Uniform Title: Puraścaryārṇava, Volume 1 Main Title: Puraścaryārṇavaḥ, Volume 1 Editor: Muralīdhara Jhā
Description: Compiled by His Highness the Maharaja Pratāpa Siṃha Saha Bahadur of Nepal.
Notes: The texts were transcribed by the staff of Muktabodha under the direction of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski. Revision 0, January 28, 2007.
Publisher: Prabhākari & Co.
Publication year: 1901 Publication city: Benares Publication country: India
Now begins the *Puraścaryārṇava*. Homage to the venerable teachers, the Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrtis!
[Salutation to Him] whose mighty staff-like arms, arrogant with power, forcibly split asunder [the foes] with fierce blows from the trunk of His elephant.

May the Lord of the hosts of Siddhas— the sovereign of the sun that destroys the darkness of obstacles, who increases the joy in the eyes of the Daughter of the Mountain King and the Destroyer of Kama, and who graces the earth with the *tāṇḍava* dance performed by the trunk-like trunks of the army of the Daitya lords— grant you prosperity. 1.1.
Brahmā, whose body consists of the essence of Umā, Madhava, and Mādhava; whose eyes resemble charming bees hovering over a blooming lotus; the witness of the world's karma;
he who is untiring in protecting all the worlds from the destruction caused by darkness—
May the sun, the leader of the gods, who is praised by the three worlds, be for your welfare. 1-2.

Adored by the hosts of the foremost gods, such as the conqueror of Tripura and the enemy of Vṛtra, who bow with true devotion, and which is illuminated by the rays of the jewels shimmering on the tips of their crowns—
by remembering Him, the wise cross the ocean of worldly existence with ease.
May that lotus-foot of Viṣṇu, who assumed the form of Nṛsiṃha, bestow upon you the highest good.

From Him whose power is Prakṛti, Mahat—the principle of the Great—arose; from that, Ahaṃkāra (the I-maker); from that, the subtle elements (tanmātras); and from those, the collection of gross elements beginning with earth.
From the elements arose the organs; thus the universe was produced from Him who is the Imperishable.
May Śiva, beautiful with the crescent moon as his crest-jewel and full of grace, protect you. 1-4.

The knowers of the scriptures declare that the path to liberation is unmanifest and difficult to traverse; yet, by dispelling their own ignorance and other afflictions through meditation, they attained the immortal pair of feet.
May she—the sister of the Sun, the savior, and the protector—protect us from the ocean of worldly existence.
May that which is without a second even for Brahmā and the other gods, and which is eternally free from diminution due to the attainment of perfected knowledge and the like, protect you.
Having bowed to the illustrious Gaṇanāyaka, the Sun, Viṣṇu, Paśupati,
Durgā who delivers one from distress, the divine Guhyeśvarī, and Īśvarī;
[and] by the illustrious King Pratāpasiṃha, [having consulted] various scriptures...
Having seen this, the ocean of *puraścaryā* rites, which benefits all people, is now being expounded. || 1-6 ||
In magnanimity he was like the son of Tapa (Bhīṣma), in great heroism like the enemy of Karṇa (Arjuna),
in beauty like the god of love, and in depth and fortitude like the ocean; in fame he was like the moon, in splendor like Indra’s horse (Uccaiḥśravas), and in majesty like the sun.
He who shines, having conquered the trees of the gods upon the earth through his acts of giving.
This composition, which has been thoroughly refined by virtuous men of perfectly pure intellect who are conversant with the meaning of all the scriptures, must be further scrutinized by those who—
driven by a thirst for hatred toward the learned and whose joy is destroyed by the sight of the excellence of others' stainless virtues— are enemies of the wise.
Let it be defiled by those who, out of anger, desire only to find fault, who are exceedingly impure and wickedly clever.
Even if this work of ours is treated with contempt by ignoble persons who are ignorant of the nature of the learned, how could it fail to be a cause for the delight of the minds of the wise?

Is not the *guñjā* berry, though cast away by the wives of forest-dwellers in the outskirts of the woods because they are enamored with clusters of *guñjā* seeds, [nevertheless] a source of joy to those who know its true value?
Why do the liberated not hold in high regard those women whose eyes are as broad as the petals of slightly opened fresh lotuses? 1-9 ||
Here, at the outset, we shall first demonstrate some of the well-known varieties of deities mentioned by Smarahara in the first wave of the *Sāmnāyabheda*, which are already known; and after that,
[we shall discuss] those of Kālī, Kaṃsāri, Tārā, Araghuvaramurajit, Śailajāvallabhā, and so forth.
The union [of the three powers] occurs through the sequence of pairs, as declared in the scriptures, and there is non-differentiation among the three powers.
(p. 3) I shall describe Rāma’s nature as Śiva and Śakti, and the unity of Sītā and the Daughter of the Snowy Mountain;
likewise, the sequence of the union between Śrī Rāma and Kāma, and between Antaka and [Rati].
Then follows the greatness of the five deities. || 1-11 ||
Thereafter, I shall describe to you the various divisions of the Tantric path and their respective qualified practitioners;
and following that, the various divisions of the Vaiṣṇavas as well.
After that, the various divisions of the Pāśupata [system]. || 1-12 ||
Furthermore, he taught the various classifications of worship and the unfitness of those who have not received initiation for it;
and thereafter, he [taught] the initiation from the true gurus.
I shall describe its majesty in due order.
Next, I shall explain the characteristics of the teacher and the disciple, as well as the characteristics of those two who are disqualified; thereafter,
the rejection of a mantra once it has been received.
And [the abandonment] of the mind acquired from a false teacher. || 1-14 ||
The prohibition and injunction regarding the reception of mantras from one's father and others, the qualified candidates for mantras,
and the purificatory rites for a mantra obtained in a dream.
And I shall explain the wheels and their prohibitions.
Then, in the second delightful wave, I shall describe the times and places appropriate for initiation,
as well as the curses within the mantras of the deities.
Having set that aside, I shall now describe the procedure for its extraction.
Thereafter, I shall describe the ritual for consecrating the site, the awakening of the mantras, the examination of the ground,
and the methods for extracting defects.
The ritual for the site and the characteristics of the pavilion. || 1-17 ||
I shall describe the characteristics of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) and the large and small ladles (sruk-sruva) in that very place; thereafter, the ritual planting of sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa);
and then I shall explain the initiation (dīkṣā) consisting of ritual action.
In that [process], it occurs during the third and fourth waves. || 1-18 ||
In this procedure for initiation, I shall first describe the selection of the gurus in the third chapter;
thereafter, I will explain the selection of the officiating priests (ṛtvij).
That which is the examination of the tooth-stick is [as follows]. || 1-19 ||
The worship of the door, the entry into the sacrificial hall,
the mandalas required for the ritual,
and then the procedure for the service as taught in the Agamas.
And I shall describe [the ritual] preceded by the installation of the water-pot (ghaṭasthāpana). || 1-20 ||
In the fourth wave, I shall describe the entire fire-ritual (agnikārya), as well as the consumption of milk-rice (pāyasa); thereafter,
I shall speak concerning the teacher and his disciple.
Then, sleep and the examination of dreams. || 1-21 ||
In that very place, on the day of initiation, I shall fully manifest all the rites appropriate for that day,
including the bestowing of the mantra;
however, I shall do so on the fifth day.
Its entire application [is explained] in the wave [chapter]. || 1-22 ||
(p. 5) Next, I shall explain the abbreviated initiation (saṃkṣepadīkṣā),
and after that, the initiation consisting of phonemes (varṇamayīdīkṣā),
and then the initiation called Kalāvatī.
After that, [he should bestow] the initiation consisting of piercing (vedha).
I shall describe the initiations of the five deities (pāñcāyatanī),
followed by the Smārta initiation, the mental initiation,
and thereafter the yogic initiation— [the initiation] of vision.
Then, [he receives] the initiation consisting of touch and the initiation consisting of contact.
I shall now explain initiation (dīkṣā) concisely: first the vocal, then the mantra-based, and then the priestly;
likewise, I shall describe the scriptural and the consecratory initiations.
And right there, [he taught] the even more concise Śāmbhavī [mudrā].
Thereafter, I shall explain the initiation of oral instruction (upadeśadīkṣā), then the designation of the sequential initiation (kramadīkṣaṇa),
and after that, I shall describe the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka).
The mind's abode [is reached] without a guide. || 1-26 ||
Now, in the sixth chapter, I shall describe the complete ritual for the act of honoring; therein,
I will first explain the proper time and the locations.
I shall speak; thereafter, I shall describe the seats.
I shall also describe there the various types of rosaries,
as well as the greatness of the rudrākṣa in this context;
and right there, the method for stringing the rosary.
And I shall explain the ritual procedure for her consecration.

(6) One should also know the characteristics of the mudrās, as well as the rules regarding what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted; the various expiations prescribed for one who has fallen from the many rules and employed [them improperly];
and the diagrams of the earth, the house, and the tortoise, as well as the Śākta seats (pīṭhas).
Now, I shall describe the morning ritual together with the procedure for the Ajapā mantra right there.

In that [treatise], there is the rule for purification, the method for cleansing the teeth, various kinds of bathing as taught in the Tantras, the procedure for applying the *tilaka*, and likewise for the sacred ash (*vibhūti*);
it contains the rules for the twilight worship (*sandhyopāsana*), the ritual of libations to the deities (*devatarpaṇa*), and the daily worship (*nityārcana*).
Next, I shall describe the fire sacrifice (homa) for the rite currently under discussion, according to the rules and in its proper sequence.
Next, I shall describe the construction of the yantra, its dimensions, and the procedure for its consecration as taught in the Āgamas; thereafter,
I shall speak of the mantras and the state of ritual impurity resulting from birth.
And [he knows] sleep and awakening as residing in the crest-lock (śikhā). || 1-31 ||
And in that very place, I shall explain the *kullukā-mantra*,
the *setu*, and the *nirvāṇa* as they have come down in succession;
likewise, the mantra for purifying the tongue in that same place.
And then, the constituent parts of the mantra uttered by Hari.
I shall now describe the procedure for recitation (japa), followed by the rules for the fire-oblation (homa) and the libation (tarpaṇa);
thereafter, I will proclaim the ritual for the consecration (abhiṣeka).
After that, there is the feeding of the Brahmins. || 1-33 ||
Thereafter, I shall explain, in the beautiful seventh chapter, all the topics concerning the characteristics of success, the groups of methods, and the designations of preliminary rites.
The sādhana of the hero accompanied by a female consort. || 1.34 ||
Then, in the eighth and most beautiful wave,
[the forms] of the Lord of the Gaṇas, of Ravi, of Viṣṇu,
of the Fish, of the Tortoise, and of the Boar incarnation—
And likewise of his own power and of the Earth. || 1-35 ||
And of Śrī Divyasiṃha, Vāmana, Trivikrama, and Kuṭhārapāṇi;
and of Śrī Rāmacandra and Bhūsutā—
And then [the hymn] of the enemy of the demon Pralamba. || 1-36 ||
Likewise, [the worship] of the Buddha Kṛṣṇa, of Kalkin,
and then of those in the forms of Hayagrīva and Rathāṅga (Viṣṇu),
as well as of the one named Ananta and Gopasundarī—
Then, [he worshipped] the image known as Śrīdhara. || 1-37 ||
And by Śiva, accompanied by Mṛtyuñjaya, Nīlakaṇṭha, and the venerable Dakṣiṇāmūrti,
along with the Kṣetrapālas in the forms of Baṭukas and others—
Likewise, [it is the same] for that which is accompanied by numerous divisions. || 1-38 ||
Of him who bears half the body of Murāri, of Purāri, of Bhavānī, and of Garuḍa,
as well as of Kārtavīrya and the son of the Wind-god.
I shall declare many mantras of Smara.
I shall now describe the meditations preceded by the ṛṣis and others, as well as their ritual honors;
however, there is no separate preliminary procedure for each of them here.
I shall speak [of this], fearing the excessive length of the treatise. || 1-40 ||
(p. 8) Then, in the ninth wave, I shall explain in succession the ten Great Vidyās together with their respective subdivisions,
as well as the ritual procedure for their preliminary worship.
One should also [worship] Nīlakrama and the others, conjoined with their respective deities.
Then, in the tenth chapter [of the *Taraṅga*], concerning the Goddess of Speech whose sandals are worshipped by the three worlds,
and therein specifically regarding the Goddess known as Tvaritā.
Of her who is endowed with Klinnā, Annapūrṇā, and the others. || 1-42 ||
Then [the worship] of Pratyaṅgirā, of Kubjikā, and of Surāpagā together with Vāgbhava,
and then of Caṇḍa and the other planets.
Then, for the flowers of the planets situated in their respective directions... || 1-43 ||
I shall proclaim the mantras ending with the preliminary rites, and then I shall declare the Mother of the Vedas,
along with all her ritual placements (nyāsa) in their proper sequence.
Meditation, the ritual machine, and the sequence of sacrifice. || 1-44 ||
I shall describe its entire procedure of worship, including the mudrās, the preparatory rites,
and the ritual for the preliminary practice of Tārā.
Likewise, there is the Vedic mantra for Mṛtyuñjaya.
The preliminary ritual for the Rudrādhyāya will be described along with various auspicious Sūktas; then the procedure for the preliminary rituals of the Vedic hymns and the mantras of the planets,
followed by the description of their *puraścaryā* as spoken by the Enemy of Tripura (Śiva).
And I shall also state, in brief, the entire measure of the sacrificial offerings.
In the eleventh wave, according to the method described above for the mantra of Durgā, I shall now explain the ritual procedure for the *puraścaraṇa* of those who follow the Tantras.
Also the complete procedure for the festival of Durgā.
I shall explain therein the procedure for the offering of oblations to the deities of animals and other objects, as well as that of the young girl.
And the ritual procedure for worship and the offering to Śiva.
In that very context, I shall likewise describe the ritual procedure for the worship of Revanta’s horses and elephants, as well as the practices for Navarātra,
as taught by Śiva.
The purification by fire and the sighting of the wagtail.
Then, upon the final, delightful wave,
[he recited] the mantras beginning with that of Brahmā, along with the rules for their preliminary rites, as well as the corresponding mantras of Gorakṣanātha.
Thereafter, I shall declare the mantra of that same Śītalā.

Then [he taught] the yantras and the ritual procedure for the preliminary service of the yantras, as well as the *bhūtalipi* (earth-script) and its preliminary rite (*pauraścaraṇa*) within that very context.
I shall now describe the ritual procedures for the placement of the scripts (lipinyāsa).

Then, [he saw] the seal (*mudrā*) of the Mother-goddess (*mātṛkā*), made of the three metals (*triloha*), possessing incomparable power, shining brightly; and right there, the ritual procedure for its consecration (*saṃskāra*).
In the same way, I shall now describe the nine-jewel mudrā. (1-52)

Following that, there is the sequential description of the preparatory rites (*puraścaryā*) for the *Ṣoḍhānyāsa*, the *Sahasranāma*, the *Kavaca*, the various *Stotras*, and likewise for the *Saptaśatī* hymn;
including the rules for its recitation along with the fruits thereof, together with the application of fire-offerings (*homaprayoga*).
Following that question, I shall explain the classification of the mantras and the ritual procedure.

The preliminary ritual for breath control (prāṇāyāma) is to be known by the best of the wise; thereafter, the preliminary ritual for mantras will be explained, as well as the method of accomplishment even without it.
[This applies] to the various Bhairavas, Yoginīs, the celestial damsels, and Jvālāmukhī, in their respective order—
And for others as well, there is the practice of sādhana preceded by puraścaryā, even on the earth.

In this context, since *puraścaryā* consists specifically in the propitiation of a deity that yields the fruit of mantra-siddhi, and because the deity to be propitiated is the most venerable, the deities included within the six *āmnāyas* are first described. Regarding this, the *Merutantra* states that a certain specific form of Gaṇeśa possesses a particular distinction residing in his mantra, by virtue of which he functions within all six *āmnāyas*:
"I shall describe the Vighna-mantra consisting of a single seed-syllable, which bestows perfect accomplishment."
In that regard, first of all, for the Vaidikas, the letter *ga* alone is considered [the primary element]. (1.55)
The letter *da* joined with a dot (*bindu*) is for the followers of the Eastern Path; it is double-dotted (*dvibindu*).
When joined with both of these, followed by *ū*, it becomes *gauṃ* in the Upper Tradition (*ūrdhvāmnāya*). (1.56)
"Glaumuttare" and "gomiti" are said to belong to the Pātālāmnāya.

Herein, in the Dakṣiṇāmnāya, there are Lakṣmī-Gaṇeśa, Haridrā-Gaṇeśa, and others; in the Ūrdhvāmnāya, Mahāgaṇapati and others; in the Pūrvāmnāya, Viriñci-Gaṇanāyaka and others; in the Paścimāmnāya, Kṣipraprasādana-Gaṇeśa and others; and in the Uttarāmnāya, Ucchiṣṭa-Gaṇeśa and others. Thus, the many varieties of Gaṇeśa are to be seen in the Merutantra. (p. 11) Although the Sun has twelve varieties, only the Dakṣiṇāmnāya [is primary]. 1–57.
It is stated in that very same place:
"His single tradition is proclaimed as the Southern one;
just as he would touch a Yavana and a Brahmin equally with his hands. (1.58)
Likewise, his worship is preceded by the practice of one's own specific duties;
this God is manifest in all four ages and is honored by everyone. (1.59)
The Lord of the World is the eye of all the gods.
There are twelve divisions:
Varuṇa, Sūrya, Vedāṅga, Bhānu, Indra, and likewise Ravi. (1–60)
Gabhastin, Yama, Svarṇaretas, then Divākara,
Mitra, and Viṣṇu— these are declared to be the twelve Ādityas in their respective order.
"Those of immeasurable splendor shine forth in succession beginning from the month of Māgha.
Thus it is stated in that very [text].

While no difference based on the Vedic tradition (*āmnāya*) is perceived between Viṣṇu and Śiva, there are indeed infinite differences arising from the application of incarnations (*avatāra*), mantras, meditations (*dhyāna*), and so forth; among these, some specific differences will become clear during the occasion of explaining the methods for *puraścaraṇa*, and thus they are not mentioned here. Although it is impossible to describe all the varieties of the Goddesses due to their infinity, some varieties mentioned in the *Vāḍavānalīya Tantra* are presented here.
Thus it is said in the Vaḍavānalīya Tantra:
"The primordial source of the universe is one alone, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss. (1.62)
Through the differentiation of various manifestations, she has attained manifoldness as distinct forms:
Pūrṇeśī, Bhuvaneśānī, Lalitā, and Aparājitā. (1.63)
Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Vāṇī, she whose feet are marked by the Pārijāta tree,
Annapūrṇā, Jayā, and others are established in the Eastern Tradition (Pūrvāmnāya).
Niśeśī, Dakṣiṇākālī, Bagalā, Chinnamastakā,
Bhadrā, Tārā, and Mātaṅgī are the deities of the Dakṣiṇāmnāya.
Kubjikā, who is endowed with many divisions, and Kulālikā, as well as Mātaṅgī, Amṛtalakṣmī, and others, are the deities of the Western Tradition (paścimāmnāya).
By this, it is established that Mātaṅgī belongs to two traditions (*āmnāya*), since she is mentioned in the Southern tradition (*dakṣiṇāmnāya*) as well. Thus:
"Siddhilakṣmī, Guhyakālī, Mahābhīmasarasvatī, Dhūmrā, Kāmakalā, Kālī, Mahākālī, Kapālinī. (1.67)
Mahāśmaśānakālī, as well as Kālasaṃkarṣiṇī, Pratyaṅgirā, Mahārātri, Yogeśī, and Siddhibhairavī. (1.68)
These are joined in many ways, the most excellent among all sciences;
they reside in the sacred seats (pīṭhas) of the Northern Tradition (Uttarāmnāya) and bestow the fruits of the four aims of human life.
In the *Muṇḍamālā*, it is also stated that Tārā and Chinnamastā belong to the Uttarāmnāya:
"There are forty-nine divisions on the path of the Uttarāmnāya."
Then Guhyakālī is proclaimed, and after that, Siddhilakṣmī.
Therein is Svarṇakoṭīśvarī, likewise Rājarājeśvarī;
she is declared to be Guhyeśvarī, and likewise Tārā in her three forms.
Then the Great Goddess Chinnamastā is described as exceedingly terrifying;
such secret conventions (saṃketa) are proclaimed to be always to be kept hidden.
Vāḍavānalī, Kāmeśī, Lalitā, Bālā, Mahātripurasundarī,
Tripurā, and Bhairavī— these indeed are based upon the Ūrdhvāmnāya. (1.73)
Since it is also stated in the *Pūrvāmnāya* of Lalitā, her presence in both traditions is indicated. In some places, however, the reading is "tvaritā.
The Yoginī, Vajrapūrvā, Pannagī, and Nairṛteśvarī reside in the seats (*pīṭhas*) of the Lower Tradition (*adharāmnāya*) and are worshipped according to the Jain path. (1.74)
In this very context, Bhīmādevī is declared as the primary deity in the Mahākālasaṃhitā;
listen now to the mantras of the deities who fall within the scope of the Adhara-āmnāya.
"Wherein Bhīmādevī, the primordial, renowned, and formidable goddess, resides. (1.75)
Kulabālā and Durgā are worshipped by all traditions;
Kulabālā is the Virgin (Kumārī). Thus— "The worship of these two, however, is prescribed as being obligatory everywhere. (1.76)
Of those two, Durgā and Kumārī. These ten deities are renowned as the Mahāvidyās.
As it is said in the Śaktisaṅgama:
"Kālī, Tārā, Chinnamastā, Sundarī, Bagalā, Ramā..."
Mātaṅgī, Bhuvaneśānī, Siddhavidyā, and Bhairavī. || 1.77 ||
And Dhūmāvatī is the tenth; these are remembered as the ten Great Vidyās.
Regarding that very point, he speaks of the Bhairava for each of these individually:
Mahākāla is the consort of Kālikā, and Laliteśvara is the consort of Sundarī.
Likewise, Akṣobhya is the lord of Tārā, Vikarālaka of Chinnā, Mahādeva of Bhuvanā, and Kālabhairava of Dhūmrā. (1.79)
Nārāyaṇa is traditionally associated with Mahālakṣmī, and Baṭuka with Bhairavī; Mataṅga is associated with Mātaṅgī, or alternatively, he may be Sadāśiva. (1.80)
Mṛtyuñjaya is proclaimed as the [consort] of the Vidyā of Bagalā;

Laliteśvara is Tripurabhairava, Vikarāla is Krodhabhairava, and Ghorakālabhairava is [the consort of] Tārā. Although in the Rudrayāmala, Sadyojāta, Kālarudra, and others are mentioned for Tārā, Chinnamastā, and so forth, there is no contradiction, because those names mentioned therein are merely alternative names for these very same Bhairavas, not different Bhairavas altogether. [This is stated] in the Śaktisaṃgama.
Just as the Yakṣiṇīs grant success through union with Krodhabhairava. || 1.81 ||
In the same way, O Pārvatī, the vidyās are accomplished through union with the Supreme Being alone.
In the Rudrayāmala it is said that one who recites only a Śākta mantra should not employ a Śaiva mantra. (1.82)
Even if recited for ten million lifetimes, a mantra will not attain success for one whose deity is other than Śiva;
for whatever be the deity of a goddess, Śiva alone shall be her [true] deity. (1.83)
By that [means], O Great Goddess, the vidyā is quickly perfected in the Kali age.
In the Merutantra, it is declared that the mantra of women bestows enjoyment (bhoga), while the supreme mantra of men bestows liberation (mokṣa).
O gods, the worship of both [Śiva and Śakti] bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
for in another Tantra it is said that without Śakti, there is no name nor abode for the withered Śiva. (1.85)
Without Śiva, the state of being a *kalā* (creative power) could never belong to the *cit-kalās* (powers of consciousness).
Due to the application of the logic of the seed and the sprout, the Great Light consists of both Śiva and Śakti. (1.86)
O Goddess of gods, she is ever awake and manifests in various forms;
the Merutantra describes the fruits of worshipping the deities of the six Āmnāyas.
The devoted lay follower, at the time of death, shall attain union [with the Divine] while standing upright. || 1-87 ||

Likewise, through devotion to the deity, one first attains supreme similarity of form (sārūpya), then proximity (samīpya) in this world; the final [stage], however, is the fruit pertaining to this life.
"Gain, renunciation, and assistance—even on the lower path—possess a future result;

'in time' (kāle) means that one becomes Śiva himself, whose nature is Mahākāla. As for the statement by some that the word *kāle* is in the locative case (*saptamī*), and thus means that a follower of the Southern Tradition (*dakṣiṇopāsaka*) and a follower of the Upper Tradition (*ūrdhvāmnāyopāsaka*) shall attain union (*sāyujya*) at the time of death, that is incorrect. "A Brāhmaṇa endowed with the five characteristics is indeed Kāla. (1.89)

This is because it contradicts the preceding text, and because it contradicts the subsequent text which states: "By whose grace you and I have been born, like another Kāla. Regarding the phrase "in the Uttara," the meaning is that a worshiper of the deity of the Uttarāmnāya shall attain *sālokya* (residence in the same world). This refers specifically to those who worship deities such as Guhyeśvarī and others within the Uttarāmnāya.
However, regarding those who worship Him, the attainment of fourfold liberation is stated in the *Mahākālasaṃhitā*, in the section on *Anusmṛti*:
"Sālokya, Sāmīpya, and Sārūpya as the third. (1.90)
O Goddess of gods, liberation is said to be fourfold, beginning with *sāyujya*;
O Īśvarī, among these, each one of the liberations belongs to those who worship other [deities].
For one who worships Guhyakālī, the fourfold liberation arises in due course;
there is no doubt about this, according to the instruction of the Destroyer of Tripura. (1.92)
O Goddess of the gods, within the six traditions (ṣaḍāmnāya) there are many deities;
among them, some are proclaimed for the Kṛta Yuga, and some for the Tretā Yuga.
In the Dvāpara age some [sciences] yield fruit, while in the Kali age others yield fruit;
these ten sciences, which yield fruit throughout the four ages, have been declared by me.
Among them, three are distinguished: Kālī, Tārā, and Sundarī.
O Śiva, among those three as well, in the Kali age, Kālī is preeminent.
Among the nine types of Kālīs, Guhyakālī is praised;
there is no vidyā equal to her within the sphere of the universe.
The Vidyārājñī Guhyakālī is never divided;
therein, Kālī is said to be of nine kinds.
Kālī is said to be ninefold, kept secret in all the tantras.
The first is Dakṣiṇakālī, and Bhadrakālī is likewise another;
another is Śmaśānakālī, and Kālakālī is the fourth.
The fifth is Guhyakālī, who was previously described by me;
the sixth is Kāmakalākālī, and the seventh is Dhanakālikā. (1.99)
The eighth is Siddhikālī and the ninth is Caṇḍikālikā.
In this manner, the distinctions of the others are to be understood from other texts, such as the Śaktisaṃgama.
Kālikā is indeed proclaimed as the queen of the four yugas.
The Vidyārājñī, the science of accomplishment, bestows swift results in the Kali age;
the identity of Kālī and Kṛṣṇa is declared in the Mahākālasaṃhitā.
She is the sole cause of the intoxication of desire for all women born within the three worlds.
Vaṃśīdhara Kṛṣṇadeva is said to be Prakṛti and Viṣṇu;
O Goddess, from the union of these two, Śiva-Śakti is indeed proclaimed.
In the *Śaktisaṃgama*, it is stated that Kṛṣṇa is the embodiment of Kālī, Rāma is the embodiment of Tārā, and there is a unity among the three Śaktis:
"At times, the primordial Lalitā assumes a male form with the body of Kṛṣṇa."
Bearing her supreme form for the purpose of deluding the world.
Sometimes the primordial Śrī Kālī is Pārvatī, who is Tārā of Śiva and capable of completely enchanting all beings by the commencement of the sound of her flute.
Once, the primordial Śrītārā assumed a male form with the body of Rāma,
for the purpose of slaying Rāvaṇa and for the establishment of the gods.
Assuming a supreme male form for the sake of destroying the Daityas, she is the primordial Tārā, the Great Power; she alone is Kālī, the Great Sovereign.
That which is the great Māyā of Mahāvaiṣṇavī is considered to be Mahāsundarī;
she is neither female, nor male, nor even neuter. (1-107)
Whatever body she assumes, she is joined with that very one;
therein the identity of Hari and Hara is declared.
At one time, both of them previously took the form of Viṣṇu.
For the sake of attaining the true nature of Viṣṇu, Hara himself performed penance;
for the sake of attaining the true nature of Śiva, Hari himself performed penance.
For sixty thousand ages, both were devoted to austerity for the sake of Śiva;
Śiva attained the form of Viṣṇu, and Viṣṇu attained the form of Śiva.
Both are indeed the very essence of Hari and Hara, the supreme Ardhanārīśvaras;
O Goddess, O Mother, this union of the two is their primary form.
"O Goddess, this mass of splendor is the eternal form of Brahman;
therein it is stated that Rāma is the very essence of Śiva and Śakti."
Rāma is known as Śakti, and he is proclaimed to be Śiva.
"Brahman, whose nature consists of Śiva and Śakti, is sung as 'Rāma, Rāma. In that very place, the identity of Gaurī and Sītā, and of Śiva and Rāma, is declared."
Sītā, the supreme leader of the great empire, is the form of Gaurī. || 1-113 ||
Rāma is to be known as Paraśiva, not as an incarnation nor even as a human being; that which is renowned as the Supreme Brahman is expressed by the two syllables "Rā-ma. (1.114)
In the *Rāmopaniṣad* (1.115): "Yogins delight in the infinite, true bliss, the self that is consciousness;
by the word 'Rāma,' that Supreme Brahman is designated."
The identity of the five deities beginning with Gaṇeśa is stated in the Rudrayāmala: "Sarasvatī is the very form of Durgā [in relation] to Gaṇeśa, the Sun, Viṣṇu, and Śiva."
The great Śyāmā, the great Vidyā, is to be worshipped in due order. || 1-116 ||
One who knows the supreme truth, whether a Kaulika or a Vaiṣṇava, should not create division among these [deities]: Gaṇeśa, the Sun, Hari, Īśāna, and Durgā. (1.117)
The wise devotee of the Goddess should worship with a sense of oneness;
he should worship all [the deities] within the circle of the Goddess, or else within the Śiva-liṅga or in Śivā herself.
Whether on a Śālagrāma stone, on the seat of the Sun, or upon Śiva,
or within the wheel of the illustrious Gaṇeśvara, a wise person should not perceive any distinction between them.
He who indeed creates division becomes a destroyer of Śiva, even if he is a devotee of Śiva (*śaiva*).
The term "devotee of Śiva" is an elliptical designation (*upalakṣaṇa*).
It has been stated that there is identity between the ten Mahāvidyās and the ten Avatāras.
In the Muṇḍamālā Tantra,
Kṛṣṇa is indeed Kālikā herself, and the form of Rāma is Tāriṇī.
Varāha is declared to be Bhuvana, Nṛsiṃha is Bhairavīśvarī,
Dhūmāvatī is Vāmana, and Chinnā is born from the lineage of Bhrigu.
Kamalā shall be in the form of a fish, while Kūrma is Bagalāmukhī; Mātaṅgī is the Buddhist one, and this sixteenth [incarnation] is in the form of Kalki.
Thus,
[the text] states the etymological derivation of the word *Kālī* in the *Kāmadhenu-tantra* on page 20.
Because she swallows time through the synthesis of time, she is Kālī;
thus [the author] speaks of the meaning of the word Tripurā in the *Sundarīstava*.
Indeed, there are exactly three powers: Brāhmī, Raudrī, and Vaiṣṇavī.
That in which the city is the body is proclaimed as Tripurā;
the meaning of the word Tārā is stated in the Matsyasūkta.
And because she grants speech through her divine play, she is therefore called Nīlasarasvatī.
Because she bestows the state of being a savior (tāraka), Tārā is the giver of happiness and liberation; and because she rescues one from fierce calamity, she is celebrated as Ugratārā.
Regarding the determination of the different paths according to the different traditions, the *Vāḍavānalīya* states:
"In the Eastern Tradition (Pūrvāmnāya), there is the Dakṣa path; in the Western and the Supreme (Para), it is Vāma."
The upward paths on the right and left are those of the left and the right [nādīs].
Having abandoned everything, the Kaula path is praised everywhere;
and the arrangement of the three paths is established in that very place.
Through the application of the five *m*s and by worshipping with the left hand. || 1-127 ||
Through recitation (japa) and burnt offerings (homa), one becomes left-handed (vāma); the opposite results from the reverse.
However, the mantra for the libation of the principles (tattva-tarpaṇa) is performed with the left hand upon the right [hand].
A distinction is proclaimed regarding the left hand as well as the right;
one who employs the actions of both the right and the left is a Kaula, being a mixture of both. (1-129)

And because of the necessity of the syllable *ma*, O Goddess of gods, due to the worship and libation performed with the right hand, the third path, the Kaula, is in some cases performed with the left.
In the Rudrayāmala, three seed-syllables of Durgā are mentioned, and accordingly, three modes of conduct (ācāra) are prescribed:
the first is Dakṣiṇācāra, and the second is Vāmācāra. (1.131)
But the third is the family tradition; listen to its rule, O beloved:
bathing, twilight prayers, and so forth at dawn, and recitation at midday, O Goddess. (1.132)
A woolen seat for one's own use, food consisting of milk-rice and sugar,
a rosary made of *rudrākṣa* beads, and a vessel made of stone.

O Goddess, this practice of enjoyment with one's own wives while following the right-hand path (dakṣiṇācāra), when performed with material substances and wine, is considered to cause the loss of spiritual attainment. 1-134.
I shall now proclaim the supreme Vāmācāra practice for the sādhana of Śrī Durgā, by performing which a practitioner of mantras will swiftly attain accomplishment in the Kali age. (1.135)
A garland made from human teeth, a begging bowl of stone or a skull, a seat such as the skin of a perfected one (siddha), and a bracelet made from the hair of a woman. (1.136)
O Śivā, the substance is the essence of the *āsava* liquor; the food consists of meat and the like;
the chewing is of small fish and so forth; the mudrā is the sound of the lute; and the discourse is the sacred narrative.
Sexual union with the wives of others and treating all castes as equal—
this is declared to be the "Left-hand Practice" (Vāmācāra), O Śivā, which bestows all accomplishments.
Otherwise, O Maheśvarī, there would be a loss of the accomplishment of this mantra.
I shall now proclaim the Kula practice, which is to be served by the most excellent yogis. (1.139)

O Maheśvarī, that which one should constantly worship—the noble woman (*kulastrī*), the family preceptor (*kulaguru*), and the family goddess (*kuladevī*)—is called the *kulācāra* (the practice of the Kula). (1.140)

O Śivā, O Maheśvarī, having recognized her as a woman of noble family, having praised and bowed to her, having brought her by force, having worshipped her, and then having provided her with enjoyment; || 1-141 ||
One should satisfy the goddess Śrī Durgā, the leader of the wheel, with light;
and one should especially perform the recitation (japa) of Nīlakaṇṭha according to the prescribed rule.
Preceded by that, one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) and adorn the beloved of the Kula;
having gratified the woman of the Kula with drinks, beverages, and likewise with foods.
"One should indeed practice thus every day; this is known as the family tradition (kulācāra).
The procedure for the Left-hand path (vāmamārga) has been described according to its divisions, such as Kaula and others, in the Merutantra."
The Kaulika [mudrā] occurs when the left thumb reaches the position of the [right] thumb and becomes equal to the index finger. || 1-144 ||
The Cīna-krama would be the middling [path], the Siddhāntīya would be the lower;
the Śābara path is the youngest—thus the Left-hand path (vāma) is fivefold. (1.145)
The distinction of eligible practitioners according to the difference in paths has been stated in the Vāḍavānala:
"Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas are the eligible practitioners of the Dakṣa path."
The three castes, excluding the twice-born, are eligible for the Vāma and Kaula [traditions].
A Brahmin who has strayed from the path of the right-hand way and follows the left-hand way attains accomplishment in this very world, but never liberation.
A Brahmin who abandons the path of the Vedas, who is devoid of the desire for liberation (kaivalya), and who seeks supernatural powers while following the Vāmamārga, shall become a denizen of hell.
(23) Having abandoned the path of the Vedas and becoming solely intent on the path of Tantra, Brahmins will experience hell and become Brahma-rākṣasas. 1-149.
A Brahmin who follows the Vedic and Tantric path, as well as the Southern way (dakṣiṇamārga),
becomes a lord of supernatural powers in this world and attains immortality at the end of the body.

By this collection of statements, it is established that the Brāhmaṇa has authority only in the Right Path (dakṣiṇa-mārga), while the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya have authority in all three paths, and the Śūdra in the Left and Kaula paths. It is further concluded that for a Brāhmaṇa who proceeds toward the Left or Kaula paths out of a desire for supernatural powers (siddhi) and the like, there is only worldly enjoyment (bhoga) and not liberation (mokṣa). However, both [liberation and enjoyment] belong only to that Brāhmaṇa who, while following the Vedic path, worships his chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) according to the Tantra as taught in the Right Path. Nor is it the case that the initiation into the Kula (kuladīkṣāṇa) should previously be performed by twice-born ones through the practices of the Left (vāmācāra).
If, however, the initiation with the Sāvitrī mantra is performed afterwards [after other rites], one becomes fallen due to that transposition. || 1.151 ||

It should not be said that there is a contradiction with this statement from the *Merutantra*, which reveals that Brahmins possess the qualification for the Vāmamārga; for in that context, the term "dvija" (twice-born) is interpreted as referring to those twice-born who are other than Brahmins, and thus no contradiction arises. For this very reason, another statement from a different tantra—“The Vāmamārga leads only to hell for Brahmins”—is also consistent; since even the Vāmamārga, when practiced by a qualified person, generates both worldly enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*), it is illogical for it to be a cause of hell for Brahmins if they were the ones qualified for it. And so it is said:
That Brahmin who worships Mahāmāyā without courtesy [shall incur sin]. || 1-152 ||
"From that sin, he falls from the heavenly world and becomes a bearer of disease.

From this statement in the *Kālikāpurāṇa*, it should be understood that the Brāhmaṇa has authority only in the Right Path (*dakṣiṇamārga*). Likewise, for the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya as well, the Right Path alone is recommended; however, the mention of their authority in the Left Path (*vāmamārga*) is intended to show that there is no loss of caste (*pātitya*) even for those who engage in it out of passion, since such a thing is heard of only in the case of a Brāhmaṇa. The Left Path, on the other hand, is recommended only for Śūdras.
The attainment of siddhi for those ranging from Śūdras to Yavanas is established on the Left Path (Vāmapatha).

Thus, according to the statement in the *Meru Tantra*. With regard to conduct (*ācāra*), it says: "A Śūdra should worship by means of the Left-hand path (*vāmādi*) and the twice-born (*dvijāti*) by the Right-hand path.

This is from the statement of Mahākāla. The term "twice-born" means Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas. By the word "Left-hand path and so forth," the *Kulācāra* (family tradition) is included; that too, as before, is recommended for Śūdras alone, while it is neither recommended nor prohibited for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, but for Brāhmaṇas it is strictly prohibited.
Because it causes the loss of one's Brahminhood, one should not practice the customs of one's family [if they are contrary to dharma].
Thus, from the words of the *Siddhāntasāra*:
"For those Brahmins who have been consumed by curses and are devoid of Vedic rites, this Kaula dharma is the means for both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (1.155)
Those Brahmins who have become sinful and are overwhelmed, consumed by curses—for them, this authority over the lineage of this path arises. (1-156)

This is because, according to such statements from the Merutantra, at Dakṣa’s sacrifice, it is understood that only those Brahmins who have fallen outside the Vedic path and whose Brahminhood has been destroyed due to the curse of the attendants (*pāriṣada*) possess the qualification for that [practice]. Furthermore, if another statement were found—due to the diversity of the independent speaker, the Lord—that teaches the qualification of even Brahmins for the Vāma and Kaula traditions, then in that case, "inferior Brahmins" (*hīnabrāhmaṇa*) characterized by any one of the five defining marks (*lakṣaṇa*) should be understood as intended; for such individuals, there is indeed their qualification for it.
And this has been made explicit by the venerable feet of Īśvara in the *Merutantra* itself:
"Just as there is the seed-vigor (*brahmavīrya*), so too the field (*kṣetra*); the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) originate from Brahman;
through the conduct of a Brāhmaṇa (*brāhmaṇācaraṇa*), and through the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), one becomes a Brāhmaṇa. (1-157)
He under whose control we are, and after whose word meaning runs—when even a single characteristic is lacking, the word does not follow the meaning. (1.158)
O Goddess, one who lacks two characteristics may become a Brāhmaṇa through his own conduct;
however, he who lacks three characteristics attains accomplishment through the path of Tantra. (1.159)
The paths such as Kaulika and others belong to those who are devoid of the four characteristics.
Furthermore, the loss of these characteristics is to be understood by reversing the sequence of their description.
In that very same [text]:
In whichever Brahmin even one of the previously mentioned characteristics is observed, [he is to be honored].
And having attained some degree of Brahminhood, he suffers through remorse: "No entitlement to any of the Vedic rites has arisen for me. (1.161)
"How shall I obtain happiness both in this world and in the next—being one who is blind toward the wealth of others and impotent toward the wives of others? (1.162)
That Brahmin who, like one mute, always reflects in this way regarding the slander of others—only he shall possess the right to this [practice]. (1.163)
"One" means being born from the vigor of Brahman;
likewise,
a Brāhmaṇa endowed with the five characteristics is Time itself.
I am Brahmā as well as Viṣṇu; we both abide under the power of his command.
If he reaches the left path and is born again as a dog, endowed with the four characteristics, that left [path] bestows its fruit upon him. (1-165)
If a certain mantra of the Tantric tradition is bestowed by those two due to the power of one's fortune,
it bears fruit immediately for the first [type of practitioner] and through ritual action for the other.
For one who possesses the three characteristics, both the Vedic and Tantric [paths] bestow their fruit simply through the practice as described; therefore, he is a *vāmaka*. (1.167)
If both his left and right [hands] are endowed with the two marks, they shall be equal and yield identical results; never, however, does this apply to one who follows the Vedic path.

Endowed with the single characteristic, the left [path] bestows its fruit upon those beginning with Śūdras and ending with Yavanas; for them, spiritual accomplishment (siddhi) resides on the left path. (1–169)
A Brahmin who follows the left-hand path (vāmamārga) should never touch *tulasī*,
nor should he touch a Vaiṣṇava Brahmin, nor should he bow to one who follows the Vedic path.
"Let all my kinsmen revile me; let my wife, sons, and others abandon me; let people laugh at me upon seeing me, or let kings punish me. (1.171)
"Even though I am constantly tormented by disease, poverty, suffering, and the like, whether Lakṣmī remains or departs, I shall not abandon this state. (1.172)
Thus, he whose devotion is firm shall attain accomplishment in the Vāmā.
In the Rudrayāmala, it is said:
"The moon-faced woman is on the left, wine is in the mouth, and a vessel is in the lotus-hand;
the contemplation of the venerable Guru is upon the head, and the mind is the locus for meditation upon the Goddess."

For those for whom the practice of recitation on the tongue, the transformation, and the arrival of the Kaula lineage are indeed constant, let them drink the divine nectar; they have attained both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
On the left is a woman skilled in dalliance; on the right, a bowl of wine;
in front, hand-gestures (mudrās), chickpea cakes, and a radish for cleansing the lips;
a lute with strings, sweet and melodious; and a true guru in the company of noble discourse.
The left-hand practice (vāmācāra) is supremely profound and inaccessible even to yogins.
"In the Merutantra, it is said that wine is to be drunk, meat is to be eaten, and the face of the beloved is to be gazed upon;
such conduct alone is supreme," so indeed do the vulgar proclaim. (1-175)
O Umā, if a human being could attain perfection through the drinking of liquor,
then why would all those who are devoted to drinking liquor not become perfected beings?
If a meritorious rebirth were to occur merely by eating meat, then the liberation of carnivorous beasts would follow; for nothing other than meat would be suitable for them. (1.177)
O gods, if liberation were produced through sexual union with women, then everyone would be liberated; who then would be subject to rebirth? (1.178)
"From walking upon the edge of a sword, from hanging by the ears of a tiger, and from being shielded by a serpent—it is certain that [this] is impossible on the path of one's lineage. (1.179)
Now, the divisions of the Vaiṣṇavas:
it is stated in the Śaktisaṃgama that "First there would be the Vaikhānasa, and likewise the Śrīrādhāvallabha."
O Maheśānī, Gaukuleśa and likewise Vṛndāvanī shall come into being. || 1-180 ||
O Maheśvarī, the Pāñcarātra is the fifth, the Śrīvīravaiṣṇava is the sixth, the Rāmānandī, the Harivyāsī, and the Nimbārka [are the remaining ones]. (1.181)
Then, O Goddess, ten divisions of the Bhāgavatas are proclaimed;
the Smārta-Vaiṣṇava is adorned with the initiations and other rites beginning with those of the Vaikhānasa.
Devoted to the conduct of a Vaiṣṇava, having reached the further shore of the Viṣṇu-mantra alone, with a mind focused on no other, tranquil in soul, and dedicated to the emblems of Viṣṇu. (1-183)
O Goddess, O beloved, hear about Gokuleśa, the Lord of Śrī Rādhāvallabha;
he is endowed with various ornaments and adorned with various fragrances.
Taking on the form of Kalikṛṣṇa who delights the herd of cows, he offered his body, wealth, and life-breaths as a dedication to him. (1.185)
O Goddess, he is devoted to power within, while externally he assumes the form of a Vaiṣṇava;
he is intent on the conduct of a Gandharva and is devoted to being entwined by creepers.
The tradition of Gaukuleśa brings about all perfections on earth;
it is free from worldly desire, serene in nature, and devoted solely to devotion for Viṣṇu.
Fickle with attachment to amorous women, taking delight in forest sports, his body adorned with fragrances, he was solely intent on meditating upon women. (1-188)
O Śivā, those who know the reality of Viṣṇu’s identity (sārūpya) are called Vṛndāvanīs;
those who have undertaken the Pañcarātra vow are proclaimed as Pāñcarātras. (1.189)
For up to five days, those called Śaivas are three-eyed;
according to the Gopālapaddhati, he who worships Viṣṇu alone through body, mind, and speech [is a Vaiṣṇava].
He who reviles other deities while knowing this entire universe, both moving and non-moving, to have Nārāyaṇa as its essence, is declared to be a Vīra-Vaiṣṇava. (1.191)
He who hates no one at all— he is this supreme heroic Vaiṣṇava,
[established] right there in the Supreme Self, Śrī Rāma, who dwells in the center of the lotus of the heart.
He who cultivates bliss is called a Rāmānandin;
he is devoted to Viṣṇu, intent on destroying sin through union with Śakti, and has conquered his senses. (1-193) p. 29)
Endowed with the restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas), devoted to disciplined conduct, accepting only what is necessary for himself, and dedicated to the welfare of others. || 1-194 ||
O Maheśānī, Hari was one who bore the very nature of Śiva and Śakti; though unable to follow the sequence of daily worship, he was solely devoted to his own independent state.
Devoted to external worship and other rites, possessing exclusive devotion, clear-minded, endowed with the side of the Noble Ones, pure, and intent upon conduct according to his own will. || 1-196 ||
The Lord Hari Nimbārka is independent, a hater of the Smārta tradition,
uniquely skilled in devotion to Viṣṇu, self-conquered, and of serene intellect.
O Goddess, filled with pride in his own traditional learning (smārta), he was intent on other practices;
through association with him, he became a hater of Śiva and devoted once more to ritual bathing.
O Śivā, one who knows only devotion to Viṣṇu is called a Bhāgavata;
however, the characteristics of a supreme Bhāgavata are described in the eleventh book [of the Bhāgavatapurāṇa].
He who perceives the state of the Blessed One within all beings— || 1.199 ||
He is the best of devotees who perceives all beings within the Blessed One’s own Self;
furthermore, he is one who, even when perceiving objects through his senses, neither feels aversion nor rejoices. (1.200)
He who perceives this world as the māyā of Viṣṇu is indeed the best of Bhāgavatas.
Likewise,
for the sake of the glory of the three worlds, he whose memory is unimpeded and who is sought after by the unconquered self and the gods;
That foremost of Vaiṣṇavas does not move even for half a moment from the lotus-feet of the Blessed One. (1.201)

Regarding the characteristic of the intermediate [yogi], it is as follows: he who practices love, friendliness, compassion, and equanimity toward the Lord, those dependent on Him, the ignorant, and his enemies—he is the intermediate one. (1.202)
The definition of the *prākṛta-bhāgavata* is given in that very same work:
"He who, with faith, performs worship of Hari only in the consecrated image (*arcā*), and not toward His other devotees, is known as a *prākṛta-bhakta*. (1.203)
Now, the divisions of the Śaivas:

according to the *Śaktisaṃgama*, they are, in order, the *śikhī* (one with a topknot), the *muṇḍī* (the shaven-headed), the *jaṭī* (the one with matted hair), the *dvidaṇḍī* (the one with two staffs), and the *tridaṇḍī* (the one with three staffs).
O Maheśānī, there is the Ekadaṇḍī as well as the Vīraśaiva. || 1-204 ||
Seven types of Pāśupatas have been declared, as well as ten types of Vaiṣṇavas.
Now, O Pārvatī, hear the underlying disposition (vāsanā) of the Pāśupatas.
O Goddess, Śikhin is the auspicious Pāśupata who wears the topknot and the sacred thread;
O Goddess, he is devoted to meditative absorption and, in that absorption, maintains the seat of Śiva.
O Śivā, one who possesses the rudrākṣa, as well as the ash and the liṅga known as Śaiva,
is proclaimed to be a celibate student (brahmacārī) whose soul is serene and whose mind is tranquil.
O Goddess, relying upon the doctrine of Śrībindumālinī, the thirtyfold Muṇḍī has been established and revealed in the Tārāsūkta.
Therein, one who is perfected in the conduct of the Pāśupatas shall have his head shaved;
he may wear three matted locks, a single matted lock, or likewise wear crooked matted locks. (1.209)
Naked, an ascetic, peaceful in soul, devoted to the mortification of the body, and perfected in the threefold ritual action—the one with matted hair is known as a Pāśupata. (1.210)
O Great Goddess, one who is endowed with the restraint of speech and mind is called *dvidaṇḍin*;
one who possesses the restraint of body, speech, and mind is proclaimed a *tridaṇḍin*. (1.211)
One who possesses only the mind as his staff is proclaimed a "single-staffed" (ekadaṇḍin);
he is endowed solely with Śiva, yet he is a reviler of his own deity. (1-212)
"He is known as a Vīraśaiva.

Elsewhere, it is shown that even those such as the Tridaṇḍins, who are renowned as Vaiṣṇavas, can also be Śaivas. He states that the predominance of different paths varies according to the distinction of the Yugas.
In the Kṛta age, the path declared by the Śrutis prevails; in the Tretā, that spoken in the Smṛtis;
in the Dvāpara, that stated in the Purāṇas; and in the Kali age, that arising from the Āgamas. (1.213)
The word "pradhāna" (the primary) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
The *Merutantra* states that scripture (*āgama*) is an auxiliary limb (*aṅga*) of the Veda.
The Veda does not exist apart from the Praṇava, and a mantra is that which is endowed with the Veda;
therefore, a mantra is considered to be devoted to the Veda, and Āgama is known as a limb (aṅga) of the Veda. || 1-214 ||
The meaning of the word *āgama* is as follows, as it appears in the Rudrayāmala: "It has come from the mouths of Śiva and gone into the mouth of Girijā."
It is great within the lotus of her heart; therefore, it is called the Āgama.
Even though scripture (*āgama*) is an auxiliary limb (*vedāṅga*) of the Veda, [the author] states the contradiction between the Vedic and the Kaulika [traditions] on that very page (p.
32): "In that regard, for one who performs a Kaulika rite, the Vedic rite is not prescribed."
Because of this contradiction, both are lost; therefore, one should walk upon the single path.
Regarding the contradiction between the left and right paths, the *Merutantra* states:
"When one who follows the left path enters the right, he is [rejected] by the gods."
He is obstructed and even afflicted; he does not attain success. || 1-217 ||
When the [breath] of the right path enters the left, O gods, they likewise cause that person to flee from both worlds and devour the one who follows the left. (1.218)
Therefore, having understood the path of one's own family (kula), one should perform worship.
The different types of worship therein have been stated;
Śrī Śiva said:
That which was spoken by Mahākāla, which was heard by Mahāmāyā.
That which is the most profound secret,
hidden within all mantras and the secret of the sacred traditions (āmnāyas), is now declared as this daily practice (āhnika).
"Listen, all you gods, to that which grants success to practitioners;
it is declared there to be eternal and threefold, according to the distinction of the three qualities. (1-221)
According to the distinction of the qualified aspirant (adhikārī), that [initiation] also becomes threefold: pure, mixed, and dissolved; it yields fruit in exactly that manner. (1.222)
Pure [devotion] bestows the complete fruit; mixed [devotion] yields some fruit.
In the case of what is unperformed, there is no transgression; and when it has dissolved, there is no excellent fruit.
That mental action which is devoid of egoism, preceded by knowledge, and performed by an ascetic with a composed mind is called pure. (1.224)
If such a [deed] is performed by a householder who is destitute of wealth, or even by one who is ill, a traveler, or one who has entered a prison; (1-225)
Or else, out of devotion, or mixed with that [devotion], by virtue of being entitled to external worship;
or due to fear of cold and so forth, from the destruction of what was desired, or because the task is minor. (1.226)
That which has flowed forth through the command of a woman or others and has been received is considered mental;
as is external worship and the like, performed with regularity in solitude. (1.227)
That which is performed by a householder with devotion is considered pure;
however, that which is done for the sake of worship after begging, or without faith and devotion, is regarded as rajasic.

That which is mixed with royal authority, undertaken out of fear of the world or fear of the gods, and requested under the pretext of the gods for the purpose of deceiving the people—[that is not true dharma]. (1.229)
That which was made as a substance has dissolved away through that very guise; it is of the nature of passion (rājasa).
Having resorted to the left-hand path and having reflected upon the Kaula doctrine...

Furthermore, an action performed out of non-aversion toward other dharmas is pure, whereas an action performed out of desire—whether it be a Vedic rite or one pertaining to the next world—is characterized by tamas. (1.231)
Resorting to the left-hand path (vāmamārga), that is indeed mixed and characterized by darkness (tāmasa);
it consists of eating out of greed for the tongue, drinking, and sexual pleasure according to one's desire. (1–232)
Alternatively, that which has dissolved for the purpose of killing and so forth is tāmasa;
through pure sattva there would be liberation, and through mixed sattva there would be heaven.
Success arises from one whose essence has dissolved; there is also success in this world and as a human being.
From the rājasa [sattva] comes heaven, and from the pure [sattva] comes desire; from that which is mixed with rajas, desire likewise arises.
From a mind characterized by rajas that has fallen away, there may even be happiness in the animal realm;
from a sattvic or tāmasa mind, a person shall attain birth in a divine womb. (1.235)
From the quality of Tamas, one becomes miserable and a hell-being through extreme Tamas;
thus, action is said to be fivefold, bestowing liberation in five ways. || 1-236 ||

On the ground: (1) spreading [the sacrificial grass], (2) gathering the materials, (3) the sacrifice, and (4) the recitation; likewise, (5) the consecrations in the temple of the deity, such as sweeping and smearing.

Worship performed with devotion is *sarpaṇa*, which brings about residence in the same world as the deity (*devasālokya*); the gathering of all the materials required for worship is the service of the devotee (*bhaktasevana*). (1–238)
That joy shall be the material cause which bestows the form of the deity,
preceded by the worship of the seat (pīṭha) with the sixteen and other ritual services.
Or else, worship may be performed upon the image or the yantra; this is the worship that brings about proximity [to the deity].
Having properly studied the scriptures concerning that [deity] and having contemplated the meaning of the mantra, [one should perform the rite]. (1.240)
Having performed [this], the recitation (japa) becomes self-study (svādhyāya), which brings about union with the Divine;
it consists of the perfect contemplation of the essential identity of the Guru, the Deity, the Self, and Time. (1.241)
The conjunction [of the soul] with the body and the subtle body (liṅga), brought about by the operation of time, is the cause of destruction.
Furthermore, the worship performed by travelers and others is described in that very same [text].
Now I shall describe the afternoon [rite], which occurs in those ten locations.

On a journey, during travel abroad, in difficult terrain, when food is not obtained, when there is mental anxiety, in prison, in an inauspicious place, and when there is fear arising from thieves, tigers, and the like. (1-243)
Upon the arrival of an enemy army, one should perform purification and so forth, in whatever manner possible;
having performed some form of mantra-bath and the like, one should carry out mental worship.
Having meditated with the mind upon the seat known as Yoga within the heart, one should perform the worship of the God right there, in the center of the earth. (1.245)
Just as worship with flowers and other offerings is performed in the external world, so too should all those same practices be performed within the heart. (1.246)
The mental oblation in the stomach and this daily ritual during times of adversity have been explained.
Now, the worship performed by one afflicted by disease is described in that very same place.
Now I shall describe the daily observance for the sick, which is always intended for one who is afflicted by suffering.
If a disease that culminates in emaciation is seen within oneself, then one should not perform worship upon a sacrificial mound or before images. (1.248)
One should not perform bathing, nor the use of a tooth-stick, nor even the fire-oblation (homa), without first beholding the solar disc or a sacred image. (1.249)
Having recited the root mantra once, one should offer a flower together with unbroken grains of rice;
even if one is exhausted by most violent diseases or has lost the faculties through old age.
Or else, he should complete his own duties with his own companions;
then, having recovered from his illness, he should bathe and worship the fires and the deities.
In the presence of the gurus and the Brahmins, he should utter these words: "The worship has been interrupted for this long; by your grace, [it is now resumed]. (1-252)
Having prayed, "May there be no fault," one should perform the rite again as before;
however, for whatever fault has arisen due to the influence of disease, one should perform its purification.
"Either by recitation, or by giving, or by fire-offering, or even through meditation.
Furthermore, the worship performed by one in a state of birth-impurity (sūtaka) is described in that very same [text]:
Now, for one in a state of birth-impurity (sūtaka), the Vedic rites prescribed by the Smṛtis must be performed constantly.
Having performed the tantric worship and so forth, one should carry it out by means of the mind alone;
if, however, the practice is for the sake of a specific desire, then one should perform it as previously described. (1.255)

Having abandoned the house of death during the period of birth-impurity through the left-hand practice (vāmācāra), and having cast aside desire with prior knowledge, the one born of the Kula attains the dharma that has arrived. || 1-256 ||
He who protects the Vāma-dharma is born as a deity.

Now, regarding what should be done when a great danger has arisen or when the requisites for worship are lacking, he says: "If, being terrified, the means such as the arghya-vessel and so forth have not been obtained... (1-257).
The worship should be performed with water; however, if water is not available at all, then one should worship the deity with flowers of meditative visualization and so forth. (1.258)
Devotion, faith, and contemplation are said to be the life-force of worship.
Now I shall describe the daily rite for the insentient, as well as their daily practice in brief.

The worship of these is prescribed: the jewel-pavilion (ratnamaṇḍapa), the fourfold [principles] beginning with Dharma, the serpent (uraga), the lotus (ambuja), the root-mantra (mūla), the form (mūrti), and the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga). || 1-260 ||
One should constantly touch the limbs according to this very sequence of ritual placement (nyāsa);
for when none of the physical objects are available, meditation alone is indeed sufficient.
With pure water alone, one of steady mind should perform the worship.
Generally, worship is of three kinds: superior (1), middling (2), and inferior (3). (1-262)
Furthermore, it is divided a hundredfold according to the qualifications and causes [of the practitioner].
When performed with all the complete requisites of yoga, it is considered the highest. (1.263)
Worship performed with materials obtained as they come is called middling;
worship performed with leaves, flowers, and water is designated as inferior. (1.264)
That worship which is performed by stainless Brahman-sages who have studied all that is prescribed in the Vedas is *sāttvika*, and it bestows liberation. (1.265)
The worship that is performed correctly by royal sages devoted to austerity and who know the true nature of the Blessed One is of the passionate (rājasa) type, which bestows happiness.
That worship which is performed constantly by women, children, the elderly, the ignorant, and others who are devoted but possess undisturbed minds, is proclaimed to be *tāmasī*.
In the forest, worship is prescribed for those with few desires for the sake of spiritual attainment;
however, for householders free from desire, worship at home is beneficial. (1.268)
The path of the Vedas must never, at any time, be abandoned by the twice-born;
for those who have fallen away from the Vedas, both the status of a Brahmin and even divinity are difficult to attain. (1.269)
Likewise, worship is said to be threefold, among which the sāttvika is the most excellent;
and within that, mental worship and silent recitation are considered the most primary. (1.270)

The southern path is characterized by passion (rājasa); the worship of the image with external offerings such as flowers and the like is especially distinguished for those of the first [category]. (1.271)
The practice of Tāmasa worship is said to consist of offering oblations (bali) at sacred seats and other locations;
that is praised as the foremost when performed according to the Vāma path, provided the initial letter [of the mantra] is omitted. (1.271)
This supreme arrangement for the left and right [paths] has been fully declared;
worship is said to be of two kinds, renowned as being with desire and without desire. (1.272)

The seed of liberation belongs to those free from desire, while for those with desire it is the seed of worldly existence. Furthermore, regarding worship, it is stated in that same work (p. 38) that one lacks the qualification [to perform it] without the instruction of a guru.
For the twice-born who have not been initiated, [the king should intervene] regarding their own duties, Vedic study, and so forth. || 1.273 ||
Likewise, those who have not been initiated have no authority regarding the worship of mantras and deities; therefore, one should make oneself consecrated by the mantra.
In the *Mantramuktāvalī*:
"The recitation of mantras and the ritual of deity worship should be performed by men who have received initiation.
Likewise, in the *Gaurīyāmala*:
A mantra heard by chance, or through deception, or by force; || 1.275 ||
Even if it is placed upon a leaf and consecrated with verses, it is fruitless;
for those who, uninitiated, perform rites such as recitation and worship in the Yoginītantra. (1.276)
Their fruit would not come to pass, like seeds sown upon a stone.
Also, in the *Mahākālasaṃhitā*:
"One should not speak, act, or even recite [the mantra] without having first examined the scripture. (1.277)

One should not look [at it], nor teach it, nor perform it, nor accomplish it—once the recitation, ritual placement, worship, and so forth have been obtained through the instruction of the Guru. (1.278)
Thereafter, one who is always permeated by that [state] should accomplish everything;
thus the Rudrayāmala states the necessity of initiation (dīkṣā).
For that living being, there is no initiation into Śiva until the end of life.
O Goddess, such a person shall never at any time cross over the ocean of hell—neither the bound soul (paśu) devoid of initiation, O Mistress of Gods, nor one of contemptible birth. (1.280)
A flood of sins approaches, while merit flees afar;
therefore, this supreme initiation should be received with effort by those who are wise. (1.281)
In the Dattātreyayāmala:
"Now, he who on this earth lives devoid of initiation experiences sin;
afflicted, he falls into the pit of hell within the darkness of delusion. (1.282)
Just as there is no protector for a mortal who lacks a lord upon this earth,
so too for one devoid of initiation, there is no master either in this world or in the next.
The gods never accept the worship of one who is uninitiated, even if it is performed with thousands of ritual services and endowed with devotion, as described in the Āgamakalpadruma.
Since all action is in vain for one who is uninitiated, such a person is a mere beast; as stated in the *Matsyasūkta*:
"O Goddess Maheśvarī, hear now concerning those mortals who are uninitiated. (1.285)
For him, food is considered equal to excrement and water equal to urine;
any śrāddha performed by him or for him goes entirely to a downward state.
The greatness of initiation (dīkṣā) is stated in the Kulārṇava: "Hundreds of thousands of minor offenses (upapātaka) and tens of millions of major sins (mahāpātaka)," [are destroyed].
For initiation, when performed according to the prescribed rule, O Goddess of Gods, burns away [impurities] in an instant.
A Brāhmaṇa initiated in the Rudrayāmala goes to the nectar-filled world of Brahmā;
likewise, a Kṣatriya goes to the world of Indra, and a Vaiśya to the world of Prajāpati. (1.288) p. 40)
By the grace of initiation, even a Śūdra goes to the city of the Gandharvas;
according to the teaching of Śiva, there can be no liberation for living beings without initiation. (1.289)
And that [initiation] cannot exist without a teacher; thus there is a lineage of teachers.
In the *Vaiśampāyanasaṃhitā*, it is said:
"Initiation brings about all accomplishments and bestows all prosperity. (1.290)
The excellent qualities of the various forms, as well as beauty, nourishment, and wealth;
and the acts of enchantment, paralyzing, attracting, killing, and driving away.
He attained mastery over others, poetic skill, and an intellect endowed with tens of thousands of powers of retention;
he achieved the crossing of the ocean, the cooling of fire, and victory in battle.
In the forest, she indeed grants fearlessness as well as the removal of grief and suffering;
she bestows dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa—of this there is no doubt. (1.293)
The meaning of the word *dīkṣā* is stated in the Rudrayāmala:
"Because it bestows divine knowledge and effects the destruction of sin."
Therefore, it is proclaimed as "dīkṣā" in this world by those who have mastered the mantras.
In the Merutantra it is said:
"Knowledge and realization are bestowed, and the heaps of sins are destroyed;
therefore, when received from the mouth of a true guru, it is indeed called 'dīkṣā' (initiation). (1.295)
How can a false guru, being himself lost, deliver another?
One should receive the great vidyā that destroys sin from the mouth of a guru, according to the essence of the Āgamas. (1.296)
Therefore, having made diligent effort, one should perform the practice of mantra-sādhana under a guru;
[as stated] in the *Cāmuṇḍātantra*:
"In all the secondary sciences (*upavidyā*) and in the accomplishment of the six rites (*ṣatkarma*) and so forth... (1.297).
In this [practice], there is no requirement for initiation (*dīkṣā*) and the like, nor is there the worship of the limbs (*aṅga*) and so forth.

The "subsidiary sciences" (*upavidyā*) refer to Yakṣiṇīs and others. The "means-mantras" (*sādhanamantra*) refer to those mantras used for the accomplishment of the six rites (*ṣatkarma*) and so on, which are distinct from the great mantras (*mahāmantra*). Here, the term "initiation" (*dīkṣā*) refers to initiations such as the *kriyāvatī*; however, the initiation of oral instruction (*upadeśadīkṣā*) is necessary everywhere.
O beautiful one, when a mantra written in a book is recited by someone... (1-298)
For him, no success arises; rather, there is only loss at every step.
All rites performed with the preceptor as the chief yield the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (1.299)

"Since all ritual acts not instructed by the Guru will certainly be fruitless," according to such statements. Furthermore, one should accomplish the mantra after learning it either from the scripture or from the mouth of the Guru. (1.300)

Based on this statement, it should not be said that knowledge of a mantra derived even from a book produces success (*siddhi*). For the meaning of that [statement] is precisely this: a practitioner who has received a mantra from a guru should accomplish the mantra after learning the method of mantra-practice either from the scriptures or from the mouth of the guru.
He states the meaning of the word *mantra* in the *Piṅgalāmata*:

"Because it brings about the realization of the universe through contemplation (*manana*) and protection (*trāṇa*) from the bonds of saṃsāra, and because it effects complete accomplishment (*saṃsiddhi*), it is therefore called *mantra*. (1.301)
Regarding the majesty of mantra, the *Merutantra* states: The mantra itself is the Lord manifest; the mantra itself is the great medicine.
Indeed, there is nothing superior to the mantra as a bestower of all accomplishments. (1.302)
In that very same [text]:
"The gods assumed those various forms in order to bestow the fruit upon practitioners;
however, their primary essential nature is the mantras alone, and nothing else. (1.303)
(p. 42) (In the *Sārasaṃgraha*):
"As it is with the deity, so it is with the mantra; as it is with the mantra, so it is with the guru;
as it is with the guru, so it is with one's own self—thus is the sequence of devotion traditionally taught. (1-304)
The greatness of the Guru is stated [in the Rudrayāmala]:
"The Guru alone is the supreme mantra; the Guru alone is the supreme recitation;
the Guru alone is the supreme knowledge; there is nothing whatsoever apart from the Guru. (1.305)
O Goddess, when one's Guru is pleased, Maheśvarī is pleased with him;
O Goddess, he by whom the Guru is satisfied is indeed Sadāśiva himself.
Therefore, one should serve the guru with devotion and constantly please the guru;
wherever there is gossip or censure concerning the guru, [one should avoid it]. (1.307)
"In that situation, one's ears should be covered, or else one should flee far away"—so it is said in the *Brahmavaivarta*.
For those disciples who have constantly served their gurus yet have insulted them... (1.308)
For those fools who are treacherous toward their guru and constantly commit evil deeds fall away from the prosperity of sons, friends, wives, and the like. (1.309)
Whatever good or evil deeds they may have committed, there is no doubt;
one should always perform mental salutations [to them] while remaining constantly free from hostility toward the guru. 1-310.
One should always worship the Guru who dwells in the same village with the thought that he is Sadāśiva; if he is far away, one should perform the salutation mentally.
Whatever fruit may arise from the worship of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others, that same fruit one obtains by saluting the Guru every day. (1.312)
Whether ignorant or possessed of knowledge, the guru alone is the deity;
whether situated on a wrong path or on the right path, the guru alone is the supreme goal. (1.313)
Just as copper becomes gold through contact with an alchemical elixir, so too does a disciple become identical with Śiva through the mere presence of the Guru. (1.314)
Likewise:
"Between the progenitor and the giver of the Veda, the father who gives the Veda is more venerable;
therefore, one should always regard him as even greater than one's biological father. (1.315)
In the *Vasantalalitabhairavī*:
One should worship with supreme devotion the Guru, the supreme lord who is the instructor of divine knowledge, and one must never transgress his command. (1.316)
As is the Guru, so is the Lord; as is the Lord, so is the Guru.
Both are to be worshipped with devotion; no difference exists between them.
One should never engage in dualistic discourse with the Guru;
one should contemplate non-duality with devotion, for thus one becomes the Lord. (1.318)
Even when Śiva is angry, the guru is the protector; but when the guru is angry, there is no one at all.
Therefore, with every effort, one should propitiate the guru alone. (1.319)
In the *Merutantra*: "Aversion (ghṛṇā), doubt (śaṅkā), fear (bhaya), shame (lajjā), and fifthly, disgust (jugupsā);
family (kula), conduct (śīla), and likewise power (śakti)—these eight are proclaimed as the fetters (pāśas). (1.320)
One bound by fetters is called a *paśu* (bound soul), while one freed from fetters is Sadāśiva.
Therefore, he who removes the fetters here is called the Guru, and no other. (1.321)
Thus, by that very doubt, the entire triple world, including all moving and unmoving beings, was consumed; he by whom that doubt itself is consumed is a Guru difficult to find on earth. (1.322)
(p. 44) (In the *Kularatnāvalī*):
"O Dear One, the venerable Guru is said to be Śiva himself with three eyes, Acyuta with four arms, and Brahmā with four faces. (1.323)
O Pārvatī, there is no difference between the god Sadāśiva and the venerable Guru; he who makes a distinction between the two is a sinner.
Just as "pot," "jar," and "vessel" are synonyms denoting a single object, so too "God," "mantra," and "guru" are said to have one and the same meaning. (1.325)
There is no object equal to the Guru; there is no deity comparable to Śaṅkara.
There is no yoga higher than Kaula, and no knowledge equal to that of Kālikā.
(Merutantra) For one devoid of devotion to the Guru, austerity, knowledge, vows, and lineage are all in vain, like the various ornaments adorning a corpse. (1.327)
He states the meaning of the word *guru* (in the *Āgamasāra*):
"The letter *ga* is said to bestow accomplishment (*siddhi*); the letter *ra* is the burner of sin;
the letter *u* is said to be Śiva. The supreme *guru* is the essence of these three. (1.328)
One who is firm in his vows, of virtuous conduct, endowed with faith and devotion, grateful, fearful of sin, and who associates with the good and the virtuous. (1.329)
One who is a believer, virtuous in charity, and devoted to the welfare of all beings—such is the characteristic of a Guru (*Kulārṇava*):
"O Supreme Goddess, the venerable Guru is of pure caste and captivating. (1.330)
Endowed with all the primary marks, beautified by all the secondary characteristics,
he knows the reality of the meaning of all scriptures and understands the preeminent essence of all mantras.
His appearance was one that deluded the world, yet he was as pleasing to behold as a god; by his gestures, expressions, and movements, he kept wicked people at a distance from afar. (1.332)
Inward-turned yet looking outward, omniscient, and knowing time and place; one who has attained mastery through command, knowing the three times, and capable of both restraint and grace. || 1-333 ||

One who is learned in the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, tranquil, devoted to compassion for all living beings, one who has mastery over the movement of his senses, and capable of conquering the group of six internal enemies. || 1.334 ||
