Foremost among the assembly, exceedingly profound, and discerning between those who are worthy and unworthy recipients;
stainless, eternally contented, free from the pairs of opposites, and possessed of constant power.
Affectionate toward his true devotees, steadfast, compassionate, and one whose speech is preceded by a smile;
fond of devotion, impartial toward all, merciful, and the instructor of disciples. (1.336)
He is a wise devotee of his chosen deity and preceptor, eager to honor women, and devoted to blameless rites— whether daily, occasional, or performed for specific desires.
Free from passion, hatred, fear, anger, deceit, and egoism, he is the illuminator of his own spiritual knowledge, of ritual practice, of austerity, and of learning. (1.338)
Content with whatever is obtained by chance, discerning between virtues and faults, unattached to women, wealth, and the like, and abandoned by the vice of evil company. || 1.339 ||
Free from greed, non-violent, impartial, and discerning;
one who does not sell mantras, yantras, tantras, and the like for the sake of wealth, learning, or other such things. (1.340)
Free from conceptualization, free from discursive thought, having ascertained the self, and supremely righteous;
equal toward blame and praise, observing silence, indifferent to worldly concerns, and self-restrained.

O Dear One, the Śrī Guru has been described as endowed with such characteristics as these. Now, the characteristics of a prohibited guru [are stated in the *Tattvasāra*]: "One who eats excessively, one who procrastinates, and one who is greedy for sense objects and the like... (1.342).

One who delights in causal theorizing, the wicked, the mere talker of words, the reviler of gurus; one without body hair, one with excessive body hair, and one who serves a censured stage of life. (1.343)
One with black teeth, dark lips, and foul-smelling breath—even if he were himself a lord—is endowed with evil characteristics. (1.344)
A teacher who is addicted to receiving many gifts brings about the destruction of prosperity.
Now, regarding the characteristics of a disciple (in the *Kulārṇava*):
O Mistress of the Kula, that good disciple is endowed with all auspicious marks. (1.345)
One who is endowed with the means such as tranquility, possessed of virtues and moral conduct,
knowledgeable regarding pure bodies and lineages, righteous, and pure-minded.
Endowed with trustworthiness and humility, free from stinginess regarding wealth, a accomplisher of the impossible, heroic, and possessed of strength and splendor. (1.347)
One who acts in accordance [with the goal], is vigilant, and discerning;
who speaks what is beneficial, truthful, measured, and affectionate; and who is free from fault-finding. || 1-348 ||
One who grasps the meaning upon being told once, possesses an expansive and clever intellect;
such a person is free from attachment to home, free from intoxication, free from the lap [of worldly indulgence], free from transformation, and free from servitude. (1.349)
One who acts with deliberation, a hero free from the poverty of mind,
highly skilled in all undertakings, steadfast, and helpful to all.
O beloved, [he is] averted from excessive censuring of others, pleasant-faced,
one who has conquered his senses, well-contented, wise, and a celibate student.

Having abandoned the fickleness of mental and physical ailments, and being free from the distress of ill-founded suspicions, one is eager for the service and devotion of practicing the meditation upon, praising, and listening to the teachings of the Guru. (1.352)
O Goddess, [he is] devoted to the guru and the deity, eager to serve women,
an observer of the guru’s commands, and a praiser of the guru’s fame.
O Mistress of the Clan, [one should choose] one who knows the authority of the Guru’s words, who delights in service to the Guru, who follows his mind, and who acts after due consideration. (1.354)
Free from shame, pride, arrogance, and the like in the presence of the guru, indifferent toward the guru’s property, and desiring his grace; (1.355)

The teacher should accept as a disciple one who is devoted to the meditation on the Guru and other such practices, who yearns for the path to liberation, and who possesses these and other similar characteristics. (1.356)

The characteristics of a contemptible disciple are given in that very same [text]: one born of a wicked lineage, wicked, devoid of virtues, deformed, a former disciple of another, a heretic, a rogue, and one who fancies himself a scholar. (1.357)
With limbs deficient, excessive, or deformed, and possessed of impaired members; lame, blind, deaf, filthy, and afflicted by disease. (1.358)
[He saw] Ucchiṣṭa, Durmukha, and the libertine Svecchāveśadhara;
[and] Durbhidagdha, Kuceṣṭa, Kuṭila, and Bhīmavīkṣaṇa.
Always possessed of sleep and laziness, afflicted by drowsiness and vices such as gambling, and with his body constantly hidden behind doors, walls, pillars, and the like.
What is the use of one who acts with empty gestures, is base, devoid of faith and devotion, a mere talker, stubborn, a slanderer, fickle, and deceitful? (1.361)
It is devoid of purity regarding wealth and women, lacking both prohibitions and injunctions, a divulger of secrets, and a destroyer of the purpose of Vedic rites. (1.362)
One who behaves like a cat or a heron, being intent on seeking out weaknesses;
one who is full of deceit, ungrateful, and a secret betrayer. (1.363)
One who betrays trust, an enemy of the gods, an evildoer, one devoid of faith, whose limbs are ignorance, and who desires the accomplishment of misfortune— (1.364).
One who seeks to kill, one who desires to seize, one who is contemptible, a false witness, a beggar everywhere, O Goddess, and one who approaches all women by force— || 1.365 ||
One who is devoted to untruth, unattached [to virtue], a speaker of many vulgar and such words, a producer of evil reflections and discursive thoughts, and one fond of quarreling; || 1-366 ||
One who causes vain distractions, who is deluded or causes others to wander, who mocks with words,
who finds fault behind one's back but speaks kindly in one's presence— (1.367)
One should know him to be a thief of knowledge who speaks harsh words, praises himself, cannot endure the virtues of others, is afraid of the virtuous, and is filled with excessive anger. (1.368)
The Cārvāka system is the friend of the wicked, despised by all the world;
it is malicious, a source of torment to others, and a cause of fear for all living beings.

O Goddess, one who speaks without affliction [of conscience], a betrayer of friends, a deceiver of his brother, one devoted to the tongue and the genitals, a thief, and one whose conduct is like that of a beast— || 1.370 ||
One who commits hatred, laughter, affliction, anger, and so forth without cause; one who indulges in excessive laughter; and one who mocks others out of delusion. (1.371)
Lustful, shamelessly flattering, indicative of false and wicked conduct, and possessed of envy, intoxication, malice, hypocrisy, and egoism. (1.372)
One who is envious, slanderous, harsh, miserly, angry, and proud;
who is lacking in fortitude, miserable, hateful, incompetent, and devoid of the true reality—(1.373).
One who possesses unestablished and poor intellect, who is deluded and whose mind is agitated by anxiety,
who is joined with craving and greed, who is wretched, discontented, and a beggar for everything— (1.374).

O beloved, [one should avoid] one who eats excessively, who is deceitful, who is a deceiver, who is crooked, and who is devoid of devotion, faith, compassion, tranquility, and righteous conduct. (1.375)
One who causes laughter to his mother, father, gurus, the wise, and great men;
one who treats with loathsomeness the family property and other such things; and one who is arrogant regarding service to his guru. (1.376)
O Maheśvarī, the Guru should abandon a disciple who is corrupted by women, who has violated the samaya, who is cursed by his own teacher, or who is possessed of such other defects as these. (1.377)
If, out of affection or even greed, one should accept [a disciple] or initiate him,
then a curse from the deity will fall upon that guru and his disciple.
Therefore, one should never accept such a disciple;
if one accepts him out of delusion, the teacher incurs those very sins. (1.378)
Just as the sin of a minister affects the king, and that committed by a wife affects the husband, so too the sin committed by a disciple generally touches the teacher as well. (1.379)
The teacher should examine the disciple through his knowledge or his compassion for a year, or half of that, or half of that again, or even half of that. (1.380)
In matters of high or low importance, and in tasks of base or noble character,
[one should act] through the offering of life or wealth, by commands, and through associations.
By means of words that pierce his vital spots, by deceptions, by cruel actions, and by many partialities as well as indifference, [he assailed him] again and again. (1.382)
One who, though afflicted, does not fall into despondency even when provoked, should always feel joy, thinking, "The Guru is showing compassion. (1.383)
Whether in the remembrance of the glorious Guru, or in his glorification, or in salutation, or in service, or in invocation, or in sending forth, or in seeking him out, O beloved— || 1.384 ||
O Goddess, those who experience physical transformations such as bliss, trembling, horripilation, changes in voice, or the eyes, would not be fit even for the accomplishment of mantras. (1.385)
(Mantramuktāvalī):
"Between those two, within the span of a single year, their mutual status as teacher or disciple will be known; it cannot be otherwise—this is the certain conclusion. (1.386)
In the Kali age, according to the Merutantra, gurus seek wealth while disciples seek supernatural powers;
therefore, neither attains success, and it is merely a mockery of the deities.
(Liṅgāgama) Having received the mantra from a true guru, the disciple should not abandon him;
a disciple who abandons his guru will certainly be subject to penance. 1.388.
(Rudrayāmala) From abandoning the guru comes death; from abandoning the mantra comes poverty;
from abandoning both the guru and the mantra, one goes to the Raurava hell. (1.389)
Regarding the reception of mantras by a bound soul (paśu) from a Kaulika, even the abandonment of that [mantra] is stated in the Devyāgama:
"If, by chance, the Vidyā is obtained from a bound soul by men born of the Kula, one should approach a Kaulika twice-born (dvija) and receive the Vidyā once again. (1.390)
For one who undertakes the initiation of a sacrificial animal, there will certainly be physical suffering or even imprisonment; of this there is no doubt. (1.391)
Having written that mantra on a banyan leaf, one should cast it into the stream;
or, having taken refuge in a true guru, one should receive the consecrated mantra.
(Kulārṇava) Having obtained a venerable Guru who possesses the [required] characteristics, who cuts through doubt, and who bestows knowledge, O Goddess, one should not resort to another Guru. (1.393)
Having approached a teacher who is ignorant and unable to sever one's doubts, a disciple who goes to another teacher is not defiled by the faults of that [first] teacher. (1.394)
(In the Śaiva Āgama:
There are many gurus who know evil mantras and medicinal herbs;
one who knows the mantras taught in the Vedas and Āgama scriptures is rare on earth. (1.395)
A wise person may rescue a fool, but a fool cannot rescue a fool;
for can a boat carry across a stone, or can a stone carry across a stone?
Just as a bee, greedy for honey, goes from flower to another flower, so too a disciple, greedy for knowledge, goes from one teacher to another teacher. (1.397)
(In the Vārāhītantra:
"One should not appoint as a guru one who bears one's own name, nor one whose wife bears the name of a mother.
Now, he states a further distinction even regarding a guru characterized by the aforementioned marks. (In the Rudrayāmala:)
A Vaiṣṇava should be accepted in a Vaiṣṇava [rite], a Śaiva in a Śaiva, and a Śākta in a Śākta.
Whether one is a Śaiva or a Śākta, he is everywhere the master of initiation; of this there is no doubt.
O Maheśānī, if the sequence is inverted, the accomplishment of the mantra will certainly not occur.
A husband shall not initiate his wife; a father shall not initiate his daughter;
likewise, a brother shall not initiate his son, nor shall he initiate his own brother.
"One should not initiate the wife [without the husband]," it says in the *Paśukalpa*. However, in the *Vīrakalpa*:
"For heroes and for Kaulikas, the husband should perform the initiation.
In the Kaulika Āgama, there is no fault in the husband bestowing the initiation. (1.401)
It has been stated: "In the past, Śiva bestowed upon Gaurī an auspicious initiation.
Likewise: "One should not receive a mantra from one's father, nor likewise from one's maternal grandfather. (1.402)
(From the *Gaṇeśavimarṣiṇī*, p. 52): Likewise, [initiation] from a younger brother, or from one who has taken the side of an enemy;
as well as the initiation of a father, the initiation of an ascetic (*yati*), and the initiation of a forest-dweller (*vanavāsin*). 1-403.
The initiation of one who dwells in a secluded hermitage does not bestow auspiciousness;
for the mantra of the father as well as that of the maternal grandfather is devoid of potency. (Yoginītantra 1.404)
When one performs the initiation of a father out of negligence or likewise through ignorance, [the father] being either a younger brother or one who has taken the side of an enemy.
"Then, having performed an expiation (prāyaścitta), one should undergo initiation again.

Here, the genitive case in "pituḥ" (of the father) is used in the sense of disregard; thus, the meaning is that if there is disregard toward the father and others in the form of a lack of devotion due to excessive familiarity and so forth, then the mantra should not be received by the son or others. This is the view of the author of the *Sudhārṇava*.
However, in the *Matsyasūkta*:
"For a mantra of the Father (Bhairava) that lacks potency does not cause harm when applied to the Śaiva or Śākta [traditions]"—thus it has been said. (1-406)

In the *Tārākalpa*, it is stated that having somehow obtained this mantra, one should bestow it upon a certain disciple who is the ornament of one's own lineage, namely one's eldest son—this refers to the subject of Tārā. Regarding the subject of Śrīvidyā as well, there is no prohibition against initiation by a father. As it is said in the *Śrīkrama*:
Having reflected, [the mantra] should be given to a wise eldest son;
however, regarding the reception of one's own mantra, no deliberation concerning a guru should be made.
Regarding the instruction of one's own mantra, one should not entertain thoughts of a guru. (1-407)
Thus, from the statement of the Bhairava Tantra:
"And likewise, it was previously told by Brahmā to the great-souled Vasiṣṭha."
Vasiṣṭha himself also gave it to my father, his own son.
With a serene heart, pure and a treasure-house of compassion, my father gave [it] at the great sacred site of Kurukṣetra during a solar eclipse. (1.409)

Thus, based on the words of Vyāsa addressed to Śaunaka in the *Vaiśampāyana-saṃhitā* concerning the Viṣṇu-mantra, there is no prohibition against a father’s initiation (*pitṛ-dīkṣā*) even for the Viṣṇu-mantra. However, according to the statement in the *Nārāyaṇīya*, "He [the teacher] may initiate his son, and likewise a son who has transgressed," the prohibition of a father’s initiation applies only to a son who is not a devotee (*abhakta*). This is the view of those who know the tradition. A "transgressor" (*vyatyayī*) is one who, having been given one mantra, subsequently receives another mantra.
In the Yoginītantra, initiation by women is declared auspicious; it is remembered as being eight times more efficacious than that of a mother. (1.410)
She was virtuous, of good conduct, devoted to her guru, and had conquered her senses;
she knew the true meaning and essence of all mantras, possessed excellent character, and delighted in worship.
For she who is fit for the Guru must indeed be a widow, free from [other] attachments.
(From the Vaiśampāyana-saṃhitā) That which is obtained in a dream or given by a woman is perfected through the very rite of consecration. 1-412.
And regarding the ritual preparation (*saṃskāra*) in that very context:
one should infuse the vital breaths of the Guru into a jar obtained in a dream;
having written [the mantra] with saffron on a *vaṭa* leaf, its reception is performed. (1.413)

From that, one attains success; otherwise, it would be fruitless. However, regarding the reception of a perfected mantra (*siddhamantra*), there is no deliberation required at all. As it is said in the *Śaktiyāmala*:
"If [the teacher] possesses a perfected mantra, then he should duly initiate his wife. (1.414)
O lady of excellent hips, she does not become a "daughter" by virtue of her capacity alone;
rather, the father should likewise bestow initiation upon his daughter in that same manner. (1.415)
A brother whose mantra has been perfected becomes a guru for his brother by virtue of his power;
a man whose mantra is perfected can bring everything that is unfit to a state of fitness.
(Mahākapilapañcarātra) 1.417: Śūdras have no entitlement to the mantra; for them, there is a supreme restriction.
Due to the absence of mantras, indeed, every ritual act is performed without a mantra.
(In the *Sātātapa-saṃhitā*):

"Prajāpati himself has declared that for as many syllables as one might cause to be imparted to women, Śūdras, and the like from the mantras, there shall be that many instances of the sin of killing a Brahmin. (1.418)
Thus ends the section concerning the Vedic and other mantras.
(Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa):
"The mantras should indeed be imparted to those Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who are pure and stainless, but not to those of mixed caste. (1.419)
(From the Devīyāmala):
A twice-born man who gives a mantra joined with *svāhā* and the *praṇava* to a Śūdra shall go to hell; the Brāhmaṇa shall attain the status of a Śūdra. (1.420)
(In the Brahmapurāṇa:
"The Vedic or the mixed [path] is prescribed for the Brāhmaṇas and others;
the Tantric [path] is proclaimed even for a Śūdra who is devoted to the Brāhmaṇas. (1.421)
(Bhāgavata Purāṇa, 11th Skandha):
"My sacrifice is threefold: Vedic, Tantric, and Mixed. One should worship me according to whichever of these three methods one desires. (1.4.22)
(In the Sāmbapurāṇa:

A Brāhmaṇa who has fallen away from the Vedas and who feels fear regarding the expiations prescribed by the Vedas should, for the sake of gradually accomplishing Vedic mastery, take refuge with him [the teacher]. (1.423)
The Lord of Kamalā proclaimed the Pañcarātra, the Bhāgavata, and the Tantra known as Vaikhānasa for the sake of those who had fallen away from the Vedas. (1.424)
(From the *Ācārakusumāvalī*):
Born from the seed of Brahman, produced from the womb of a Brāhmaṇī, consecrated by all the purificatory rites prescribed in the Vedas, he is always pure. (1-425)
Having studied the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas, he was proficient in the meaning of the Vedānta;
he performed the ritual baths, twilight prayers, and libations as prescribed for the three periods of the day.
He who constantly recites the Gāyatrī a thousand times, performs the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, maintains the sacred fire, and is attentive in rites for the gods and the ancestors; || 1.427 ||
Fearing the loss of his own specific duties and fearing the transgression of time, he is fearless regarding penances and respectful toward virtuous conduct. (1.428)
"Averse to censurable conduct, tranquil, self-controlled, and clear-minded—one endowed with such characteristics as these is declared by the wise to be a Vaidika. (1.429)
Those other Brāhmaṇas who have fallen away from the Vedas are considered such;
for twice-born men who have fallen from the Vedas, a mixed path yields success in the Kali age.
The path of a twice-born person who follows the Vedic tradition must be that which is declared in the Vedas;
a twice-born person who has abandoned the path of the Śruti is called fallen.
In the *Nāradapañcarātra*:
"One should give the mantra to women and Śūdras, excluding the word *svāhā* and the *praṇava*.
(In the *Kulārṇava*)
For women and Śūdras, this mantra ending in "namas" brings happiness.
Having understood this, O Maheśānī, one may initiate even Cāṇḍālas.
(In the Yājñavalkyasaṃhitā:
A Śūdra and women should never recite Vedic mantras. (1-433)
The wise desire either a Śaiva mantra or a Vaiṣṇava mantra ending with "namas" (Meru-tantra).
Out of delusion or desire, a Śūdra [should not recite] a Purāṇa, a Saṃhitā, or a Smṛti (1.434).
A sinful Śūdra who intentionally listens [to it], and a twice-born man who causes it to be heard, both go to hell together with their ancestors. (1.435)
O Veda, those two are suffering in this very existence, whereas others [who act thus] become denizens of hell;
this is so for one who, out of pride in his authority or even his wealth, acts with arrogance.
But a Śūdra who should listen to the Veda becomes destitute of lineage and destitute of wealth;
if the Veda is heard or recited by a twice-born man out of ignorance, [the same penalty applies].
"By performing three *prājāpatya* penances, those two shall become pure.
These are the statements written in the *Tantracintāmaṇi*, as cited in the *Bhūtaśuddhi-tantra*:
"Through the utterance of the *praṇava*, through burnt offerings (*homa*), and through the worship of the *śālagrāma* stone... (1-438).
And by having sexual intercourse with a Brāhmaṇī woman, a Śūdra shall become a Caṇḍāla;
O beloved, the utterance of the Praṇava by a Śūdra is not approved in the Purāṇas.
Therefore, that which is declared in the Tantra must be performed with effort by one of the Śūdra caste;
through the power of the Mahāvidyās, a Śūdra indeed attains the status of a Vaiśya.
O Maheśānī, those of the Śūdra caste should receive [the mantra] beginning with the Praṇava.
This supreme reality of initiation is to be kept strictly secret, O Parameśvarī.
(Rudrayāmala) When the Bhairavī-tantra prevails, all castes are twice-born;
when the Bhairavī-tantra has ceased, all castes remain distinct. 1-442.
In this context, "the twice-born" refers to those born of two castes; "Kuṇḍas and others" refers to Nāgojibhaṭṭa. (In the *Sautrāmaṇitantra*:
"The seed-syllable *māyā* is for the Brāhmaṇa, and the seed-syllable *śrī* is remembered as being for the Kṣatriya."
The seed-syllable of desire (KĀM) belongs to the Vaiśya, while Vāgbhava (AIM) is said to belong to the Śūdra.
The mantra known as Paulastya is devoid of four seed-syllables;
for Brāhmaṇas it consists of four seed-syllables, while for Kṣatriyas it consists of three seed-syllables.
The Vaiśyas have two seed-syllables (*bīja*), while the Śūdras have only one.
(In the *Brahmapurāṇa*) it is stated that [the mantra] is preceded by the syllable *oṃ* and ends with a salutation (*namaskāra*).
One's own name is designated as the "mantra" for all sentient beings. || 1-445 ||
In the *Yāmala*:
"One should employ mantras that are favorable to the zodiacal signs and houses of one's own star;
having ascertained from the wheels what is favorable to the disciple, the Guru should bestow the mantra. (1.446)
Now, the consideration of the *cakra*: it has been said in the *Bhuvaneśvarī Tantra*:
"The purification of the *tāra* [syllable] belongs to the Vaiṣṇavas; the purification of the *kośa* belongs to Śiva;
the purification of the *rāśi* belongs to the Traipuras; and for Gopāla, the *akaḍama* is prescribed. (1.447)
The akaḍama [mantra] belongs to Gaṇeśa; the dantacakra [belongs] to Vāmana;
the dantacakra [belongs] to Varāha; and the kulākula [belongs] to Mahālakṣmī. (1.448)
Having thoroughly purified the defects in the wheel of names and likewise in the wheel of all beings, the reciter should grasp [the mantra] according to the word of the Guru. (1.449)
(From the Vārāhasaṃhitā:
"The wheel of stars, the wheel of zodiac signs, and likewise the wheel of names—if the mantra is endowed with qualities here, one need not examine any other wheel. (1.450)
Now I shall explain this investigation for the sake of accomplishing the wheels (*cakras*);
first, therefore, I shall describe the wheel of one's own *kula* and *akula*.
Since the *mātṛkā* has arisen from the cause of the five elements, therefore the phonemes consist of the elements through their division into five groups of five. (1.452)
Air, fire, earth, water, and space are the fifty letters in sequence;
five are short, five are long, ending with the bindu, and they arise from the junctions.

The consonants beginning with *ka* and ending with *ṣa*, *kṣa*, *la*, and *sa* are said to consist of five each; that is to say, there are ten letters in total. These correspond to air, fire, earth, water, and ether. Specifically: *a, ā, e, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, ya, ṣa* belong to air (*māruta*); *i, ī, r, kha, cha, ṭha, tha, pha, ra, kṣa* belong to fire (*āgneya*); *u, ū, o, ga, ja, ḍa, da, ba, la, la* belong to earth (*bhauma*).

(58) *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *au*, *gh*, *jha*, *ḍh*, *dh*, *bh*, *va*, and *sa* belong to the watery [element]. *ḷ*, *ḹ*, *aṃ*, *ṅ*, *ña*, *ṇ*, *na*, *ma*, *ś*, and *ha* belong to the ethereal [element]. The five short vowels are *a*, *i*, *u*, *ṛ*, and *ḷ*. The five long vowels are *ā*, *ī*, *ū*, *ṝ*, and *ḹ*. "Ending with the *bindu*" means that which has the *bindu* at its end; thus, it refers to *aṃ*. "Arisen from conjunction" refers to *e*, *ai*, *o*, and *au*.
Regarding those whose initial letter is their own name, a friend or one of the same family is best. (1–454)
For example:
the first syllable of the practitioner and likewise the first syllable of the mantra—if one should know them to have the same elemental deity, that indeed belongs to one's own family. (1-455)
"Friend" (*mitra*) means mutual friendship. As it is said in the *Dīpikā*:
"The earthly, the watery, and the friendly [are the allies] of the fiery; even for the fiery, the airy is [an ally].
Among the earthly syllables, the airy stands as their enemy. (1.456)
The fiery element is known as the enemy of water, while the luminous (taijasa) element is the enemy of water;
however, the ethereal (nābhasa) element is not in conflict with any of these.
A wise person should not bring together those things that are mutually contradictory;
thus has been described the Kula-Akula wheel, which fulfills all human goals.
Wind, fire, and earth.
Water and space.
i u e

Aṃ ka kha
ga gha ṅa

jha ña ṭa
ṭha ḍa ḍha
Not that,
not this.
da dha ṇa
pa pha ba (the three labial consonants)
Bhaṃaya

śa ṣa kṣa
The earth is indeed.
Thus ends the *Kulākula-cakra*. (p.
59) I shall now describe the *Akathaha* wheel: one should first draw a square;
in its center, one should place two lines, one directed eastward and the other directed northward. (1.459)
There, it should be square and provided with four compartments; then, one should draw two lines in the middle extending from east to west.
Then, one should draw two lines, long from north to south;
from that, the supreme wheel, consisting of sixteen squares, is produced.
The knower of mantras should write the letters from *a* to *kṣa* in this sequence:
in the directions [of the compass] corresponding to 2, 3, 11, 9, 2, 4, 12, and 10;
and in the elements corresponding to 6, 8, 16, 14, and 5.
O wise one, you should write the letters in their proper sequence within fifteen (15) squares, which are [calculated as] Pātāla (7), Pañcadaśa (15), Vahni (3), and Himāṃśu (13).
First, one should arrange the Siddhas and the others in four squares each, proceeding in a clockwise direction starting from the first letter of their respective names. (1.463)
The wise one should count [the beads] according to the sequence of *siddha*, *sādhya*, *susiddha*, and *ari*.
Among these, the *siddha* bestows success through recitation (*japa*), while the *sādhya* is accomplished through burnt offerings (*homa*) and other rites. (1.464)
A well-perfected (susiddha) enemy would devour the practitioner merely by being encountered;
those with accomplished syllables (siddhārṇa) should be known as kinsmen, while those to be accomplished (sādhya) are considered servants. (1.465)
Thus, those that are well-accomplished (*susiddha*) are nourishers, while those that are enemies are known as destroyers.
According to the *Piṅgalāmata*: "The accomplished (*siddha*) mantra succeeds in due time, whereas the one to be mastered (*sādhya*) succeeds through recitation and fire-offerings. (1.466)

One who is well-accomplished (*susiddha*) cuts the very roots of the enemy from the moment of seizing [the weapon]. (From the *Merutantra*) First, one should know that among the four squares, the *siddha* and the others are located in the intermediate directions. (1.467)

(p. 60) From the square corresponding to that position, one should again count according to the teacher’s instruction; the practitioner of mantra should then purify the *siddha* and other categories by means of the *siddha* and others—so it is traditionally taught in the *Piṅgalāmata*. (1.468)
One who is *siddha-siddha* attains success through recitation (*japa*); one who is *siddhi-sādhya* attains success through double that amount;
one who is *siddha-susiddha* attains success with half the recitation; but one who is *siddha-ari* destroys his kinsmen. (1.469)
A *sādhya* that is established is doubled; a *sādhya-sādhya* is useless;
a *sādhya-susiddha* is accomplished by half the recitation; and a *sādhya-ari* kills those born of one's lineage.
A *susiddha-siddha* mantra bestows the desired fruit from half the recitation;
a *susiddha-sādhya* mantra grants success through constant recitation, and not otherwise. (1.471)
That mantra which is "well-accomplished and accomplished" (susiddhasiddha) is one for which effort was exerted in previous births;
therefore, one should employ that mantra for the attainment of all siddhis.
A *susiddha* enemy especially destroys one's own family with certainty;
an *ari-siddha* kills one's son, while an *ari-sādhya* kills one's daughter. (1.473)
But when well-mastered, Aryari, the destroyer of the root, [protects] even one's wife;
thus spoke Uṅapa.
The *ākhada* scale has six notes (*ṣaḍja*, *ṛṣabha*, *gāndhāra*, *madhyama*, *pañcama*, *dhaivata*),
and the *ūcapha* scale has five notes (*oḍava*).
Ḷ jha ma au ḍha śa ḹ ñ ya
O straight one,
come hither.
The Ṛgveda is its pedestal.
Aṃnaṣa eṭara (p.
61): Now, the wheel of debtors and creditors (*ṛṇidhanicakra*). Regarding that, [the *Tantrarāja*] states the reason for the state of being a debtor or a creditor for both mantras and practitioners:
Due to the practice performed in a previous birth, this [person] brings about the non-attainment of the fruit from sin.
When evil has been destroyed, there is the attainment of the fruit upon the dissolution of the body in due time;
by the mere acquisition of the mantra, one becomes purified beforehand for the sake of spiritual accomplishment.
Having obtained perfected mantras from a guru, that practitioner who becomes a possessor of siddhis is always fortunate and worthy of worship; he shall attain the enjoyment of the mantra. (1.476)
That mantra should be known as his debtor, and its worship is the prerequisite;
therefore, the purification of that debt must be performed by everyone in every way. (1.477)
As it has been said in the *Sundarīrahasyavṛtti*:
"One should draw twelve lines extending from east to west in succession;
by this very sequence, eleven squares are produced here in order. (1.478)
In those [squares], the practitioner of mantra should write the letters according to the sequence beginning with the vowels:
two vowels each in five squares,
and the remaining vowels— six— in six squares, one by one.
Then one should write the letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *ha*, each letter individually within the eleven prosodic measures.
One should write the figures of the person to be defeated (*sādhya*) above and write the figures of the practitioner (*sādhaka*) below.

The figures of the *sādhya* are multiplied by fourteen (Indra), twenty-seven (constellations), two (eyes), twelve (Suns), fifteen (days of the waxing and waning moon), six (seasons), four (Vedas), three (fires), and eight (weapons).
Then, multiply the letters of the practitioner by eight, ten, one, seven, four, eight, three, seven, five, four, six, and three.
One should fill in the figures of the person to be proven (sādhya) and the figures of the prover (sādhaka) according to the number of houses.
Having determined the remainder after dividing the letters of both names by eight, nine, and seven, the greater remainder of the two shall be the debt or the wealth. (1-481)
If the mantra has an extra syllable, then the wise practitioner should recite it;
even if it is equal [in length], the reciter of the mantra should recite it, but he should not recite it if it is deficient.
In the *Merutantra*:
"The practitioner should be known as a debtor when the marks of the practitioner are fewer;
for as long as they remain deficient, he should perform that same number [of rites]. (1.483)
When these are known as *puraścaraṇa*, then there will be equanimity for him;
having performed the *puraścaryā* once again, he shall then become an achiever of his purpose.
(Sundarīrahasyavṛtti) But when the multiplication of the digits has been performed, whatever remainder clearly arises— that digit situated in the eleventh house, I shall declare here. (1-485)
The letters of the *sādhya* (the name to be accomplished) are indeed: six, six, six, fire (3), ocean (4), Vedas (4), ether (0), space (0), zero (0), and three fires (3).
[The letters of the *sādhaka* (the practitioner's name) are: two pairs (2, 2), five, ether (0), sky (0), joined with two (2), and the moon (1).
The letters of the practitioner are indeed [counted as] zero (vyoma), four oceans (abdhi), four Vedas (veda), and one moon (śaśin). || 1-486 ||

Having determined the remainder after subtracting nine from the letters of the name and eight from the letters of the question, the greater of the two remainders shall be the debt or the wealth. (1-486ef)

Thus ends the wheel of debtors and creditors (*ṛṇidhanicakra*).
Now, the wheel of classes (*vargacakra*). As it is said in the *Tantrarāja*:
"For the purpose of purifying the enemies of mantras, [the calculation] begins with the first letter of the name."
Having drawn eight squares, one should then write the eight groups [of consonants].
Birds, cats, lions, dogs, snakes, mice, and elephants, along with rams—these, in order, are associated with the groups of letters beginning with 'a' and ending with 'va'. (1.488)
There is enmity between the bird and the cat, and enmity between the cat and the bird;
there is enmity between the bird and the serpent, and hostility between the elephant and the lion. (1.489)

One should consider the enmity between the ram and the dog, as well as their friendship through reasoning; likewise, there is friendship between the serpent and the lion, and similarly between the ram and the mouse. (1.490)
And that which is to be known as other than worldly [reality] is understood through the application of conventional usage;
having thus understood this supreme machine, one should grasp the most excellent mantra. (1.491)
As it is said in the *Vārāhī-tantra*:
"Cats, dogs, and serpents shall have enmity toward birds;
the cat with the dog and the rat, and the lion always with the elephant. (1.492)
Of the dog with the crow and the owl, of the bird and the mouse, and of the serpent; of the mouse with the cat and the snake, and of the elephant together with the deer. (1.493)
There is enmity between the Garuḍa and the serpent, and likewise between the elephant and the lion.
A 16-pakṣī, ka 5.
And the cat [is] the lion.

The serpent,
the leaf,
the mouse.
The elephant is five;
the arrow is four.
"Aries" is the wheel of the classes (*vargacakra*).
Now, the wheel of the zodiac signs (*rāśicakra*) is likewise [described] in that same place:
Two lines are drawn extending from east to west; in their middle, two more are drawn according to the division between the south and Kubera (the north).
Then one should draw [lines] toward the northeast and the southwest, and toward fire (southeast) and wind (northwest); thereafter, one should write the syllables.

One should write down all the letters starting from Aries (Meṣa) in groups of four: ending with the Vedas (4), Agnis (3), Vahnis (3), pairs (2), Śravaṇas (2), the numberless (0), the five arrows (5), the five arrows (5), the five arrows (5), the arrows (5), and the four (4).
Then one should write the letters beginning with Śa, ending with Va, situated in the Kanyā (Virgo) sign.
(In the Vārāhī Tantra: The numbers four, three, three,
two, two, five, five, five, five, five, five, and four [are the syllables].
Having written the six vowels beginning with 'a' in the compartments starting from Aries, and having written them in the [compartments of] the young woman; || 1-496 ||
As the teachers have said:
"The letter *kṣa* should be together with the four beginning with *ya*, residing in Pisces (*mīna*)."
The first, the fifth, or the ninth from one's own sign is a kinsman;
the tenth, together with the second, from the sign becomes a servant; and the eleventh, the third, and the sixth are declared to be one's nourishers.
As for the mantra, it is said to be self-sustaining when its syllable count is eleven, three, or six.
If this mantra, measured by the syllables of the eighth year, should be recited, it would become its own slayer. || 1-497 ||

The twelve zodiac signs are: the Ascendant (1), Wealth (2), Brothers (3), Enemies (4), Children (5), Friends (6), Wife (7), Death (8), Dharma (9), Action (10), Gain (11), and Expenditure (12). (1-498)

In this zodiacal wheel, the fourth house is an enemy and not a friend; likewise, some maintain that the sixth house is neither a friend nor an enemy. Furthermore: for the reciter, auspicious planets situated in the sixth, eighth, or twelfth houses from one's own sign are to be avoided.
They reside in one, two, three, four, five, seven, ten, and eleven [spheres]. (1.499)
The Ascendant, Wealth, Brothers, Siblings, Children, Enemies, Wife, Death, Virtue, Action, Income, and Expenditure are the twelve zodiacal signs. (1–500)
One should indicate the auspicious or inauspicious fruit for these according to their names; the wise should count from one's own sign up to the mantra. (1–501)

The purity of the zodiac signs (rāśis) is to be understood; one should abandon the enemy sign, the eighth house, and the twelfth house. This is the instruction for it: draw two lines extending east-west and two lines extending north-south. Draw two lines from the northeast to the southwest corner and two lines from the southeast to the northwest corner. Thus, there are eight lines. In the resulting squares, one should write the fifty letters starting from Aries (Meṣa) according to the sequence to be described below.

Namely: a ā i ī in Aries; u ū ṛ in Taurus; ṝ ḷ ḹ in Gemini; e ai in Cancer; o au in Leo; aṃ aḥ śa ṣa sa ha in Virgo; ka kha ga gha ṅa in Libra; ca cha ja jha ña in Scorpio; ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha ṇa in Sagittarius; ta tha da dha na in Capricorn; pa pha ba bha ma in Aquarius; ya ra la va kṣa in Pisces. (p. 66)

And here are the four: ta, tha, da, dha, na (10); and the five: o, au (5).

Ca, cha, ja, jha, ña— 8;
thus is the wheel of the zodiac signs.
Now, regarding the circle of the lunar mansions (nakṣatracakra) in that very place: ten lines extending from east to west should be drawn with care. (1-502)
Four lines should be drawn, long from north to south, joined by three sets of nine [lines], resulting in twenty-seven squares. (1–503)
And one should act in such a way that [the mantra] is produced; one should write the syllables within them.
Two, one, three, four, one, earth (one), arms (two), moon (one), pair (two), pair (two), earth (one), pair (two), fortnights (two), non-pairs (two), one, two,
three, one, three, earth (one), moon (one), moon (one), two, one, fortnights (two), fire (three), and Vedas (four)—
these syllables are declared here in the order beginning with Aśvinī; for the remaining asterisms, there are the bindu and the visarga.
Then, while reciting, one should calculate the constellations and elemental spirits according to the sequence of birth and prosperity.
Birth, prosperity, adversity, security, enemy, achiever, and death;
friend, great friend, and neutral—these are indeed the nine [houses], occurring through three repetitions. (1.505)
One should calculate the result according to that very sequence and in accordance with the name:
there will be loss at the birth asterism, and prosperity during prosperity. (1-506)
In the *vipattāra* [lunar mansion], there will be misfortune; in the *kṣema*, one should predict auspiciousness.
In the *pratyari*, there will be an increase of enemies; in the *sādhaka*, it brings about the attainment of success. (1-507)
In the enemy constellations, harm is to be known; in the friendly constellations, there is the increase of friends;
and in the exceedingly friendly ones, there will be happiness—this is remembered as the Tārācakra.
O Dear One, when the zodiac signs are unknown, one should take the first letter of one's own name and so forth; [then] the *vipatbādha* and the *pratyari* [signs] must be avoided by the wise. (1-509)
"From the first syllable of the mantra up to the final letter, they are to be counted by the wise"—
this refers to cases where the *rāśi* (astrological sign) and other such factors are unknown.
And so it is said:
For one whose birth star (janmarkṣa) is manifest, the wise [astrologer] should calculate from that birth star.
According to the Piṅgalāmata, for one whose birth star has been lost, the wise man [should calculate] from the natal star:
fire (3), moon (1), qualities (3), Vedas (4), form (1), form (1), Yama (2), and moon (1). (1–511)
Prāyaṃ, prāyaṃ, and likewise candra; triprāya, soma, and yugmaka;
guṇa, eka, tri, and guṇasoma; and that which is called yama, namely soma, yu, gu, and guṇa.
One should assign the Vedas (4) to the limbs, as well as their respective numbers and the syllables;
and the six (rasa), eight (aṣṭa), nine (nava), and auspicious (bhadra) [squares] according to the division of pairs and pairs.
The other [results] are not auspicious; this should be understood by those skilled in mantras, beginning from one's birth asterism and ending with the asterism of the mantra. (1.514)

The deity of Anurādhā is Ta-tha-da.

The Rākṣasa Na-pa-pha-mūla.

The god Maśravaṇa.

Śatabhiṣā is Rākṣasa.
The human being under the constellation Pūrvabhādrapadā is one who possesses self-control.
The human being [born under] the asterism Uttarabhādrapadā is one who possesses the syllables ṣa, sa, ha, and u.
Lakṣa Aṃ Aḥ,
the deity Revatī.
Thus ends the wheel of constellations (*nakṣatracakra*).
Now, the wheel of groups (*gaṇacakra*) (in that same place):
the three [constellations] beginning with Aśvinī and ending with Uttaraphalgunī, followed by Bharaṇī, Ārdrā, and Rohiṇī.
The wise call these the lunar mansions (nakṣatras) belonging to human beings.
Jyeṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣaj, Mūla, Dhaniṣṭhā, Āśleṣā, Kṛttikā, Citrā, Maghā, and Viśākhā—these stars have the Rākṣasas as their presiding deities. (1.516)
Aśvinī, Revatī, Puṣya, Svātī, Hastā, Punarvasu,
Anurādhā, Mṛgaśiras, and Śravaṇā are the asterisms presided over by deities.
Furthermore, in the Jyotiḥśāstra: "De, mā, rā, mā, de, mā, de, de, rā, rā, mā, ma, de, rā, da, rā, de, rā, rā, ma, ma, de, rā, rā, mā, mā, de—these are the groups of asterisms. (1-518)
As it has been said in the *Dīpikā*:
"The hands, Svātī, Mṛga, Aśvinī, Puṣya, Anurādhā, Āditya, Ārdrā, Rohiṇī, the three Uttarās, and Bharaṇī— these are the three sets of Pūrvā constellations."

Jyeṣṭhā, Āśleṣā, Viśākhā, Mūla, Varuṇa (Śatabhiṣaj), the Vasus (Pūrvābhādrapadā), Agni (Kṛttikā), Citrā, and Maghā—these, in their respective order, are declared by the sages to be the gods, humans, and rākṣasas. (1.519)
Thus ends the section on the *gaṇacakra*. Now, regarding the *akaḍamacakra*, it is said in that very same place:
"I shall describe the well-known wheel called *akaḍama*, which bestows all accomplishments."
When receiving mantras, the practitioner of mantra should examine them in every respect.
The wise mantra-practitioner should draw the zodiacal wheel (rāśicakra), writing the letters excluding the neuter ones;
the intelligent one should write them in order from the letter 'a' to the letter 'kṣa'. (1.521)

Just as the syllables *a*, *ka*, *ḍa*, and *ma* arise sequentially in the first square, one should write them out and count them starting from the first letter of the name of the person reciting. (1-522)
Again and again, according to the sequence of *siddha*, *sādhya*, *susiddha*, and *ari*;
and furthermore:
from the letter *a* to the letter *kṣa*, following the sequence on the right side.
The wise practitioner of mantra should count in order from Aries (Meṣa) to Pisces (Mīna), according to the first syllable of the mantra of the reciter's own name. (1.524)

Again and again, according to the sequence of *siddha*, *sādhya*, *susiddha*, and *ari*, that which is already accomplished (*siddha*) becomes perfected in time; as for that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), it may or may not be perfected.
When fully perfected, the enemy cuts off one's very root from the moment of grasping it:
*aḥ ṭha bhajñaḥ*.
Aṃ ṭabakṣa a kaḍama.
The mouse has been killed.
O man,
the fruit of the auñja tree is like a sword-blade.
O Jha,
come here, O people!
The sixteenth is the one who has transcended all.
Thus ends the Akadamacakra.
Now, the Uditacakra. As it is said in the *Sundarīrahasyavṛtti*:
"I shall explain in brief the great cakra known as Uditā. (1.526)
One should draw a six-cornered wheel with equal lines, beautiful to behold;
one should inscribe the letters from 'a' to 'kṣa' in order, starting from the east.
When [the moon] has risen, prosperity is declared; in the second [watch], there is the destruction of prosperity;
in the third, one should know there is stability; and in the fourth, the ruin of kinsmen. (1-528)
In the fifth [syllable], one becomes of a doubting nature; in the sixth, a destroyer of all.
This continues from the first syllable of the name until the appearance of the first syllable of the mantra. (1.529)
71) Thus ends the described wheel.
Now follows the six-pada mātṛkā wheel (in the Merutantra).
As for the mantra that consists of the seed-syllable, therein the six-limbed Mātṛkā should be known; one should fashion there a beautiful six-petalled lotus. (1.530)
Therein, one should place the letters of the Mātṛkā, excluding the *kūṭas* and the neuter (*ṣaṇḍha*) vowels;
one should then investigate starting from whichever letter is the first syllable of one's own name. (1.531)
Prosperity, poverty, fortitude, conflict with kinsmen, and danger—these result from the sequence of total destruction according to the grid of the first letter of one's name. (1-532)
The *kūṭa* is the letter *śa*; the neuter vowels are the four beginning with *ṛ*. (p.
72) From the first wave of the *Puraścaryārṇava*.
A, E, Ka, Cha, Ḍa, Dha, Ma, Ṣa, Ū, AḤ, Ca, Ṭha, Da, Bha, Śa, Ā, Ai, Kha, Ja, Ḍha, Na, Ya, Sa.
va ṅa ba tha ṭa aṃ u o i ṇapa gajha raha la pha gha ñata au lakṣa ī

Thus ends the six-pada *mātṛkācakra* (according to the *Vārāhītantra*). In the *Varāha* [tantra] there is the purification of the grid (*koṣṭhaśuddhi*), and in the *Mahālakṣmī* [tantra] there is the *kulākula*.
The wheel of names and so forth belongs to all, and likewise the wheel of the elements.
For the Vaiṣṇavas, there is purification by the stars (tārā); for Śiva, purification by the square (koṣṭha);
for the Traipura, purification by the zodiac signs (rāśi); and for Gopāla, the "akaḍama" is prescribed. || 1-534 ||
The *Yāmala* states an exception:
"If mantras do not shine forth by any means through [critical] examination, then one should adopt an excellent mantra by relying on [the authority of] prohibition. (1.535)
One should never purify the mantras of Nṛsiṃha, Arka, and Varāha, nor the Praṇava of the temples, nor the eternal Haṃsa-mantras, nor those that are already perfected (siddha) and so forth.
And likewise, in the *Kālikā Purāṇa*:

"In the case of Nṛsiṃha, Arka, and Varāha, as well as for the temples and the Praṇava, and for single-syllable and two-syllable [mantras] such as Siddha and the others, one should not perform purification at all. (1.537)
(In the Agni Purāṇa:
"In the case of the eight-syllabled Haṃsa mantra, as well as the five-syllabled one, and of neuter mantras, one need not examine the *siddha* and other [categories]. (1.538)
The neuter [mantras] end in *namaḥ*.
As it has been said in the *Śāradā*:
"All mantras were born from the various phonemes of the Mātṛkā."
The classes of mantra are of two kinds, distinguished by the division between mantra and vidyā. || 1-539 ||
Mantras are to be known as male deities, and Vidyās are recorded as female deities;
all mantras are declared to possess the nature of male, female, and neuter.
Mantras for males should end in *hūṃ* and *phaṭ*; those for females are considered to end in *svāhā*; and those for neuters should end in *namaḥ*. Thus, mantras are said to be of three kinds. (1.541)
(From the Sanatkumāra-saṃhitā):
O Nārada, the categories of *siddha*, *sādhya*, *susiddha*, and *ari* are not to be recognized in the cowherds, because they are self-luminous by their very nature. (1.542)
(In the *Gaṇeśavimarṣiṇī*):

In the case of a single-syllable mantra, a *kūṭa*, a *mālāmantra*, or a three-seed mantra; or one obtained in a dream, or given by a woman—one should not examine it for [the presence of] *siddha* and other [categories]. (1.543)

Regarding the characteristics of the *mālāmantra*, it is stated in the *Nārāyaṇī Tantra*: "Mantras consisting of more than twenty syllables are proclaimed as *mālāmantras*. [Also] in the *Devīpurāṇa*:
And in Kālikā, Tārā, Kullukā, and Trikūṭaka. || 1-544 ||
Likewise, [this applies] to the single-syllable *kūṭa* mantra, as well as to the five-syllable mantra of Śiva,
to the six-syllable mantra of that very [deity], or even to the eight-syllable [mantra] of Viṣṇu.
In the twelve-syllable mantra of Viṣṇu, in the Rāma-mantra, and in the Tāraka; in the Vaiṣṇava mantras, in the Bhairavī, and in the excellent Sundarī-mantra.
In the *Sārasvata* and the *Bālā*, one should not purify the *siddha* and other [categories] at all.
(From the *Gautamīya*) Among all the classes of mantras, the Vaiṣṇava is said to be the most excellent. (1.547)
Among all Vaiṣṇava mantras, the mantras of Kṛṣṇa yield the greatest fruits;
this ten-syllable mantra, in particular, is perfected through mere recitation.
Initiation for a woman is declared auspicious, and that of a mother is said to be eight times more efficacious; furthermore, there is no doubt regarding a mantra obtained in a dream. (1.549)
In the *Yoginītantra*,
in the *Gāruḍa* and other solar tantras, in the Vaiṣṇava, Buddhist, and Jaina traditions,
and in the great mantras and *kūṭas*, there is no purification of the *siddhas* and so forth. (1.550)

In this highly esteemed confluence of rivers of excellent compositions, which abounds in streams of nectar variegated by the wonderful diversity of words that purify all beings through their marvelous majesty,
there has arisen a lofty wave, radiant with the luster of a multitude of pearls made manifest by sound reasoning.
The first [chapter] shines forth in the *Puraścaryārṇava* composed by the illustrious Naradeva.

Thus ends the first wave, titled "An Examination of the Cakras," preceded by the determination of the deities and the conduct of the six Āmnāyas, in the *Puraścaryārṇava* composed by the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja Pratāpasiṃha Sāh.
Now follows the determination of the time for initiation (*dīkṣā*).
Regarding that, first is the fruit of the months. As it is said in the *Yāmala*:
In Vaiśākha, initiation from Śiva bestows abundant prosperity;
in Jyeṣṭha, it brings death; and in Āṣāḍha, it grants happiness and wealth.
In Śrāvaṇa there shall be the acquisition of jewels; in Bhādra it is considered to bestow suffering;
in Āśvina there shall be success in all things; and in Kārtika it grants the attainment of knowledge.
In Mārgaśīrṣa it is the path of auspicious deeds; in Pauṣa it destroys ignorance;
in Māgha it increases intelligence; and in Phālguna it brings everything under one's control.
One should avoid the intercalary month (*malamāsa*), which causes affliction, during the month of Caitra.
(In the *Siddhāntaśekhara*):
Initiation (*dīkṣā*) during the autumn season and in Vaiśākha bestows the most excellent fruit. (2–4)
Initiation in the months of Phālguna, Mārgaśīrṣa, and Jyeṣṭha is considered middling;
that in Āṣāḍha and the month of Māgha is proclaimed as the lowest.
The months of Caitra, Pauṣa, and Bhādrapada are indeed censured; however, even Caitra is recommended for initiation into the Gopāla mantra. As it was stated by Gautama:
"The commencement of the mantra in the month of Caitra bestows all human goals. (2-6)
In Vaiśākha there will be the acquisition of jewels; in Jyeṣṭha, however, death is certain.
In Āṣāḍha there will be the loss of kinsmen, while in Śrāvaṇa one shall have a full lifespan.
In Bhādrapada there would be the destruction of progeny; in Āśvina, a collection of jewels;
in Kārttika, there would be the accomplishment of mantras; and it would be the same in Mārgaśīrṣa.
In Pauṣa there will be affliction from enemies; in Māgha, there is an increase in intelligence;
in Phālguna, all desires shall be fulfilled; one should avoid the intercalary month (mala-māsa).

(p. 76) Now, the fruit of the lunar fortnights (*pakṣaphala*). As it is said in the *Rudrayāmala*: "Initiation (*dīkṣā*) is auspicious during the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*), and also during the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*) up until the fifth day.
However, the knower of mantras (*mantravittama*) should not perform a vow (*vrata*) or initiation when the moon is waning. (2.10)
From the eighth day of the dark fortnight until the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, the moon is waning.

Now, the results according to the lunar days (*tithi*): it is stated in the *Yāmala*: "An initiation (*dīkṣā*) performed on the first lunar day (*pratipad*) is considered to cause the destruction of knowledge."
On the second [day] knowledge shall arise; on the third day one shall become happy. || 2-11 ||
On the fourth day there will be loss of wealth; on the fifth, an increase in intelligence;
on the sixth, a decline in knowledge; and on the seventh day, one obtains happiness.
On the eighth day there would be loss of intellect; on the ninth, the decay of the body;
on the tenth, royal fortune; and on the eleventh, one becomes pure.
On the twelfth day there shall be all success; on the thirteenth day, poverty;
on the fourteenth day, birth as an animal; and at the end of the month, one becomes a worm.

At the end of a lunar fortnight, all success shall be attained; one should avoid Vedic recitation during these times, as well as when there is thunder at twilight, an earthquake, or the falling of meteors.
The practitioner of mantra should avoid [certain foods] for three nights; he should also avoid those things prescribed in the Vedas.
(From the *Tattvasārasaṃhitā*):
Having carefully considered each respective lunar day (*tithi*), one should initiate there those who are devoted to that [deity]. 2-16.
The full moon day is declared for Brahmā; the twelfth day for the Wielder of the Discus (Viṣṇu);
the fourteenth day is declared for Śiva; and the thirteenth day is said to be for Vāc.
The second is said to belong to Śrī, the third to Pārvatī,
the fourth to Gaṇanātha, and the seventh is said to belong to Bhānu.

Among the regular paths [of time], for Pārvatī, the eighth and fourteenth days are auspicious; furthermore, since it is stated that "the end of the month and the end of the fortnight" are [auspicious], the end of the month refers to the day following the solar transit (*saṃkrānti*), and the end of the fortnight refers to the full moon and new moon days. As it is said in the *Gautamīya* (p. 77):
"Initiation is auspicious in the solar month, not in the lunar nor the sidereal. (2.19)

According to this statement, the end of the month should be understood as the end of the solar month (*sauramāsa*). Now, the results for the days of the week: on Sunday there will be wealth; on Monday, it is said, there will be peace.
On Tuesday, it destroys longevity; therefore, one should avoid initiation on that day.
Under Mercury one attains beauty; under Jupiter, there will be knowledge;
under Venus, one attains good fortune; and under Saturn, there is loss of fame. (2-21)
Now, the results of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*). As it is said in the *Tripurārṇava*:
"Under Aśvinī one attains happiness; under Bharaṇī death is certain;
under Kṛttikā one becomes miserable; under Rohiṇī one becomes a master of speech. (2.22)
In Mṛgaśīrṣa there is the attainment of happiness; in Ārdrā, the loss of kinsmen;
in Punarvasu, one becomes wealthy; and in Puṣya, the destruction of enemies. (2.23)
In Āśleṣā there may be death; in Maghā, liberation from suffering;
and in Pūrvaphālgunī, one attains beauty—of this there is no doubt. (2-24)
Knowledge shall prevail under Uttaraphalgunī and one becomes powerful under Hastā;
there shall be attainment of knowledge under Citrā, and the destruction of enemies under Svātī. (2.25)
In Viśākhā there will be happiness; Anurādhā bestows intelligence;
in Jyeṣṭhā there may be loss of sons; and in Mūlā there is the increase of fame. (2-26)
Pūrvāṣāḍhā and Uttarāṣāḍhā bring fame;
under Śravaṇā one becomes miserable, and under Dhaniṣṭhā there is poverty. (2.27)
Intellect shall arise under Śatabhiṣā; one shall become happy under Pūrvabhādrapadā;
there shall be happiness under Uttarabhādrapadā; and under Revatī, there is the increase of fame. (2-28)
(In the *Ratnāvalī*):
The first lunar day (*pratipad*) with Pūrvāṣāḍhā, and likewise the fifth with Kṛttikā;
on the sixth, Pūrvabhādrapadā, and likewise the tenth with Rohiṇī. (2-29)
The twelfth lunar day with the asterism Āśleṣā, and the thirteenth with the asterism Punarvasu—
these are known as "asterism-deprived" (nakṣatraluptā), and they bring destruction even to the gods.
Now, the results of the ascendant (*lagnaphala*) [from the *Rājamārtaṇḍa*]: "If initiation (*dīkṣā*) takes place when Jupiter, the Sun, or Venus are not in their proper positions, it causes poverty;
however, on an auspicious day and at an auspicious ascendant, initiation bestows sovereignty. (2-31)
(In the Rudrayāmala:
The Guru should always bestow initiation on a day when the moon and the stars are favorable, during the zodiac signs of Taurus, Leo, Virgo, Sagittarius, or Pisces. (2–32)
In the *Merutantra*:
"For the Vāmins, there is always suffering and always loss; for the Yavanas, there is auspiciousness in the sign of Gemini, and many kinds of auspiciousness are obstructed. (2-33)
(In the *Smṛtisaṃhitā*):
A fixed ascendant is prescribed for the Viṣṇu-mantras, while a movable one is remembered for the Śiva-mantras;
an ascendant situated in a dual nature is commended for the Śakti-mantras. (2–34)
In the *Gautamīya* and the *Saubhāgyaratnākara*:

"Malesfic planets situated in the third, sixth, and eleventh houses, and benefics situated in the angles (kendras), the trine (trikona), and the tenth house, are declared auspicious for initiation; however, those situated in the eighth house cause total destruction. (2-35)
If the ascendant is fixed (*sthira*), initiation is auspicious; if it is dual-natured (*dvisvabhāva*), it is middling.
Those who desire what is auspicious should never perform initiation when the ascendant is movable (*cara*). (2-36)
The Moon is auspicious when situated in the third, eleventh, sixth, or tenth house.
Now, regarding the results of the yogas (*Merutantra*):
for the yogas beginning with Viṣkambha, the result shall correspond to their respective names. (2–37)
The fruit of the yogas beginning with Ānanda is everywhere complete;
initiation on the days of Manu and the other [Yuga-beginnings] bestows all prosperity. (2.38)
And these have been stated [in the Muhūrtacintāmaṇi]:
"In Madhu (Caitra), the lunar days and the sun [are the first]; in Ūrja (Kārttika), three lunar days; in Śuci (Jyeṣṭha), ten lunar days;
in Jyeṣṭha and the last [month, Māgha], one lunar day; in Īṣa (Mārgaśīrṣa), nine; in Tapas (Phālguna), seven; in Sahasya (Pauṣa), eleven."

In the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, on the eighth day, is the Amāvāsyā of Nabhas; in the dark fortnight of Nabhas, on the first day, is the Yugādi; in the dark fortnights of Vaiśākha and Jyeṣṭha, they are respectively Gaurī and Agnī; and in the dark fortnights of Bhādrapada and Māgha, they are Madana and Darśa. (2-39)
In the *Agnipurāṇa*:
"On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, the Kṛta age departed;
on the third day of the dark fortnight of Vaiśākha, the Dvāpara age [departed]. (2.40)

On the new moon day of the month of Māgha, and on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of Nabhasya, as well as on the fourteenth day [of the dark fortnight], these should be known as the beginnings of the Manvantaras during the Kali age. (2.41)
(In the Yoginītantra:
At the transit of the sun and likewise during a solar eclipse, one should never consider any [astrological factor] such as the ascendant (*lagna*) at that time. (2.42)

Especially on the Great Eighth day, for the sake of attaining dharma, kāma, and artha; [and] at the equinoxes, at the two solstices, at the transition of the sun, and during the festival of Madana— (from the *Bṛhacchrīkrama*)— 2.43.
Initiation performed on a Guru-parva day indeed bestows auspicious results.
Regarding the Guru-parvas, the Bhuvaneśvarī Tantra states:
"The sixth [tithi] in the month of Bhādrapada, and the thirteenth of the dark fortnight in the month of Īṣa. (2-44)
The ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, the third of Mārgaśīrṣa, the ninth of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa, and likewise the fourth of Māgha. (2–45)
The ninth day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, Kāmatrayodaśī in Caitra,
Akṣayā in Vaiśākha, and likewise Daśaharā in Jyeṣṭha.
The fifth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha and the fifth day of the dark fortnight of Śrāvaṇa—these, the wise declare, are the meritorious festivals of the Guru. (2.47)
(In the *Sārasaṃgraha*):
The fifth, eleventh, seventh, thirteenth, and especially the tenth and twelfth days of the bright fortnight [are auspicious]. (2.48)
The third lunar day is prescribed as obligatory, while the sixth is censured in all cases.
In the Viṣṇuyāmala: "Beginning from the day of the Goddess's awakening (Kārttika śukla pratipadā) until the ninth lunar day... (Viṣṇuyāmala 2.49).
(In the *Ratnāvalī*):
Yoga, Prīti, Āpuṣman, Saubhāgya, Śobhana, Śubha, Sukarman, Dhṛti, Vṛddhi, Dhruva, Siddhi, and Harṣaṇa. (2-50)
Varīyas, Śiva, Siddha, Brahmā, and Indra are the sixteen [deities].
Now follows the determination of the Karaṇas (according to the *Gautamīya-tantra*): they declare the Karaṇas to be auspicious, especially for initiation (*dīkṣā*). (2.51)
One should especially avoid Śakuni and the other [yogas], as well as Viṣṭi.
Now, the results of the Sun's zodiac signs (according to the *Sārasaṃgraha*):
Aries is a bestower of wealth and grain when one begins the practice of mantras and so forth. (2–52)
In Taurus one meets death; in Gemini there is the loss of offspring;
in Cancer there shall be success in all things; and in Leo there is an increase in intelligence. (2-53)
In Virgo, Lakṣmī is eternally bestowing [wealth]; in Libra, all perfections are attained;
in Scorpio, there shall be perfection in all things; in Sagittarius, there is the destruction of knowledge. (2.54)
Capricorn is said to bestow sons, Aquarius grants the abundance of wealth, and Pisces always brings suffering; such, O beloved, is the fruit of the zodiac signs.
(In the Gārgya-saṃhitā:
Even during censured months, initiation is declared to be auspicious during an eclipse;
there is nothing on earth equal to the time of a solar eclipse. (2.56)
In that regard, whatever action is performed therein shall yield infinite fruit.
O Maheśānī, these alone are proclaimed as the ten Vidyās. (2.57)
In this [practice], there is no dependence on perfected beings (siddhas) and the like, nor is there any deliberation regarding constellations and such;
there is no purification of time and so forth, and indeed no defect regarding the object to be accomplished (sādhya) and the like. (2.58)
(In the *Samayātantra*):
During the solstices and the equinoxes, as well as on the anniversaries of the Yugas, during eclipses, and at great sacred sites, there is no consideration of time. (2.59)
Near a *tulasī* plant, at the root of a *bilva* tree, likewise at the foot of a *dhātrī* tree, in the presence of the Anādi-deva, in a great sacred field (*mahākṣetra*), or in a cowshed; || 2-60 ||
On the day of the worship of the Goddess, there is no fixed determination regarding the time.
(In the *Yāmala*):
On the anniversaries of the Manus and the anniversaries of the Yugas, initiation bestows all prosperity. (2.61)

And these [Manvādi days] have been described in the Muhūrtacintāmaṇi: three lunar days in the month of Madhu; two lunar days in Ūrja and Śuci; ten lunar days in Jyeṣṭha; one lunar day in Āśvina; nine in Tapas; and eleven in Māgha.
In the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, the eighth day (Aṣṭamī) is the Agni-yuga; in the dark fortnight of Nabhas (Śrāvaṇa), it is the Yuga-ādi;
in the dark fortnights of Bhādrapada and Vaiśākha, they are the Go-agni and Madana-darśa respectively.
(In the Agni Purāṇa:
On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, the Kṛta age emerged;
on the third day of Vaiśākha, the Tretā and Dvāpara ages [emerged]. (2.63)

On the new moon day of the month of Māgha, and on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of Nabhasya, as well as on the fourteenth day [of the dark fortnight], these should be known as the beginnings of the Manvantaras. (2.64)
(In the Yoginītantra):
At the transit of the sun and likewise during a solar eclipse, one should never at all consider such things as the ascendant or other astrological factors. (2.65)

Especially on the Mahāṣṭamī for the sake of accomplishing dharma, kāma, and artha; (in the *Bṛhacchrīkrama*) at the equinoxes, at the two solstices, at the transits of the sun, and during the festival of Madana. (2.66)
Furthermore, initiation performed on a Guru-parva day bestows auspicious results.
Regarding the Guru-parvas, the Bhuvaneśvarī Tantra states:
"The sixth [lunar day] in the month of Bhādrapada, and the thirteenth of the dark fortnight in the month of Īṣa (Kārttika). (2-67)
The ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, the third of Mārgaśīrṣa, the ninth of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa, and the fourth of Māgha. (2–68)
The ninth day of the bright fortnight in Phālguna, the Kāma-trayodaśī in Caitra,
the Akṣayā in Vaiśākha, and likewise the Daśaharā in Jyeṣṭha.
The fifth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha and the fifth day of the dark fortnight of Śrāvaṇa— these wise men declare to be meritorious festivals of the Guru.
(In the *Sārasaṃgraha*):
The fifth and eleventh days of the bright fortnight, as well as the seventh, thirteenth, tenth, and especially the twelfth, [are auspicious]. (2.71)
The third lunar day is prescribed as obligatory, while the sixth is censured in all cases.
In the Viṣṇuyāmala:
"Beginning from the day of the Goddess's awakening (Kārttika śukla pratipadā) until the ninth lunar day... (2.72).
The wise have performed initiation in these [images], which bestows all desired fruits;
and for the awakening of Durgā, one need not examine whether the time is auspicious or inauspicious. (2.73)
Wherein the eighth lunar day is called Aśoka and the ninth likewise Rāma; (according to the Smṛtisaṃhitā), Vyatīpāta and Vaidhṛti, as well as the Dīkṣā yogas, bring auspiciousness. (2–74)
As it is said in the *Rājamārtaṇḍa*:
"If the new moon day (amāvāsyā) occurs on a Sunday under the asterisms of Śravaṇā, Aśvinī, Dhaniṣṭhā, Ārdrā, Āśleṣā, or Abhijit, that is called Vyatīpāta. (2.75)

(83) Āśleṣā is the deity of the serpents. [It is located] at the head in the first quarter. If Mars and Saturn should be in Virgo or Aries, and it is a Saturday on the seventh lunar day (saptamī) with the Sun in Aquarius, that is the Tāmasī [Yoga]. (2.76)
That which is equal to a hundred solar eclipses is called *vyatīpāta*.
*Tāmasī* means black (*kṛṣṇā*). (In the *Mahogratārākalpa*): On the eighth day of the dark fortnight, at an auspicious *lagna* and at a favorable moment. (2–77)
In the bright fortnight of Pūrvabhādrapadā, when well-conjoined with the Maitra asterism (Anurādhā), or likewise under Anurādhā or Revatī, it is highly commended. (2.78)
One should know the auspicious time for the reception of the mantra;
this is especially so in the month of Āśvina and particularly in Kārttika.
According to the Mahācīna-krama, there is no fault in the Nīlaśārada [period] (as stated in the Śaiva Āgama):
the morning time bestows merit, while the period of union bestows sovereignty. (2-80)
At midday there shall be all success; the afternoon would be mediocre; however, the night is forbidden for the imparting of mantras by the best of teachers.
(Kriyākāṇḍaśekhara) Furthermore, for one desiring liberation, no restriction regarding time and so forth is prescribed;
all those [actions] are censurable, yet they are praised for the sake of liberation. (2.82)
All the stars, all the planets, all the lunar mansions, and all the zodiac signs—on that day, when the Guru is satisfied, they all bring about auspiciousness. (2.83)
When the guru is satisfied therein, all the deities are satisfied;
whenever there is a desire, then initiation [is granted] in accordance with the command of the guru.
In that matter, there is no restriction of time, nor likewise any restriction of place;
one should satisfy the Guru with devotion, and thus one will become [perfected] by oneself. (2.85)
(p. 84) Now follows the determination of the locations for initiation (*dīkṣā*). As it is stated in the *Pūrṇapaddhati*:
"In a cow-pen, in the house of the Guru, in a temple, in a forest, in a sacred field (*puṇyakṣetra*), likewise in a garden, on a riverbank, or in one’s own hermitage. (2.86)
Whatever is performed near the Dhātrī and Bilva trees, on a mountain peak, in caves,
or at the Gaṅgā, all that becomes multiplied ten million-fold.
(In the *Yāmala*):
At a sacred pilgrimage site, at Kurukṣetra, at the four seats of the Goddess (*devīpīṭha*), at Prayāga, on Śrīgiri, and at Kāśī, one need not distinguish between the proper and improper time. (2.88)
(In the Yoginītantra:
At Gayā, in the field of Bhāskara, at Virajā, on Mount Candra, at Catvara, at Mataṅga, and likewise at the hermitages of Kanyā. (2.89)
Therefore, O Pārvatī, one should not receive initiation at these sacred sites (*tīrthas*).
Now, regarding specific mantras, the curses of specific deities have been declared in the *Merutantra*: "In former times, the gods were deluded by the gods [of old] through wine and nectar. (2-90)
Then, at that time, the Blessed One Madhusūdana said: "Tell me, who among you is worthy of worship? Who is the most excellent? Let that be declared to me. (2.91)
Then the gods, becoming intoxicated, each said, "I am the best!
But the Blessed One, smiling slightly, deluded them by means of his own *māyā*.
Thus he spoke, whose word is capable both of cursing and of favoring;
that very deity is the most excellent here, whether he be the first or even the last.
Having heard these words of Viṣṇu, they cursed one another;
therefore, O Goddess, the release from the curse was achieved through consecrations by means of the forms of mantras.
"But without the release from the curse, what person could attain perfection?
The Illustrious Goddess said:
"By whom and how was the curse given? And what is the fruit when it is cursed and when it is recited? (2.95)
"Tell me, how can there be freedom from curses for them, and how may they attain accomplishment?
Śrī Śiva said:
"He in whose [mantra] the letter *vāyu* (ya) is established at the beginning, middle, and end... (2.96)
Where the four and so forth, as well as the single seed-syllable, are joined together in manifold ways—by whom has that mantra been overcome, or has it been severed with the sword? (2.97)
By reciting that [mantra] with Kārttikeya, his desires are fulfilled;
at the beginning, middle, or end, there should be a pair of earth-seeds (laṃ).
At first, the Vajrin was twofold; in the middle, he was threefold; and thereafter, he was twofold again.
Bound by the curse of Śukra, they were deprived of both enjoyment and liberation.
The mantra has arisen; both the left and right paths have been practiced, yet not a single seed-syllable such as *hrīḥ*, *moḥ*, *phreṃ*, *śrīḥ*, or *ṣve* is seen therein. (2-100)
Or that mantra may consist of the syllable *hūṃ*, rendered powerless by the gods; if such a mantra is recited, it destroys the efficacy of the practitioner. (2.101)
For one who is powerless and left-handed, death occurs; there is no doubt about this.
Neither at the beginning is *hrīṃ* seen, nor in the middle *klīṃ*, nor indeed at the end is *kroṃ* seen. (2-102)
This mantra has become turned away due to the curse of the Sun;
if a practitioner of mantra resorts to one that is turned away, the deity will likewise be turned away. (2.103)
Even if a task is successfully accomplished through fate, the world may turn its back on it;
for neither "I" nor "we" is seen at the beginning, the end, or in the middle. (2.104)
Those mantras have been rendered deaf by the curse of the preceptor of the gods;
when a mantra is recited that has been deafened, forgetfulness of it arises for him. (2.105)
One will surely become deaf by what Mahākāla has spoken.
The letter *ha* is the seed-syllable of the Sun, while *sa* is remembered as the seed-syllable of the Moon. (2.106)
The letter *ra* is declared to be the seed-syllable of fire; this constitutes my three eyes.
If even one of these is absent from the five-syllable mantra or yantra, [it is defective]. (2-107)
By my curse, he shall be deprived of sight and a bringer of suffering, grief, and disease;
neither at the beginning, nor in the middle, nor at the end shall there be "hsa," "haṃsa," or "hau. (2-108)
Whether it be *ai*, or *phre*, or *hū*, or *namaḥ*, or *hrī*—that is the mantra, O Goddess Pārvatī, which was pinned down by a curse from King Deva. (2-109)
But when a mantra is "staked" (kīlita) and does not attain success, if there is a single *la* in the middle, or *phaṭ* at the end, or two *la*s [at the end], [it is staked]. (2.110)
If that mantra is not paralyzed at the end by two or three *phaṭ*s, then, due to this terrible curse, what is accomplished becomes auspicious. (2.111)
Sometimes there will be no suffering at all, and for the most part it will be abundant;
provided that the mantra begins with seven syllables in sequence. (2-112)
If that mantra is joined with the letter *ra* or the letter *ya*, scorched by the curse of wind and fire, it will cause torment to the practitioner. (2.113)
Therefore, O Goddess, the best of practitioners should perform consecration for the sake of accomplishment;
it is seen to be performed with two, three, six, or eight [mantras]. (2.114)
When the *phaṭ* syllable is interspersed with other syllables, it is called [the *phaṭkāra*];
terrified by the curse of Nārasiṃha, it shall always strike fear [into enemies]. (2.115)
In dreams and the like, no accomplishment or attainment is ever seen; moreover, that mantra is fearful if it begins with *oṃ*, *vā*, *ha*, or the letter *sa*. (2-116)
Due to the curse of Brahmā, one's spiritual attainment (siddhi) becomes diminished and brings about extreme suffering. The four "Ma"s should be combined together at the beginning, middle, and end.
That mantra is defiled by the curse of Māyā and causes defilement.
There should be *hūṃ* at the beginning, or in the middle of the mantra, or at the end, followed by a pair of *phaṭ*s. (2-118)
One who has been humiliated by the curse of Rudra should perform the rite of humiliation;
first there are two *tāra*s (oṃ), at the end is *vaṣaṭ*, and in between is the *astra* mantra.
One who is divided by the curse of a child shall cause strife within the family;
that which consists of three syllables, devoid of the letter *ha* and the letter *sa*, [is such]. (2.120)
That which begins with eighteen syllables and is preceded by five *phaṭ* sounds was declared to be "asleep" due to a lion's curse, and it bestows desired fruits. (2.121)
If [the syllable] *ma* occurs in the middle, he becomes intoxicated with pride due to the curse of Cāmuṇḍā and is not auspicious;
however, if there are five *phaṭ*s in the middle, that is due to the curse of Kālikā. (2.122)
One who is swooning should cause another who is swooning to act, especially one who is a left-hander;
and at the end, he should utter five *phaṭ* syllables along with the *rambhā* mantra.
But his vitality having been stolen by the curse, he was rendered one whose skin was withered;
in that [mantra], there are four *phaṭ* sounds at the beginning, middle, and end. (2.124)
If it lacks eighteen syllables, there is loss due to the curse of Bhairava;
and [the mantra] consisting of nineteen letters is joined with the syllables Hrīḥ, Krom, and Oṃ. (2.125)

Corrupted by the curse of Kāma, he would destroy [others] for the sake of desire. The seven-syllable mantra is known as Bāla (the Child), while the eight-syllable one is remembered as Kumāra (the Youth). || 2-126 ||

The sixteen-syllabled mantra is the "youthful," while the one consisting of forty syllables is the "mature. That mantra, however, in which there are thirty kalās, one hundred, four, and eight syllables, is the "ancient" (vyoma).
For these, when cursed by Time even once, bring about sufferings;
and the mantra consisting of nine syllables joined with the syllable *oṃ* [is ineffective] due to the curse of Cāmuṇḍā. (2-128)
A sword [mantra] would cut the practitioner with its own sword; of this there is no doubt—provided that at the end it has either "namas" or "svāhā," or that these do not occur in its middle. (2.129)
*Vaṣaṭ*, *vauṣaṭ*, *sahū*, and *phaṭ*—this mantra does not exist for that practitioner of Bhuvaneśī; he is declared to be "seedless" (*nirbīja*). (2.130)
He who performs service [with a mantra] that has the sound "phaṭ phaṭ" at its beginning, middle, and end shall suffer the destruction of his lineage starting from three generations.
But due to the curse of Kaumāryā, that [mantra] is devoid of power and does not grant success;
as for the ten-syllable mantra, it [too is ineffective] because of the curse of Gaṇeśa. (2-132)
If muttered slowly, it causes stupidity in birth after birth;
when combined with an initial consonant, there should be only a single vowel. (2-133)
That peak was known to have been diminished from its summit due to the curse of Mātaṅgī;
it became two-colored and devoid of essence due to the curse of Āśvineya. (2.134)
He would destroy the strength of the practitioner and annihilate the king’s army;
born from the excessive curse of the Sun, he was one of the four castes who was squint-eyed. (2.135)
Having recited the *kekara* mantra, he no longer sees with his eyes;
the six syllables have become seedless due to the curse of Rāvaṇa. (2-136)
