It would destroy the power of the practitioner and annihilate the king’s army; through its recitation, there is no increase of the lineage, nor indeed is there happiness from women. (2-137)
Due to the curse of Dhūmāvatī, whose name consists of three and a half times seven suns (twenty-one syllables), the mind of the practitioner becomes agitated by smoke-like confusion. (2.138)
With twenty, twenty-one, or thirty syllables, this [mantra] is embraced by Tārā;
through its recitation, death occurs for one who indulges in dreams. (2-139)
The twenty-two-syllable mantra of Sarasvatī, however, through its curse, may cause the practitioner to become deluded and distracted by vices such as drinking and the like. (2.140)
That which consists of twenty-four syllables or twenty-seven syllables causes poverty through the curse of Rājamātaṅgī when one is afflicted by hunger. (2.141)
The twenty-three Rudras became the [three] castes due to the curse of the Kaulikas; their mantras became arrogant, and by reciting them, a person becomes a mere follower of the Vedic hymns. (2.142)
Consisting of twenty-six, twenty-nine, thirty, or thirty-six syllables, [the mantra] was deprived of its limbs due to the curse of Pūṣan; it did not fulfill desires. (2.143)

If the syllables are twenty-eight or thirty-one due to the curse of Nandīśa, the mantra becomes extremely cruel; having brought about the destruction of the subject, the practitioner himself shall perish. (2.144)
The thirty-eight syllable mantra [is effective] through the curse of the Mātṛkās;
by its recitation, one who is exceedingly angry brings about his own destruction. (2.145)
Beginning from forty up to sixty-three syllables, [the mantras] are accompanied by shame due to the curse of Mālikā; the practitioners of those [mantras] are likewise accompanied by shame. (2.146)
Those mantras which consist of sixty-five syllables are peaceful in nature;
due to the curse of desire, there is no fruit from the exertion of reciting them. (2.147)
From sixty-six up to ninety-nine, those who have fallen from their status due to a curse within the family are born as such practitioners (sādhakas). (2.148)
Wherein are *kvātidhṛti*, *vyatidhṛti*, *kvaṅkayugma*, and *dvigokara*;
wherein there are three hundred syllables, as sworn by Chinnamastā. (2.149)
May you become free from attachment and the dispellers of fear for practitioners;
when recited by those whose minds are devoid of desire, you destroy the craving for worldly existence. (2-150)
Starting from four hundred and going up to one thousand syllables, those that are excessively long are excluded from rites for nourishment and the like due to the curse of the sacrifice. (2.151)
Mantras exceeding one thousand syllables belong to Daṇḍapāṇi;
due to his curse, they are afflicted by the name "Daṇḍaka," and from their recitation, one incurs suffering. (2.152)
Due to the curse of Bhārgava, more than two thousand mantras were split into seven parts; they are remembered as those that cause the fragmentation of spiritual accomplishment (siddhi).
O gods, listen to another thing: when no success was achieved by the chanting sages, then a most terrible curse was uttered. (2.154)
Consolation for the deities arises from the absence of [external] means for accomplishment;
therefore, one should appoint a guru for the instruction and perform the purification of that mantra. (2-155)
He describes the method for purifying the mantra:
"I shall proclaim that method; let all the gods listen!
The Guru, seated in the Siddhāsana, [presses] the space between the anus and the genitals firmly. (2-156)
Having pressed [the left foot] with the left heel, one should place the right foot upon it, so that the two ankle-joints press against each other. (2.157)
One should perform that [action] so that it may be accomplished; then, having firmly pressed the base of the *liṅga* with the right heel, one should sit with the body steady. (2-158)
Having contracted the anus, the Guru should likewise raise the wind known as apāna;
then, he should properly restrain the prāṇa-vāyu. (2-159)
With a one-pointed mind, one should effect the union of the apāna and prāṇa breaths within the mūlādhāra, in the kuṇḍalinī whose nature is consciousness, which is the Supreme Self. (2.160)
In that case, the true guru should contemplate his own mantra which has become defective;
then, he should [contemplate] the syllables of that mantra one by one in their proper sequence. (2.161)
One should cause it to enter the *mūlādhāra* by way of the *suṣumṇā* channel, and then into the *svādhiṣṭhāna* cakra, the *maṇipūra*, and the *anāhata*. (2.162)
p. 91) One should cause [the breath] to enter the pure *ājñācakra*, piercing it again and again;
having thus led it to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), from the lunar mandala located there— (2-163)
One should clearly visualize the syllables of the mantra as being sprinkled with the nectar that has emerged;
then, one should cause them to descend again by way of the suṣumṇā channel into the ājñācakra.
One should cause [the breath] to enter the Viśuddha, the Anāhata, or the Maṇipūra cakra, and then, through the process of piercing, into the Svādhiṣṭhāna and the Mūlādhāra. (2-165)
Then one should again recite that mantra, preceded by the nyāsa of the ṛṣi and other elements;
by doing so one thousand and eight times, the mantra becomes purified.
Once he has been released from the unspoken curse, one should thereafter instruct him.

"From an unspoken curse" means from a mental curse; the implication is that verbal curses are destroyed by the ten purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) which will be described later. That defects such as being "cut" (*chinna*) are removable by the aforementioned causes has also been stated by Nāgabhaṭṭa:
"Those mantras which are cut, obstructed, paralyzed, pinned down, asleep, fainted, or deprived of their potency..."
Terrified by the burning weapons, those who stood on the enemy's side—
whether children, the elderly, or those arrogant in their youth— [perished].
Those who are soulless, those who are devoid of vitality, those who have become impotent, and those who are deprived of their limbs and mantras—
these [are purified] by the very binding of the mudrā in the womb.
All mantras become possessed of power. || 2-168 ||
(From the *Śāradātilaka*):
"The fool who practices mantras without understanding these defects will not attain accomplishment even in hundreds of millions of aeons. (2-169)
The ten consecrations of mantras are described in that very same [text]:
first, birth (janana); second, life-giving (jīvana); then, striking (tāḍana) and awakening (bodhana);
likewise, consecration (abhiṣeka), purification (vimalīkaraṇa), and again, nourishment (āpyāyana). (2.170)
Satisfying (tarpaṇa), kindling (dīpana), and protection (gupti)—these ten are the purificatory rites for mantras.
Now, the methods beginning with "birth" (janana) are described for the purpose of destroying the verbal curses [of those mantras] (as stated in the Merutantra). || 2-171 ||
On a seat made of *śrīparṇī*, sandalwood, or mango wood and the like, one should draw the *pāñcabhautika* [maṇḍala] with musk, saffron, and clarified butter. (2.172)
One should invoke there the Goddess Sarasvatī, known as Mātṛkā;
having performed worship according to the prescribed rite, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times.
Having recited the Mātṛkā, from its midst [one should extract] one's own desired mantra, including the vowels, consonants, and *bindus*, as well as the syllables joined with the *visarga*. (2.174)
Having extracted [the components] individually and then unified them according to the instructions of the Guru, one should grasp the mantra; this is declared to be "generation" (saṃjanana). (2.175)
Having placed the *praṇava* at the beginning and end, one should recite the mantra with the *praṇava* interspersed;
this recitation of the mantra one hundred and eight times along with its syllables is indeed the "life" of the practice. (2.176)
One should write the mantra on birch bark with yellow pigment (rocanā) and saffron (kuṅkuma),
and strike it one hundred times for each syllable with sandalwood water.
Uttering this seed-syllable of Vāyu is called "striking" (tāḍana).
Mantras that have become blunted by the Śabaras, when thus struck, bring about success. (2-178)
Having drawn [the diagram] upon the previously mentioned pedestal according to the number of syllables of that mantra,
and then taking *karavīra* flowers while reciting [the mantra], || 2.179 ||
One should offer oblations with those flowers one hundred times for each syllable while reciting the seed-syllable of fire; this is called "awakening. (2.180)
In the *Śāradā-tantra*, however, where "one should offer oblations" (*hunet*) is stated, it is said "one should strike" (*hanyāt*).

[The text reads: "The practitioner of mantra should draw with flowers born of the *karavīra* tree, numbering according to the syllables of that mantra; one should strike, as indicated by the word 'end' (*rānta*). Thus it is taught.
With the fire-seed syllable ending in *rāṃ* (in *mairau*), as before, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus on the seat with those same substances. || 2-181 ||
Upon its pericarp, one should draw a single *mālatī* bud;
then, according to the number of syllables in that mantra, one should write each individual syllable of the mantra.
Taking sprouts from the *bodhidruma* tree while reciting this mantra, one should consecrate [the disciple] with the words "I consecrate this mantra; obeisance! (2.183).
With various fragrant waters and a single sprout, one should sprinkle [the deity] once with the syllable; this is remembered as the rite of one hundred and eight [sprinklings].
Just as water performs the purification of mantras through consecration for human beings, so too should the light-mantra be contemplated within the fire-mandala at the mūlādhāra. (2.185)

One should contemplate the Manu as being thus to be purified; above that, one should likewise visualize [the fourfold impurity] known as the āṇava, the innate (sāhajika), the adventitious (āgantu), and the kārmaṇa. (2-186)
The one called Yoga is said to be illusory; within his own mantra, one should contemplate each of the three impurities as being individually consumed by the fire-mantra. (2.187) p. 94)
One should contemplate that in this way [the deity] has become pure as one's own mantra;
the *jyotirmantra* is considered to be the two-syllabled mantra beginning with the Vedas, namely "hauṃ. (2-188)
For this is the purification; one should perform it even at the conclusion of the ritual application.
As before, one should inscribe the mantra upon the pedestal with substances such as saffron. (2.189)
Having filled a vessel made of copper or other metal with pure water scented with camphor,
one should recite the written mantra one hundred and eight times.
Having consecrated water with that mantra, one should sprinkle it three times for each syllable using drops of *kuśa* grass; this is considered to be "nourishing" (*āpyāyana*).
For those who have been exhausted by the preliminary rites (puraścaryā), this [rite] is like the formal graduation ceremony (samāvartana):
one should inscribe the mantra within a copper vessel using musk and other substances. (2.192)
And having taken pure water scented with camphor and other substances in another vessel, one should take it with the *argha* vessel while reciting this mantra: (2-193)

"One should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) with the words 'I satisfy [you], obeisance' (tarpayāmi namaḥ). One should then recite the mantra preceded by 'Oṃ Hrīḥ Śrīḥ' one hundred and eight times. (2.194)
One should mutter this [mantra], for it serves as an illuminator; this is desired in the case of all mantras as well.
The concealment of the mantra being muttered, however, means its non-disclosure. (2.195)
Ten consecrations (saṃskāras) have been proclaimed, hidden in all tantras;
by performing them according to the tradition, the mantra-practitioner attains his desired goal.
Now, the awakening of the mantras occurs therein as well.
Now, first of all, I shall proclaim the awakening of all mantras. (2.196)
The Guru should perform that [initiation] for the sake of the disciple’s accomplishment;
it is joined with the final letter of *Tārā*, fire (*ra*), and space (*ha*), and that [mantra] in which [these are present] is the one belonging to Agni. (2.197)
The other, gentle time of sleep belongs to the one in the form of fire within the *iḍā* channel;
that of the gentle one [the moon] would be in the *piṅgalā*. Their waking state occurs elsewhere than in those two. (2-198)
At the time of awakening, the mantra of the waking state arises when [the seed-syllables] have been recited;
or else, by enclosing the letters beginning with *la* and ending with *na*, together with their nasal bindus. (2.199)
Furthermore, one should recite the letters ending with the visarga and the letter *kṣa* alone.
If recited in this manner as desired, it awakens [the practitioner] and swiftly bestows accomplishment. (2-200)
The specific procedure regarding the Śabara mantras is stated in that very same place:
"Now listen, O Pārvatī, to the awakening of the Śabara mantras.
Having brought a pure bell-metal vessel prepared with ashes and other substances... (2.201).
During the day and night, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times during each watch;
with a staff made of *khadira* wood, one should strike a bronze vessel, and it is said that one should speak thus: (2-202).
While awake, one should recite the mantra; then, during the fourth watch, one should offer the bali-oblation to Kālī and to Bhairava, born of the mantra.
One should crack a coconut upon another deity [than the primary one] with the mantra: "O Kukkuṭa!
The meaning of "in the language of the mantra" is that one should address the Śabara mantra in the very language of the region to which it belongs, saying, "Be awake!
Now follows the examination of the ground for the purpose of the sacrificial site (*maṇḍapa*) required for initiation (*dīkṣā*).
And the place for the raft is deep, being a refuge with a long-lasting reservoir of water. || 2-204 ||
It was a renowned sacred site for those who maintain the sacred fires in their fire-halls,
and it was either a refuge for twice-born men observing their vows or his own hermitage.
O Pārvatī, these locations are highly praised for initiation;
however, one should not perform the initiation in a dense thicket or a deep forest.
In a great forest at the boundary between two regions frequented by predatory beasts,
(according to another tantra), on the banks of great rivers, or at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean. (2-207)
And the praiseworthy holy fords, sacred fields, and hermitages as well;
all the forests and even all the mountains. (2.208)

One who is expert in the science of architecture should examine the ground there— whether it be near a mountain with waterfalls or at a sanctuary of the gods— in accordance with the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*. (2.209)
Ground that is cracked, pierced by stakes, or overrun with anthills should be avoided from afar; it robs the builder of his life-span and wealth.
A cracked [footprint] brings death; one that is saline causes the loss of wealth;
one with a thorn constantly gives rise to affliction; and one that is uneven brings fear from enemies. (2-211)
If it flows toward the northeast corner, it certainly bestows prosperity upon the performer quickly;
if it flows toward the east, it brings about increase; and if it flows toward the north, it grants boons. (2-212)
Land that slopes toward the south always brings the fear of death;
and that land which slopes toward the southwest (Nairṛta) causes the destruction of one's home.
Land flooded by Varuṇa is said to cause the loss of wealth;
likewise, land flooded by Vāyu constantly causes agitation. (2-214)
And that which flows toward the southeast corner destroys sons, longevity, and wealth.
(From the *Gautamīya*:
One should perform the formal acquisition of the ground as far as the temple site extends. (2-215)
The ground that is white soil is proclaimed as Brāhmī;
the red soil is Kṣatriyā, and the yellow is proclaimed as Vaiśyā. (2.216)
Black soil is Śūdra; thus it is proclaimed as fourfold.
(In the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*):
Land endowed with *kuśa* grass is Brāhmaṇī, while land abounding in *śara* grass is Kṣatriyā. (2-217)
The Vaiśya woman is filled with Kuśa and Kāśa grass; the Śūdra woman is filled with all kinds of grass.
(In the *Gautamīya Tantra*) the Brāhmaṇī leads to the accomplishment of all aims, and likewise the Kṣatriyā bestows sovereignty. (2-218)
O Sage, the Vaiśya woman brings wealth and grain, while the Śūdra woman is censured.
(In the Vāsiṣṭhī rite:
when the pit is being dug, if stones are found in the earth... (2-219)
Then, [the appearance of] bones, hair, or charcoal portends untimely death; the loss of wealth is indicated by ashes; and poverty is said to be foretold by husks. (2.220)
Regarding the wheel of great power for the purpose of knowing [hidden] shafts (*śalyajñāna*), it is said in the *Ādiyāmala*:
"I shall proclaim the snake-wheel (*ahicakra*) as spoken by the Omniscient One, by which practitioners come to know substances, shafts, and likewise voids. (2.221)
Wherever on the surface of the earth a treasure (*nidhi*) is located, being the sole site for its extraction, there this wheel should be placed, situated at the entrance of that place. (2-222)

And having ascertained the lunar mansion in which the moon is at that time, there the substance or the splinter [of bone] shall be located, produced by the conjunction of the moon and the sun. (2.223)
Eight vertical lines and likewise five horizontal lines should be drawn;
thus, in the snake-wheel (ahicakra), there are twenty-eight squares.

In that [diagram], the asterisms Pauṣṇa (Revatī), Āśvinī, Yāmya (Bharaṇī), Kṛttikā, Maghā, Bhāgya (Pūrvaphalgunī), and Uttarāphālgunī should certainly be written in a single row within that group of seven. (2.225)
One should mark Ahibudhnya, Ājapada, Arka, Śatabhiṣaj, Bhrāmya, Sārpabha, Puṣya, and Hasta, situated in the second row. (2–226)
Abhijit, Viṣṇu (Śravaṇa), Dhaniṣṭhā, Saumya (Mṛgaśiras), Raudra (Ārdrā), Punarvasu, and Citrā are in the third row, beginning with the first of the seven constellations. (2-227)
Having placed Viśvarkṣa (Śatabhiṣaj), the water asterism (Pūrvāṣāḍhā), Mūla, Jyeṣṭhā, Maitra (Anurādhā),
and the Viśākhā asterism in a row, one should observe the wheel on the fourth day.
The Wheel of Serpent-Power (ahibalacakra):
Re 27 Caṃ.
A,
Caṃ, Bha.
2 caṃ kṛ 3 caṃ
Ma 10 Caṃ U (Moon)
U Pū 25 Caṃ (Uttaraphalgunī)
Śaro śle (arrow and glue)
9 and 8 lunar mansions (nakṣatras) in the east.
Ha!
Listen!
22 caṃ dha 23 caṃ
Mṛ āa 6 caṃ (The *mṛ* [vowel] is the sixth [consonant] of the *ca*-group.)
Pu 7 Caṃ Ci
u 21 caṃ pū (the twenty-first lunar mansion, Citrā)
20th lunar day,
Mūla,
Jyeṣṭhā.

(On page 99: Viśvā, Revatī, Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā, Maghā, Pūrvaphalgunī, and Uttaraphalgunī are in the first row. Uttarabhādrapadā, Pūrvabhādrapadā, Śatabhiṣā, Rohiṇī, Āśleṣā, Puṣya, and Hasta are in the second row. Abhijit, Śravaṇā, Dhaniṣṭhā, Mṛgaśiras, Ārdrā, Punarvasu, and Citrā are in the third row. Then, Uttarāṣāḍhā, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, Mūla, Jyeṣṭhā, Anurādhā, Viśākhā, and Svātī are in the fourth row.
In this way, the diagram in the form of a serpent is generated upon the wheel.
The two door-posts are Maghā and Yāmyā (Bharaṇī), while Kṛttikā is considered to be situated at the door.
The three asterisms beginning with Aśvinī, the four beginning with Pūrvaṣāḍhā, Revatī, and Pūrvabhādrapadā belong to the Moon; the remaining ones belong to the Sun. (2.230)
The nadīs elapsed since sunrise, when reduced by sixty and taking the remainder, added to the moon’s motion for that day, will be the moon at that specific time. (2.231)
Multiply that lord of the night (the lunar day) by sixty, then add four and five (nine).
Whatever remains when divided by four is the [planet's] direct or retrograde motion starting from the east.
One should calculate the Sun, situated in its asterism at the time of the query, in the same manner as for the Moon;
afterwards, one should observe whether those two are situated in their own asterisms or in other asterisms. (2.233)
When the Sun and the Moon are in the lunar mansion of Candra (Mṛgaśīrṣā), a treasure is certain to be there;
if they are situated in the lunar mansion of Bhānu (Punarvasu), then there is a splinter, and not otherwise.
One should know that there are two [results] in their respective signs; nothing exists in the opposite case.
No substance situated [therein] can be obtained when the Moon is conjoined with a malefic planet. (2-235)
One should know that when the moon is situated in the planets beginning with the sun, there will be copper-colored iron, copper-colored gems, copper-colored metal, tin, lead, and silver. (2-236)
A substance mixed with others becomes mixed; it is empty when there is a reversal of views.
When the Moon is situated in Sarvagraha, that great treasure is indicated. (2-237)
When the moon is situated in an auspicious field, gain occurs with certainty;
when in an inauspicious field, there will be no gain—this is to be known by those who understand the science of vowels. (2-238)
When the moon is waxing, the treasure will be abundant; when the moon is waning, the treasure will be small.
Furthermore, by virtue of the aspects of the planets, that [treasure] should be understood by the wise as being of nine kinds. (2-239)
When the Moon is in the houses of the Sun and other planets, there arises merchandise consisting of gold, copper, stone, earthenware, and iron. (2-240)
"The measurement of the ground is by means of *kāṃvika* cubits according to the measure of the degrees of the consumed sign.
For example:
a treasure is to be known in the position of the Moon, and a thorn in the position of the Sun. (2-241)

And this *nirvartana* should be performed only once on a limited area. As for the nature of the *nirvartana*: a staff (*daṇḍa*) shall be ten cubits long, and thirty such staffs constitute a *nirvartana*.
Thus it is said.

Alternatively, the extraction of the thorn (śalyoddhāra) should be performed according to the method taught in the Mahākapila-pañcarātra. It is as follows: "And at the time of commencing the temple, whichever limb a man touches... (2-242).
A wise person should recognize that there is a firm thorn within the body of the site;
if a man scratches his head, one should extract the thorn from the head. (2.243)
In that case, when digging three hand-spans deep, a bone should be recognized as a "thorn" (śalya);
it causes a burning sensation from fire, disease, and loss of wealth. (2-244)
One who desires his own success should extract the splinter with effort;
if there is itching in the arm, one should indicate an iron chain.
The characteristic described by you regarding the two hands standing together is this:
one should know it portends the death of the master, as well as his departure to a foreign land. (2.246)
One who desires his own welfare should extract the splinter with effort;
if there is itching in the thigh, one should diagnose it as a bronze splinter.
If it remains with only one hand, that characteristic has been described to you:
the wife will be unchaste and loss of reputation will arise. (2-248)
One who desires his own welfare should extract the thorn with effort;
however, if one scratches with the hand, one should predict a skeleton. (2-249)
When being excavated, it should remain at three cubits and not otherwise;
[if it is less], there will certainly be a fire, a disease, a splinter, and death. (2-250)
One who desires his own welfare should extract the splinter with effort;
however, if there is itching on the back, one should diagnose it as a splinter in the arm. (2-251)
It should remain with only one hand; no deliberation is required here.
In that case, the death of the husband occurs, or the wife becomes unchaste. (2.252)
If there is itching on the foot, one should indicate a hand-bone as the cause;
it stands at a distance of one and a half cubits—thus has the characteristic been described to you. (2.253)
Destruction of cattle, royal punishment, and loss of crops shall arise;
one should extract the thorn with effort if one desires success for oneself. (2-254)
If there is itching in the belly, one should indicate a stone there;
the characteristic has been described to you as measuring two cubits.
In that case, there would be a snakebite; therefore, one should extract the thorn.
However, if the knee itches, one should prescribe ashes for that spot. (2.256)
The characteristic described by you regarding the two hands is as follows:
there will be a great conflagration, intense heat, and the fears of affliction and suffering. (2-257)
One performs such an action; therefore, one should indeed rescue him.
[The materials are] a cow’s horn, yellow-colored frogs, a conch shell, mother-of-pearl, and a pavilion. (2-258)
Śambūkas and other such varieties of precious gems are commendable;
however, one should avoid charcoal, husks, hair, bone, and splinters. (2.259)

Alternatively, having identified the *śalya* (the "thorn" or defect) according to the method taught in the *Brahmayāmala*, its extraction must be performed. Regarding that, the knowledge of the *śalya* is as follows:
"In a wheel consisting of nine compartments, the letters va, ka, ca, ta, e, ha, sa, pa, ya, and ra are to be written in sequence within the directions starting from the East. (2.260)
The wheel for extracting the shaft as taught in the *Brahmayāmala*;
another method.
p.
Va-ka-pa
Va-ka-sa (Vakasa)
And whoever that is...
And whoever indeed...
And this indeed.
And thus, in the home, with perfumes, flowers, food offerings, incense, lamps, and so forth—
Having brought a young boy who has bathed well, he should be questioned with fruits and flowers.

In the first half [of the day], it is known by the name of the flower, and in the remaining half, by the name of the fruit; there is no "thorn" (defect) of the day based on the color of the fruit, flower, and so forth. (2-262)
If the initial letter of the name of a flower or fruit occurs in the stomach-house (koṣṭha), then there will be a thorn (śalya) in that house; if it is not there, then there is none. (2-263)
A human thorn standing at one and a quarter cubits (sapādahastabhūmistha) causes the destruction of men;
a donkey thorn and a snake thorn, extending from one and a half cubits (sārdhahasta), are terrifying.
The *vājiśalya* at both hands brings death and suffering to householders; the *hastiśalya* at two and a half cubits brings the emptiness of the home and exile. (2-265)
Death occurs from a buffalo with a thorn-like wound at a distance of two and a quarter cubits;
a cat-thorn at one cubit brings about the loss of a friend at three cubits.
In a house measuring three and a half *kapa*s, there is a thorn of a bad dream that causes the loss of wealth;
in a house of the size of a *vāstu*, there is a thorn of a rat that destroys the family and its riches. (2-267)
The arrows beginning with man and so forth are to be known in sequence starting from the letter *va*;
whichever limb the messenger touches, an arrow arises from that very limb. (2-268)

Having divided the house into nine parts, and then dividing each of those parts again and again, the fruit is determined by the primary color found in whichever part corresponds to the flower or fruit. (2-269)
In the *Tattvakaumudī*, however, it is stated:

"If, at the commencement of building a house, itching occurs on the body of the owner, it should be declared that there is a splinter [of wood] present, whether in a palace or even in a dwelling. (2-270)

The syllables of the *śalya* [alphabet] are derived from armor (*kavaca*), weapons (*taihasa*), and vehicles (*paya*). The names of hell-beings, donkeys, camels, porpoises, cats, cows, monkeys, men, birds, bones, rivers, flowers, fruits, and deities are used. A syllable that has just emerged from the mouths of infants, women, or fools—having doubled that syllable and quadrupled its *mātrā*—[is employed]. (2.271)

One should divide by nine; there is no piercing [of the earth] when it is even. "Obeisance to the one who brings about the bearing and supporting of the earth"—this is stated as the specific mantra for extracting the splinter (*śalyoddhāraṇa*). Everything else is as described in the *Brahmayāmala*.

Four methods for extracting the *śalya* (subterranean defects) have been shown. Having extracted the *śalya* by one of these methods and having ascertained that the ground is free from defects, one should construct a pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) there after performing the *vāstuyāga* according to the method to be described. Alternatively, the examination of the ground should be performed using another method for extracting the *śalya*; that method is [described] in the *Prayogasāra*:
"Having fashioned a hole in the earth with an extent of one *vitasti*... (2.272).
One should cast those clods of earth into it; when some remain, it is auspicious.
One should know that it is middling if they are equal in number, and inferior if they are fewer. (2.273)
(Gautamīyatantra) Then, one who is skilled in the knowledge of sites should examine the ground;
he should perform the purification of thorns and the like, and remove husks, charcoal, and so forth. (2.274)
If this is not performed, the practitioner shall obtain no fruit whatsoever.
(From the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*):
As long as water is found while digging, the defect caused by the *śalya* (impurity/remnant) is destroyed. (2-275)
Water situated at a great depth cannot be reached by digging;
it must be excavated to a depth of five cubits for the sake of pacifying the defects caused by hidden obstacles. (2.276)
Then, having extracted the splinters, one should fill [the pit] so that it is perfectly level;
thereafter, one should perform the Vāstuyāga for the pacification of all obstacles. (2.277)
Yama states the necessity of the Vāstuyāga:

"In the construction of a house or similar structures, wherever the deity of the site (Vāstudevatā) is not worshipped, everything therein shall become empty, destroyed by demons, obstacles, and the like. (2.278)
Therefore, those who desire prosperity should perform the ritual worship of the site properly;
likewise, [it should be done] first when taking possession of the ground and when establishing the foundation stones. (Mahākapilapañcarātra, 2.279)
One should especially strive for a suitable site for the purpose of constructing a water reservoir or a house, as well as for other tasks such as sacrifices and fire-offerings. (2.280)
The Guru, having measured it out with a cord, should make the Vāstumaṇḍalaka level.
Regarding the origin of the Vāstu sacrifice, the *Merutantra* states:
"In ancient times, there was a certain very powerful Asura named Vāstu. (2.281)
By him the three worlds were conquered, as well as the fifty-three deities; those who came before him in battle were crushed by him. (2-282)
He who had been repeatedly conquered in battle remained as Prajāpati;
at the end of a thousand divine years, the gods came to him for refuge.
That was heard by Viṣṇu, by me, by Pārvatī, and even by the lord of the Daityas;
urged on by Nārada, he rushed forward, desiring to fight. (2.284)
A battle was waged by us with him for five years;
thereafter, the Daitya became arrogant with pride, deluded by the illusory power (māyā) of Viṣṇu.
Being pleased, he spoke these words: "Choose, choose!
Neither Indra nor Kubera has performed anything so pleasing for me. (2-286)
Indeed, even with that army, that battle was fought by you while wearing matted locks,
aided by Viṣṇu, and bearing half the body of Pārvatī.
Therefore, I, the supreme lord of the three worlds, have attained satisfaction;
there is nothing whatsoever that I cannot give, so let all three of you ask for whatever you desire.
Having heard those words of Śiva and Pārvatī, Hari, impelled by their eyebrows, said: "O most fortunate lord of Daityas, who is there equal to you?"
If you grant the truth three times, then I shall ask for a boon;
even from Śiva and Pārvatī together, there is only one such boon, and no other.
Then the Daitya spoke three times, and Viṣṇu made this request:
"Let that means be shown by which your death may come swiftly. (2.291)
Realizing that this was a ruse of Viṣṇu, the lord of the Daityas spoke:
"One must certainly go to the mouth of Time, O Hari, along with everyone else."
And so, he who proceeds for the sake of his own promise lives;
however, there is but one exception in my lineage: those by whom service to me has been performed. (2.293)
"Having shown him the way, let this body be cast down.
And at that time, O gods, an incorporeal voice spoke: || 2.294 ||
O Lord of the Daityas, do not grieve; your birth was from the Earth. Go to dissolution in that very place, and hear a boon for the sake of your satisfaction. (2.295)
Those castes who will build a new house for their own enjoyment will, there, be afflicted by various miseries, except for your festival. (2-296)
"The female servants Kālavarṇī and the others, as well as those with the faces of Vināyakas, shall be the attendants who will torment [them]; such is the command of the Supreme Lord. (2.297)
Having heard these words, he too went to a great pit and entered the vast cavern,
which was then filled by the gods with earth and stones.
Therefore, those gods who had been defeated by him, fearing a renewed uprising, prepared themselves and established fifty-three abodes for his sake. (2.299)
Therefore, they must certainly be worshipped by those who desire the happiness of domestic life. Now follows the ritual procedure for the Vāstu-sacrifice;
O gods, listen to that procedure according to the left and right paths. (2-300)
"O Vāstoṣpati, you are present in this stone or image"—with this Vedic mantra, one performs its invocation and worship. (2-301)
Having performed worship for others with their respective name-mantras, one should fulfill [the rite] by constructing an auspicious square shape in the southwest corner of the house. (2-302)
Having made the ground level and a raised altar (vedikā) one span high,
the wise practitioner should draw [the mandala] there, measuring one cubit in width and length.
In the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*, however, there is this distinction:
"For houses, palaces, wells, pavilions, and water [reservoirs], a site-plan (*vāstumaṇḍalaka*) measuring eight cubits must be made, and not otherwise. (2.304)
One should purify the auspicious ground and draw ten lines;
by drawing them downward, further downward, and horizontally from the beginning, there will be eighty-one squares.
My wheel consists of eighty-one squares; therein, the Vedic deities reside.
One should first worship Brahmā in the nine central compartments.
Āpavatsa is in the northeast; Aryaman is in the east within three compartments;
Savitṛ is in the southeast, and Vivasvat is in the three [compartments] below.
Indra in the region of the southwest, Mitra in the three [directions] facing west, Rājayakṣman in the northwest, and Sumeru in the three [directions] to the north. (2-308)
And in the Vedic squares, starting from the northeast and the corner of Īśa, the deities are Śikhin, Parjanya, and Āpa; and Diti is in the two eastern squares. (2.309)
These five deities are to be known in succession from the left-hand path:
Jayanta, Indra, Sūrya, Satya, and Bhṛśa, located in the south-eastern corner. (2.310)
Antarikṣa, Vāta, Pūṣan, and Sāvitra—these four gods belong to Īśāna; thereafter, in the southern pentad, [are the others]. (2.311)
And from the pair-wise sequence [of the directions], Vitatha, Bṛhatkṣetra,
Yamī, Gandharva, and Bhṛṅgarāja are likewise located in the fourfold group of eight belonging to Nairṛta.
From the northeast (Īśānī) are Jaya (28) and Mṛga (29), as well as Pitṛ (30) and Dauvārika (31);
thereafter, in the next pair, are the five [deities] Sugrīva (32) and Puṣpadantaka (33).
Varuṇa, Asura, and Śoṣa [are located] in the northwest; Ahi resides in the northeast. Rudra, Pāpayakṣman, and Roga are in the five northern [directions]. (2.314)
Mukhya, Bhallāṭa, Soma, Bhujaga, and likewise Āditi—these forty-five deities should be worshipped with devotion. (2.315)
This is the Vedic Vāstu-maṇḍala consisting of eighty-one squares.
On the Tantric path, the Vāstu-maṇḍala consists of sixty-four squares, as stated in that very [text]:
"Now, on the Tantric path, likewise in the sixty-four-square [maṇḍala]," (2-316).
One should worship Brahmā in the center with a pair of threads at the two corners,
preceded by auspicious rites, the chanting of the Vedas, and the blessings of Brahmins (Gautamīya Tantra 2.317).
One should construct the maṇḍala of Vāstu according to its beauty and according to the prescribed rule;
[it is] the Vāstu-cakra consisting of eighty-one squares.
Śikhin, Parjanya, Jayanta.
Indra is the true Sun.
The wind in the atmosphere is intense.
Diti, the waters, and the conquerors.
Indra is the true Sun.
The son of Savitṛ is Pūṣan, the exceedingly powerful one.
Aditi is Aditi; she is the waters.
The calf is Aryaman; Aryaman [is he].
Aryaman, Savitṛ,
Vitatha.
The serpent is false;
it is a serpent.
Sumeru is Brahmā; Brahmā is Sumeru.
Brahmā, Vivasvān, Bṛhatkṣetra.
Soma is the vast field; Soma is Soma.
Sumeru is Brahmā; Brahmā is Sumeru.
Brahmā, Vivasvat, and Yama.
Yama is Bhallāṭa; Bhallāṭa is Yama.
Sumeru is Brahmā; Brahmā is Sumeru.
Brahmā, Vivasvat, and Gandharva.
The Gandharva is the foremost, the foremost.
Consumption is a friend;
consumption is a friend.
Indra is Mitra, the king of bees.
Bhṛṅgarāja, Ahi, Rudra.
Śoṣa is the Asura Varuṇa.
Puṣpadanta,
Sugrīva,
and Jaya.
The deer, the disease, the evil consumption.
Śoṣa is the Asura Varuṇa.
Puṣpadanta, Sugrīva, and Dauvārika.
The father [the preceptor] should lay down a thread extending from east to west, measuring one cubit, upon the Śāradā [mandala]. (2-318)
Taking a small portion of that center as a reference point, one should draw two fish-shaped marks on either side;
then, one should lay down a thread situated between those two, running from south to north.
One should draw crocodiles in the corners using two lines each, including the foremost ones; there, one should drop threads whose tips rest in the middle of the fish. (2–320)
There, it should be square and provided with four compartments;
the mantra-practitioner should further divide that so as to consist of sixty-four squares.
From Īśāna to Rākṣasa, and from Agni to Prabhañjana—one who is composed should thus lay down two threads as the ear-thread (karṇasūtra). (2.322)
One should first worship Brahmā in the four central squares;
thereafter, one should worship Ārya in the four directions, starting from the east.
Then [place] Vivasvat, Mitra, and immediately after him Mahīdhara;
again, in the pairs of half-cells at the corners, starting from the southeast (Agni) and proceeding around. (2–324)
The wise one [should worship] Sāvitra and Savitṛ, Śakra and Indrajaya again, Rudra and Rudrajaya, Āpa, and then Apavatsaka. || 2.325 ||
The instructor [should place] Śarva (14), Guha (15), Āryamāṇa (16), Jṛmbhaka (17), and Pilapicchikā (18) in the pairs of squares on both sides of that ear-thread. (2–326)
One should worship Carakī, Vidārī, and Pūtanā in sequence;
one should worship these in the directions starting from the east, in the half-squares at the beginning and end of each.
The best of teachers [should worship] the deities in eight groups of eight, in sequence: Īśāna (22), Parjanya (23), Jayanta (24), Śakra (25), and Bhāskara (26). 2-328.
Satya, Vṛṣa, and Antarikṣa are established in the eastern direction;
as are Agni, Pūṣan, Vitatha, Yama, and Gṛharakṣaka. (2.329)
Gandharva, Bhṛṅgarāja, and Mṛga are situated in the southern direction;
then come Nirṛti, Dauvārika, Sugrīva, and Varuṇa. (2–330)
The two Asuras Puṣpadanta and Śoṣa, as well as the diseases, are situated in the western direction;
and Vāyu, Nāga, Mukhya, Soma, and Bhallāṭa likewise.
Argala, Aditya, and Aditi are situated in the direction of Kuvera;
these fifty-three deities should be worshipped with great effort.
(In the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*):
An eighty-one-square plot is recommended for the construction of houses;
a sixty-four-square plot is praised for palaces. (2.333)
The sixty-four-padded Vāstu-cakra is Īśāna.
Aditi, Parjanya, and Jayanta.
Śakra is the sun, the truth.
The bull is Agni, the intermediate space.
Aditi, Parjanya, and Diti.
Jayanta, Śakra, and Bhāskara.
Pūṣan is the true bull.
Pūṣan is the bolt; the bolt is Pūṣan.
The waters are like a calf;
Aryaman is the waters.
The noble Savitṛ, the son of Savitṛ.
Vitatha,
Vitatha,
Bhallāṭa.
Bhallāṭa, Mahīdhara, and Brahmā.
Brahmā, Vivasvat, and Yama.
Yama is Soma; Soma is Yama.
Mahīdhara is Brahmā;
Brahmā is [Mahīdhara].
Vivasvat is the guardian of the house,
the guardian of the house.
Rudra is the foremost, the most eminent.
Rudrajaya is Mitra, Mitra.
Śakra, Indrajaya, and Gandharva.
Gandharva,
Nāga, Nāga.
Śodha is the Asura Puṣpadanta.
Varuṇa, Sugrīva, and Bhṛṅgarāja.
The doorkeeper is Bhṛṅgarāja,
the wind.
Disease, consumption, and the Asura.
Puṣpadanta, Varuṇa, and Sugrīva.
The deer is the doorkeeper;
Nirṛti.
Aryaman knows [this]. (In the *Merutantra*):
The station of Brahmā is colored red; the cardinal directions yellow; and the intermediate directions white.
Then the cardinal directions were filled with green [beings], and the intermediate directions with those of black color.
The surrounding border (paridhi) should be made reddish-orange so that the mandala becomes beautiful;
having cleared away nine squares in the center, one should fill them in. (2–335)
Having further swept the six [squares] in all four directions with white powder, one should fill them completely with red powder. || 2-336 ||
Between those two, having cleared away twelve compartments in the four directions, one should fill them with yellow pigments as beautifully as possible. (2.337)
In each corner, one should fill two sets of eight [squares] with yellow color;
the remaining squares here should be arranged according to what is aesthetically pleasing.
Then, in the center of those various [deities], one should fully worship Brahmā;
having filled the squares of even the aforementioned deities with the five [offerings]— (Gautamīya Tantra 2.339).
Then, one should offer an oblation (bali) to them with dust from those [sites] and with milk-rice (pāyasa);
one should worship all of them with sweet milk-rice mixed with sweets.
Or, for the pacification of defects, the wise one should perform worship with various substances,
such as rice, mung beans, and barley, sequentially soaked in honey, clarified butter, and milk. (Meru Tantra, 2.341)
One should offer oblations one hundred and eight times, or twenty-one times,
with each of those substances, and likewise with milk-rice (pāyasa) accompanied by the mantras.
And one should offer them an oblation (bali) consisting of milk-rice accompanied by side dishes, mixed with sugar, and combined with milk, plantains, cakes, and other such items.
Thus, when the sun has entered Leo, on the full moon day of every year,
one should perform the worship of Vāstu in one's own home within pavilions.
There shall be no untimely death, no disease, nor [disturbance from] bhūtas, pretas, and the like;
there shall be no affliction by serpents, nor any inauspicious events such as mutual quarrels. (2-345)
Possessing sons, grandsons, wealth, health, and an abundance of cattle and female slaves, he lives long in that house, free from disease, victorious, and renowned. (2-346)
In all royal palaces, as well as in the quarters of the queens,
and likewise in the residences of ministers, counselors, and generals.
The teacher should perform [the rite] every year for the sake of the aforementioned accomplishment;
otherwise, there would be constant suffering through results that are contrary to what was taught. (2.348)
For the Bhairavas, the Kṣetrapālas, and especially for the Yoginīs,
an offering (bali) should be made according to the left-hand practice (vāmācāra), using either buffaloes or cocks.
If propitiated with offerings on the left, they become exceedingly hungry;
the deities desire the bali offering, and if it is deficient, they destroy the practitioner. (2-350)
Meditation on Vāstu (from the Somaśambhutantra):

In ritual worship, one should visualize Vāstu as having the form of an Asura, with its hands contracted and its body supine; however, when constructing walls and so forth, one should visualize it with its face turned downwards. (2.351)
The knees and elbows are in the direction of Vāta and Hutāśa (the northwest);
the feet are in the direction of Pitṛ (the southwest); the head is in the direction of Raudrī (the northeast); and the hands joined in añjali are at the heart.

Regarding the term "paitryām": it should be understood that this refers to the direction of the Rākṣasas within the natural cosmic sphere (*prakṛtimaṇḍala*), presided over by the ancestral deities (*pitṛdevatā*), and not to the southern direction.
(As stated in the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*:
"In the past, there was a great demon, terrifying to all living beings."
Slain by the gods, he fell to the earth; he is known as Vāstupuruṣa. || 2-353 ||
As long as the earth remains firm in the world, so long does the Vāstu-asura remain;
but at the time of dissolution, he goes to his rest along with the gods, all the planets, and the rest. (2-354)
Its extent all around is one hundred crore yojanas;
it stands pervading the earth, turned face upwards, and is black in color.

In this regard, the sequence is as follows: first, the patron (yajamāna) should speak to the preceptor (ācārya). Then, the preceptor, having selected a ground possessing the prescribed characteristics and having performed its purification, should sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). In the center of that [ground], he should stretch out a white cord and, using either a golden needle, a gem, a silver needle, or—in their absence—any one of flowers, fruits, or grains, [he should mark the lines].
The nine [lines] are considered to be: Śāntā (1), Yaśovatī (2), Kāntā (3), Vilāsā (4), Prāṇavāhinī (5), Satī (6), Vasumatī (7), Nandā (8), and Subhadrā (9). (2–356)

Having thus drawn nine lines extending from east to west, beginning from the south and ending in the north, [the following rivers] have been enumerated by the wise: Hiraṇyā (1), Suvratā (2), Lakṣmī (3), Vibhūti (4), Vimalā (5), Priyā (6), Jayā (7), Kālā (8), and Viśokā (9) as the ninth. (2–357)

Having thus drawn nine lines extending from south to north, beginning from the west and ending at the east, one should construct the sixty-four-square Vāstu-maṇḍala. Then, having filled the squares with five-colored powders and constructed an eight-petaled lotus in the center according to the method to be described, one should meditate upon and invoke Brahmā in its center. Having invoked the respective deities in their respective squares, one should worship them with their name-mantras preceded by *Oṃ* and ending in *namaḥ*. Outside the maṇḍala, having constructed four additional squares in the four corners, one should worship the Guru, Gaṇeśa, Durgā, and Kṣetrapāla there. Rāghavabhaṭṭa states that one should place a water-pot (*kalaśa*) in the northeast and worship Varuṇa therein according to the prescribed rules.
Among these, their meditative absorptions (dhyānas) are described in that interval;
and the physical forms of all the aforementioned gods are now declared:
[they hold] a rosary and a sacrificial ladle in the right hands, and a staff and a water-pot in the left. (2.358)
One should worship the eight-eyed one seated upon a lotus in the center;
all the gods, possessing four arms, are established within the body of Vāstu.
With palms joined in reverence, holding swords and shields in their hands,
they gaze upward at Brahmā, facing toward his face.
When they are situated in their respective places, it is declared to be the common [form].
Marīci is white in color, and Vivasvān is the color of a cloud.
Mitra is like molten gold, while Bhūdhara has a black face;
Savitṛ has the luster of a blue color, and Sāvitra has a smoky body.
Indu has the luster of the color of dawn, and Indrajaya is white;
Rudra resembles coral, and likewise Rudrajaya is yellow.
Āpa is white as cow’s milk; Āpavatsa has the luster of a japā flower;
Īśāna is white as milk; Parjanya is like collyrium. (2–364)
Jayanta is like black aloe-wood (añjana); Mahendra has a dark-blue luster;
Āditya should be red in color; and Satyaka is variegated in hue. (2.365)
Vṛṣa has the luster of a bandhūka flower, while Antarikṣaka has the luster of a kunda flower;
Agni has the brilliance of the rising sun, and Pūṣan resembles the radiance of jewels.
Vitatha is like a rainbow, Vidyutvarṇa is the guardian of the house, Nirṛti has the luster of fire, and Dauvārika is remembered as yellow. (2-367)

Sugrīva has the luster of a peacock’s neck; Candrābha is like the moon; Puṣpadantaka is like a flower-toothed one; Varuṇa has limbs with the brilliance of crystal; and the Asura is considered to have the luster of a bumblebee. (2-368)
Yama is like collyrium in appearance, the Gandharva is like a ruby;
Bhṛṅgarāja has the luster of a bumblebee, and Mṛga resembles a cloud. (2.369)
Wasting away (śoṣa) resembles a blue lotus, and the disease (roga) is like sapphire;
Vāyu is blackish in color, and the serpent Śeṣa is like the crescent moon. || 2.370 ||
Mukhya resembles a pearl, Bhallāṭa is like a white lotus,
Soma is like crystal, and Argala has the luster of a red lotus.
Diti is remembered as white as a jasmine flower or the moon, while Aditi is tawny;
Carakī resembles a conch shell, and Vidārī has the brilliance of fire.
Pūtanā resembles snow, has the luster of a cloud, and possesses a tuft of hair;
she likewise holds a sword, a drinking vessel, a knife, and a pair of scissors.
Those who assume terrifying forms are proclaimed to be the Rākṣasīs;
Skanda and the other Grahas are white, red, yellow, and black. (2-374)
Holding a vajra, a spear, a sword, and a noose, those with distorted faces are declared to be the terrifying grahas, beginning with Skanda. (2.375)

Having meditated thus and worshipped with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*), one should likewise meditate upon Vāstupuruṣa as described. Then, according to the Vedic tradition, with the aforementioned Vedic mantra, or according to the Tantric tradition, with the mantra *oṃ vāstoṣpataye namaḥ*, one should worship him with the five offerings. To the east or west of that, having constructed a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) or a leveled altar (*sthaṇḍila*) measuring one cubit and possessing three ridges (*trimekhala*), one should establish the fire there according to the procedure to be described hereafter, and invoke the deities beginning with Brahmā from the mandala into that place.

p. 115) Having offered oblations to them according to the previously stated number and having performed the *pūrṇāhuti*, one should again invite the deities into the maṇḍala and offer a *bali* to each of them.
The *balimantras* and the varieties of substances [are described] in the *Gautamīya* and the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*:
"Combined with milk-rice, boiled rice, and parched grain, along with incense and flowers..."
And it was joined with rice and other foods, adorned with black gram cakes and the like.
"O Brahman, accept this offering and destroy the defects of the site;
it consists of scents and other ingredients in the form of sugar, combined with milk-rice. (2-377)
"O Noble One, accept this; destroy all defects!
O Lord, it is honored with sandalwood and the like, and adorned with camphor and agallochum. (2.378)
O Vivasvat, indeed, accept this; destroy every defect, O Lord—this milk-rice with molasses, well-provided with flowers and other offerings. (2–379)
"Accept this pleasing bali-offering, O friend, and grant me peace;
it consists of black-gram rice with meat, combined with perfumes and the like, along with milk. (2-380)
"O King, take this and destroy every defect.
Having thus worshipped in the center, one should offer the bali-oblation starting from Īśāna.
By this [rule], even when the sequence begins with the southeast (āgneya) during worship, the sequence for the *bali* offering begins with the northeast (īśāna).
This applies elsewhere as well:
"The *bali* offering is generally said to proceed clockwise from the northeast."
Indeed, for all things, the distinction lies in the determination of their status. (2.382)
In some places, however, worship is likewise prescribed:
"One should worship the deities in the northeast and other corners according to the rule;
the wise one should worship those situated in the four corners beginning with Īśāna. (2.383)
Likewise: "Accept this offering (bali) joined with milk and sugar, adorned with flowers and other [offerings]; having accepted it, O Āpa, grant me peace. (2-384)
"O child, accept this curd mixed with molasses and well-endowed with perfumes and other offerings; receive this bali-offering and destroy all obstacles here. (2-385)
O Savitṛ, accept this water with flowers and kuśa grass, scented with sugar and agallochum; grant me peace in this matter.
O Lord Sūrya, accept this offering of flour-cake with molasses, adorned with red perfumes and the like; destroy all obstacles here.
O Lord Śakra, accept this cold food, as well as these flowers beautifully adorned with saffron and other substances; having accepted this domestic offering, salutations be unto you.
O Indrajaya, accept this domestic offering (bali) consisting of rice mixed with clarified butter and adorned with garments, perfumes, and other ornaments; homage be unto you! (2-389)
O God Rudra, accept this offering consisting of cooked and uncooked meat, along with cloth, flowers, and other items; we pay homage to you.
Accept this offering (bali), consisting of meat cooked with ghee and combined with perfumes, flowers, and other ingredients; O Rudrajaya, may there be well-being; salutations unto you!
O Vidārī, take this red flower together with meat, accompanied by red garments and the like; destroy this obstacle of the Rākṣasa.
Joined with bile, blood, and bone, and adorned with the scent of blood and other things—O Pūtanā, accept this; destroy the obstacle of the Rākṣasa.
O Śarva, accept this offering of black gram cooked with rice and ghee, combined with red perfumes and other substances; destroy the obstacles caused by Rākṣasas.
O Skanda, accept this bali-offering, provided with meat, flowers, and the like, and adorned with black gram cakes; destroy the Rākṣasas and obstacles.
Dog meat mixed with flour, accompanied by cooked meat and water—O Aryaman, accept this and destroy all obstacles! (2-396)
O Jṛmbhaka, accept this blood, meat, rice, fish, along with perfumes and incense; destroy the obstacle of the Rākṣasa. (2-397)
O Pilapiccha, accept this meat provided with goat's ears, accompanied by garments, perfumes, and other offerings; destroy this obstacle of the Rākṣasa!
O Carakī, accept this meat prepared with clarified butter and endowed with garments, perfumes, and other offerings; destroy this obstacle caused by the Rākṣasas. || 2-399 ||
O Lord, accept this bali offering— consisting of cooked rice with ghee and unbroken grains, adorned with garments, perfumes, and other ornaments— which removes all defects of the site (vāstu).
"O King of Clouds, accept this offering consisting of blue lotuses mixed with milk-rice and accompanied by garments and other gifts; homage be unto you! (2-401)
O son of Jiṣṇu, accept this five-cubit long, bright yellow banner adorned with offerings such as rice; accept this household oblation, salutations be unto you!
O King of Gods, accept this domestic offering of cooked rice filled with clarified butter and adorned with the five jewels and other gems; homage be to you!
Accept this pleasing bali-offering consisting of cooked food mixed with red flowers and endowed with red perfumes and other such items; obeisance be to you, O Bhāskara! (2-404)

O Satya, accept this canopy, which has the luster of smoke-colored clouds and is beautifully adorned with perfumes and other offerings; accept this red flower and this bali-offering; salutations be unto you!
But please accept this offering of meat, as well as this worship with garments, perfumes, and other items;
take this bull-offering and destroy the defects of the site.
But take this grassy meat, together with the sacrificial offerings and the like;
accept this pleasing bali-offering, O Vyoman, and grant me peace. (2-407)
O Saptajihva, accept this gold, flour-cake, and garments, perfumes, and so forth, accompanied by clarified butter; homage be to you! (2.408)
O God Pūṣan, accept this pleasing offering consisting of milk mixed with parched grain and joined with perfumes, flowers, and other articles; salutations be unto you! (2.409)
O Lord of Vitatha, accept this offering of meat-rice accompanied by perfumes, garlands, and ornaments such as clothing; destroy the defects of the site! 2-410.
O King Yama, accept this bali offering consisting of cooked rice mixed with fish and meat, adorned with perfumes, flowers, and other ornaments; grant me peace.
Accept this pleasing cooked meat, rice, fresh butter, and ornaments such as clothing; O Guardian of the House, homage be to you! (2.412)
O Gandharva, accept this offering combined with various fragrances and joined with red perfumes and the like; destroy all defects.
But take this tongue of a bird placed upon a meal of black beans;
accept this offering of *bhṛṅgarāja* and grant me peace. (2.414)
Thus, [O] Mṛgadeva, accept this pleasing bali-offering provided with sesame and ghee, joined with perfumes, flowers, and so forth; homage be to you! (2-415)
O King of Rākṣasas, accept this offering with pleasure; it is adorned with sugar-candy, cloth, perfumes, and other ornaments. Homage be to you! (2.416)
O Gatekeeper, accept this pleasing offering consisting of pieces of sandalwood, agallochum, and kākhaṇḍa, combined with garments, perfumes, and other items; homage be to you! (2.417)
But this milk-rice, O Lord Sugrīva, mixed with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings—accept this oblation and grant me peace. (2.418)
O God of Water, accept this pleasing offering of milk adorned with barley-gruel and accompanied by cooked rice; salutations be unto you!
"O Puṣpadanta, accept this black-gram rice and a bunch of *kuśa* grass combined with ghee, fragrance, and other offerings; destroy the defects of the site (*vāstu*). (2-420)
O Lord of Asuras, accept this offering of ground flour prepared with honey and adorned with perfumes and other substances; destroy all defects.
"O Śoṣa, accept this offering (bali) consisting of ghee combined with food and mixed with camphor and other ingredients; grant me complete peace."
O Lord, accept this offering of barley and rice, adorned with perfumes, flowers, and the like; O Disease, destroy all defects. (2-423)
O Lord whose vehicle is the deer, accept this pleasing offering of a sweetmeat ball with ghee, adorned with various foods; salutations be unto you! (2.424)
But this *kṛsarā* food, prepared with the scent of milk and other ingredients—O Lord of Pātāla, accept this and destroy whatever obstacle is here. (2.425)
O Chief One, accept this offering consisting of coconut water, cooked rice, yellow garments, and other items; destroy the defects of the site.
"Endowed with the fragrance of curd and other such qualities, and accompanied by yellow flowers—O Soma, may this offering be accepted; destroy all defects. (2-427)
O Bhallāṭaka, accept this domestic offering of cooked rice mixed with clarified butter and accompanied by fragrant flowers; homage be unto you! (2.428)

O you named Argala, accept this pleasing offering of black gram cooked with rice, anointed with clarified butter and adorned with perfumes, flowers, and other ornaments; salutations be unto you! (2.429)
O Mother of the Daityas, accept this [offering] combined with milk and sugar-candy and adorned with various flowers; destroy all defects.

O Mother of the Gods, accept this domestic offering (bali), consisting of parched grain flour mixed with honey and combined with garments, perfumes, and other articles; accept it, O Goddess, salutations be unto you! (2.431)
May the deities and the deities of the site in heaven, the netherworld, and the mortal realm accept this pleasing bali offering; being satisfied, may they depart for their own abodes. (2-432)
May the Mothers, the Bhūtas, the Vetālas, and whoever else desires the bali-offering,
as well as those who are the attendants of Viṣṇu— they too should accept this bali.
Having offered the bali-oblation to the ancestors and the guardians of the field according to one's desire,
one should worship with kuśa grass, flowers, and so forth, in the absence of the prescribed path.
In the *Prayogasāra*:
"The remainder of the site-offering (*vāstuśeṣa*), purified by ritual action, effects all protective rites;
it brings about prosperity and joy, and in this [context], one should offer the oblation to the quarters (*diśāṃ bali*). (2.435)

That which is intended for all beings, including the assembly of the guardians of the directions, and consists of worship ending with the ritual dismissal (visarjana) by means of their names, should be known as the bali offering to the directions.

One should offer the directional oblation (bali) by means of substances consisting of curd, water, turmeric, flowers, parched grain, flour-meal, sesame seeds, and food, according to the sequence of the directions.
Furthermore, it [is the source] of the gods, of the luminaries, of living beings, and even of the Rākṣasas;
likewise of the waters, of the vital breaths, and of the stars. (2.438)
One should not offer oblations to the lords of the sciences in any other manner than as stated;
for their retinues and powers, the formula is said to include the term "with vehicle" (savāhana).
Then, joined with "to all those attendants," and further with "to the spirits" (bhūtas) in succession, one should cast the bali offering while moving clockwise.
For those who desire protection from enemies, piśācas, vetālas, and rākṣasas in this world, the offering to the directions (diśāṃ bali) specifically bestows the abundance of all prosperity. (2.441)

For the consecration of a site, the sprouting of a house, injury to living beings, the entry into a new home, and when a peace-offering (śāntihoma) is performed, the offering to the quarters (diśāṃ bali) should be employed for the sake of success. || 2-442 ||
Having thus offered the *bali*, having again worshipped them, and having recited [mantras] according to one's ability, praised them, and prostrated, one should dismiss them.
The mantra for dismissal is as follows:
"May all the hosts of deities depart, taking with them this earthly worship."
For the sake of fulfilling desired wishes and for the purpose of returning once more. || 2-443 ||
Having thus dismissed the deities, one should worship the spade;
as it is stated in another [text]:
"Resorting to an auspicious moment (muhūrta), let the site-grid (vāstukoṣṭhaka) be excavated."
The state of being a golden spade [is attained] by the act of digging the earth. (2-444)
"O you whose weapon is Viśvakarman, eternal salutations to you who are the very embodiment of the divine missiles.
Having thus worshipped the golden spade, one should worship the man who digs with the thought that he is Viśvakarman himself:
"He has two arms, a yellow body, wears matted locks, and sits upon a lotus. (2-445)
Viśvakarman is eternally fair-complexioned, holding the gesture of knowledge (jñānamudrā) and a rosary;
O Viśvakarman, you who pervade the universe and are the creator of the manifestation of worldly existence.
O Viśvakarman, here you stand with a spade in hand; salutations to you, whose work consists of the universal self within the Vāstu divided into eighty-one squares.
"Take this spade and now perform the digging here.
Thus he should place the spade and the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) into his hand. Then he should pray to the Earth:
"Even by the hundreds of millions of insects torn apart here by the spade... (2-448)
"Forgive me, O Goddess Earth, for the purpose of establishing Viṣṇu.
Having thus entreated the Earth, the person acting as the digger, who is of the nature of Viśvakarman, should perform the digging within the side-sections of the Vāstupuruṣa.
As it is stated in another Tantra:
I shall now describe, in due order, the auspicious and inauspicious characteristics of sites.
One should always indicate auspiciousness in the armpit and everywhere else; however, if it occurs on the head, there will be death, and if on the neck, one will surely experience suffering. (2-450)
One should know that [a tremor] in the hand indicates fear of thieves; on the chest, the loss of cattle; on the knees, travel to a foreign land; and on both feet, fruitlessness. (2-451)
The site of the temple (vāstukṣetra) is declared to be thus, [divided] as left and right;
the skillful mantra-practitioner should cause auspiciousness to be performed for the sake of perfection. (2.452)
Having become composed in mind, one should dig in the site-section.
This is the ritual procedure for the Vāstu-sacrifice.
Now follows the determination of the pavilion required for initiation (dīkṣā).
In that regard, first is the means for knowing the directions such as the east for the purpose of constructing the pavilion.
As it is said in the *Kriyāsāra*:
"Having made the ground level there, one should draw a circle measuring one cubit. (2.453)
The wise practitioner should place there a gnomon made of khadira wood, twelve finger-breadths in height; or, if that is unavailable, one made of sacrificial wood.
Wherever its shadow touches, that point in the middle is known as the center;
one should extend a cord transversely through the center, and those two points are known as south and north.
The other four corners are formed by the extension of four lines; thus has the clear understanding of measurement been fully explained. (2-456)
Having understood this, the wise practitioner should properly construct the pavilion and other structures.
When the sun has reached the equinox, one should perform the measurement with a gnomon (*śaṅku*). (From the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*, 2.457)
One should fix a stake made of khadira wood, twelve finger-breadths in width;
having rendered it immovable, one should strike it while holding an iron mallet.
One should strike oneself eight times, beginning from the left and proceeding in order;
when the stake is being struck, if the mallet falls from the hand, [it is a sign of success]. (2.459)
Then a great and insurmountable grief arises for the one who strikes;
[this applies to] a belt made of muñja grass, cotton, silk, or even that derived from the hair of living beings. (2.460)
One should wrap a thread four *yava*s in circumference around the peg; at the very moment the thread being wrapped leaves the peg, [it marks the point]. (2-461)
One should know that the death of a son indicates one's own destruction when the [thread] is severed;
even in that case, the destruction of inauspiciousness occurs through a *nārasiṃha* oblation. (2.462)

(From the Śāradātilaka: On an auspicious day favorable to the lunar mansion, the zodiacal sign, and the day of the week, one should then [proceed] upon a pure patch of ground, free from husks, charcoal, and the like. (2.463)
Having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), one should construct a beautiful pavilion measuring five,
seven, or nine cubits, O best of men.

Regarding this, Rāghavabhaṭṭa has explained in his *Padārthādarśa* that, according to the literal interpretation of the text, since the requirements for the eight sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍas*), the altar (*vedi*), the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), and the area for their movement would otherwise be untenable, the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) is twelve cubits (*hasta*) by the phrase "with five and seven," fourteen cubits by the phrase "with five and nine," and sixteen cubits by the phrase "with seven and nine. Nṛsiṃhaṭhakkura also stated the same in his *Tārābhaktisudhārṇava*. By this, it is said that there are three types of pavilions: the smallest at twelve cubits, the medium at fourteen cubits, and the largest at sixteen cubits.
As it has been said in the *Pratiṣṭhāsārasaṃgraha*:
"This [measurement] begins with twelve cubits as the smallest; from there, it increases successively by two at each step.
As for that which...
But for the purpose of performing the fire-oblation, consecration, and other rites for kings, [one should construct] a pavilion.
"One should construct [the pavilion] with nine cubits, endowed with specific width and length"—
this statement from the *Tantrarāja* refers to a pavilion intended for ritual acts other than initiation (*dīkṣā*).
(In the *Siddhāntaśekhara*)
The ground for the pavilion is said to have a height of twelve finger-breadths from the base.
In the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*, however, it is stated:
"The height shall be one cubit, perfectly level and very beautiful. [In the *Śāradā*:]
It is provided with sixteen pillars, four of which are situated in the center. (2.468)
Twelve [pillars] should be erected all around, eight cubits in height;
they should measure five cubits [in circumference], be without gaps, straight, and auspicious. (2.469)
The best knower of the tantra should bury one-fifth of that in the earth;
according to the Vāstuśāstra, one should place one-fifth in the ground—this is the rule common to all. (2.470)
(In the *Śāradātilaka*): One should cover it on the outside all around with coconut leaves.
The phrase "with coconut leaves" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*).
And likewise, [it is stated] in the *Merutantra*:
"One should further cover it with coconut leaves, bamboo, and mats. (2.471)
"Just as there would be no fear from storms, rain, and the like, so too, according to the *Vāstuśāstra*,
the pavilions such as the Vijaya and others should be well-covered with mats. (2–472)
The establishment of the pillar should be performed in the sequence beginning with the southeast (Agni), according to the statement:

"In the case of raising the pillar, laying the stone, the application of the cord, the peg, and the commencement of the excavation and the preparation of the pit, [these] are within the domain of Fire. (2.473)
(In the *Siddhāntaśekhara*):
In the center there should be a set of four pillars, and in their midst a pedestal (*vedikā*) is prescribed. Having placed pillars that embody the Vedas at the corners of the pedestal... (2.474).
In the *Pañcarātra*:
"One should make the pillars firm, straight, and equal, fashioned from heartwood.
In the *Kriyāsāra*: [same].
For the work of making pillars, one should use a sacrificial tree, bamboo, or betel-nut wood. || 2.475 ||
Others may be pure trees, not inferior plants;
[but one that is] a thorn in the house, naturally withered, crooked, and ancient [should be avoided]. (2-476)
That which is produced from inauspicious ground should be abandoned for the rite of pillar-installation.
(From the *Mantramuktāvalī*):
One should construct four doors in the cardinal directions, each measuring one-fifth [of the total]. (2.477)
In the *Pañcarātra*, the door for the smallest [size] should be two cubits, increasing by four finger-breadths for the medium and the largest; thus one should behold the beautiful gate. (2.478)
According to the system of Somaśambhu, arches made of Plakṣa, Udumbara, Aśvattha, and Vaṭa wood should be constructed in order starting from the east;
or alternatively, there may be a reversal of the sequence at the beginning and end. (2.479)
If not one of these is available, one should establish even a single [linga] in all directions.
(From the *Siddhāntaśekhara*):
"If not even one of these is available, there may be [one]; in its absence, a *śamī* tree. (2.480)
The Jambu, Khadirasāra, and Tāla trees are prescribed for the archways (toraṇa). (In the Mahākapila-pañcarātra:
The gods are stationed in the form of archways within the sacrificial pavilion. (2-481)
For the purpose of destroying obstacles and for the protection of the sacrifice,
one should place a *nyagrodha* tree in the eastern direction and likewise an *udumbara* tree in the southern direction.
One should place a Pippala tree in the west and a Plakṣa tree in the north;
moreover, a very beautiful tree in the east should be consecrated with mantras from the Ṛgveda and other Vedas.
With the mantra "iṣe tvā," one should place the one named Subhadra in the south;
with the mantra beginning with the Sāmaveda, one should place the one named Sukarman in the west.
One should place Suhotra on the north with the mantra *śanno devī*.
"From the Ṛgveda, etc. means it is consecrated with the mantra *agnim īḷe purohitam*. [It is consecrated] from the Sāmaveda, etc., with the mantra *agna ā yāhi*.
(In the *Śāradātilaka*, p. 126).
At the gateways, there should be arches made, in sequence, from the milky trees.
The height of each of those pillars is recorded as seven cubits;
their circumference is said to be ten finger-breadths. (2.486)
The measurement of the horizontal beam (tiryakphalaka) should be half the measurement of the pillar;
one should fashion the spikes (śūla) in the middle of the archway (toraṇa) according to the measurement of a cubit.
"By seven cubits" refers to the case of the inferior pavilion.
As it is stated in the *Vāstuśāstra*:
"They [the pillars] are five cubits in measure, and two cubits in width."
But by increasing [the length] by six finger-breadths and so on, it is likewise seven cubits in the highest [grade].

"Six finger-breadths, etc. means that, according to this, the ground between the two *toraṇa* pillars in the lowest pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) is two cubits; in the middle one, it is two cubits plus six finger-breadths; and in the highest one, it is two cubits plus twelve finger-breadths. By this, the measurement of the horizontal beam (*tiryak-phalaka*) of the pavilion is also stated. Since the heights of five and seven cubits are mentioned for the lowest and highest [pavilions] respectively, the height of six cubits is thereby stated for the middle one; so says the author of the *Sudhārṇava*. "One should arrange the trident, etc. refers to the placement of the trident (*triśūla*) in the Śaiva and Śākta systems. However, a specific rule is stated for the Vaiṣṇava system in the *Merutantra*: [The *Merutantra* continues: "In the Vaiṣṇava tradition, the trident should be drawn with its points directed downward, and the *yantra* should be fashioned from the center of the lotus. It should be made with three spokes (*ara*), or else with four spokes, or even with eight spokes. It should be fashioned with the *yantra* of the *Śrīvatsa*, or likewise with the *yantra* of the *Kaustubha*. Or it may be fashioned with the *yantra* of the *Vanamālā*, or else with the *yantra* of the *Garuḍa*. Or it may be fashioned with the *yantra* of the *Cakra*, or likewise with the *yantra* of the *Śaṅkha*. Or it may be fashioned with the *yantra* of the *Padma*, or likewise with the *yantra* of the *Gada*. Or it may be fashioned with the *yantra* of the *Vajra*, or likewise with the *yantra* of the *Dhvaja*. Or it may be fashioned with the *yantra* of the *Mudgara*, or likewise with the *yantra* of the *Muṣala*. Or it may be fashioned with the *yantra* of the *Kheṭaka*, or likewise with the *yantra* of the *Pāśa*. Or it may be fashioned with the *yantra* of the *Aṅkuśa*, or likewise with the *yantra* of the *Śakti*. Or it may be fashioned with the *yantra* of the *Brahmāṇḍa*, or likewise with the *yantra* of the *Viśvabimba*. Or it may be fashioned with the *yantra* of the *Mahābhūta*, or likewise with the *yantra* of the *Navagraha*. Or it may be fashioned with the *yantra* of the *Rāśicakra*, or likewise with the *yantra* of the *Tithicakra*. Or it may be fashioned with the *yantra* of the *Nakṣatra*, or likewise with the *yantra* of the *Yoginī*. Or it may be fashioned with the *yantra* of the *Mātṛkā*, or likewise with the *yantra* of the *Mantra*. Or it may be fashioned with the *yantra* of the *Tattva*, or likewise with the *yantra* of the *Kalā*. Or it may be fashioned with the *yantra* of the *Varṇa*, or likewise with the *yantra* of the *Bīja*. Or it may be fashioned with the *yantra* of the *Mudrā*, or likewise with the *yantra* of the *Āyudha*. Or it may be fashioned with the *yantra* of the *Loka*, or likewise with the *yantra* of the *Deva*. Or it may be fashioned with the *yantra* of the *Pīṭha*, or likewise with the *yantra* of the *Sthāna*. Or it may be fashioned with the *yantra* of the *Tīrtha*, or likewise with the *yantra* of the *Puṇya*. Or it may be fashioned with the *yantra* of the *Mantra*, or likewise with the *yantra* of the *Japa*. Or it may be fashioned with the *yantra* of the *Homa*, or likewise with the *yantra* of the *Arcana*. Or it may be fashioned with the *yantra* of the *Dhyāna*, or likewise with the *yantra* of the *Samādhi*. Thus, O King, the *yantra* should be fashioned according to the specific injunctions of the various *tantras*."

In the Vaiṣṇava [mandala], one should place the conch, discus, mace, and lotus with a twelfth part [of the area] according to the sequence starting from the east; even a Saura may likewise be a Vaiṣṇava in this regard.
(From the Śāradā-tantra:
One should tie banners to the directions that possess a splendor equal to that of the world-protectors;
one should adorn the pavilion with canopies, garlands of darbha grass, and other such items. (2.490)
In the *Pratiṣṭhāsārasaṃgraha*:
"The banners are recorded as being yellow, red, and other colors, measuring five cubits;
they are joined with poles made of bamboo, measuring ten cubits, and are [to be] straight. (2-491)
At other places as well, it is said:
"The banners should be made five cubits long, or in an alternative case, two cubits. (p. 127)
And the staff, ten cubits long, one should place those in the ten directions.
(In the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*):
One should decorate the pillars with mirrors, chowries, and bells, as well as with cloths, jars, small bells, and likewise with bases and pebbles. (2.493)
In that regard, one water-pot (kalaśa) should be placed at each archway (toraṇa); two at each side of every door; and one at each corner. As it has been said:
"One should place within those pots vessels provided with perfumes, flowers, and garments."
Upon those archways,
one should certainly worship Dhruva, Dharā, Vākpati, and Vighneśa.
In the pitchers located at the corners of the pavilion, these [deities] are to be placed in sequence:
Amṛta, Durjaya, Siddhārtha, and likewise Maṅgala. (2.495)
In the jars situated at the entrance of the worship hall, Śakra and the other deities [should be invoked] with their respective supreme mantras.
Furthermore, it is stated elsewhere:
"One should place two jars at each and every door within the pavilion. (2.496)
Filled with water that has flowed [from the source] and adorned with mango sprouts (as described in the Śāradā-tantra),
one should construct [a structure] three parts of that [area] in size, rising to the height of one aratni.
Then, one should prepare a square altar for the mandala.
(From the *Tripurāsārasamuccaya*):
Then, in the center of that [mandala], which is provided with four gates,
the wise one [should construct] a pedestal (*vedī*) using one-third of that [central area].
One should also make it one cubit in height, as beautiful as the reflection within a mirror, and captivating to the mind. (2.498)
