In this context, O Śivā, a fist is formed by those four [fingers] raised to the measure of one *aratni*; a *vitasti* consists of three such [fists]; an *aratni* is made from two of those; and a *hasta* is likewise [formed] from two [of the former]. (2.499)
Thus, according to the words of the *Mantrarāja*, the author of the *Sudhārṇava* states that the terms "cubit" (*aratni*) and "hand" (*hasta*) are synonyms.
(Also in the *Kriyāsāra*:
Having divided the pavilion into three parts, there shall be an altar in the middle portion.
Its height should be one cubit, and it should be square and level.
In the *Merutantra*:
"In the initiation of the Left-hand path (*vāmamārga*), it has three channels; in the Vaiṣṇava sacrifice, it is white like a conch shell.
A square altar with four corners bestows all fruits. (2.501)
In that very place:
one should fasten a very white canopy over the pavilion;
one should decorate it with flower garlands and the like, and encircle it. (2.502)
With a long garland made from mango and *aśvattha* leaves joined together,
one should wrap the pillars with fine silk cloths (*dukūla*) and construct an altar in their center.
One should construct a pedestal for the pavilion using unbaked bricks, measuring one cubit in width and [respectively] five, eleven,
nine, seven, five, and three cubits in length.
Or else, having observed the relative proportions of the various parts, the pavilion should be constructed so that there is a complete integration of all the constituent elements. (2.505)
Thus ends the description of the pavilion. Now, the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas).
(In the Śāradā-tantra:)
In the pavilion previously described, the wise man, having divided the area outside the altar into three parts,
should designate the directions starting from the east within the central portion.
In the eight directions, sacrificial pits of beautiful form should be arranged in sequence: square, yoni-shaped, half-moon, triangular, and circular. (2.507)
(129) A six-cornered [pit] shaped like a lotus and an eight-cornered one—these are their names.
The pit for the Preceptor (ācārya) should be in the center, between the Lord of Gaurī and Mahendra. (2-508)

(Also in the *Tripurāsārasamuccaya*): Beginning from the direction of Indra (the East), one should construct within that [mandala] a four-cornered [figure], a yoni-shaped [figure], one resembling half a boat, a fire-weapon-shaped [figure], a perfect circle, a six-cornered [figure], a lotus-shaped [figure], and an elephant-trunk-shaped [figure].

In the center there is a circle; some scholars have stated that in the direction of Gaurī’s husband (the north-east) there is a square, in the north-west a five-cornered [kuṇḍa], and in the direction of Madana’s enemy (the north) a seven-cornered kuṇḍa.
The definitions of these [terms] follow in sequence in that very same source:

"First, having laid down a thread in the east, a person of pure intellect should mark its middle with half [of its length], forming a pair of fish (two intersecting circles) between the directions of Yama and Kubera."
Having stretched out a cord from those two [points], one should then mark the four corners;
thus the field shall be square, and one may construct other sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) within it. || 2-510 ||
Having cast one portion of the *bhūta* (the outer square) outside the field here in front, one of sharp intellect should grasp it and rotate it by half of a corner and again half of that;
likewise, one should drop two threads as far as the next corner.
One should fashion it in the center; this becomes the Manmathāvāsa kuṇḍa.
Having set aside two parts,
the wise one should properly rotate [the cord] by that measure above and below in what has been made into rows.
This pit shall be known as the "Half-Moon" (ardhacandra). || 2-512 ||
Having divided the field into two halves of the night, the wise man should place two parts on both sides;
with that measurement, he should lay down two lines.
This pit shall have nine eyes as its garland. || 2-513 ||
From the portion consisting of lines exceeding those of the world-elephants (*diggaja*), one of sharp intellect should lay out the field externally;
by rotating a single part of this in every direction, an excellent circle is produced. (2.514)
Having placed two large portions outside on both sides from the center, one of pure intellect should, by that measurement,
mark the placement of six lines forming a pair of fish-tails on both sides at the edge of the field.
One should construct the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa); this one, having three corners, is pleasing to the mind. || 2-515 ||
Having laid out one-tenth of this [circle] on the outside and rotated by that same measure, one should draw the circle of the petals;
furthermore, one should fashion the pericarp between the outer and middle [circles].
A wise man should construct a lotus-shaped bathing pool with eight petals.

Having cast [the cord] here on the field toward each of the outer directions, having made one part out of a portion equal to two pairs of suns (twelve), and then again taking half from the corner by means of two oceans and a corner (four and a half), the wise man should place marks all around here using that measurement from those two corners; thus there shall be an octagon, and he should extend the application of eight lines on all sides.
Having projected [the center] here at the horse-portion (hayāṃśa) and drawn a circle externally, one should again divide it into four parts;
with three of these parts, the length of the cloth (paṭṭa) shall be five threads.
Therefore, by means of this application, there is this five-pronged sacrificial pit.

Having laid out one part out of ten parts of the field's width here on the outside, and having made it perfectly circular by this measurement, and then again dividing this [circle] into sixty-four parts;
the wise one [should determine] the length of the cloth-strip by these thirty-three parts plus three.
One should construct a seven-cornered sacrificial pit; for this indeed comes about through the application of seven threads. (2.519)
In this context, twenty-four finger-breadths constitute the diameter of a fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) measuring one cubit (*hasta*).
As it is said in the *Śāradā-tilaka* (p. 131):
"Those who know the ritual diagrams (*yantra*) recognize a cubit as beginning with twenty-four finger-breadths."
Of the middle finger-joint of the performer's right hand. || 2-520 ||
The measurement of the middle finger is declared to be the *mānāṅgula*.
In another tantra: "That subtle particle which is seen when the sun's rays pass through a lattice window... (2.521).
First, they declare that to be a *trasareṇu* according to the treatises on valid cognition; eight such *trasareṇus* are known by the wise as a single hair-tip (*bālāgra*). (2.522)
Eight tips of a hair are one *likṣā*, and eight *likṣās* are said to be one *yūkā*.
They say eight *yūkās* are a *yava*, and eight *yavas* are one *aṅgula*.
A *hasta* is declared to consist of twenty-four *aṅgulas*.

Regarding the method of doubling and so forth starting from two *hastas*: the central line of a two-*hasta* pit is to be understood by means of the corner-line of a one-*hasta* pit; likewise, the central line of a four-*hasta* pit is to be understood by means of the corner-line of that [two-*hasta* pit]. The same applies to what follows.
As it has been said in the *Gautamīya-tantra*:
One should excavate a pit measuring two cubits according to the measurement of the ear-piercing cord.
In all fire-pits (*kuṇḍa*) and everywhere, one should expand [the dimensions] according to this rule.
Here, the term "ear-line" (*karṇasūtra*) refers to the diagonal line (*koṇasūtra*).
This has been stated in that very same [text]:
Whatever diagonal cord (koṇasūtra) there may be of each preceding pit (kuṇḍa), [that is used for the subsequent one]. || 2-525 ||
The measurement of each successive sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is declared to be likewise.

By this [calculation], the diameter of a two-cubit (*dvihasta*) pit is thirty-four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*); for a three-cubit pit, it is forty-one finger-breadths and five barley-grains (*yava*); for a four-cubit pit, forty-eight finger-breadths; for a five-cubit pit, fifty-three finger-breadths and six barley-grains; for a six-cubit pit, fifty-eight finger-breadths and seven barley-grains; for a seven-cubit pit, sixty-three finger-breadths and four barley-grains; for an eight-cubit pit, sixty-seven finger-breadths and seven barley-grains; for a nine-cubit pit, seventy-two finger-breadths; and for a ten-cubit pit, seventy-five finger-breadths and seven barley-grains. The area (*kṣetraphala*) of a one-cubit pit, however, is five hundred and seventy-six finger-breadths. In this same manner, it should be understood for the two-cubit and other sizes as well. Although only the one-cubit pit is required for initiation (*dīkṣā*), and thus the two-cubit and larger pits are not used in initiation, they are nevertheless shown here because they are employed in the fire-oblation (*homa*) that is a subsidiary part of the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*), which will be described later.

Regarding the measurement of the excavation and the characteristics of the girdle (*mekhalā*) (in the *Tripurāsārasamuccaya*, p. 132): whatever measurement has been stated for the width of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), that same measurement is prescribed for the excavation as well.
A wise person should fashion the girdle in whatever shape that sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) has. || 2.526 ||
One who is unable to construct so many sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) should make five; one who is unable even for that should make just one.
For it is said in the secret tradition of the Āgamas: "Nine, five, or else one [pit] should be made, endowed with the proper characteristics."
But if there is no capacity for eight, there should be four fire-pits in the cardinal directions according to the Tantric tradition.

"In the event of inability [to construct all five], one should arrange only a single square" (from the *Merutantra*). Regarding the placement of the five sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) according to the position of the five [deities] (as stated in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*): "In the cardinal directions, there are squares and circles; the fifth, however, is within the domain of Īśa. (2.528)
Thus, the placement [of the fire-pit] in the case of a single pit has been described by the teachers;
or else, one should construct a single square pit in the northern direction.
(From the Piṅgalāmata:

A circular pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one cubit, provided with a girdle (mekhalā), a neck (kaṇṭha), and a navel (nābhi), is considered auspicious for daily rites, initiation, pacification, and nourishment. (2.529)
Regarding the measurement of the neck, the *Mahākapilapañcarātra* states: "The neck is proclaimed to be one twenty-fourth part [of the pit].
Outside the excavation, the neck is one finger-breadth wide; this is the rule for all fire-pits. (2.530)
One should calculate one twenty-fourth part as a finger-breadth (aṅgula). || 530ef ||
One should make three girdles in the pit, or two girdles, or indeed one girdle;
above the girdle, one should fashion [the shape] like an elephant's lip.
And also the womb of the builder (kārā) is in the direction of the Hotṛ priest here. || 2-531 ||

(p. 133) By this, having stated that the *yoni* is an integral part (*aṅga*) of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the rules regarding its location, essential form, and orientation have been declared. (In the *Kriyāsāra*):
"A sacrificial pit provided with a navel and a *yoni*, and possessing three girdles (*mekhalā*), is excellent;
a pit with two girdles is middling; one with a single girdle is inferior. (2-532)
(Somaśambhu):
"The sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) for a Brahmin has three ridges (*mekhalā*); for a Kṣatriya, two ridges;
and for a Vaiśya, one ridge... [2.533]
The gradation of the girdles according to the gradation of the sacrificial pit has been stated [in the *Tripurāsārasamuccaya*]:
"In the case of a pit measuring one fist, those girdles should have heights and widths of two finger-breadths, one finger-breadth, and half a finger-breadth, respectively."

In a space measuring one cubit (ratni), those [arches] should have heights and spans of three finger-breadths, two and a half finger-breadths, one and a half finger-breadths, and one finger-breadth respectively, starting from the front. || 2-534 ||
In a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) measuring one cubit (*hasta*), these [measures] for the eye-pupils should be, respectively, four, three, two, and one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*).
In a pit measuring two cubits, they should be six, four, three, and two [finger-breadths].
The stars in front should be one finger-breadth in height. || 2-535 ||
In this temple of four cubits,
the pillars should be two fingers and a palm-tree span (tāla) in height; in this temple of six cubits, ten cubits—
They are equal in height to the span of five fingers. || 2-536 ||
In this [mandala] measuring eight cubits, these [lines] should be joined with a height and width of twelve hundred and eighty-nine finger-breadths;
one should fashion the lotus here at the navel.
It has eight petals together with a pericarp within.

(134) "The navel" (*nābhi*): the meaning is that one should fashion the navel in the center of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) in the form of an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp (*karṇikā*). The dimensions for the womb (*yoni*) and other features therein are stated according to the size of the pit: "The wise declare the *yoni* to be one *muṣṭi* [in area], with a length, width, and height of six, four, and two *aṅgulas* respectively; the *nābhi* here also possesses a height and width of two and four *aṅgulas*, and the lip of the *yoni* is one *aṅgula*. (2.538)
This characteristic of the womb [of the fire-pit] has been declared for a pit measuring one aratni;
indeed, that very same [characteristic] has been stated by me for a pit measuring one hasta.
Regarding the method for increasing the dimensions of the *yoni* and other parts in sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) of two cubits and more, it is stated in that very same source:

"One whose intellect is pure and sharp should increase this *yoni* and the *nābhi* in the other pits by one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) each; likewise, the lip (*oṣṭha*) of the *yoni* here should be increased by a pair of barley-corns (*yava*)."
One may fashion the navel in a circular shape, or even in the form of a pit (kuṇḍa) or some other shape;
however, in this case, one should not place the yoni in the shape of a womb within a lotus-like [design], nor should one fashion the navel there.

By the word "should make," the option for a navel-shape is stated. Regarding the phrase "in the shape of a yoni": the meaning is that one should not make a yoni in a *yoni*-shaped pit (*kuṇḍa*), nor a navel in a lotus-shaped pit.
He states another opinion on that very point:
"Some [authorities] [prescribe] a yoni for a pit measuring only one cubit."
They say it should be two finger-breadths in length and width;
one-third of its width should be its height,
and it should be made in accordance with the petals of the earth-born lotus of awakening.
Regarding that position, he describes its increase and the manner of its construction:
"The navel is provided with a radius equal to the height of two fingers, and there are eight petals on both sides of it."
A wise person should fashion its pericarp in the central portion, measuring one-sixteenth part of the width of the sacrificial pit.
Regarding the measurement of the rim (*nemi*), it is stated in that very same source:
"The beautiful rim of a one-cubit pit should be [one] finger-width all around; from that, one should increase [the size] starting from two cubits."
Within the pit, up to the limit of the directional pits, the wise one should [place] half a finger-breadth for each;
indeed, outside of that, he should construct the three girdles according to the prescribed sequence. (2.543)
In the Vedic tradition, however, fire-pits (kuṇḍas) that lack a navel, a neck, or a womb must not be constructed.
These types of fire-pits are well known in Tantric rites and Smārta rituals;
for according to the Śruti, those lacking a navel, a neck, or a womb are "of bad birth" (viyoni). (2-544)
Thus, from the statement in the *Merutantra*: "The stalk (*nāla*) is said to begin from the base and extend to the middle of the womb (*yoni*), being perforated. (From the *Śāradā* and *Pañcarātra*).
"But it has a thick base and a fine tip, level with the outer girdle. (2.545)
In the *Jñānārṇava*:
"The location situated outside the girdles is called the *sthalam* (ground/base). The *nāla* (tube/axis), obtained from the square *sthalam*, is in the center and possesses a perforation. (2.546)
The gradation of the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) has been stated according to the gradation of the oblations (*āhuti*).
Indeed, for an offering of fifty [oblations] (*śatārdha-homa*), the measure is merely a handful (*muṣṭi-mātra*). (From the *Tripurāsārasamuccaya*)...
The sacrificial pit for one hundred oblations is one *maratni* in measure;
for one thousand, it is one *hasta*; for ten thousand, two *hastas*; and for one hundred thousand, this [pit] is prescribed as four *hastas*.
At ten lakhs [of oblations], there is a hand of mercury; at a crore-homa, a hand of wealth (eight hands);
those who know the eightfold path declare that at half a crore, there is a hand of eight in the homa.
He states another opinion: some [hold] that the pit should be one cubit for a hundred-thousand oblations (lakṣahoma), two cubits for two hundred-thousand, and three cubits for three hundred-thousand.
They say that for a home-altar (kuṇḍa) measuring four cubits, the number [of bricks] is one hundred thousand; for five cubits, it is five hundred thousand.
A sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) of six cubits [in length] is for one hundred thousand [recitations], seven cubits for seven hundred thousand;
for eight hundred thousand it is eight cubits, and for nine hundred thousand it is a pit of nine cubits. (2.550)
A pit measuring ten cubits is prescribed for a sacrifice of one million oblations, and likewise ten cubits for a sacrifice of ten million;
indeed, there is no pit on this earth greater than ten cubits.
The specific fruit of each type of sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) is described in that very same place:
"The pit at the corner of the ocean (northwest) brings about all accomplishments; the one at the end of the abode of the Mind-born (southeast) bestows sons;
the one resembling a half-moon (northeast) grants auspiciousness; and the one at the corner of fire (southwest) is the cause for the increase of enemies. (2-552)
For rites of pacification (śāntika), the pit should be perfectly circular; for rites of destruction (māraṇa), it should be hexagonal.
Here, a lotus-shaped pit causes rain, while an eight-cornered one pacifies disease. (2.553)
He states the distinction of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa) according to the division of castes: "For Brahmins here, the pit is square; for kings, it is circular;
for merchants, it has the shape of a half-moon; but for Śūdras, it is triangular. (2.554)
Some teachers say that for all [types of rites], the square is recommended;
that fire-pit which bestows the desired fruit grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation on this earth. (2.555)
A fire-pit (kuṇḍa) shaped like a hexagon or a half-moon bestows progeny;
one with five corners bestows liberation; and the womb-shaped (yoni) pit with eight corners grants sovereignty.
Likewise,
those of very keen intellect have declared that for both obligatory (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) rites,
a pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one cubit, triangular like the abode of Smara, and elevated, is highly recommended.

A six-cornered sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), resembling the moon with its half-defect [i.e., a crescent], measuring one *ratni* in extent, well-leveled, and fashioned from sand, should be prepared so that it is elevated first at its own thumb-side. || 2-557 ||
(From the Merutantra:
If the pit possesses many defects, such as its measurement being either too small or too large, then one who desires auspiciousness must examine this thoroughly before proceeding. (2.558)
If the pit is too deep, there will be disease; if it is too shallow, there is loss of cattle and wealth.
In a curved pit, there is suffering, while in one with a broken rim, death occurs.
(137) If it lacks a girdle, there is excessive grief; if it lacks wealth, there is danger to one's fortune.
A *kuṇḍa* fashioned without a vulva is said to cause the destruction of one's wife. (2.560)
A sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) that is devoid of a neck is said to cause the destruction of offspring;
likewise, a pit that lacks aesthetic beauty and has a shattered girdle [is also destructive]. (2.561)
If the [mandala] is split, there will be the eradication and destruction of the patron;
if there is an excess of threads, hatred toward friends; if there is a deficiency of threads, poverty. (2.562)
Disease in the stomach when there is no food, and untold suffering when the vessel is broken. (562ef)
Thus is the description of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa):
it is square;
[and] the womb (yoni).
A half-moon.
A triangle.
The meter;
the hexagon; the lotus.
Eight-cornered; five-cornered; seven-cornered.

Regarding the characteristics of the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) (as stated in the *Śāradā-tantra*, p. 139): "The sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) is of one kind; however, one should perform [the rite] on a sacrificial ground.
A square sacrificial ground is recommended for all ritual actions. (2-563)

"On the lunar seat (*candrapīṭha*), however, a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) one cubit in measure should be fashioned from sand and other materials; it is said to be triangular and square, and one span (*vitasti*) in height. (2–564)
Now, regarding the characteristics of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles (*Śāradāyām*):
"The Guru should fashion the *sruk* for the sacrifice according to the method that will be described hereafter, using one of the following trees:
*śrīparṇī*, *śiṃśapā*, or any tree with milky sap. (2.565)
Having taken [the measurement], one should divide it by thirty-six to the extent of one cubit;
the staff (daṇḍa) shall consist of twenty parts, and the altar (vedi) shall consist of eight of those parts.
The neck is measured by one part, and the mouth is measured by seven parts;
the width of the neck is proclaimed to be three parts of the pedestal (vedī). || 2-567 ||
The opening at the mouth should be made equal in width to the throat, measuring one finger-breadth of the little finger, in order to allow the clarified butter to flow out. (2.568)
In the center of the altar, the pericarp (karṇikā) should be fashioned with one part;
one should then fashion a pit (avaṭa) all around it with one part on the outside.
Its pit should be circular with three parts, and with half a part extending outward;
one should fashion the petals all around with a single part.
The rim (nemī) of the Mekhalā and Mukhavedī should be one-and-a-half parts in measurement;
at the tips of the staff (daṇḍa) and trident (śūla), there should be a pitcher (kumbha) measuring three and four finger-breadths respectively.
The pair of *gaṇḍī* (bosses) shall consist of Yama’s parts (two); this is declared to be the *anāha* (circumference) of the staff.
The back portion of the altar (*vedī*) should be shaped like a tortoise and consist of six parts. || 2-572 ||
One should draw the face of either a swan, an elephant, or a boar; the characteristics of the *sruk* ladle are said to be on the back part of the face. (2.573)

*Śrīparṇī* is well known as *gambhārī*. The "milk-bearing trees" (*kṣīraśākhinaḥ*) are the *aśvattha*, *udumbara*, *vaṭa*, *plakṣa*, and *nyagrodha*. "The measure of a hand" (*hastamātram*) means the measure of an arm (*bāhumātram*). This is because of the statement in the *Agastyasaṃhitā*: "One should indeed fashion a *sruk* ladle for the purpose of oblation with the measurement of an arm. *Gaṇḍī* refers to a water-pot (*kalaśaḥ*).
(In the Phetkāriṇītantra:
Also with kāraskara, āmalakī, palāśa, and khadira. (2.574)
One may have them made of gold, silver, copper, or even iron.
(In the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā:
The *sruk* and *sruva* ladles should be taken as being made of metal, not of bell-metal, iron, or lead. (2.575)

Alternatively, they may be made of sacrificial wood according to the Tantras as approved by craftsmen; or they may be made of the leaves of the *brahmavṛkṣa* and other such trees, provided they are without holes, raised in the middle, and intact.
In this context, the injunctions and prohibitions pertain to the domains of the cruel and the gentle.
As it is stated in another tantra:
"The *sruk* and *sruva* ladles should be made entirely of gold in rites pertaining to the gentle."
These two should be made of iron for rites such as immobilization (stambhana) and others.
(In the Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā:
The *sruk* and *sruva* ladles are considered to be made from flawless and beautiful *palāśa* leaves;
or one may prepare them from small *aśvattha* leaves for the performance of the *homa* ritual. (2.578)
(From the *Mantramuktāvalī*):
The wise man should cause the piercing at the difficult passage below the throat on the path of the clarified butter;
he should perform the piercing from the mouth with a heated iron probe. (2.579)
Now, regarding the characteristics of the *sruva* ladle (*Śāradā-tantra*):
One should fashion the *dhruvā* ladle with twenty-four parts;
the measurement of its handle is proclaimed to be twenty-two parts. (2.580)
The swelling (ānāha) has four parts, with its head drawn out by a *karṣa* of clarified butter;
one should bury it two parts deep so that it takes the shape of a deer's footprint in the mud. (2.581)
The gaṇḍī should be at the root and tip of the staff, adorned with a bracelet;
thus has the procedure for the *sruva* been declared. || 2.582 ||
Now, regarding the offering of the germinating seeds (*aṅkurārpaṇa*), [it is said in the *Śāradā-tantra*]:
"Prior to the day of initiation, one should perform the offering of the germinating seeds for seven days according to the rules, in order to ensure the attainment of all auspiciousness. (2.583)
(From the Siddhāntaśekhara:

"In the consecration of an image, in initiation, in the ritual bathing, as well as in festivals, in the sprinkling for the sake of pacification, in marriage, and in the tying of the sacred girdle. (2.584)
In all auspicious rites, one should perform the rite of sowing the seeds (*aṅkurārpaṇa*) seven or nine days prior to the day of initiation (*dīkṣā*), according to the *Merutantra*. (2.585)
This rite of sowing the seed, which grants all desires,
should be performed in the northern part of the pavilion, in a place that is most excellently enclosed.
One should construct the mandala in the dwelling, extending from the east toward the west;
it is highly recommended for the left-hand initiation (vāmā-dīkṣā) when it extends from the south toward the north.
"Bhavana" refers to the interior of the pavilion, which should be understood as having a single entrance on the south side. Likewise:
"On the ground smeared with cow dung, either to the right or to the left..."
With rice mixed with oil, and with the juices of Vijayā mixed with oil.
In that regard, there should be five lines, each five cubits in length; likewise, eleven long lines should be drawn at intervals of one span (vitasti).
There should be forty-four squares; with twenty-four outer squares, there shall be a pathway (vīthī), which one should fill with red powders.
p. 142) Subsequently, that which consists of four squares is declared to be the station of Brahmā;
one should fill it starting from the southeast square and ending at the northeast. || 2-591 ||
With yellow, red, white, and black powders, one should fill two squares from the principal path, and then fill the pathway with red powder alone.
In front of that, however, the four compartments should be known as the station of Viṣṇu;
having filled them with red powders as before, there is also a pathway in front of that.
The four squares situated in the east are declared to be the place of Rudra;
to its east, as before, all the lines are colored with reddish-red.
The four *pālikās*, dedicated to the deity Viṣṇu, should be made in the shape of hand-drums (*ḍamaruka*), each measuring one cubit in width, height, and length. (2.595)
Adorned with dūrvā grass, mango sprouts, and leaves of the aśvattha tree, and bound with thread, one should place them within the four squares of Viṣṇu’s abode.
Those five-faced [deities] belonging to Vairiñca, born from the womb, measuring sixteen finger-breadths in height, elevation, and length, one should subsequently install them. (2.597)
In the station of Brahmā, four Śaiva bowls, twelve aṅgulas in height, are joined with threads made of sprouts and other materials as before. (2.598)

Having washed them and wrapped them with threads, one should place them as before upon heaps of śāli rice, along with fragrant substances and pairs of darbha-grass brushes, in the eastern and other directions.
The *pālikās* are indeed shallow bowls (*śarāva*) shaped like hand-drums (*ḍamaruka*), being exceedingly deep; such specific vessels, when endowed with five faces, are called *pañcamukhyas*.
As it is stated in another Tantra:
"There are four faces in the cardinal directions, and one face situated above them."
One should fill those vessels with sand, clay, and dried cow dung.
The specific procedure for fetching the clay is stated [in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*]:
"On another day, having worshipped the spade with perfumes and other offerings, accompanied by song and dance, and attended by elephants and horses... (2.601).
The preceptor and others, some mounted on chariots and others likewise on elephants, having gone to the bank of a pond, a river, or a flower grove; (2-602)
There, having swept a pure portion of the ground with *darbha* grass while reciting the weapon-mantra (*astra*),
and having sprinkled it with water from the *argha* vessel, one should recollect the respective mantra for each.
Having invoked the Earth with the heart-mantra, one should worship it with perfumes and flowers;
then, having dug the ground with a spade while reciting the weapon-mantra, [one takes] the earth.
Having taken [the earth] with the Vāmadeva mantra, one should fill a bronze vessel;
having worshipped the clay with the Hṛdaya mantra and covered it with a cloth, one should hold it. || 2.605 ||
Having performed a circumambulation of the preceptor amidst the sounds of all auspicious instruments, one should then lead him to the pavilion, whether it be to the city or the dwelling.
A wise person should perform this action during the day, not at night.
"This action" means the action of fetching clay.
However, the sowing of seeds should indeed be done at night.
Soma is the lord of the earth; therefore, one should perform the offering at night.
Thus, from the very statement found therein;
likewise:
"By the sound of the conch, by the fivefold sounds, and by the benedictions of the Brahmins..."
Then, one should sow ten seeds in a vessel made of gold or other precious materials.
The practitioner of mantra should recite the seed-syllable *vaṃ* and then wash [the vessel] with milk;
these [materials] should be consecrated with the root mantra—thus it is stated in the *Śāradā*. (2.609)
Likewise: "Priyaṅgu, śyāmāka, sesame, mustard, and śāli rice; mung beans, āḍhakī, suniṣpāva, khalva, and māṣa beans—these are proclaimed [as the grains]. (2.610)
*Śyāmāka* is well known in common parlance as *sāmā*; *āḍhakī* is well known in common parlance as *rahara*; *niṣpāva* is *simbi*; and *khalvāḥ* are *kulatthāḥ*. Likewise:
"One should scatter [the offerings] first in the vessel of Brahmā, and then in that of Viṣṇu."
Then, in the Śaiva rite, preceded by the sounds of the five musical instruments and the chanting of the Veda, || 2-611 ||
Then, having sprinkled [the area] with yellow water and covered it with cloths,
one should offer the bali-oblation during both twilights and at midnight as well.
Following the path instructed by the guru, one should properly offer the bali-oblation for nine days before the three vessels, dedicating each to its respective deity.
On the first day, this offering (bali) intended for the spirits (bhūtas) is considered to consist of śāli rice, sesame seeds, parched grain, and roasted flour,
combined with turmeric powder.
Thus, on the second day, [offerings] of sesame and rice are for the ancestors;
on the third, groats mixed with curd are for the yakṣas.
One should joyfully offer to the Nāgas a bali of parched grain soaked in coconut water, and on the fifth day, an offering of lotuses and unbroken rice grains to Brahmā.
On the sixth day, rice mixed with ghee and flour is recommended for Śiva;
on the seventh day, one should offer molasses-water to Viṣṇu.
On the eighth day, an offering of milk-rice for Viṣṇu alone is prescribed;
on the ninth day, rice mixed with sesame (kṛsarānna) is likewise recommended for Viṣṇu alone.
The specific rule for the Left-hand Path (vāmamārga) is stated in that very same place:
"In the Left-hand Path, one should offer an oblation (bali) to the mandala in the four directions;
in the station of Brahmā, however, there is a Vetāla, and its oblation is a ram placed before it. (2-619)
In the place of Viṣṇu, Bhairavī should be present, and a goat is considered her sacrificial offering;
but Bhairava, in the place of Śiva, desires a buffalo as his offering.

Gauḍī, mādhvī, and paiṣṭī are considered to be the types of *surā* (alcoholic liquor) there, in that order. Fish, meat, and liquor are prescribed as an offering (*bali*) for the spirits (*bhūta*). (2.621)
For the ancestors, a portion of wine; for the yakṣas, a cock and honey;
for the nāgas, a frog and a mouse; this is the offering on the left-hand path.

(Siddhāntaśekhara) One should worship Soma daily until the day of the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa). When the day of the preliminary consecration has arrived, the preceptor should perform the dismissal (udvāsana) of Soma. (2.623)
(According to the Sārasvata-mata:
One who is not [the teacher] should never look at the fully grown sprouts;
only the teacher himself, or his disciple by his command, may enter. (2.624)
(Merutantra) When these nine days have passed, one should examine:
"Whose emergence has occurred correctly? What has been lost? And what is the intermediate state? (2.625)
If [the seed] has risen perfectly, there is success; if it is blunted, one encounters obstacles.
If it is eaten by insects, the fruit is very small; if it is rotten, there is total destruction. (2.626)

Success is to be known through *priyaṅgu* flowers; with *śyāmāka* grains, there shall be happiness from women; with sesame seeds, there is delight among those worthy of worship; and with mustard seeds, there is malevolent sorcery. (2-627)
Through rice (*śāli*), one attains preeminence over all; through mung beans (*mudga*), there shall be the grace of the gods.
Likewise, through *āḍhakī* beans, one gains four-footed animals; and through *niṣpāva* beans, one gains fields and a house. (2.628)
With *khalva* seeds, there is success in virtuous deeds; with *māṣa* seeds, there shall be peace from enemies.
If all [seeds] emerge on the left, there is success; otherwise, there is a fall. (2-629)
(Siddhāntasāra) 2.630: If the sprout has not emerged or has perished, one should perform a propitiatory oblation (śāntihoma);
one should offer a hundred oblations with either the root mantra or the Aghora-weapon mantra.
Thus concludes the ritual for the offering of the sprout. (p.
146) [I bow] to that most venerable confluence of rivers of excellent compositions, which possesses streams of nectar variegated by the wonderful splendor and the diverse, sacred words of the Bhūtas.
This second wave in this *Puraścaryārṇava* composed by Śrī Naradeva has reached its conclusion, possessing the wonder of a multitude of pearls made clear by sound reasoning. (2.631)

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Rite of Planting the Germinating Seeds (Aṅkurārpaṇa)," preceded by the determination of the time and place of initiation, the sacrifice for the site, the sacrificial pit, the pavilion, and so forth, in the *Puraścaryārṇava* composed by the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja Śrī Pratāpasiṃha Sāhi. || 2 ||
Now, in this pair of waves, the *kriyāvatī-dīkṣā* (initiation involving ritual action) is described.
In the *Śāradā-tantra*,
it is taught to be fourfold, according to the distinctions of *kriyāvatī* and the others.
She consists of action, she consists of form, she is the essence of the kalās, and she is also composed of piercing.
These, which bring about prosperity, are described in sequence in this tantra:
"Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim that which is hidden in all tantras" (Merutantra, 3.2).
The fivefold procedure for initiation is the most excellent of all for kings;
it is superior for those of great wealth, while for ordinary people it is middling.
That which has been spoken for the Brahmins is little, and that for the ascetics is also slight;
therefore, I shall first proclaim that which is equal and most excellent of all.
Upon knowing which [this], the scope of the highest and other divisions becomes manifest.
First, however, a devoted disciple, for the purification of his own body— (Prakaṭayoginī)— 3-5.
Having bathed at a sacred ford (tīrtha), one should recite the Gāyatrī mantra a thousand times while observing a vow for two days, such as eating only one meal a day or fasting.
One should perform the acceptance [of the invitation] on the third day and the initiation on the fourth day;
one should not perform the initiation immediately with a body that has not been consecrated.
According to the Piṅgalāmata and the Mantratantraprakāśa, however:
"Or else, one who is skilled in the ritual of initiation should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) immediately or according to the rule, completing it within two days. (3–8)
It has been stated [in the *Merutantra*]: "The consecration (*adhivāsana*) may take place immediately, or on the same day;
having performed the morning rites on the day prior to the initiation (*dīkṣā*), etc. (3-9).

Having adorned his own body, he should perform worship in his own home according to the ritual for Gaṇeśa; thereafter, he should have the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha-vācana) recited. (3.10)
Having gratified the Nāndīmukhas accompanied by the five musical instruments, and having prepared the materials as prescribed, he should proceed toward the teacher’s house. (3.11)
Five kinds of musical instruments are mentioned in the *Saṅgītiśāstra*:
"The stringed, the wind, the percussion, the metallic, and likewise the solid—these are the five kinds of instruments for the dance of the God of Gods. (3-12)

Stringed instruments (*tata*) include the *vīṇā* and others; wind instruments (*śuṣira*) include the flute (*vaṃśī*), the conch (*śaṅkha*), and others; percussion instruments (*ānaddha*) include the *ḍiṇḍima* drum, the *mṛdaṅga*, and others; and metallic instruments (*ayas-sāra*) include the bell (*ghaṇṭā*) and others.
According to the *Merutantra*, the preparation for the selection of the preceptor (*ācārya*) and the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) is considered to be tenfold.
The seats made of Śrīparṇī wood should be one cubit in measurement according to the standard.
It should be twenty-seven strands of *darbha* grass, equal in length and together eight finger-breadths in height, with its tip adorned by a knot.
The *viṣṭara* (seat) is proclaimed as the characteristic feature in all sacrifices;
copper basins filled with pleasantly warm water are for the purpose of the *pādya* (water for washing the feet).
Conch shells filled with water, scents, and flowers for the offering of *argha*, and water-pots of fine copper filled with water for the ritual sipping (*ācamana*). (3.16)
They brought brass vessels filled with curds and other ingredients for the *madhuparka* offering,
as well as costly garments and fine ornaments such as finger-rings.
One should collect parasols made of peacock feathers along with turbans,
and there one should also fetch sandals adorned with leather ornaments.
Having performed this, one obtains a fruit comparable to the honor accorded at a great sacrifice;
the honoring of other Brahmins with the honey-mixture (madhuparka) is thus prescribed.
One who possesses true devotion should give twice that amount to the teacher with great devotion;
for in that [rite], the worship of the instructor is equal to that of the other twice-born [brahmins].
In that sacrifice, the fruit is meager, just as [the harvest] on the earth is due to drought;
likewise, having gone to the teacher’s house and bowed to the teacher’s sandals— (3.21)
Having presented the materials for the formal offering and having made the formal resolve, he should choose a guru, saying:
"O best of the twice-born, for the purpose of receiving such-and-such a mantra. (3.22)
"Having addressed you with the words, 'I choose you as my guru,' the disciple should say, 'I am chosen,' and then the guru [should accept him]. (3.23)
The disciple should say, "Perform the rite for the Guru as is appropriate," and then the preceptor, by the command of the Guru, should say, "I shall do so. (3.24)

One should choose eight Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas, as well as those who worship the respective deities, for the office of officiating priests (ṛtvij). Or, when [performing the rite], [one may choose] them as such. (3.25)
At that time, four sacrificial pits are prescribed and four officiating priests are appointed;
then the Guru, accompanied by his disciple, shall proceed to the sacrificial hall.
Having sat down at its door, he should then begin the examination;
he should give the disciple a tooth-stick over which the root-mantra has been recited.
Having cleansed his teeth, he should thereafter cast it upon a square sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) measuring one cubit;
the Guru should then examine it.
Regarding that which is situated at the tip of the direction, this is the result starting from the east:
prosperity, mental anguish, loss of kinsmen, and likewise death. (3.29)
Grief, agitation, happiness, knowledge, and gain are the results in successive order;
if it falls upon an inauspicious place, one should perform an expiation.
Or one may recite [the mantra] one thousand and eight times, or one hundred, or even twenty times,
using their names joined with the weapon-mantra (*astra*) and suffixed with *svāhā*.

One should offer oblations with pure clarified butter alone, reciting the mantra "jahi jahī" (slay, slay) until the end of each word; indeed, one should do exactly the same even in the case of a bad dream.
The tooth-stick should be offered again; if it is still defective, it should be offered four times over. If it is defective even for the third time, that deity must not be accepted. (3.33)
On the left-hand path, [the teacher] may destroy both the guru and the disciple even with a single [transgression].
(From the *Siddhāntasaṃgraha*): Having approached the guru, having circumambulated the sacrificial enclosure, and having washed his feet and hands... (3.34).
Having sipped water and standing at the doorway, the preceptor, having bowed to the deity and the guardian of the direction,
should recite two mantras for the purpose of removing sins.
O Deva, this ordinary mind of mine is overcome by evil;
extract that evil from my mind—phaṭ phaṭ! And homage to you! (3-36)
The sun, the moon, Yama, Time, and the five great elements—these nine are the witnesses here in this world of both auspicious and inauspicious actions. (3.37)
Uttering "huḥ phaṭ," one should gaze at the two sides with a wrathful look;
when this is done, whatever great sin exists remains far away. (3.38)
At that very moment, all other sins of the practitioner perish;
for one who has abandoned sin through worship, whatever is desired shall be attained in an instant. (3.39)
Then, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should prepare the general offering (sāmānyārgha).
Regarding the procedure for establishing the general offering (as stated in the *Gautamīya*):
"Thereafter, one should fashion a mandala consisting of a circle and a triangular ground-form. (3–40)
Having worshipped the foundational power (ādhāraśakti), one should place the support (ādhāra) therein;
having purified the vessel with the weapon-mantra (astra), one should fill it with the heart-mantra (hṛnmantra).
Having invoked the sacred ford (tīrtha), one should pour it out while reciting the Praṇava;
then one should indeed display the Dhenu-mudrā—this is known as the general arghya.
One should indeed consecrate [it] with the *praṇava*—[as stated in the Merutantra]:
"Having sprinkled [the area] with water for the *argha* offering, one should perform the worship of the door. (3-43) (Merutantra, p. 151)
The procedure for the worship of the door is as follows:
having sprinkled the door with water for the *argha* offering, one should worship the Lord of Obstacles (*Vighnapa*) in its center;
to its right, Mahālakṣmī, and to its left, Sarasvatī. (3–44)
One should worship Śrī at the door, and in its center, on the right and left branches,
in five divisions each, from the upper part down to the base.
Having uttered the first syllable of each name joined with the bindu, followed by the name ending in the dative case (ṅe) and the word "hṛt," one should worship these deities. (3-46)
Then, with a stream of wealth, one should worship Gaṇapati and Kṣetrapāla,
together with the Śaṅkha treasure on the right and Vasumatī on the left.
Having worshipped Padmanidhi beneath that, one should likewise worship Māyāśakti and Cicchakti on the right and left, as well as Gaṅgā and Yamunā.
Salutation to Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ, and below, salutation to the threshold (dehalī).
This worship is first proclaimed for the western door. (3–49)
The rivers Mahānadī and Mahākālī are to be worshipped at the right and left gates respectively; having thus worshipped the northern gate, one should then worship the eastern and southern gates.
In those [positions], the two gatekeepers are Gaṇeśa and Vṛṣabha respectively;
likewise Bhṛṅgīrīṭa, Skanda, Umā, and Caṇḍeśvara.
Nanda and Sunanda of Viṣṇu, as well as Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍaka;
Bala and Prabala, and also Bhadra and Subhadraka.
Vakratuṇḍa, Ekadaṃṣṭra, Mahodara, Gajānana,
Lambodara, and Vikaṭa are the Gaṇeśas who serve as gatekeepers.
Vighnarāja, smoke-colored, [is positioned] successively from the western door.
(p. 152) These eight—the Goddess, the Sun, and the Yoginīs—are the gatekeepers. 3.54.
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, Cāmuṇḍā, and Śrī. (3.55)
Likewise:
"And then the guide [perceives] the divine obstacles by means of his vision. (3.56)
One should gradually dispel those situated in the intermediate space with water-weapons;
having diligently driven away the terrestrial ones with three kicks of the heels. (3.57)
Having slightly contracted his limb while touching the branch extending to the left,
he bestows armor upon the right side for the sake of dispelling obstacles.
Then, one should enter the sacrificial pavilion with the right foot;
or else, in the Śākta path, one should enter with the left foot first.
One should worship Brahmā and Vāstvadhiśa in the southwestern direction.
(From the *Śyāmārahasya*, cited verses:
"Worship performed without the five purifications leads to malevolent magic (*abhicāra*). (3.60)

Purification of oneself, purification of the place, as well as the purification of the mantra, purification of the substances, and purification of the deity—thus purification is said to be fivefold. (3.61)

O Dear One, self-purification is said to be accomplished through bathing, purification of the elements, breath control (prāṇāyāma), and so forth, as well as by all the ritual depositions (nyāsa) beginning with the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga). || 3.62 ||
(Merutantra) One should sprinkle the interior of the pavilion with the five products of the cow and with water for the arghya offering;
having made it smooth like the surface of a mirror by means of sweeping, smearing, and other such acts. (3.63)
Adorned with pure incense, lamps, flowers, garlands, and so forth, and variegated with five colors—this is considered the purification of the place (sthānaśuddhi). (3.64)
Having taken up the letters of the *mātṛkā* and the syllables of the root mantra, repeating them in successive order twice over—this is considered the purification of the mantra. (3.65)

Having consecrated the materials for worship and other items with the root mantra and the weapon mantra according to the rules, one should display the *dhenu-mudrā*; this is considered the purification of the substances. (3.66)
Having established the Goddess upon the pedestal and performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, the knower of mantras,
radiant in spirit, should consecrate her with water while reciting the root mantra.
The wise one should sprinkle [the materials] three times; this is called the purification of the deity.
Having thus performed the fivefold purification, one should thereafter carry out the sacrifice.
What is performed by one devoid of the five purities is as if not performed at all.
In that very [context]:
"When the place of sacrifice has been well-sprinkled with water for the guest-offering (*arghya*) and with products of the cow (*gavya*). (3.69)
"With the products of the cow" means with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
As it is said in the *Gautamīya*:
"One *pala* of milk is prescribed as one portion, and the cow's urine is desired to be of the same amount."
There should be one pala of ghee and two tolas of cow dung.
The curd should be the measure of one handful; this is remembered as the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Alternatively, equal portions of the five products of the cow are prescribed.
Having consecrated it with the root mantra, one should purify it with the tip of a blade of kuśa grass;
by that, there shall be total purification and the eradication of all sins. (3.72)
In the Smṛti scripture:
taking cow’s urine with the *gāyatrī* mantra, cow dung with "gandhadvārā," milk with "āpyāyasva," and curd with "dadhikrāvṇo. (3.73)
One should purify the ghee with the mantra "tejo 'si" and the kuśa-water with "devasya tvā"; however, if the mantras and so forth are not known, one should purify them with the *praṇava* alone.
(From the *Merutantra*, p.
154): Then one should perform the purification of the four doors by means of the rites beginning with inspection (*vīkṣaṇa*).
Having inspected [the site] with the root mantra, one should then sprinkle it with the weapon mantra (*astra*). (3.75)

One should perform the striking with the weapon-mantra and sprinkle [the object] with the armor-mantra; having been fumigated seven times with sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor using the weapon-mantra.
Having recited the mantra over sandalwood, white mustard seeds, dūrvā grass, ashes, unbroken rice, kusha grass, and parched grain,
the practitioner should scatter them within the pavilion, for they indeed destroy all obstacles.
In another tantra:
"First, having dispelled the obstacles, one should afterwards arrange the seat;
or else, the wise one, remaining on the seat, should dispel the obstacles. (3.78)
(From the Śāradā-tantra:
Fried grain, sandalwood, white mustard, ashes, dūrvā grass, kuśa grass, and unbroken rice—these are designated as the *vikira* offerings, which destroy the entire multitude of obstacles. (3.79)
The mantra for dispelling obstacles (from the *Merutantra*):
With the Nārāca-mudrā and the Astra-mantra, the preceptor [should say]:
"May the bhūtas, piśācas, pretas, and guhyakas depart! (3.80)
And whatever other deities dwell here, established upon the earth— let those beings depart, whatever beings are established upon the earth.
"May those beings who create obstacles perish by the command of Śiva.
Reciting this at the end of the two verses, one should employ the *nārāca* mudrā while reciting the *astra-mantra*.
Having cast them into that pavilion... [as previously stated].
In that very place, the mantra-practitioner should sweep them away with a handful of *darbha* grass using the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*). (3.83)
One should place that *vardhanī* for the seat in the northeast,
having caused the Brahmins to pronounce the auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) and having diligently satisfied them.
(p. 155) One should subsequently draw the Sarvatobhadra maṇḍala upon the altar.
The Sarvatobhadra maṇḍala is described [in the *Śāradātilaka*]: "In a square divided into four compartments and provided with diagonal lines... (3.85).
In each of the four quadrants as well, one should drop four diagonal lines (koṇasūtra) so that fish-shaped figures (matsya) are formed at every intersection.
The practitioner should drop four equal lines upon those fish-marks, two extending from east to west and two extending from south to north.
As before, one should drop diagonal threads into the corner squares;
then, upon the fish-figures produced by those [threads], one should apply four threads.
Then, there should be fish in the corners; one should drop threads upon them.
In the center, with thirty-six squares, one should draw a lotus endowed with excellent characteristics.
Outside, one should arrange the pedestal (pīṭha) with one row [of squares], and the pathways (vīthikā) with two rows;
one should designate the door-decorations (dvāraśobhā) and sub-decorations (upaśobhā) using the remaining [squares]. || 3.90 ||
Then, following the procedure prescribed in the treatises, the wise mantra-practitioner should draw a lotus,
having set aside one-twelfth part of the area of the lotus field on the outside.
One should divide that center into three equal parts by means of three circles:
the first shall be the place for the pericarp (karṇikā), and the second for the filaments (keśara).

Therein, the third [measurement] is the tip of the petal by the stated portion; the wise one [should determine] the measurement of the interval between the outer and inner circles according to the rule. (3.93)
Having placed half-moons around the tips of the filaments and having drawn them situated at the junctions, one should then drop the lines there.
The wise one should draw a circle with the same measurement as that of the tips of the petals;
within that space, in its center, on both sides of the thread— || 3.95 ||
One should draw [the lines] all around with the outer hand along the tips of the petals; at the bases of the petals, one should arrange the filaments in pairs. (3.96)
This common lotus design has been proclaimed by those who know the tantras.
One should clear away three squares for the sake of the [central] foot in the corners of the pedestal.
With the remaining squares, the learned one should fashion the limbs of the pedestal;
he should sweep the squares situated along the pathways according to the undivided rows.
Then, one should construct doors in the cardinal directions using two or four squares;
furthermore, the *śobhās* (ornamental projections) on both sides of the doors should consist of three or one square each.
The ornaments (upaśobhās) should be formed with one [square] each, followed by three squares;
the four corners should be formed with the remaining six squares. (3-100)
One should color that captivating maṇḍala with five colors:
yellow should be made from turmeric powder, and white from rice flour. (3.101)
Red is the powder of safflower; black is that produced from burnt husks;
and dark-grey is said to be that produced from the leaves of the bilva tree and others—thus the five colors are described.
The boundary lines, one finger in height and width, are white and auspicious;
the pericarp is yellow in color, and the filaments are reddish.
The artisan should color the petals with white pigment and their joints with black;
alternatively, the pericarp itself may be yellow.
The filaments should be yellowish-red, and the petals should also be reddish;
the joints should be black in color, and [the interior] may be either yellow or black. (3.105)
One should color the interiors of the pedestals; the feet should have a reddish luster, and its limbs should be white in all four walkways. (3-106)
One should draw wish-fulfilling creepers (*kalpalatikā*) endowed with leaves, flowers, and fruits;
they are described as being variegated with various colors and beautiful with red adornments. (3.107)
The ornaments are yellow in color, and the corners are black.
One should draw three lines on the outside in sequence: white, red, and black.
This Sarvatobhadra mandala is known as the common one;
having divided the square ground into twelve parts from the cardinal directions, the wise practitioner [should proceed]. (3.109)
One should drop the lines there so that one hundred and forty-four squares are seen; thereafter, with thirty-six [squares], there is a lotus.
One should fashion the pedestal with chambers arranged in rows; there are no pathways here.
The door-decorations are as before, and no secondary decorations (upaśobhā) are seen. (3.111)
The knower of the tantra should form the corners with the remaining six squares;
he should perform the rest as before—thus is the mandala traditionally taught.
The wise one should arrange sixty-four squares within a square;
there shall be a lotus in the center consisting of four lotuses, and again surrounding that. (3.113)
One should fashion four pathways that terminate at the edge of the mandala;
in the four squares situated at the cardinal directions, one should draw lotuses.
Having divided the four diagonal squares into sixteen parts,
the wise one should erase them to form the shape of a svastika with white, yellow, red, and black [colors].
One should fill those svastikas with powders, beginning from the northeast (śiva), by the very path previously described; one should perform the rest in the same manner.
This mandala with nine centers is proclaimed as bestowing all accomplishments;
this mandala with five lotuses is said to be devoid of the svastika.
For the purpose of worshipping the deity during initiation, four types of mandalas have been taught according to all the tantras; they bestow all prosperity. (3.118)
(Yāmala) Having worshipped him who is of a reddish color, possessing that same color, and joined by twelve Śaktis, one should pray to Bhairava, the Lord of the Lamp, as follows: (3.119).
O you of exceedingly sharp fangs and massive body, resembling the fire at the end of an eon;
homage to you, Bhairava! You are worthy to grant me permission.
Having recited the *kānta* mantra, one should then enter the altar of worship;
having consecrated the place of the seat and spread out the prescribed seat, [one should sit] according to the *Vaiṣṇavīkalpa*. (3.121)
Having brought water, one should consecrate it with the left hand according to the prescribed rule.
The consecration of the water is stated in that very [text]:
"Having purified it with the seed-syllable of air (vāyu), one should burn it away with the seed-syllable of fire (vahni). (3.122)
One should wash it with the water-seed mantra and then sprinkle it with the Gāyatrī;
thereafter, having rendered it nectar through the Dhenu-mudrā, one should consecrate it with the Praṇava.

Likewise: Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) three times with that water using the principles of the Self-knowledge and Śiva, beginning with the Praṇava and ending with the Śiras [mantra], one should then purify the seat. (3.124)
The wife of Agni is the head. Regarding this, the traditionalists maintain that purification is performed with the Astra-mantra, [conceiving] water as having a single form.
Likewise: Meru-pṛṣṭha is declared the Seer (ṛṣi), and Sutala is said to be the Metre (chandas).
The tortoise is declared to be the deity here for the purpose of settling upon the seat.
The application (viniyoga) has been stated; then, having assumed a seat, one should recite:
"O Earth, by you the worlds are supported; O Goddess, you are supported by Viṣṇu. (3.126)
And you, always support me and prepare a pure seat;
then, having uttered the seed-syllable of Māyā, [say] "to Ādhāraśakti."
Having addressed Kamalāsana with the mantra ending in "namaḥ," the best of preceptors should sit upon the seat while reciting his own personal mantra.

p. 159) For the pacification of various defects such as being poorly crafted, the personal mantra (*ātman-mantra*) is as follows: "The first letter of one's own name for a man, conjoined with *soma* (the moon) and *sāmi* (fire). (3-129)
One should understand the mantra of the self... || 3-129ef ||
Thus it is stated in the Siddhāntasaṃgraha. "Somasāmi" means the half-moon. (In the Merutantra:
Then he should sit upon his seat on the altar facing the east.
Seated in the bound lotus posture, observing silence, with the body straight and the senses subdued. || 3-130 ||
The supreme guide, having established the articles of worship,
should place an auspicious water-pot on the right and on the left side.
Then, having placed a vessel filled with fragrant water for the washing of the hands,
one should subsequently light auspicious lamps.

The knower of mantras should place the mirror, the umbrella, and the fly-whisks in the various directions—this is the ellipsis to be supplied. "Facing east" and "seated in the bound lotus posture" are illustrative;
one may face north or east while established in the svastika posture. (3.133)
Thus it is stated in the Bhairava [Tantra] (in the Nibandha):
"Then, having made the formal resolve according to the rule, one should offer the *arghya* to the Sun."
The mantra for offering the arghya to the Sun is stated in the *Merutantra*: "Hrīḥ Hrīḥ Saḥ; one should then utter the words 'along with the planets, zodiac signs, and lunar mansions'. (3-134)
And then: "O you who have turned your seat through the practice of yoga, salutation to the venerable Sūryā; this is your *argha*, svāhā. This is remembered as the mantra. (3-135)
This thirty-four syllable [mantra] is for the offering of the arghya to the Sun.
Having introduced the materials for worship in that very context:
"The self-possessed one, having arranged them in their proper places, should consecrate them. (3.136)
One should gaze upon the flowers, the food offerings, the perfumes, and so forth with the mantra *hrāḥ hūṃ phaṭ*, using the nārāca-mudrā, the [appropriate] gaze, and the samaya. (3.137)
One has seen or heard of, or personally known, the defilement caused by flowers and such;
likewise, the touch of the untouchable, or that which is acquired through unjust means. (3-138)

Likewise, whatever has come into contact with floral offerings (nirmālya) or has been ascended upon by insects and the like—all that goes to destruction simply by the sight of the food offering (naivedya) and so forth. (3.139)
Then, with the mantra *raṃ*, one should touch the crest of the lamp;
that lamp shall be auspicious, free from the smell of raw flesh, and bestow happiness. (3.140)

[The body] is consumed by the burning of moths, insects, hair, and so forth; it is joined with the flesh-eaters' [remains], and it is utilized through substances such as clarified butter produced from fat, marrow, and the like. (3.141)
All that defect, which is of the nature of ignorance, is destroyed by touch;
while reciting the seed-syllable *kṣrauḥ*, the practitioner of mantra should touch [the body] with the divine *tīrtha*. (3.142)
Having clearly observed the water situated within the jar, the practitioner, holding the jar located at his left side with his left hand, [should proceed]. (3.143)
Purifying with the mantra for the vessel-support, one should touch the water;
[one's own] name-initial syllable joined with the bindu and the half-moon (the crescent). (3.144)
The name of that vessel should end in the dative case, while the mantra of the vessel ends with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya);
for it is through ignorance of this that contact with impure substances and the like occurs here. (3.145)

Whatever other defilement may occur through ignorance regarding the vessel or the water—whether from contact with a corpse in a reservoir, or from contact with the place where the water stands—[it is removed by this]. (3.146)
Thus, such defects as these shall perish when one worships the deity, O beloved;
thereafter, with palms joined in reverence, [one should worship] on the left and right sides. (3.147)
Having bowed to the Guru, Gaṇapati, and one's own chosen deity before them,
[one should contemplate] that which has the form of an unbroken circle, by which the moving and the unmoving are pervaded. (From the *Yāmala*) 3.148.
"Salutation to that venerable Guru by whom that state has been revealed.
Having thus bowed to the Guru, the practitioner of mantra should perform the purification of the hands and other preliminary rites. (3.149)
As for the method of purifying the hands (*karaśuddhi*), [it is stated] in the *Merutantra*:
"The knower of mantras, having taken fragrant flowers smeared with sandalwood paste, should rub them on both hands with the mantra *hsauḥ* and the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*). (3-150)
Having taken that flower with the left hand, one should whirl it around the head while reciting the *tāra* mantra; then, one should smell it again.
One should first recite this verse, which is declared as follows:
"May all those harmful ones who injure me go to their destruction. (3.152)
"May death, disease, fear, and afflictions fall upon the head of the enemy!
With the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra) and the iron-arrow gesture (nārāca-mudrā), one should cast [the offering] toward the eastern direction. (3.153)
Then, for the purification of the hands, the preceptor should perform the triple *tāla* with the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*),
and subsequently perform the binding of the directions (*digbandha*) above and above using the weapon-mantra.

The fire generated by that [mantra], by means of the mudrā of the fire-fence (vahniprākāra), one should protect oneself with the root mantra; then one should perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma). || 3-155 ||
The definition of *prāṇāyāma* is stated [in the *Sārasamuccaya*]:
"Prāṇa is the vital air of the body; its extension (*āyāma*) is its restraint. This is declared to be *prāṇāyāma*, and it is said to be of two kinds. (3-156)
The *sagarbha* [breath] is produced by the recitation of mantras, while the *nigarbha* arises through the measure (*mātrā*).
And the characteristic of the form of the measure is described in the *Agastyasaṃhitā*:
"In the piercing with the tip of a fine needle through a stack of lotus petals. (3-157)
The time that elapses from one *dala* to the next is designated as a *lava*.
Thirty *lavas* constitute a *truṭi*, and they consider thirty such *truṭis* to be a *kalā*. (3.158)
A *kāṣṭhā* should be known as a certain duration of time; that same duration is a *nimeṣaka*.
It is also equal to the snap of one's own fingers and is recorded as consisting of eighteen *mātrās*. (3.159)
(From the Merutantra:
When the base of the middle finger is pressed down to its tip with the thumb, that is called a *mātrā* by the wise; it bestows whatever is desired in yoga. (3-160)
The duration of time it takes for one to circumambulate the knee once is the measure known as a *mātrā*, which is also equal to the duration of one's own exhalation. (3-161)
(Also in the Agastyasaṃhitā: "The time required for the hand to revolve around the left knee is to be known as one *mātrā* by the sages who have reached the further shore of the Vedas. (3-162)
In that very same [text]:
"Whatever action is performed without breath-control (prāṇāyāma) is useless;
therefore, those who seek auspiciousness should practice breath-control with effort. (3.163)

In this context, the plural form "prāṇāyāmāḥ" (breath-restraints) refers to three, according to the principle established in the *Kapiñjalādhikaraṇa*. Thus it is said: "One should perform three breath-restraints... and so forth.
In the Kālīkrama, one should perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma) using either the root mantra or the syllable Om. (3-164)

Alternatively, the wise one, being composed, should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) using the seed-syllable of the mantra according to the prescribed rule—specifically with the Vāgbhava syllable—as it has been stated: "Then, being concentrated, he should perform prāṇāyāma with the Vāgbhava [syllable]. (3-165)
Regarding the regulation of the fingers in breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), [it is stated in the] *Jñānārṇava*:
"The holding of the nostrils with the little finger, the ring finger, and the thumb—excluding the index finger and the middle finger—is to be known as *prāṇāyāma*. (3-166)
It is threefold: inhalation (*pūraka*), retention (*kumbhaka*), and exhalation (*recaka*).
The method for this is stated in the *Yāmala*:
The knower of mantras, having pressed the right nostril with the right thumb, [should perform the rite].
One should fill the breath with the *īḍā* [nostril] in sequence by sixteen measures (*mātrā*), then hold both nostrils with the thumb and ring finger. (3.168)
Then, one should retain the breath for four times the duration of the inhalations (pūraka),
holding the right nostril with the ring finger while keeping the left nostril open.
One should perform the exhalation of the breath with thirty-two measures; having placed one's own mind in the root-cakra, one should practice the vital breaths. (3-170)
(Also in the *Mahākālasaṃhitā*):
"Indeed, by means of the recitation of the root mantra sixteen times, one should forcefully fill the air through the left nostril alone. (3-171)
Furthermore, O Pārvatī, having restrained the breath by repeating [the mantra] sixty-four times,
one should again repeat the root mantra thirty-two times.
One should expel all the air through the right nostril;
indeed, by such a method, one single breath control (prāṇāyāma) is accomplished. (3.173)
For those three [practices] are essential, as there is a greater abundance of fruit when they are combined.
Regarding the second breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), the *Yāmala* states:
"Then, one should perform the breath control by means of the path of exhalation. (3.174)
Furthermore, the practitioner of mantra should perform the retention (kumbhaka) for sixteen mātrās,
holding the two nostrils with the sixty-fourth [mudrā].
Furthermore, the wise man should exhale the breath with a duration of thirty-two mātrās;
the remainder [of the instruction] implies that this is done through the left nostril.
The third prāṇāyāma is described in that very same place.
One should inhale the breath through the left [nostril] alone, in sequence, by means of sixteen measures (mātrās).

Then, having pressed the two nostrils together, the wise practitioner should exhale the air through the right [nostril] with thirty-two measures, which are four times the duration of the inhalation (*pūraka*).
In another tantra:
"One should draw in the breath through the *iḍā* in succession by sixteen measures;
then, having pressed the two nostrils, [one should hold it] with four times the measure of the inhalation (*pūraka*). (3.178) p. 164)
The wise one should exhale the breath through the *dakṣiṇa* [nāḍī] with thirty-two *mātrās*.
In another tantra: "One should draw in the external breath through the *iḍā* with sixteen *mātrās*. (3-179)
The best of those who know yoga should properly exhale this [breath] slowly through the piṅgalā channel for thirty-two mātrās, while it is correctly situated within the suṣumṇā.
One should perform this again and again in sequence, alternating it.
"Of that" refers to the previously mentioned breath control (*prāṇāyāma*). "Alternating" means by way of reversal. As it has been said in the *Sanatkumārasaṃhitā*:
"By the same [nostril] through which one should expel the air, by that very same one one should fill it again. (3-181)
Having performed *prāṇāyāma* in this manner, one should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*).
(From the *Śāradā*) [and the *Yāmala*].
That which is the purification of the elements that have taken the form of the body. || 3-182 ||

This purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) is considered to arise from union with the non-dual Brahman (*advayabrahma*). (In the *Yāmala*): "He who performs worship without the purification of the elements and the installation of the letters (*lipinyāsa*)... (3.183).
Just as worship performed without devotion yields a contrary result, [the text] describes the method for the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) in the *Merutantra*:
"From the feet to the knees, it is a square marked with a vajra. (3-184)
The earth element, conjoined with the letter *la*, is yellow in color and has Brahmā as its presiding deity;
this station is said to be presided over by the *kalā* (aspect) called Nivṛtti. || 3-185 ||
At the time of the birth of living beings, one should contemplate their form in this way:
from the knees up to the navel is the locus of water, possessing a white luster. (3.186)
The two prongs, resembling a half-moon, are marked with a lotus;
it is hexagonal, joined with six dots, and endowed with the seed-syllable *vaṃ*.
One should meditate on that which has Viṣṇu as its deity, endowed with the power of *pratiṣṭhā*;
from the navel up to the throat, it is reddish-pink and has Rudra as its deity. (3.188)
It is joined with the seed-syllable and endowed with the digit known as Vidyā;
radiant and accompanied by the svastika, it has assumed the form of a triangle.

One should contemplate the fire element (vahnitattva), which has the configuration of the great dissolution (mahāpralaya) and assumes the form of a hexagon extending from the throat to the space between the eyebrows. (3-190)
Marked with six dots, encircled by a circle, and black in color;
it is the locus of wind, presided over by the power of peace (śāntikalā), and has Śiva as its deity. || 3-191 ||
One should contemplate the form of the vital breath (prāṇa) of all [beings] as joined with the seed-syllable;
the space from the middle of the eyebrows to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) is called the station of space. (3.192)
Circular in shape, smoke-colored, and marked with a high flag;
it is presided over by the digit known as Śāntyatīta and has Śiva as its deity.
Having meditated thus upon [the lotus] joined with the seed-syllable, one should assign the elements to the body:
[a lotus] arisen from the root-stalk of Dharma and beautifully adorned with the stem of Knowledge. (3.194)
One should join the individual soul (jīva) to the Supreme Self by means of the path of the *suṣumṇā*, [visualizing] that lotus situated in its pericarp, resembling the flame of a lamp. (3.195)
The practitioner, by means of the method joined with yoga and the "so 'ham" mantra, should contemplate all beings as dissolved right there. (3.196)
In another tantra:
Having placed both hands face upwards upon one's own lap, [one proceeds] by means of the power residing in the *mūlādhāra* and through the sequence of piercing the cakras. (3.197)
By means of the swan-like path of Brahman, one should unite the individual soul with Brahman;
[as stated] in the *Mahākālasaṃhitā*:
"From the lotus of the heart, one should [visualize] the Self in the form of a blazing lamp-flame. (3-198)

p. 166) Having joined [the soul] to the Supreme Self, situated in the center of the thousand-petaled lotus at the crown of the head by means of the *suṣumṇā* path and the *brahmabīja* mantra, || 3-199 ||
(Siddhāntasaṃgraha) Thereafter, one should dissolve all the principles (*tattva*) right there: earth into water, that [water] into fire, fire into air, and air into space. (3-200)
Having thus dissolved space into space, and then that [space] into primordial nature (prakṛti),
one should dissolve that power of illusion (māyāśakti), which is of the nature of the lower Brahman, into the Supreme Self.
Having thus dissolved the entire manifold of the body and so forth into the Supreme Self, one should remain for some moments in the form of the Supreme Brahman. (3-202)
(Merutantra) One should contemplate the personification of sin in the left side of the body;
the personification of sin situated in the left side of the abdomen, with the luster of lampblack. (3.203)
It has the murder of a Brahmin as its head, the theft of gold as its two arms,
the drinking of liquor joined with its heart, and the violation of the Guru’s bed as its two hips.
The pair of feet through contact with which causes sin to every limb and member,
whose hair consists of minor offenses, and whose beard and eyes are red— (3.205)
One should contemplate [the enemy] as holding a sword and shield, cruel, the size of a thumb, face-down, most terrifying, harsh, and sinful. (3.206)
(In the Mahākālasaṃhitā:
Then, having filled the air through the left nostril and having visualized the seed-syllable of Vāyu, together with the bindu, as smoke-colored; 3-207.
O Goddess of the Gods, one should utter that very seed-syllable fifty times;
then, one should contemplate the body as being dried up by the wind produced thereby.
Simultaneously, one should exhale the breath through the nostril;
having drawn up the breath through the left [nostril], it should be placed in the center of the thousand-petaled lotus. (3-209)
O fair-faced one, having visualized the Supreme Self in the form of the moon,
one should utter the fifty letters of the wind-seed syllable together with the anusvāra.
Therefore, O beautiful one, having bathed the body with a shower of nectar from that moon,
and having joined the purified form with the seed-syllable of the earth (Bhū-bīja) together with its resonance (nāda), [one should proceed].
Having established those five elements here that were previously dissolved according to their respective places, one should again recite the seed-syllable of Brahmā.
Having drawn the individual soul (jīvātman) together with the principles beginning with egoism (ahaṃkāra) into the Supreme Self, he should establish it within the lotus of the heart.
Then, being empowered, one should contemplate oneself in the form of the Goddess for a moment.
Here, the practice of *pūraka* and so forth is described as consisting of fifty recitations of the seed-syllable of Vāyu (*ya*) and others. (However, in the *Yāmala* and other texts:)
And at the region of the navel, one should contemplate the syllable *ya*, which is smoke-colored wind. || 3-214 ||
One should purify the body of the *liṅga* with sixteen measures (*mātrā*) using that very [breath];
having performed the retention (*kumbhaka*) for sixty-four [measures] pertaining to action (*karmātmaka*), one should proceed.
"Exhalation is performed with thirty-two *mātrās*, or again by that [other method].

Thus, it should be understood that there is an option regarding the number, as filling (*pūraka*) and the other [breath-controls] have been described using sixteen *mātrās* and so forth (in the *Siddhāntasaṃgraha*).
One should cause the body of the Supreme Self to arise once more as something pure.
The supreme Vidyā, whose essence is the Parābrahman, is Prakṛti, the supreme Mātṛkā;
from her was born the Mother of the World, and from her came space, and from space, the wind.
From wind arose fire; from fire, water; and from that, earth.
From these very elements, he [the Lord] assumed a body whose form was splendor. (3.218)
One should contemplate that what has arisen is fit for the propitiation of the deity.
This is declared to be the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), which destroys the flood of great sins. (3-219)
