He states the abbreviated method (*Uḍḍīśa*):
"Alternatively, having joined the goddess Kuṇḍalinī together with the five elements and so forth within the Supreme Self, and having meditated upon the identity of those two... (3.220).
Through the yoga of meditation, one should contemplate with the mind "I am He, I am He.

However, in certain specific cases of power (*śakti*), it is taught that one should join the seed-syllable "Haṃsa" and so forth with Paraśiva, and by means of the mantra "So 'ham," bring [the deity] to its own place. Having thus performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) on Mount Meru, one should carry out the installation of the vital breath (*prāṇasthāpana*). (Meru 3.221)
(Jñānārṇava) Thereafter, one should enjoin the life-force (*jīva*) into the body by means of the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā*.
Having uttered the "mouth-circle" (*mukhavṛtta*), the *haṃsa* [mantra] is then reversed. (3.222)
One should extract [the mantra], O Supreme Goddess; this shall become a three-syllabled Vidyā.
This is the Prāṇapratiṣṭhā mantra; it accomplishes every ritual action. || 3-223 ||
(From the Merutantra: Having performed three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should perform the ritual placement of the Mātṛkās (mātṛkānyāsa).
(From the Phetkāriṇītantra:)
Mantras become mute without the placement of the letters.
For the sake of the accomplishment of all mantras, one should therefore first place the *lipi* (the alphabet).
Therein, first is the internal *mātṛkā*-nyāsa. (In the *Merutantra*):
"Now I shall describe the internal *mātṛkā*-nyāsa, which brings about purification. (3.225)
By performing this, the mind of yogins does not engage in sin;
having heard the sound of the *mūlādhāra*, the *kuṇḍalinī* power is awakened. (3.226)
Resembling a blazing fire, subtle and consisting of the nature of light, she has the form of lightning, touching the lotus of the head from the *mūlādhāra*. (3.227)

From the lotus of his head touched by her, the letters of the Mātṛkā emerged in the form of a flood of nectar; [he should contemplate] these as issuing from his body through the path of the Suṣumṇā. (3.228)
Having established these [deities] thus and meditated upon them as remaining [there], one should place [the lotus] in the throat;
it is the sixteen-petaled lotus known as the Viśuddhi-cakra.

With its face turned upward, the sixteen vowels are situated there starting from the eastern petal; having thus visualized [the lotus] beginning with *tāra* (oṃ), joined with the *bindu*, and ending with *namaḥ*. (3.230)
One should utter the sound according to the method for all these phonemes;
one should meditate upon the twelve-petaled wheel struck by the heart. (3.231)
One should arrange the letters beginning with *ka* on the inner petals of the eastern leaf as before;
then, one should contemplate the Maṇipūra-cakra in the region of the navel.
There, one should contemplate the ten petals with the letters beginning with 'ḍa' as before;
this is called the six-petalled wheel of the Svādhiṣṭhāna at the base of the genitals. (3.233)
There, one should contemplate the six syllables of Bālā as before;
the wheel called Mūlādhāra is lotus-shaped and has four petals. (3.234)
Va, Śa, Ṣa, and Sa; there, one should contemplate [these] in the petals starting from the eastern direction.
The wheel called Ājñā, shaped like a lotus with two petals, is located in the middle of the forehead. (3.235)
HA / KṢA / This [meditation] should be performed with the mind alone;
it should be performed within one's own body by means of the "sickness-free" [syllable], and upon flowers for the forms of the deities. (3-236)
Because it is beginningless, it has no seer (*ṛṣi*) and so forth; its meditation (*dhyāna*), however, is like that of Brahman.
Now follows the external placement of the *mātṛkās* (*bahir-mātṛkā-nyāsa*). (In the *Śāradā-tantra*):
"Brahmā is declared to be the seer, and the *gāyatrī* is said to be the meter. (3.237)
Sarasvatī is proclaimed as the deity by the most excellent of teachers;
she is represented by the six groups of consonants in their respective order, excluding the semi-vowels and ending with both short and long vowels. (3.238)
The teachers should perform the six ancillaries (ṣaḍaṅga) conjoined with the [mantric] birth-syllables.
(Merutantra, p. 170) Next, I shall describe the external placement (bahirnyāsa) in the previously mentioned aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). (3.239)
One should meditate upon Sarasvatī, known as Mātṛkā, within the lotus of the letters.
Meditation is on that very [deity]:
her face, arms, feet, belly, and chest fashioned with the distinctions of fifty letters;
she is resplendent with a radiant *kaparda* (matted hair) adorned by a digit of the moon, and is as white as the moon or a jasmine flower.

I bow to that Bhāratī, who holds a rosary, a water-pot, and a book written upon her palm; who has three eyes, is seated upon a lotus, is as radiant as the moon, and bears the weight of full breasts and hips. (3.240)

One should place the vowels on the forehead, the perimeter of the face, the eyes, the ears, the nose, the two cheeks, the two lips, the two rows of teeth, the crown of the head, and the mouth. (3.241)

The wise practitioner should place the *ka*-group and the *ca*-group at the joints of the arms and at their tips; likewise, the *ṭa*-group and the *ta*-group [should be placed] on the feet, on the sides, and on the region of the back. (3.242)

Having assigned the *pavarga* to the navel and the belly, and then the four letters beginning with *ya* to the heart, shoulders, and hump, one should thereafter assign the six letters beginning with *śa*.
This placement (nyāsa) is performed on the heart and other centers, as well as on the two hands, the two feet, the belly, and likewise the mouth;
it fulfills the recitation by supplying the missing syllables and measures.
In the *Śāradā*, one should place [the letters] accompanied by the *sarga* (visarga) according to the process of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) and meditate upon the Goddess according to the rule;
one should place them there joined with the *bindu* according to the process of withdrawal (*saṃhṛti*) in reverse order. (3-245)
(Merutantra) If the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) is performed starting from the letter *kṣa* and ending with the letter *a*,
it shall be known as the "placement of withdrawal" (*saṃhāranyāsa*), and it is called the "placement of the bindu" (*bindunyāsa*). (3-246)

He describes the meditation according to the sequence of withdrawal: [one should meditate on her] who holds in her hands a rosary, a young deer, a formidable axe, and a lore-mantra, and who has three eyes.
Prostrate before Varṇeśvarī, who rests upon a red lotus, whose head is adorned with a crescent moon, and who is bent by the weight of her breasts. (3.247)
(In the Śāradā-tantra:

Having placed [the syllables] ending with *sarga* and *bindu* according to the path of maintenance (*sthiti*), the wise one should know the previously mentioned seers (*ṛṣi*) and so forth, together with their limbs (*aṅga*). (3-248)
During the phase of maintenance (*sthiti*), one should place the letters beginning with *ḍa* and ending with *ṭha*, joined with the emission of the bindu (*vindusarga*).
The sages and so forth are the same as previously mentioned; this is called the meditation on the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga-dhyāna*).
[He who has] the splendor of vermilion, is adorned with immeasurable ornaments, possesses three eyes, and holds a rosary of knowledge, a deer-cub, and a boon-granting gesture;
and [who has] the Blessed Lady standing at his side, possessing a golden luster— [to him I bow].
One should meditate upon her holding a book and a rosary of beads in her lotus-like hands.
The ritual placements (nyāsa) of maintenance, withdrawal, and emanation should be performed by students;
however, a householder should perform the placements of withdrawal, emanation, and maintenance in their proper sequence.

Forest-dwellers and ascetics should perform the ritual depositions (nyāsa) according to the sequence of creation, maintenance, and dissolution; thus has the detailed procedure for the *sthitinyāsa* been proclaimed. (3.252)
Now, regarding the Kalāmātṛkā-nyāsa, it is stated in that very same [text]:
"I shall describe the Nyāsa of the Kalāmātṛkā; Prajāpati is remembered as its Seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is its metre (chandas), and its Deity is [the aforementioned]. (3.253)
Sarasvatī is known as Mātṛkā; her application is for the fulfillment of one's desires.
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with the *tāra* (om) situated between the short and long vowels. (3.254)
He describes her meditative posture:
she holds in her hands a lotus, a wheel, a rosary, a deer, a book, a string of letters, a chisel, a white skull-cup, a leaf, and a golden jar overflowing with nectar.
I bow to that Śāradā, who resembles the full moon, whose breasts are heavy, who possesses three eyes and five faces as beautiful as pearls, lightning, clouds, crystal, and coral. (3.255)

Having thus meditated upon that [goddess] preceded by the syllable *Tāra* (Oṃ), as well as the Mātṛkā beginning with the letter *A*, joined with the *bindu*, ending in the vocative case (*ṅe*), and followed by the name [of the deity] and the word "namas" (salutation)— (3.256).
One should place [the mantras] of the previously mentioned pure *mātrās* in the locations for their assignment (*nyāsa*).

Regarding the phrase "preceded by *tāra*" (*tārapūrvām*) and so forth: by this, the practical applications such as *oṃ aṃ nivṛttyai namaḥ* and others are established. He states the names of the *kalās*:
"Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, Śānti, and likewise Indhikā. (3.257)
She is called Dīpitā, Recikā, and the supreme Mocikā;
she is Sūkṣmā, Sūkṣmāmṛtā, Jñānāmṛtā, and Āpyāyanī. (3-258)
Pervasive, of the nature of space, infinite, and the source of prosperity is Sṛṣṭi;
then follow Smṛti, Medhā, Kānti, Lakṣmī, Dyuti, Sthirā, and Sthiti. (3.259)
Siddhi, Jayā, Pālinī, Śānti, Īśvarikā, Rati, Kāmikā, Varadā, and another, Hrādinī, who is joined with Prīti. (3.260)
Dīrghā, Tīkṣṇā, Raudrī, Bhayā, Nidrā, and Tandrikā; then Kṣudhā, Krodhinī, Kriyā, Utkārī, and Samṛtyukā. (3-261)
Yellow, white, reddish, and finally black, accompanied by Anantā;
one should thus place the Ulkā and Kalāmātṛkā in the positions beginning with the letter 'a'.
He states the place of origin for the arts (*kalā*):
"In that regard, those born from *nāda* arise from Sadāśiva;
they hold a rosary, a book, a noose, and also a skull-cup. (3.263)
Holding [objects] with their hands, white-complexioned, and adorned with white ornaments,
these ten digits of the *ka*-group were born from Brahmā through the letter *a*.

Yellow in color, holding a rosary of beads, a lotus, the gesture of fearlessness, and a water-pot in their hands, they should be meditated upon as being anointed with yellow perfumes and unguents. (3.265)
The ten digits born from the letter *u* of Viṣṇu belong to the *ṭa*-group;
they are described as dark-complexioned, with hands holding the gesture of fearlessness, a conch, a discus, and a lotus. (3.266)
From the letter *ma*, nine digits born of Rudra arise;
they resemble the autumn moon and hold in their hands the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*) and a trident.
And they should be meditated upon by practitioners as holding a skull-cup and a boon-granting gesture;
these five, beginning with Śākārā, arose from the Lord through the Bindu.

Holding in their sprout-like hands the gesture of fearlessness, a deer, a chisel, and a boon, and being red in color, they are to be meditated upon during the ritual placement (nyāsa) consisting of the kalās.
Now, the Keśavādi-mātṛkā-nyāsa is described in that very same place:
"For the Keśavādi-mātṛkā, the sage is Sādhyanārāyaṇa;
the meter is Amṛtādā-gāyatrī; and the deity is Lakṣmī-Hari. (3.270)
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with the [mantras] *śakti*, *śrī*, and *kāma* repeated twice.
*Śakti* refers to *lajjā*.
He states the visualization (*dhyāna*):
A conch, a discus, a mace, a lotus, a water-pot, a mirror, a lotus, and a book. || 3-271 ||
I worship Lakṣmī-Hari, who bears a complexion as fickle as a cloud;
his Śaktis, with smiling faces, are seated upon his own limbs. (3.272)
Having meditated thus, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the syllables encased by Śakti and Śrīkāma;
the powers (śaktis), beginning with Tārā and ending with Hṛdayā, are indeed those beginning with Keśava.

Those ending in *bhyām* and those ending in *namaḥ* should be recited and placed in their respective positions beginning with the letter *a*. The form ending in *bhyām* is correct because it follows the Tantric convention. This is the concise method; however, in the *Agastyasaṃhitā* and other texts, the separate utterance of the names in the singular dative case is prescribed. For example, in the *Vaiṣṇavīkalpa*, it says: "To Keśava and to Kīrti," and so forth. (*Merutantra*)
Having uttered Tāra, Māyā, Ramā, and Kāmā, one should pronounce the syllables.

Having likewise pronounced the [mantra] ending with *bhyām* for the Goddess, and then again the triad beginning with Śakti, one should perform the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*) upon the forehead and other parts, up to the heart. (3.275)
In some cases, however, the utterance of the seed-syllables of Śakti and so forth is not mentioned again after the name of the deity.
(Regarding Vaiṣvaksenī:
This [seed-syllable] may be preceded by Tāra (Om), or by Manmatha (Klīm), or by Ramā (Śrīm).
Thus the alternative [method] for the *praṇava* and the others has been stated. (In the Śāradā-tantra, however:
"Having performed the placement of the Mātṛkā beginning with *smara*, conjoined with [the names] Keśava and the others followed by *namaḥ*... (3.276).
"Among those devoted to Viṣṇu (vaiṣṇava), [the practice] consists of the elements, the vital breath, power, the self, yoga, and so forth;
thus, only the seed-syllable of desire (kāmabīja) is employed. But for the Śāktas, it is merely a fraction (kalā); this [practice] is eternal for the servants of Viṣṇu. (3.277)
He states the names beginning with Keśava: Keśava is endowed with fame; Kānti is possessed by Nārāyaṇa;
Mādhava is endowed with contentment; and Govinda is endowed with nourishment. (3.278)
Viṣṇu is endowed with fortitude; Madhusūdana is joined with peace;
Trivikrama is joined with action; and Vāmana is possessed of compassion.
Śrīdhara is joined with Medhā, while Hṛṣīkeśa is joined with Harṣā;
Śraddhā is united with Padmanābha, and Lajjā is accompanied by Dāmodara. (3.280)
Vāsudeva is joined with Lakṣmī, Saṃkarṣaṇa with Sarasvatī,
Pradyumna is joined with Prīti, and Aniruddha is joined with Rati.

The wielder of the discus is joined with Jayā, the mace-bearer with Durgā, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow is endowed with Prabhā, the sword-bearer is united with Satyā, and the conch-bearer is joined with Caṇḍā.
Hali was joined with Vāṇī, and then Mauśali with Vilāsinī;
Śūlin was united with Jayā, and Pāśin was accompanied by Virajā.
Aṅkuśī is joined with Viśvā; Mukunda is accompanied by Vinadā.
Nandaja is endowed with Sudayā, and Nandin is possessed of Smṛti. (3.284)
Nara by his supernatural power, Naraka-jit by his prosperity, Śuddhi-yug-hari;
Kṛṣṇa by his intellect, Satya by his enjoyment, and he is remembered as the eternal one endowed with wisdom. (3.285)
Śaurikṣama with Śūradamā, Janārdana with Umā,
Bhūdhara with Kledinī, and Viśvamūrti with Klinnā.
Vaikuṇṭha is joined with Vasudhā; Vasudā and Puruṣottama are likewise joined.
Balī is joined with Parā, and Balānuja is devoted to Parāyaṇā.
Bāla is joined with Sūkṣma; Vṛṣaghna is joined with Saṃdhyā; Prajñā is joined with Vṛṣa; Haṃsa is joined with Prabhāsā; and Varāha is accompanied by Niśā. (3.288)
Vimala is endowed with intelligence, and Nṛsiṃha is joined with lightning;
Keśava and the others are declared according to the Mothers, and the conjunction of the vowels (ya, etc. is as before. (3.289)

The application of this [mantra] is as follows: *oṃ hrīḥ śrīḥ klīḥ aṃ keśava-kīrtibhyāṃ hrīḥ śrīḥ klīḥ namaḥ*, and so forth. Regarding the phrase "the conjunction beginning with *ya*": the meaning is that in the sequence beginning with the letter *ya*, there is the conjunction of the skin (*tvak*) and so on, such as: *oṃ hrīḥ śrīḥ klīḥ yaṃ tvag-ātmabhyāṃ vasudā-puruṣottamābhyāṃ hrīḥ śrīḥ klīḥ namaḥ*, and so on.
Now, the *mātṛkā*-nyāsa of Śrīkaṇṭha and others is in that very same place:
"Now I shall describe the *mātṛkā*s of Śrīkaṇṭha and others, which are beneficial for the followers of Śiva."
The sage is Dakṣiṇāmūrti, and Gāyatrī is declared to be the meter. (3.290)
Lord Hara, born from the half-mountain, is the command for the attainment of all perfections;
the consonants (hal) are the seeds in the secret place, while the vowel-powers (svaraśakti) reside in the feet.
Having placed the short and long vowels in between, he should form the groups [of consonants] with the *ha* sounds as before;
having formed the six limbs with those joined by the six long vowels, he should place them upon his body.
(176) "Short and long intervals" means that one should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with *a*, *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ṅa*, *ā*, *hsām*, and so forth.
He describes the visualization (*dhyāna*):
[one should visualize the deity] resembling the Bandhūka flower and gold, holding a beautiful rosary...

We perpetually take refuge in that body which bears a noose and a goad, as well as the gesture of granting boons, with its own staff-like arms; which wears the crescent moon as an ornament, possesses three eyes, and has the Lord of Ambikā as its half. (3.293)
Having uttered the Mātṛkā, one should perform the worship of Īśa at the end of the [mantra of the] deities;
ending in -ṅ, -ṅaṃ, and a, [one should worship] that Śakti with [the suffixes] ending in -namaḥ in the place of the Mātṛkā. (3-294)
One should state the skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen as the "life-breaths" (asūn).
Likewise, one should state power, anger, and the self with the suffix -Ṅ in all ten [categories]. (3.295)
The practical application is as follows: *hsau a śrīkaṇṭheśāya pūrṇodaryai namaḥ*.

Regarding the word "skin" (*tvak*): *hsau ya tvagātmane bālīśāya sumukhyai namaḥ*. The meaning is that in this manner, the association with skin and the other [elements] should be performed for the ten syllables beginning with *ya*. He now states the names of Śiva and Śakti.
Śrīkaṇṭha with Pūrṇodarī, Ananta accompanied by Virajā, Sūkṣmeśa joined with Śālmalī, and Trimūrtika joined with Lolākṣī. (3-296)
Amareśa is with Vartulākṣī, Arghīśa with Dīrghaghoṇā,
Bhāramūrti with Dīrghamukhī, and Tithīśa is joined with Gomukhī.
Sthāṇvīśa is joined with Dīrghajihvā, Yugghara with Kuṇḍodarī, Jhiṇṭīśa with Ūrdhvakeśī, and Bhautika with Vikṛtāsyā. (3.298)
Sadyojāta is joined with Jvālamukhī and Anugraholkāmukhī; in Akrūra is Mahāsena, joined with Śrīmukhī and Vidyāmukhī.
Krodhīśa is with Mahākālī, and Sarasvatī is with Caṇḍeśa;
Sarvasiddhi is proclaimed to be joined with Gaurī in the [mandala of] Pañcāntaka. (3.300)
Śivottameśa, joined with Trailokyavidyā, is to be deposited;
Ekarudra with Mantraśakti, and Kūrmeśa joined with Aṣṭaśakti.
Ekanetra is joined with Bhūtimātrā, and Caturānana is joined with Lambodarī; Ajeśa is said to be joined with Drāviṇī.
Sarveśa is joined with Nāgarī; Someśa is joined with Khecarī; Lāṅgalīśa is joined with Mañjarī; and Rūpiṇī is joined with Dārukeśa.
With Vīriṇī he becomes Ardhanārīśa, and with Umā he is again united as Umākānta;
likewise, with Kākodaryā he is Aṣāḍhī, and he is said to be joined with Pūtanā.
Daṇḍīśa is joined with Bhadrakālī; Yugadrīśa is joined with Yoginī;
Mīneśa is joined with Śaṅkhinī; and Meṣeśa is joined with Tarjanī.
Lohita is joined with Kālarātri, and Śikhīśa with Kūrdinī;
Chagalaṇḍa is with Kapardinī, and Dviraṇḍeśa with Vajrā.
Mahākāla is joined with Jayā; Bālīśa is joined with Sumukhī;
Bhujaṅga is joined with Revatī; and Pinākin is joined with Mādhavī. || 3-307 ||
Khaḍgīśa is joined with Vāruṇī; Vakeśa is united with Vāyavī;
Śveta is with Rakṣovadhāriṇī; and Bhṛgu is joined with Sahajā.
Nakulīśa conjoined with Lakṣmī, Śiveśa conjoined with Vyāpinī, and Saṃvartaka conjoined with Mahāmāyā—these indeed are the Mātṛkās. (3.309)
(178) Regarding the statement "from Śrīkaṇṭha up to Īśa," one should not employ the word *Īśa* there.

The meaning of "ya" (who/which) is that at the end of whichever [name] ends in *Īśa*, the word *Īśa* should not be added again. By this, it is authorized that the addition of the word *Īśa* at the end of names beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha is necessary.
Likewise:
All the Rudras are remembered as being red in color, holding tridents and skull-bowls.
The Śaktis, residing in the seats of Rudra, have bodies as red as vermilion;
their lotus-like hands are adorned with red lotuses and skull-cups. || 3.311 ||
Now, regarding the *mātṛkā-nyāsa* of Bhuvaneśvarī, it is said in that very same [text]:
"O gods, those who have worshipped the ten Great Vidyās possess the qualification for the *mātṛkā-nyāsa* preceded by the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Bhuvaneśī. (3.312)
The seer is Śakti, the metre is Gāyatrī consisting of the Mātṛkās, and the deity is Bhuvaneśī; its application is for the attainment of one's own desired goal. (3.313)

With the six groups [of consonants] situated between the short and long vowels, joined with the long vowels, there shall be the six limbs as before; likewise, starting from the thumb, it is exactly the same.

"Of Hari" means by means of the letters *ha* and *ra* joined with the six long vowels beginning with *ā*. The practical application (*prayoga*) is as follows: *a*, *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ṅa*, *ā*, *hrā*, [and so on], ending with "Salutation to the Heart" (*hṛdayāya namaḥ*), etc.
He describes the visualization (*dhyāna*):
"Resembling ten million rising suns, with high, broad, and full breasts..."
Adorned with a crown, necklace, girdle, and anklets in the form of a bound crescent moon,
holding a rosary, noose, goad, and a book in her lotus-like hands,
may the three-eyed Mistress of the Universe, seated comfortably upon a lotus, grant us prosperity.
Having first uttered the seed-syllable of Laḍḍā, this is indeed the Mātṛkā-nyāsa;
it is employed in those practices where there is the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the Mātṛkās of Bhuvaneśī.
Now, the *nyāsa* of the *Lakṣmīmātṛkā* is described in that very same place:
"Those householders who desire Lakṣmī should perform [this ritual] preceded by the *Śrī-bīja*.
Bhṛgu is the *ṛṣi*, Gāyatrī is the meter, and she whose form is the Mother is the deity. (3.317) p. 179)
Lakṣmī is declared to be the deity; place her in the position of Hara.
For the purpose of the assignment (nyāsa) of the six limbs and so forth, the remainder [of the mantra] should be preceded by the Śrī-bīja.

"Harasthāne śarau" means that in place of the letters *ha* and *ra* mentioned by the Mother Bhuvaneśī, one should substitute the letters *śa* and *ra*. By this, in place of *hrām* and so forth, *śrām* and so forth are established.
He states the visualization (*dhyāna*):
"She whose radiance is equal to a flash of lightning, [seated] upon four elephants resembling the snowy mountains..."

One should meditate upon the Mistress of the World, who is being sprinkled with jars of nectar drawn up by the trunks of elephants, who holds a rosary of *japā* seeds, two lotuses, and a book in her lotus-like hands, whose breasts are bent under the weight of her bosom, and who is radiant with shining jewels. (3.319)
Now, regarding the placement (nyāsa) of the *saṃmohana-mātṛkā*, it is stated in that same [text]:

"For the sake of accomplishing merely one's desires, the sage should perform the placement of the *mātṛkā* preceded by the seed-syllable of desire (*kāmabīja*) as before; this is considered the *saṃmohana* [placement]. (3.320)
The Gāyatrī is declared to be the meter, and the deity is composed of the Mātṛkās;
the goddess named Saṃmohinī is worshipped with the six limbs according to the previously mentioned method.

Regarding "with the previously mentioned method": by means of the method stated in the *Lakṣmīmātṛkā*, one should perform the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) after placing the conjunct consonants *ka* and *la* in place of the letters *ha* and *ra*, due to the *Saṃmohanamātṛkā* being preceded by the seed-syllable of desire (*kāmabīja*).
He states the visualization (*dhyāna*):
[She who is] as radiant as ten million rising suns, [holding] a crystal rosary...

One should meditate upon the Mother of all beings, who has three eyes and the crescent moon as her crest-jewel, holding in her lotus-like hands a bow and the five arrows of Smara born from sugarcane, as well as the Vidyā-mantra. (3.322)

He states another *saṃmohana-mātṛkā*: "By the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *mātṛkā* beginning with the seed-syllables of Śakti, Śrī, and Kāma, the defects of mantras arising from many syllables—such as enmity and the like—are destroyed for men. (3.323)
The seer is Mahāsaṃmohana, the meter is said to be Gāyatrī;
the goddess is named Saṃmohinī, and the ritual placement (nyāsa) is the same as that of the Mātṛkā. (3.324)
As for the meditation:
one should meditate upon [the deity] holding a rosary, a sugarcane arrow, a noose, two lotuses, a goad, an arrow, and a fresh book.
She who bears the dawn with her own arms, distressed by the weight of her breasts,
enchanting, three-eyed, and crowned with the new moon.
Now, regarding the *Gaṇeśamātṛkānyāsa* in that very same [text]:
"For the purpose of dispelling all obstacles, one must certainly perform this nyāsa.
As for the *Gaṇeśamātṛkā*, the sage (*ṛṣi*) is said to be Gaṇaka. (3.326)

With the Nivṛt-Gāyatrī meter and Śakti-Vināyaka as the deity, one should meditate upon the elephant-faced god after having performed the ritual placement of the limbs with the long mantra beginning with "smṛti. (3.327)
The letter *ga* is mindfulness (*smṛti*).
As for meditative concentration (*dhyāna*):
[He] has in his hands a trident, a goad, the gesture of granting boons, and the gesture of fearlessness, while [his consort] holds a red lotus in her hand.
I worship Gaṇeśa, embraced by his beloved, red in hue, and possessing three eyes.
Having meditated thus, one should place [the mantra], conjoined with the syllables preceded by one's own seed-syllable.

Regarding the word *svīya*: the meaning is that one should install the aforementioned Śaktis and the aforementioned Gaṇeśas in such a way that they are conjoined with those letters beginning with *a* which have their own respective seed-syllables (*bīja*)—namely *gaṃ*—preceding them. Likewise:
"Vighneśa is joined with *hrīṃ*, and Vighnarāja is united with *śrīṃ*."
Vināyaka is endowed with nourishment, endowed with peace, and is the supreme Śiva.
Vighnakṛt is joined with Svasti; Sarasvatī is joined with Vighnahartṛ;
Gaṇa is joined with Svāhā; and Ekadanta is joined with Medhā.
Dvidanta is conjoined with Kānti; Gajavaktra is with Kāminī;
Nirañjana is with Mohinī; and Kapardin is with Nadī. (3.331)
Dīrghajihva is joined with Pārvatī; Jvālinī is joined with Śaṅkukarṇaka;
Vṛṣadhvaja is joined with Nandā; and Suyasas is joined with Gaṇanāyaka. (3.332)
Gajendra [was born] from Kāmarūpinī, Śūrpakarṇa likewise from Umā; Trilocana from Tejovatī, and Lambodara from Satyā.
Mahānanda is with Vighneśī, who has four forms and is beautiful;
Sadāśiva is with Kāmadā, Yugāmoda is with Madajihvā. (3.334)
Durmukha is joined with Bhūti; Sumukha is joined with Bhautika; Pramoda is joined with Sitā; and Ekapāda is joined with Ramā. (3.335)
The double-tongued one is joined with the queen; even the hero is joined with the female serpent;
the hero is also joined with Karṇā; the six-faced one is endowed with a frown. (3.336)
Varada and Lajjā, Vāmadeva and Dīrghaghoṇā;
Dhanurdhara and Avakratuṇḍa; Dviraṇḍa and Yāminī. (3-337)
Senānī is conjoined with Rātri; Kāmāndha is joined with Grāmaṇī;
Matta is joined with Śaśiprabhā; and Vimale is joined with Lolalocanā. (3-338)
In the state of the restlessness of a rutting elephant, he is one with matted hair and endowed with radiance;
likewise, as one with a shaven head, he is joined with Subhagā, and as one with a sword, he is joined with Durbhagā.
Vareṇya is joined with Śivā; Bhagīyu is the bull-bannered Lord (Śiva);
Gaṇeśa, who is fond of devotion, is joined with his sister Bhoginī.
Meghanāda is associated with Subhagā, while Kālarātri is joined with Gaṇeśvara; thus is declared the Vighneśa-mātṛkā.
The association of the letters *ya* and the others with the skin and so forth has been proclaimed as before.
(In the Nibandha:
[The mantra] begins with *om* and ends with *namaḥ*, either with the nasal bindu or devoid of the bindu. (3.342)
The arrangement of the fifty phonemes has been taught in sequence by the wise.
The Mātṛkā is said to be fourfold: the pure [vowels], those joined with the bindu, [those joined with the visarga], and those joined with both. (3.343)
Listen, the secret is being told: [the mantra] with the *visarga* and with both [parts] is the secret;
the *vidyākarī* alone, together with both [parts], bestows enjoyment (*bhukti*). (3.344)
With the *visarga*, she bestows sons; with the *bindu*, she grants wealth.
(In the *Kulāvatāra*) she is preceded by the seed-syllables of Māyā and Lakṣmī, or alternatively, by the *vāgbhava* syllable. (3-345)
The three stars (tritāra) or the three syllables beginning with Ramā (ramādi) should be installed by the most excellent practitioners. And the three stars are:
Vāgbhava, Kāmarāja, and Śrībīja; this is the tritāraka.
"Or the sages know [the mantra] as the Śakti, Śrī, and Kāma-bījas, or as the three tāras;
thus it is declared in another Tantra. But in the Bījakośa:"
The Vāgbhava, O Bhuvaneśānī, the Śrībīja, and the Tritāraka—thus it has been stated. (3.347)
In the *Siddhāntasāra*:

"The Mātṛkā preceded by the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable] bestows speech; preceded by the three Tārās, it grants desires; and preceded by the Śrī-bīja, it is remembered as the bestower of great sovereignty. (3.348)
In the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*:
"One should perform the triad of Mātṛkās as creation, withdrawal, and maintenance;
O Maheśānī, one should especially perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) as prescribed in the Kalpa. (3.349)
In the *Kulāvatāra*:
"From creation comes the prosperity of sons and so forth; from maintenance comes their protection;
from withdrawal comes the removal of defects; therefore, one should practice this triad. (3.350)
(In the *Siddhāntasāra*):

During the act of creation, one should place the letters from *ḍa* to *ṭha* together with the vowels; during dissolution, they should be accompanied by the nasal bindu (*m*); and during maintenance, they should be endowed with both. (3.351)

(But in the *Triśaktiratna*, having divided the mantra and the script according to the threefold distinction beginning with Akatha: "One should first place the *ka*-group, and after that, the *a*-group. (3-352)
"One should then place the *tavarga* (the dental class of consonants); this is proclaimed as the *sthitimudrā*. Thus it was said.
The *mātṛkānyāsa-mudrās* are described in another tantra:
"One should place [the fingers] with the middle of the ring finger on the forehead and around the face. (3.353)
The best of practitioners should place the index, middle, and ring fingers upon the two eyes; having joined the index and ring fingers together, he should then place them [upon the ears]. (3.354)
Placing the thumbs on the two ears and the little fingers and thumbs on the two nostrils, one should place the middle fingers on the two cheeks and the middle fingers on the two lips. (3.355)
Placing the ring finger on the two teeth, the middle finger on the head, the ring and middle fingers on the mouth, and [the remaining fingers] on the hands, feet, and sides. (3.356)
The little finger, the ring finger, and the middle finger should likewise be placed on the back;
all of them, together with the thumb, should be placed at the region of the navel and in the belly. (3.357)
The practitioner [should place] the palms upon the heart, both shoulders, and the crown of the head;
likewise, the palms alone [should be placed] on the heart, the two hands, the feet, the belly, and the face. (3.358)
These mudrās of the Mātṛkās have thus been proclaimed in their proper order;
for him who performs the ritual placement (nyāsa) without knowing them, that placement shall be fruitless.
(In the *Mantratantraprakāśa*):
One should project the vital breaths (*asūn*) either with flowers, or with the *anāmikā* finger, or even mentally.
Regarding the term "with the *anāmikā*," it means "together with the thumb."
The ritual placement (nyāsa) performed with the thumb and the ring finger is approved for all instances. || 3.360 ||
Thus, according to the statement in the *Padyavāhinī*:

"By that [method], the placement (*nyāsa*) with flowers upon the form of the deity should be understood as being performed with the thumb and ring finger; and upon one's own body, it should be understood as being performed mentally at the *mūlādhāra* and other centers. Furthermore, this refers to instances other than the *ṛṣi*-etc., the six-limbed (*ṣaḍaṅga*) placement, the external *mātṛkā*, and so forth, because another mudrā is prescribed therein.
(Ḍāmara, p. 184)
Having performed the Mātṛkā-nyāsa, one should perform the other nyāsas;
then one should perform the nyāsa of the seer (ṛṣi) and so forth, as well as the hand and limb nyāsas, for the root mantra.
"O Goddess, one should assign the Ṛṣis and so forth [to the limbs], ending with the Heart-mantra in the fourth case," as stated in the Yoginītantra.
(Bṛhanmatsyasūkta)
The placement of the Ṛṣis is on the region of the head, while that of the Chandas is in the lotus of the mouth.
One should place the deity in the heart, the seed-syllable (bīja) in the secret region, the power (śakti) in the feet, and the wedge (kīlaka) upon all the limbs.
In the *Merutantra*:
"Because the seer (*ṛṣi*) is the teacher, he is placed on the head; because the meter (*chandas*) consists of phonemes (*varṇa*), it is placed in the mouth;
its retention (*dhāraṇā*) is said to be in the mind; and because the deity (*devatā*) is that which is to be known, she is placed in the heart. (3.364)
But the sage is he who, having learned [the mantra] directly from the mouth of Maheśvara through austerity, accomplishes it with a purified soul; he is declared to be its *ṛṣi*. (3.365)
Thus it is declared in the *Kālānalatantra*:
"Likewise,
because of its weightiness, the placement (*nyāsa*) of this [syllable] upon the head is proclaimed."
In the *Merutantra*, it is held that from the verbal root *ṛ* in the sense of "going," the vowel *ṛ* is considered the "attainer. (3-366)
The meaning of the syllable *ṣi* is consciousness (*vijñāna*); therefore, it is that which brings about its attainment.
(From the *Bṛhanmatsyasūkta*) Because it conceals all the principles of mantra (*mantratattva*), it is called *chanda*. (3-367)
Because it consists of syllables and words, the Vedic meter is said to reside in the mouth;
one does not partake of the fruit of the mantra through ignorance of the seer and the meter. (3.368)
Moreover, there is weakness in the mantras for those who do not know their application. (p.
185) The *ṛṣi*, *chandas*, and *devatā* placements, as well as the mudrās, are taught in other tantras:
"The fingers are prescribed for the placement of the *ṛṣi*, *chandas*, and *devatā*. (3-369)

Then, the foremost of practitioners should place the four fingers, excluding the thumbs, up to the end of the Śakti; thereafter, the best of adepts should place the Kīlaka upon all limbs with both hands interlaced.
The mudrās for the limbs of the meaning are in that very same place:
"The wise one should place [the fingers] at the heart with the middle, ring, and index fingers;
and he should perform the placement on the head with the middle and index fingers. (3.371)
One should place [the mantra] on the crest with the thumb, on the armor with ten fingers, and on the eyes with three; the weapon [mantra] should be placed three times, moving upwards from above.
These are known as the limb-mudrās (aṅgamudrā) formed with the middle and index fingers.
He speaks for the sake of the six limbs:
by the word "to the heart" (hṛdayāya), the deity residing in the heart is meant in embodied form. (3-373)
It is said that the knowledge of the word "name" has that [name] as its object;
the word "head" (śiras) denotes the excellence of the deity. (3-374)
With "svāhā," all sense objects are offered into the deity;
that state of being the very nature of the crest-lock (śikhā) is also expressed by "vaṣaṭ. (3.375)
The pervasiveness of the deity is designated as the armor (kavaca); the syllable *huṃ* manifests the pervasive radiance of the deity. (3.376)
By the word *netra*, the eternal knowledge of the Lord is revealed;
that very same [knowledge] is called *vauṣaṭ*, and by the word *astra*, it is the warding off [of obstacles]. (3.377)
By the word *phaṭ*, the burning fire of that which is undesirable is expressed.
He who, having understood the meaning of the limb-mantras in this way, performs the ritual placement (*aṅganyāsa*)— || 3-378 ||
All his purposes are fulfilled, and he is worshipped even by the thirty gods.
(From the *Merutantra*):
From the root *div*, meaning "to play," the word for a deity (*devatā*) is fully derived. (3.379)

She is proclaimed as the deity because she bestows [attainment] upon the practitioner. Being colored by passion, the self consisting of consciousness exists within the heart as the essence of the heart. (3.380)
Therefore, one should pay homage there and touch with the primary thumb, because by means of the *svāhā* [syllable], the withdrawal of the sense objects is properly performed. (3.381)
By those [fingers] drawn forth with the ring finger and the index finger, what is served?
The crest (śikhā), the splendor (mahaḥ), the exclamation vaṣaṭ, and the limb; by the crest, there is the grasping of one's own body.
Therefore, the word "vaṣaṭ" is uttered with the middle finger;
for the purpose of grasping, that [deity] is seized by means of the mantra containing the root *dhṛ* (to hold) and the word *kavaca*. || 3-383 ||
Therefore, one should place the armor upon the body with the index and ring fingers;
"vauṣaṭ" produces that which effects the knowledge of reality, and it arises from the two eyes. (3.384)
Therefore, it is said that *vauṣaṭ* is used there; that [mantra] is remembered as being performed with the index finger and the other fingers.
Because it consists of a single syllable, one should utter the name of the deity, such as Kubera, ending in the dative case (*ṅe*). (3-385)
In the case of Viṣṇu and others, it ends with *bhya*; however, in the case of Rudra and others, it consists of three eyes.
That which is of the nature of the spiritual and so forth would destroy the practitioner. (3.386)

That weapon, born of ignorance, is expanded by means of *phaṭ* and *tāla*; one should then perform the placement (*nyāsa*) upon the thumb and the other fingers with the seed-syllables (*jāti*) followed by *namaḥ*, according to the *Yāmala*. (3.387)
One should perform the ritual placement (vinyāsa) upon the six limbs, beginning with the heart, using the six seed-syllables:
*namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *huṃ*, *vauṣaṭ*, and *phaṭ*; these are the [six] *jātis*. (3.388)
Elsewhere also:
"The group of six birth-mantras is proclaimed as being joined with [the mantras] beginning with the heart and ending with the weapon.
And likewise in the Śāradā:
Then the wise practitioner should assign the limb-mantras to the heart and other parts of the body. (3.389)
First, "Hṛdayāya namaḥ" [is for the heart]; "Vahnivallabhā" (the beloved of fire, i.e., *svāhā*) is said for the head;
"Śikhāyai vaṣaṭ" is uttered, and "Kavacāya huṃ" is recited. (3.390)
One should apply the six limb-mantras, as previously stated, to the six limbs in sequence: "vauṣaṭ" to the three eyes and "phaṭ" to the weapon. (3.391)
The necessity of *aṅganyāsa* has been stated [in the *Jñānamālā*]:
"Even if worship, recitation, adoration, and fire-offerings are performed with mantras that have already been mastered, these will not yield their fruits if they are devoid of *aṅganyāsa*. (3.392)
The practitioner of mantra should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of six limbs or five limbs according to the prescribed rule.
For whichever mantra has only five limbs, the eye-limb is omitted. (Merutantra 3.393)
One should provide a limb for the mind that is devoid of limbs by means of that very [mind] itself.
Likewise: "He who constantly performs the ritual placements (nyāsa) according to the path taught in the Āgamas... (3.394).
O Dear One, he who recites the mantra while protected by the armor of the ritual placement (nyāsa) attains the state of a deity and achieves success in the mantra. 3-395.
Upon seeing him, obstacles flee just as elephants do upon seeing a lion;
yet that foolish soul who performs recitation without having first established the net of the nyāsa-mantras [is like one who attempts this without preparation]. (3.396)
He will surely be afflicted by obstacles, like a young deer by tigers;
yet, due to the abundance of deposits, there will also be an abundance of rewards. (3.397)
The previously mentioned ritual placement (nyāsa) must certainly not be abandoned; one may perform further [placements] according to one's desire. (In the *Yāmala*):
Thereafter, one should perform the ritual placement known as the Yoga-pīṭha within one's own body. (3.398)
[He worships] the foundational power (ādhāraśakti), primordial nature (prakṛti), as well as Kūrma and Ananta.
However, in another [tradition], after the root-nature (mūlaprakṛti), Kālāgnirudra is also mentioned;
thus it is said: "Then the root-nature, Rudra, and the one called Kalānala. (3-399)
In my own system, however, Kālāgnirudra was mentioned even before the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti); immediately after that, the foundational power (ādhāraśakti) was mentioned.
Likewise:
[He beheld] Varāha, the Earth, the Ocean of Milk, and the Island born of jewels.
In the Vaiṣṇava tradition, however, Śvetadvīpa is described as having a pavilion made of jewels, a wish-fulfilling tree, and a jeweled altar.
The practitioner of mantra should likewise place these [elements] upon the jewel-throne within the heart itself.
In some [traditions], a Nandana garden is also mentioned following the jeweled pavilion; as stated in the *Śāradā*:
The wise preceptor [should perform this] by moving clockwise around the pair of shoulders and thighs.
One should sequentially place knowledge of Dharma, dispassion, and sovereignty [upon the lotus].
Dharma and the others are remembered as the feet, while the others are the limbs of the pedestal. (3.402)
One should visualize Adharma and the other [principles] on the face, the sides, and the sides of the navel;
and Ananta upon the heart-lotus, wherein are the sun, moon, and fire.
In these [deities], one should assign their respective arts (kalās), preceded by the first letter of each name.
One should assign the Sun, beginning with the letter 'a', and the Moon, beginning with the letter 'u'.

The best of gurus should place the fire, beginning with the letter *ma*, conjoined with the circle of its digits (*kalā*), and likewise place the three qualities (*guṇa*) here, beginning with *sattva*. (3.405)
Sattva, rajas, and tamas are declared to be its divisions;
yet herein [it is also] the Self, the inner self, and the supreme self.
Having placed the three initial seed-syllables preceded by the seed-syllable of Śakti,
and having duly placed the one whose essence is knowledge (jñānātman), one should then place the mantra of the seat (pīṭhamantra).
In this way, one should meditate upon the chosen deity within the seat consisting of the body.
Regarding the two types of meditation on the deity, it is stated in the *Merutantra*:
"Then one should perform meditation according to the very path prescribed in the respective ritual manual (*kalpa*). (3-408)
That [meditation] is also said to be of two kinds: with attributes (saguṇa) and likewise without attributes (nirguṇa).
It is performed within the lotus of the heart of the Self, radiant with its pericarp and filaments.
(189) There, resplendent with the blossoming mandalas of the Moon, Sun, and Fire, one should perceive one's own chosen deity as revealed by the scriptures. (3.410)
Thus, that which is the realization [of this] is indeed called meditation with attributes (saguṇa-dhyāna);
it is the realization that "I am He," which is the oneness of the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman. (3-411)
"The knowers of Brahman know that very [state] to be meditation devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa-dhyāna*).
Here, in the *Merutantra*, the display of the mudrās is stated to occur immediately after the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and prior to meditation.
One should perform other ritual placements (nyāsa), primarily the placement of the hands and limbs (karāṅganyāsa). || 3-412 ||
"Subsequently, one should display the respective mudrās prescribed for each particular kalpa"—thus [it is said].
But elsewhere it says: "O Maheśānī, having meditated in this manner, one should then display the mudrās. (3-413)
The intermediate meditation (*dhyānāntara*) has been described [in that work].
However, in the *Mahātharvaṇarahasya*, after describing the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), meditation, and the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*), it is stated:
"Then, having become one with That, one should display these mudrās."
In that regard, the temporal variation is to be understood.
Regarding the binding of the mudrā, as well as its display and release, the specific mantras are stated in the *Merutantra*:
"The binding of the mudrā is traditionally taught by means of the two seed-syllables *oṃ* and *klīṃ*. (3-414)
One should show [the deity] with the root mantra; one should dismiss [it] with the seed-syllable *hsū*. (In the *Sanatkumārasaṃhitā*):
Without performing the mental sacrifice, one should not perform external worship. (3.415)
The Procedure for the Inner Sacrifice (*Antaryāgavidhi*) [from the *Bṛhaduttaratantra*]:
Having meditated upon Her seated upon the Yoga-pīṭha in the center of the pericarp of the heart-lotus, one should worship Her with mental offerings such as scents, flowers, and so forth. (3.416)

Having worshipped according to the prescribed rules, one should thereafter perform the mental fire-sacrifice (*mānasahoma*). (From the *Śrīmad-Rahasya*, verses on the observances): "Free from deceit, free from egoism, likewise free from passion and pride... (3.417).

Absence of delusion, absence of pride, and absence of hypocrisy, as well as absence of hatred, absence of agitation, absence of envy, and absence of greed—the wise know these to be the ten flowers. (3-418)
Non-violence is the supreme flower; the restraint of the senses is a flower; compassion is a flower; dharma is a flower; and wisdom is the fifth flower. (3.419)
One should worship the Supreme Deity with these aforementioned excellent flowers. (In the *Merutantra*:
One should contemplate a four-cornered fire-pit at the *mūlādhāra*. (3–420)
There, one should meditate on the fire in the form of Kuṇḍalin and recite the root mantra;
with the mind as the sacrificial ladle, one should offer the oblation of merit and demerit into the blazing fire of the Self.
I constantly offer the functioning of the senses through the path of the *suṣumṇā*;
at the end of each verse, one should further utter: "I offer merit, svāhā! (3-422).
Again I offer the root, again the verse, and again the evil; as well as intention and non-intention, conceptualization and non-conceptualization, and even dharma itself. (3-423)
Having offered separately with the word *svāhā* at the end, one should again recite this verse:
"Holding the *unmanī*-ladle with the hands of *prakāśa* and *amarṣa*... (3.424).
I offer the moisture of the portions of merit and demerit into the full fire;
having given this oblation with the word "svāhā" at its end, through the restraint of breath-control (prāṇāyāma).
One should meditate upon the Self as consisting of pure consciousness, with all limiting adjuncts cast away.
However, in the *Śyāmārahasya* and other such texts, at the end of the root mantra, [one should offer] with the ladle of the mind oblations of fire into the locus of the navel-consciousness. (3.426)
"Enkindled by wisdom, I perpetually offer the functions of the senses;
Svāhā!"—this is the first oblation. [At the end of the root mantra:]
With the mind as the sacrificial ladle, one should offer the oblation of dharma and adharma into the fire of one's own self, which is kindled by them.
"By means of the path of the *suṣumṇā*, I perpetually offer the functions of the senses;
Svāhā!"—this is the second oblation. At the end of the root mantra:
Having grasped it with the hands of light and space, by means of the sacrificial ladle of *unmanī*.
I offer into the fire that which is filled with the moisture of the subtle particles of merit and demerit.
The third oblation is with "svāhā," at the end of the root mantra: "blazing within, without interval, and without fuel..."
Into the fire of consciousness, which is the adversary of the darkness of delusion and the ground for the unfolding of certain wondrous rays,
I offer as an oblation the entire universe, beginning with the earth and ending with Śiva. (3.429)

" Svāhā"—this is the fourth oblation. Thus, four oblations have been described by means of these four verses. (In the *Merutantra*), a specific instruction is given: having drawn in the breath through the *iḍā* [left nostril], slightly contracting the anus, placing the tongue against the palate, and having raised the *kuṇḍalinī* from the *mūlādhāra*, one should unite her with the Supreme Śiva residing within the pericarp of the thousand-petaled lotus and worship the deity upon the aforementioned seat.
(As follows:)
Having drawn in the left channel, one should slightly contract the anus;
one should exhale through the central path and cause the tongue to reach the palate.
Having joined the *śakti* to the state of Śiva, one should slightly contract [the perineum] below;
having done this, the knower of mantras should worship the seat (*pīṭha*) by way of ritual deposition (*nyāsa*).

Having meditated upon one's chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) seated upon that pedestal in embodied form, one should worship her with sandalwood paste and other offerings, beginning mentally and ending with food.
At the time of eating, however, one should perform the Vaiśvadeva rite internally.
In that very context: "At the conclusion of that, becoming absorbed in Him, one should mutter [the mantra] one hundred and eight times. (3.433)
One should offer that root [garland] to the deity for the sake of all prosperity.
(In the *Mātṛkāraṇava*: "The garland is said to consist of fifty [beads], and the thread is of the nature of Śakti and Śiva. (3.434)
The knot is said to be Kuṇḍalinī; at the end of the *kalā*, it is situated on Meru.
(In the *Kumārīkalpa*), however, recitation (*japa*) is prescribed prior to the fire-oblation (*homa*);
therefore, one should indeed perform mental recitation even before the beginning of the oblation. (3-435)

"Having paid homage and likewise offered praise, one should then perform the external sacrifice"—thus [it is said]. (In the *Candrikā*: "Having performed this internal sacrifice, one becomes directly identical with Brahman. (3-436)
Neither his sins nor his merits remain; he becomes liberated while living on this earth.
Thus ends the procedure for the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*).
Now follows the preparation of the vessels (*pātrāsādana*). As it is said in the *Yāmala*:
Between the object of proof and the means of proof, there should be thirty-six finger-breadths.
Twelve finger-breadths above and twelve finger-breadths below that, with twelve finger-breadths situated in the middle—therein the wise one should establish it. (3-438)
(Merutantra) Now I shall describe the auspicious and inauspicious results of vessels for the arghya and other offerings.
Gold bestows all desires; silver bestows long life and sons. (3-439)
Good fortune is attained through a copper vessel, while the increase of dharma occurs with one made of clay;
satisfaction of the gods is achieved with a coconut, and that which is made of glass brings about nourishment.
The attainment of fortune occurs through a vessel made of bilva wood; Brahminhood is attained through one born from the Brahma-tree (aśvattha);
for killing and expulsion, it should be made of iron; and for paralyzing, it should be made of stone. (3-441)
For the propitiation of the mantra, wood from the left-hand path is used, as is copper;
likewise, vessels made of gems and other materials that are marked with auspicious lines [are employed]. (3-442)
One should prepare [the offerings] for the purpose of worship with *argha* and *naivedya*, as well as for the offering of the *bali* (Mahāhāratantre):
"The gifting of ten million maidens, and likewise hundreds of gold pieces. (3-443)
O Maheśānī, whoever offers this when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu,
the fruit thereof is multiplied ten millionfold by means of the coconut vessel for the *argha* offering.
(p. 193) This concerns the [appropriate] capacity [of materials].
Regarding specific vessels for specific deities, the *Merutantra* states:
"For Śiva, a vessel of bell-metal or silver is best; for Viṣṇu, a conch shell is best."
The great conch is on the left path, and crystal is in the leader of the planets.
One should show reverence toward worthy recipients, for they alone are supreme;
indeed, rites such as offerings and oblations do not succeed without a worthy recipient. (3.446)
A vessel of thirty-six finger-breadths is proclaimed as the best;
the medium is three parts less than that, and the smallest is twelve finger-breadths. (3.447)
One should never have a vessel made that is less than eight finger-breadths [in width];
its forms, including the navel and the openings, should be shaped like lotuses. (3-448)
One should fashion bowls with the luster of a conch or a blue lotus;
those that are white and so forth are highly praised for the Brahmins and the other castes in their respective order.
(From the *Tattvasārasaṃhitā*):
A conch shell bestows knowledge; a pearl-oyster shell grants learning;
and vessels made of skull or gourd bring about the perfections of yoga. (3.450)
The ritual involving the skull and other implements is intended for the heroes. (In the *Samayācāra*):
Then, having prepared the general *argha* offering with milk, the most excellent practitioner—
Having prepared a mandala with those waters, he should then place the vessels there.
The general procedure for the *argha* offering has been stated previously.

Now follows the procedure for the installation of the water-pot (*kalaśasthāpanavidhi*) [from the *Siddhāntasāra*]: having purified the ground with the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*) and with the water from the general *argha* offering...
To his left is a mandala consisting of a dot, a hexagon, a circle, and a square.
Having inscribed [the mantra], one should pronounce the name of the deity at the end of the root mantra;
one should worship the base of the jar with the mantra "Homage to the Maṇḍala" (maṇḍalāya namaḥ).
There, one should place a support that has been washed with the *hetimantra*; there, one should worship the fire-maṇḍala as pervaded by the ten kalās. (3.454)
Having empowered the water-pot, one should place it there with the thought that it is the deity;
there, one should worship the solar disc conjoined with its twelve digits.
One should fill the jar with pure water using the root mantra; this is on the left-hand path.
However, on the right-hand path, the practitioner of mantra should fill it with pure causal [substances] using the root mantra. (3–456)
Thus the statement from another mantra is found in the *Sudhārṇava* and other texts. "By the pure" means by the refined [Sanskrit]. Likewise:
"There one should worship the lunar orb conjoined with its sixteen digits."
The practitioner of mantra should worship the triad of images with three portions of *tāra*.
Having invoked the sacred site (tīrtha) there, the knower of mantras, having protected it with the *hetivarma* and *svamūlaka* mantras, should veil it, gaze upon it, and sprinkle it with water.
O Goddess of the Gods, one should worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, covering [the vessel] with the *matsya-mudrā*, and consecrate the *kalaśa* with this mantra: 3-459.
Viṣṇu resides at the mouth of the jar; Rudra is situated at its neck;
Brahmā is stationed at its base; and the hosts of Mothers are said to dwell in its middle. (3-460)
Within his belly were all the oceans and the earth with its seven continents;
likewise, the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda, and Atharvaveda.
"Accompanied by all their limbs, they have all taken refuge in the jar.
Having said this, one should consecrate the jar eight times with the root mantra.
Having displayed the *kumbha-mudrā*, one should then contemplate oneself as being of the nature of the deity.
The *kumbha-mudrā* will be described later [in the *Yāmala*].
Having placed the *prokṣaṇī* vessel to his right, he should fill it with water.
Having taken some of the arghya water, he should pour it into the water for sprinkling (prokṣaṇī).
Then, the wise one should place the vessel together with its support in front of him.
To its side is the offering of water for the feet (pādya), and to its side the offering of the respectful oblation (argha);
to its side is the water for sipping (ācamanīya), and to its left is the honey-mixture (madhuparka).
Furthermore, one should place the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) and the water for bathing (*snānīya*) in their respective order.

"Arghyāmbu" means the general offering water (*sāmānyārghodaka*). Since the general offering water must be placed to one's own right even before the arrangement of the vessels, one should therefore set aside a small space to the right of that [general offering water] for the purpose of placing the vessel for the water for washing the feet (*pādya*), and there place the sprinkling vessel (*prokṣaṇīpātra*). "Beside that, the vessel for the offering of *argha*" means that the *argha* vessel is on the left side of the vessel for the water for washing the feet.
(In the *Merutantra* and other texts, however...)
To the north of the *argha* water, one should place the water for washing the feet (*pādya*) and the water for sipping (*ācamanīyaka*).
"And having placed the *madhuparka* in the three triangles in due order.

Thus, after the placement of the *argha* vessel, the placement of the vessels for the *pādya* and other offerings is stated to be on its left side. Furthermore, at the time of presenting the ritual services (*upacāra*), the offering of *argha* is stated therein to precede the giving of the *pādya*.
(From the *Navaratneśvara*)
One should not use a single vessel, even if it were Maheśvara himself.
The mantras turn away, and misfortunes arise at every step;
in this world there is poverty, and after death one goes to the state of an animal. (3-468)
In that very same [text] (the Gautama-sūtra):
"One may use two vessels due to the absence [of one], but one should not perform [the rite] with fewer."
There should be three vessels for the *argha* offering, and likewise three for the foot-washing water (*pādya*).
In the same way, vessels for water for sipping should be provided separately;
however, due to the weakness of performing [the ritual] in that manner, a single vessel is recommended. (3.470)
The substances for the water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings are described in the *Phetkāriṇī*:
"One should prepare *uśīra* and *rocanā* in the vessel for the water for the feet, as well as the tips of *kuśa* grass, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), barley, grain, and sesame seeds. (3.471)
One should cast clarified butter, white mustard seeds, and flowers into the vessel for the *argha* offering,
as well as jasmine, camphor, *kaṅkola*, *bahumūla*, and *tamālaka*.
Having ground these according to the rule, one should pour them into the water for sipping (ācamanīya),
along with honey, sugar, clarified butter, curd, and milk.
Having prepared the madhuparka, one should offer it according to the prescribed rite. (In the Merutantra:
The water for washing the feet (pādya) is said to consist of śyāmāka grain, dūrvā grass, lotus, and viṣṇukrāntā. (3.474)
Likewise:
"O gods, fragrance, flowers, unbroken rice, barley, tips of kuśa grass, sesame seeds, mustard seeds, and dūrvā grass—these are declared to be the eight substances for the arghya vessel. (3.475)
"Surā" is an address to the gods. Likewise:
"The *ācamanīyaka* (water for sipping) is considered [to be prepared] with *jātī*, *lavaṅga*, and *kaṅkola*."
Kuśa grass, flowers, barley, rice, and many roots of the tamālaka tree. || 3-476 ||
One should cause it to be poured into the water of the *prokṣaṇī* vessel with the *praṇava*.
(In the *Mahākālasaṃhitā*):
"Water that has not been offered to others, remaining in its natural state and well-cooled... (3.477).
The water for bathing is said to be contained in jars or vessels made of gold and other materials.
(In the *Candrikā*:
"One should cause the bath to be performed with fragrant waters... (3.478).
The water for sipping (ācamanīyaka) has been prepared by me with pure waters;
however, in the absence of these substances, auspicious washed rice grains should be offered. (3-479)
In the worship of Viṣṇu, the placement of the conch (śaṅkha) is mandatory.
This was stated by Agastya (Kumbhasambhava):
"That Vaiṣṇava who worships Hari without a conch [is deficient]."
Even though he is a perfect worshipper, he does not obtain the fruit of worship.
The procedure for installing the conch is described in the *Merutantra*, beginning with the words "on one's own left":
"One should properly encircle that [with a line] using sandalwood water to form a triangle;
outside of that, one should fashion a square using the *matsyamudrā*. (3.481)
Having worshipped with fragrances, one should offer the *arghya* to the deity with the mantra "Obeisance to the maṇḍala" (*namaḥ-aṇu*).
Then, one should place the limbs (*aṅga*) in the four corners starting from the southeast (Agni) and likewise in front.
Having worshipped the weapon-mantra in the cardinal directions, one should place the conch-vessel;
for without a support, there is a risk of spilling, and the Mothers are not satisfied.
Therefore, according to the prescribed rule, the support should be made of metal and be either three-footed or four-footed, shaped like a lotus, a triangle, or resembling a womb. (3.484)
At the end of the root mantra, having said, "And I establish the support-vessel for [the deity] so-and-so," one should then place the conch and other supporting vessels within the mandala.
Having said "Ma Ra Dharmaprada," one should speak [the name] ending in the dative case for the one whose self consists of ten digits;
one should then proclaim the mandala of Fire and the name of the deity. (3.486)
Then, having uttered "Salutation to the support of the argha vessel," one should worship it;
there, the ten kalās of Agni are to be worshipped as previously described in a clockwise direction.

It should be understood that the mention of both the conch and the *arghya* vessel here is because the procedure for placing the specific *arghya* vessel described above applies equally to both. Then, with the *astra-mantra*, one should [purify] a vessel made of gold or other materials, or else a conch, with water using the *astra* mantra. (3-488)
"Having washed the arghya vessel for [the deity] so-and-so, I establish it.
Having spoken thus, one should place it upon its base and speak again as follows: || 3-489 ||
p. 198) Then one should say "the twelve [suns] that bestow wealth," which is the essence of the *kalās*;
having uttered the solar orb, one should then utter the name of the deity ending in *-ṅ*. (3-490)
One should worship the argha vessel with this mantra;
then, one should visualize that very vessel as a mandala of the earth.
Then, one should worship the six limbs there in the hexagon as before;
thereafter, the twelve digits of the Sun are said to be worshipped in the vessel while circumambulating clockwise.
Then, reciting the Mātṛkā in reverse order from the root-mantra to the end, the worshipper should fill that [vessel] with nectar-like water while reciting this mantra.

Having uttered "O bestower of desires" (u/ sa/ kāmaprada), followed by "to the sixteen" (ṣoḍaśa) and "to the self of the kalās" (kalātmane), this fifteen-syllable mantra, ending with "namas," is for filling the conch. (3-494)
Likewise, in another tantra it is said:
"The two ears (karṇa) and the moon (candra), joined with the bindu; then the word 'kāmaprada';
then the word 'kalā' at the end of the sixteen; and at the end of the self (ātman), [one recites] with the heart-mantra. (3.495)
Having worshipped with perfumes and flowers, one should worship the sixteen *kalaśas*.

Here, Karṇa is the letter *u*, Candra is the half-moon (*ardhacandra*), and Bindu is the *anusvāra*; thus, having established the single seed-syllable *um*, it is extracted in the *Muktāvalī*. That very same method was adopted without further deliberation by Nṛsiṃha Ṭhakkura in his own work, the *Tārābhaktisudhārṇava*. In reality, however, Karṇa is the letter *u* and Candra is the letter *sa*; through the addition of the *bindu* to these two, there are indeed two seed-syllables: *u* and *sam*. "The letter *sa* is named Śakti, and it is cooled by the nectar of the moon. (3-496)
Thus, from the *Varṇakośa*:
Śiva, Śakti, Kāma, Earth, then the Sun, the Moon,
Smara, Haṃsa, Śakra, and thereafter Parā, Māra, and Hari.
O Mother, these letters, joined at their endings with the three *hṛllekhā* syllables, attain the status of being limbs of Your name. (3-497)

This is because, in such passages as these, we observe that the word *śītakiraṇa*, which denotes the moon, is followed by the letter *sa*. Nor should it be argued that since the word *candra* is seen in some instances to refer to the half-moon (*ardhacandra*), there need be only one seed-syllable (*bīja*) here; for that would contradict the *Merutantra*, which reveals two distinct seed-syllables.
Thus:
"Having worshipped that water with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should perform the ritual adoration."
And thereafter, the sixteen digits (kalās) of the Moon are present within all the digits.
Then, at the conclusion of the worship, one should perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breaths) along with the *dhāka*.

The digits (*kalās*) of Fire, Sun, and Moon have been mentioned previously, as well as the methods for their worship in the *Kulārṇava*: "The ten digits that bestow merit arise from the letters beginning with *ya*, starting from the southeast (*āgneyī*). (3.499)
The twelve vowels beginning with *ka* and ending with *ḍha* are said to be the *saurāṣṭhas*, bestowers of wealth;
the sixteen vowels born of the primary sounds (*svaras*) are the *saumyas*, granters of desires. (3.500)

The meaning is that one should worship the sixteen digits of the Moon (*candrakalā*) by first placing the ten letters from *ya* to *da* joined with the *bindu*, preceded by the fire-digits (*agnikalā*). Then, having placed the letters from *ka* to *ṭha* and from *bha* to *ḍha* in reverse order joined with the *bindu*, one places the solar digits (*sūryakalā*) at the beginning. Finally, having placed the sixteen vowels from *a* onwards joined with the *bindu*, the lunar digits are to be worshipped. (In the *Merutantra*):

Having invoked the sacred site (*tīrtha*) as before, one should join it there with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), place a flower with the eye-mantra (*netramantra*), and [perform the rite] with the crest-mantra (*śikhāmantra*). (3.501)
Having displayed the Gālinī mudrā and having rendered [the offering] nectar-like according to the rule by means of the Dhenusaṃjñā mudrā and the seed-syllable of nectar, the practitioner—
Having meditated there upon one's chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā), one should perform the ritual of integration (sakalīkaraṇa);
and by means of the assignment of limbs (aṅganyāsa) and the weapon-mantra (astra), one should ward off the ten directions.
Having gazed [at it] with the Netra-mantra, having secured it with the mudrā known as the conch (śaṅkha),
and then with the radiant mudrā in the form of the womb (yoni).
There, one should worship the chosen deity with perfumes, flowers, and so forth;
having worshipped the six limbs as well, one should consecrate [the site] with the root mantra. (3.505)
Then, having offered the *arghya* eight times, one should cover it with the *matsyamudrā*.
However, in the Vaiṣṇava tradition, the *dhenumudrā* is used in place of the *yonimudrā*. As stated by Āgastya:
"Having protected it with the *astra-mantra*, one should veil it with the *kavaca-mantra*. (3.506)
"One should display the *dhenumudrā* and awaken [the deity] with its own *mudrā*.

By "its own *mudrā*" is meant the *śaṅkhamudrā*. We shall explain the *mudrās* further below. (In the *Meru* [rite]) one should pour a little of that water contained in the conch into the water of the *kumbha*. (3.507)
In another tantra:
Having placed the *prokṣaṇī* vessel on his own right, the best of practitioners should arrange the *pādya* vessel and the pair of *arghya* vessels to its north. (3.508)
"Two *argha*s" means the general *argha* and the special *argha*.
The measurement of the *argha* vessel is stated in the *Siddhāntasāra*:
"The vessel for the *argha*, according to its base measurement, should be four finger-breadths (*vedāṅgula*) in height."
Or one should make it eight finger-breadths wide and raised to the height of one eye-measure (two finger-breadths). || 3-509 ||
One should increase the quantity in the *prokṣaṇī* vessel; one must not make it less than that. (In the *Mahākālasaṃhitā*):
It should be known that at the beginning, the most important [vessel] measures sixteen finger-breadths. (3-510)
The medium [vessel] should be measured at twelve [finger-breadths], while the inferior should be ten finger-breadths;
however, one should never have a vessel made that is deficient by eight finger-breadths.
Everywhere, a copper vessel for the *arghya* offering is more highly esteemed than one made of gold.

Regarding this, the procedure for establishing the ordinary *arghya* has been stated previously. However, the establishment of the special (*viśeṣa*) *arghya* should be performed as was previously described for the establishment of the conch (*śaṅkha*). But in the case of the *Śyāmā* and other *vidyās*, a specific rule is stated, as follows (in the *Triśaktiratna*):
"To the right side of the *kalaśa*, [one should draw] a triangle joined with a circle. (3.512)
Having drawn a hexagon and a square, one should depict within its central portion a radiant crescent moon and a Gandharva.

One should worship the sacred seats (pīṭhas), such as Uḍḍiyāna, Pūrṇagiri, and others, in the four directions; and in the hexagon, one should worship the Śakti with the limb-mantras (aṅgamantras) according to the threefold division of the root-mantra.
Having worshipped the foundational power (ādhāraśakti) as before, as well as the yantra,
[he should worship] the great conch, a coconut, and likewise one made of gold or silver.
One should place there a vessel made either of copper or of mother-of-pearl. (3.515ef)

"Gandharva" means the vowel *ī*. "U-jā-pū-kā-dī" refers to the sacred seats (*pīṭhas*) known as Uḍḍiyāna, Jālandhara, Pūrṇagiri, and Kāmarūpa. Regarding the phrase "in the Śakti," the mention of the "Great Conch" (*mahāśaṅkha*) is made with reference to the Trikoṇa, according to the Kaulika doctrine.
The different types of vessels are also mentioned in other Tantras:
"The vessel may be produced from gold, glass, silver, pearl, or skull."

The vessel made of gold brings joy to Viśvāmitra and fulfills all desires; that of crystal is dear; the copper one bestows affection and generates the attainment of desired goals; that produced from a noble coconut destroys sins; and the pearl vessel clearly generates the perfection of mantras and grants liberation.

(Triśaktiratna) Having worshipped as before, the practitioner of mantra should fill the vessel with the substance while reciting the letters of the root mantra in reverse order, radiant with its splendor. (3.517)
(In the Bhairavatantra:
Having placed a beautiful vessel together with a *kūrca* [purifier] and pure water, or [with] that which arises from the *kuṇḍa* and *gola*, or with a *svayambhū* flower; (3.518)

The hero, having filled [the vessel] with flowing water while reciting the root-mantra—beginning with "śuddhapātha" and so forth—the practitioner of the right-hand path (dakṣiṇamārgī) uses pure water; if he follows the left-hand path (vāmamārgī), it means he fills it with water originating from the *kuṇḍa* and *goḷa*, and so on. Having worshipped there as before, he should draw a circle and a hexagon. (Triśaktiratna, 3.519)
From two lines starting from the "A" syllable, one should draw a triangle in the center of the circle;
then, with the three root-sections, one should worship that triangle.
In the hexagon, one should meditate on the six limbs; then, one should contemplate the Tīrthamaya and, having visualized Ānandabhairava, worship him according to the prescribed rite.
One should worship the five jewels and cast in the family substances.
Regarding "the five jewels," they are the Gaganaratna and others, which will be described in the *Paddhati* (in the *Kumārīkalpa*).
The wise practitioner should carefully place the materials for the *argha* offering into the *argha* vessel.

O fair-browed one, there is no unrighteousness in the accomplishment of the great mantra, whether it involves substances produced from the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*, or likewise the *svayambhū* flower. (3.523)
"One should perform the remainder as before; this is remembered as the procedure for the *argha* offering. (*Triśaktiratna*) "In the *Bhairavatantra*: [it is stated].
Having covered [the mouth] with the left hand, one should then recite the root mantra eight times.
One should display the *bhūtinī*, the *dhenumudrā*, and the *yonimudrā*.

Herein, the procedure for depositing the *kuladravya*—such as the *svayambhū* flowers arising from the *kuṇḍa* and *goḷa*—is intended for the *vīra* [practitioner]. (In the ritual for the *paśu*, however:
fragrant substances, flowers, unbroken rice, barley, tips of *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, and mustard seeds. (3–525)
"O gods, *dūrvā* grass is declared to be the eighth substance of the *argha* vessel.

Thus, it should be understood that this is the deposition of the very eight substances mentioned in the *Merutantra*. Furthermore, the phrase "with the left hand" refers specifically to those who follow the Left Path (*vāmamārga*). On the Right Path (*dakṣiṇamārga*), however, covering [the vessel] with the right hand alone is established by tradition.
(Bhairavatantra) Having taken a little water, one should pour it into other vessels. (3.526)
One should sprinkle the articles of worship and oneself with that water.
(In the *Devīpaddhati*):
To the north of the special *argha*, there is the vessel for the *ācamana* rite. (3.527)
And one should place the madhuparka to its left, O Goddess praised by the gods;
the madhuparka should consist of honey mixed with curd and ghee. (3.528)
It is proclaimed that a bell-metal vessel brings joy to all the gods;
moreover, the bell-metal vessel is common to all [deities].
According to the *Meru-tantra*, there is a distinction in the vessels for the *madhuparka* offering based on the specific deity and other factors.
For Śiva, it should be made of bell-metal or silver; for Hari, it is best if it is made of conch-shell.
p. 203) On the left path, there is a great conch; [the offering] for the Lord of Planets is crystal.
In that very place:
"The honey-mixture (madhuparka), however, consists of curd with honey; if that is not available... (3.530).

Curdled milk, sugar, and honey—clarified butter is not a substitute for these; they are declared to be the constituent elements of the *madhuparka* offering. Regarding this very point, it is said: "That which is the supreme state of the gods is called by the name 'Madhu' (Honey). (3-531)
That action by which [the goal] is attained is called *madhuparka*.

The meaning is that the offering made with a deity as the intended recipient, which has the attainment of the supreme state (*paramapada*) as its fruit, is the referent of the term *madhuparka*. This [verse], however, is primarily intended to proclaim the fruits arising from the offering of *madhuparka*. In reality, however, the etymology of the word *madhuparka* is "that in which honey (*madhu*) is mixed (*pṛcyate*) with curds and other ingredients," according to the verbal root *pṛcī* in the sense of "to mix" (*saṃparka*).
(From the *Śrīnṛsiṃhacaraṇārcanapaddhati*)
Then, one should place a vessel for the purpose of water for sipping (ācamanīya). || 3-532 ||
The bathing of the God of gods, the Wielder of the Discus, is performed with water from a conch alone;
however, in the Śaiva tradition, water from a conch is prohibited.
As it is said in the *Siddhāntasaṃgraha*:
One should not worship Viṣṇu with unhusked grains, nor Vināyaka without tulasī.
One should not worship Durgā with *durvā* grass, nor Śambhu with water from a conch shell.

However, the placement of the vessels for the *pādya*, *ācamanīya*, and other offerings should be performed in the same manner as the placement of the *sāmānyārghya*. This is stated in that very [text]:
"One should prepare the vessels for the *pādya* and so forth according to the procedure prescribed for the *sāmānyārghya*. (3.534)
(In the Mahākālasaṃhitā:

One should fill those [vessels] with perfumes, unbroken rice, water, and flowers; in the vessel for the foot-water (pādya), the substances prescribed for the foot-water, and in the vessel for the respectful offering (arghya), those prescribed for the arghya. (3.535)
The materials for bathing, sipping water, and so forth have indeed been described previously;
all the vessels should be prepared provided with those very items.
(Merutantra) One should consecrate each individual vessel eight times with the root mantra;
one should then display the *dhenumudrā*... (3.537).
In another tantra, namely the *Vīrakalpa*, the installation of the *śrīpātra* and the *śaktipātra* and so forth is taught. (In the *Mahākālasaṃhitā*:
"At this very occasion, one should perform the installation of the *śrīpātra*."
A Kaula should perform [the rite] with milk, honey, and so forth, using the *prasannā* liquor along with the twice-born.

The ascetic (yati) should perform neither of these two, for the twice-born (dvija) does not desire them. [This refers to] with clear liquor (prasannayā surayā). [The term] "by the twice-born" (dvijaiḥ) refers to the Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas. "The twice-born" (dvijaḥ) refers to the Brāhmaṇa. The meaning is that he does not desire even these two—milk and honey. The sense is that he has no entitlement to them in this ritual procedure (kalpa). Likewise:
Therefore, for the sake of the Kaulika task, I shall speak of that specifically. || 3-539 ||
The procedure for that is not written here because it is uncommon; however, in some places it is said:
"Having drawn a mandala on the right, the wise one should place the Śrīpātra."
It has been stated [in the scripture]: "By means of the procedure prescribed for the special *argha* offering... (3.540).
