Having described the placement of the *śrīpātra* on the right, [the text] states the sequence for placing the *śaktipātra* and other vessels (in the *Mahākālasaṃhitā*):
"O you who are worshipped by the thirty gods, one should place the *śaktipātra* on the left."
In the center, one should further join four other bowls. || 3-541 ||
The Guru, Bhoga, Vīra, and Kula are thus proclaimed;
and whatever mantras belong to the Śrīpātra, those mantras reside in all vessels.
For whatever rite belongs to the Śrīpātra, that rite belongs to all vessels; however, one who is currently unable to perform such a rite should worship even by means of the common [rite]. (3.543)
The separate digits (kalās)—ten, twelve, and sixteen—are not to be worshipped;
likewise, the invocation of Śakti is performed within Śakti, and that of the Guru within the Guru.
Having invoked the retinues—the vessels of enjoyment—and the Kaulikas, who consist of obscurations, into the Hero and the vessel of the Kula, one should worship them gradually. (3.545)

Likewise: "The one who is entitled to the *śrīpātra* is indeed himself and no other. The vessel for the *śakti* belongs to the *śakti*, and the vessel for the Guru belongs to the Guru as well. (3.546)
The vessel for enjoyment belongs to sons and the like; the vessel of heroes belongs to disciples; the vessel of the Kula belongs to the Kaulikas—such is the declared determination. (3.547)
But in another tantra:
"One should place all the vessels between the *śrīpātra* and the jar;
the guru’s vessel at the end of the jar, and the vessel for enjoyment at its end. (3.548)
At the end of that is the vessel for the Śaktis, and near that is the vessel for the Yoginīs;
at the end of that is the vessel for the Vīras, and near that is the vessel for the bali offering.
One should place the vessels for water for the feet (pādya) and water for sipping (ācamanīya) in their proper order;
nine vessels are considered best, while seven vessels are middling.
It is stated that one should not have three vessels for the lowest [grade] nor a single vessel;
this refers by implication to the *pādya* and *ācamanīya* vessels. Vessels for the *arghya*, the bath-water (*snānīya*), and so forth should also be placed there.
In the case of being unable to provide this much, [as stated in the *Triśaktiratna*]:
Alternatively, there may be a water-pot, a conch, and three vessels for the śakti.

The author of the *Sudhārṇava* maintains that even in this ritual (*kalpa*), vessels for the water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth must be placed, because they are required for worship. The reading cited by the author of the *Mantracintāmaṇi*—"they know the water for the feet, the water for sipping, and the *argha* as the ninth"—is erroneous, as such a reading is not found in numerous texts such as the *Sudhārṇava* and the *Kalpalatā*. Furthermore, if the *argha* vessel were the ninth, it would result in the *śrīpātra* being an additional vessel beyond that number.
For this very reason, the *Kularatnāvalī* states:
"The *kulakumbha*, the *śrīpātra*, and likewise the *śaktipātra*."
The vessel of the Guru, the vessel of enjoyment, and the vessel of the Yoginī.
It is said: "The vessel of the family, the vessel of the hero, and the ninth, the vessel of the offering.
(In the *Triśaktiratna*):
"Having drawn up [the substance] with flowers and so forth, [one takes] the drop (*bindu*) and the nectar from the conch. (3.553)
One should cast [the offering] into all the vessels and visualize everything as divine;
having meditated thus, the wise practitioner should satisfy both of them at the crown of the head. (Tattvārṇava, 3.554)
"Those two" means Ānandabhairava and Ānandabhairavī; their visualization will be described further on. (In the *Triśaktiratna*:
"The practitioner, at his own *brahmarandhra*, [should worship] with the mudrā known as *tattva*."
The wise one should satisfy the three lineages (oghatraya) with the substance intended for the vessel of the Guru.
Having especially gratified his own gurus three times or once,
[he should meditate on the Goddess] surrounded by her retinue within the lotus of his own heart.
One should also satisfy the Mistress of the Kula with the nectar from the Goddess’s vessel.

The "Goddess’s vessel" refers to the Śrīpātra. The *tattvamudrā* will be described [later]. Regarding the phrase "the three lineages" (*oghattraya*), it means the Divine Lineage (*divyaugha*), the Siddha Lineage (*siddhaugha*), and the Human Lineage (*mānavaugha*).
Among these, the Divine Lineage of the Guru-succession for Śyāmā has been stated in the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*.
Therein, first is the goddess Kālikā; hear her lineage of gurus.
Mahādevī, Mahādeva, Tripura, and Bhairava are declared to be the Gurus of the Divine Current (divyaugha); now I shall describe to you the Gurus of the Siddha Current (siddhaugha).
Brahmānanda, Pūrṇadeva, Calacitta, Calācala, Kumāra, Krodhana, Varada, and Smaradīpana. || 3-559 ||
O beloved, hear now of Māyā and Māyāvatī, who [liberate] the multitudes of human beings: Vimala, Kuśala, Bhīmasena, and Sudhākara. (3.560)
Mīna, Gorakṣaka, Bhojadeva, Prajāpati, Mūladeva, Avantideva, Vighneśvara, and Hutāśana. (3.561)
Contentment and the bliss of the covenant are remembered as the gurus of Kālikā;
the divine ones dwell eternally in the sky, and the Siddhas likewise here upon the earth.
Among human beings, there are always multitudes of humans who bear my form;
these gurus, ending with the name Ānandanātha, bestow all spiritual accomplishments.
Even women who possess the form of a guru are proclaimed to be included among the mothers;
O Goddess, at the end of the multitude of human beings, one should also join one's own gurus.
(p. 207) The lineages of gurus for the Tārā-vidyā are also found in that very [text]. Now I shall describe the gurus of Tārā, who bestow both seen and unseen fruits:
Ūrdhvakeśa, Vyomakeśa, Nīlakaṇṭha, and Vṛṣadhvaja. (3.565)
The divine lineages, O child, bestow supernatural powers; now hear from me the truth regarding the lineages of the Siddhas:
Vasiṣṭha, Kūrmanātha, Mīnanātha, and Maheśvara.
Now Harinātha shall speak of the multitudes of men and the true gurus:
Tārāvatī, Bhānumatī, Jayā, Vidyā, and Mahodarī. (3.567)
Sukhānanda, Parānanda, Pārijāta, Kuleśvara, Virūpākṣa, and Kerarī— thus is the Tāriṇī-kula described.
The gurus, ending with the word Ānandanātha, bestow all accomplishments; even women, in the form of gurus, are proclaimed to end with the title Devī.
Now, the teachers of the Śrīvidyā are right there. Now, O Mistress of the Gods, I shall declare the lineage of gurus of the venerable Ṣoḍaśī:
Ānandanātha-deva and likewise Paraprakāśaka. (3-570)
Beyond that is the god Paraśiva, and beyond that is Paraśakti;
then Kauleśvara, the god Śaktideva, and Kuleśāna, the lover.
I shall describe the lineages of the Siddhas, as well as Bhairava who sports in enjoyment; [the lineages of] Samaya, Deva, and Sahaja. Listen, O beloved, to the lineages of the Mānavas. (3.572)
Gaṇeśa, Viṣṇu, Vimala, Sahaja, Bhuvana, Nīla, and Supriya are said to be the gurus in succession.
Now, the lineage of Durgā’s gurus is as follows: Listen, O child Mahādeva, to the gurus born from the mantras of Durgā:
Paramātman, Parānanda, Parameṣṭhin, and Mahodaya. (3.574)
Kṛṣṇa, Kāla, Kalānātha, Divyaugha, Bhairavāntika, Nārada, Kāśyapa, Śambhu, Bhārgava, and Kulakaulika. (3.575)
O Mahādeva, these five streams of perfected ones (siddhaugha) have been proclaimed:
Rudrācārya, Kṣamācārya, and the one known as Pavanāśana; [3-576]
Kumārīśa, Śaktidhara, Ghanānanda, Prakāśaka, Hariśarman, Viṣṇuśarman, Dattātreya, and Priyaṃvada. (3.577)
The goddess Bahulā Śākinī is proclaimed as Caryānātha.

In this manner, the respective lineages of Vidyās and Gurus are to be understood from their respective Kalpas. Their libation (*tarpaṇa*) is performed thus: "I offer libation to the venerable *śrīpādukā* of [Name] Ānandanātha," and likewise, "I offer libation to the venerable *śrīpādukā* of [Name] Ambā," and so forth. The fourfold lineage of Gurus has been described in the *Bhāvanirṇaya*.
The Guru, the Paramaguru, and likewise the Parāparaguru.
Parameṣṭhin and Guru likewise should satisfy [the deities] according to their own respective lineages.
(In the Kulacūḍāmaṇi:
"In the absence of knowledge of the names of the gurus, one should indeed worship the triad of gurus. (3-579)
Or rather, there should be no restriction beyond these four [initiations].
(From the Bhāvanirṇaya:
O Goddess, in all cases, at the outset, the giver of mantra is the supreme guru. (3.580)
For you are indeed the supreme and subordinate gurus, since I am the Parameṣṭhin.

Now, the purification of the principles (tattva-śuddhi) is as follows: therein, "Oṃ! May my prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna be purified; may I become light, stainless, and free from evil, svāhā!"

*Oṃ, may earth, water, fire, air, and ether be purified for me—jyotiḥ, etc.* *Oṃ, may primordial nature (prakṛti), ego (ahaṃkāra), intellect (buddhi), mind (manas), and the ears be purified for me—etc.* *Oṃ, may speech, eyes, ears, tongue, nose, and the organ of action be purified for me—etc.* *Oṃ, may the hands, feet, anus, genitals, and sound be purified for me—etc.* *Oṃ, may touch, form, taste, and space be purified for me—etc.* *Oṃ, may air, fire, water, earth, and the self (ātman) be purified for me—etc.* Reciting these seven mantras while touching all the limbs seven times with both hands constitutes the purification of the principles (*tattvaśuddhi*).
In this very Vāmācāra tradition, at this same time, one offers the bali-oblation to Vaṭuka and the others; the procedure for that will be explained further on. As stated in another Tantra (p. 209):
"Having thus performed the purification of the principles (tattvaśuddhi), one should purify the materials of worship. (3.581)

(Merutantra) One should sprinkle oneself, the sacrificial materials, the articles of worship, and the mandala with the water from the *prokṣaṇī* vessel while reciting the root mantra and the *astra* mantra. (3.582)
One should display the dhenu-mudrā; this is considered the purification of the substances.
One should worship the deities of the yoga-pīṭha-nyāsa in their respective locations. (3.583)
Then, on the jewel-throne, one's own deity should be worshipped through meditative cultivation;
one should meditate upon oneself in the form of the deity five times with the root mantra.
One should offer handfuls of flowers at the head, the heart, the anus, the feet, and all the limbs; one should worship with sandalwood paste and other offerings.
One should not offer the food offering (naivedya) with the four types of service; one should complete the remainder according to the procedure taught by the Guru. || 3.586 ||
With a concentrated mind, one should employ all of this with the sprinkling waters;
having performed the six-limbed ritual placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa), one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times.
Having performed the recitation, one should offer it to the deity with the arghya water;
then, having discarded the water remaining in the prokṣaṇī vessel, one should fill it again as before.
One should worship the Guru in the maṇḍala with services such as sandalwood paste and other offerings;
first one should worship the pericarp with *śāli* rice, and thereafter with *taṇḍula* rice. (3.589)
One should place darbha grass upon these, and then a *kūrcaka* (a bundle) containing unbroken grains (*akṣata*).
These long kuśa blades, with their roots cut off, are twenty-seven in number. (3.590)
A tuft of hair (kūrca) joined with the Brahma-knot at its tip is what is described here;
one should worship [the deity] beginning from Ādhāraśakti and ending with the mantra of the pedestal (pīṭha).
Regarding the method for the worship of the *pīṭhas*, it is stated in that very same [text]:
"The lineage of gurus is to be worshipped to the north, while Mahāgaṇapati is to the south.
One should worship the seven [levels] below the deity, beginning from the netherworld (*atala*) downwards. (3.592)
Above that, one should also [visualize] Maṇḍūka, then Rudra, and then Kālānala; (according to the Śāradā-tantra:
below, she is mounted upon the tortoise-stone, with a luster like the autumnal moon. (3.593)
One should worship the Support-Power (Ādhāraśakti), who holds two lotuses and is seated upon the Tortoise-Stone;
that is to say, she stands upon that stone which has the form of a tortoise. (Likewise...)
One should worship a blue-colored tortoise mounted upon its head.
Above, one should worship Ananta, who sits upon the Brahma-stone (brahmaśilā), resembling a jasmine flower, bearing a discus on his head, and supporting the earth. || 3.595 ||
There, one should worship the Earth, dark as the tamāla tree, bearing blue lotuses, and girdled by the shimmering ocean.
Upon that [island] is an island made of jewels, and upon that is a pavilion of gems;
there one should worship the wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣa), which grant the desired accomplishments to the practitioner.
Below those [deities], one should worship the altar, radiant with the mandala;
thereafter, one should again worship the seat (pīṭha) upon it with Dharma and the other [qualities]. (3.598)
One should worship Dharma and the others, who have the forms of a bull, a lion, and an elephant, and whose feet possess the luster of red, dark-blue, and sapphire Indra-nīla gems. 3-599.

One should worship those [deities] on the limbs, preceded by the negative particle (*nañ*), as described by their characteristics. "A *bhūta* is a divine progenitor. "Preceded by the negative particle" means Adharma and the others. "As described by their characteristics" means having forms such as a bull and colors such as red.
In the *Merutantra*, however, Adharma and the others are said to be multicolored (*citravarṇa*).
Dharma has the body of a bull and is red; Jñāna is black and like a lion. || 3-600 ||

One should worship detachment as yellow like the element earth and sovereignty as black like the hand of Kṛṣṇa; one should worship Adharma and the others, which are of variegated colors, beneath the pedestal. (3.601)
Likewise: "One should worship the lotus in the corners beginning with the southeast (āgneya) and in the cardinal directions. He states the method for that as follows:
First is the bulb of bliss (ānandakanda), and immediately following it is the stalk of consciousness (saṃvinnāla).
Immediately thereafter, the mantra-practitioner should worship the lotus which consists of all principles (tattvas),
with petals representing the primary elements (prakṛti) and filaments consisting of the transformations (vikāra).
Then one should worship the pericarp, enriched with the fifty seed-syllables of the letters;
therein, one should worship the designators of the sun and the moon together with their digits (kalās).
Then, with three divisions of the Praṇava, one should worship the qualities beginning with Sattva— namely, the Self (Ātman), the Inner Self (Antarātman), and the Supreme Self (Paramātman).
And one should worship the Self in the form of Knowledge according to the rule, ending with the seat-mantra (pīṭhamantra);
[one should worship] the powers of the seat (pīṭhaśaktis) in the filaments and in the center [the goddess] together with Varā and Abhayā.
The meaning is that the ninth *pīṭhaśakti* is to be worshipped in the center.
As it has been stated (also in the *Merutantra*):
"In the filaments, as well as in the center and in the directions starting from the east, [they are to be worshipped] in due order."
One should worship the nine Śaktis of the sacred seat (pīṭha) mentioned in its respective mantra. || 3-607 ||

Then, one should worship the pedestal in the center of the seat with perfumes and other offerings using the pedestal mantra, employing each deity's own name joined with the dative case ending and the word "namaḥ. (3.608)
The practitioner should offer a handful of flowers in the center with the seat-mantra (pīṭhamaṃtra), having uttered the root-mantra followed by the name of the seat in the genitive case. (3.609)
Thinking, "I shall fashion the image," one should place the image in the center.
(From the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*):
The beautiful vessel should be made of gold, silver, or even copper. (3.610)
It should be free from defects, made of clay, and smeared with sandalwood paste.
Its size should be equal to that of a water jar (*kalaśa*):
fifty finger-breadths in width and sixteen finger-breadths in height. (3.611)
"The measurement of the jars is such that the mouth should be eight finger-breadths [in width]," so it is stated in the *Siddhāntasāra*. In the *Śāradā* [Tantra], it is said:
A pitcher fashioned from gold or other materials, its interior washed with water consecrated by the Astra-mantra.
It is fumigated with sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor, possessing a beautiful form,
its body wrapped tightly with a triple-stranded thread.
A specific detail is stated in another tantra within the Sūtra:
"With a triple-stranded thread spun by a maiden, which consists of the three qualities (guṇas) themselves, one should wrap it evenly all around along the path. (3-614)
(From the Śāradā-tantra:

Reciting the Tāra mantra, the practitioner should place [the vessel]—which has been worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, provided with a tuft of grass and unbroken rice grains, and contains the nine gems—into the interior. 3-615.
(From the Merutantra:
Reciting [the mantra] constantly according to the prescribed rule, the most excellent of preceptors should place nine gems into the pitcher and then a *kūrca* [bundle of grass] on top. (3.616)
One should place [the offerings] combined with *dūrvā* grass and sandalwood, accompanied by a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
The nine gems (*navaratna*) are mentioned right there:
"The flower (1), sapphire (2), lapis lazuli (3), coral (4), and likewise pearl (5)... (3.617).
Then, emerald, diamond, agate, and ruby—these nine gems have been proclaimed by the teachers who are most proficient in the tantras. (3.618)
Mentally reciting the mantra from beginning to end along with the Mātṛkā,
and at the conclusion reciting the root mantra while contemplating the oneness of the self.
The supreme practitioner should contemplate the non-difference of the jar from its pedestal;
immediately thereafter, he should fill it with decoctions of fifty medicinal herbs. (3.620)
These medicinal plants (varṇauṣadhi) are accompanied by one [other substance]; they are as follows:
sandalwood, the variety known as red sandalwood, and likewise agallochum (aguru).
Camphor, uśīra, kuṣṭha, bālaka, and keśara;
kaṅkolaka, jātiphala, jaṭāmāṃsī, and likewise murā. (3.622)
Granthika, rocanā, jātīpatra, pippalī, bilvaka, pṛśniparṇī, citraka, lavaṅga, and likewise kattṛṇa.
Kaṭphala, guñjā, udumbara, kāśmarī, padmaka wood, śaṅkhapuṣpī, and likewise the crest of a peacock; || 3.624 ||
Plakṣa, agnimantha, as well as mudgaparṇī, kuśa grass, pāṣāṇabhedaka, kṛṣṇaśaṅkhapuṣpī, and rohiṇī; || 3.625 ||
Syonāka, bṛhatī, pāṭalī, mūṣakarṇikā, tulasī, śikharī, indravallī, and the king named bhṛṅga; || 3.626 ||
Then Aparājitā and Tālamūlī, with palms joined in reverence, as well as Dūrvā, Śrī, Devikanyā, Bhāryā, and Bhadramustaka [spoke]. (3.627)
And these fifty [leaves] are to be used excluding the cloves.
[One should prepare them] with decoctions of the bark of milky trees and that produced from the bark of the Brahma-tree (Ficus religiosa). || 3-628 ||
The word "should fill" is to be understood as the ellipsis. (In the Śāradā-tantra:
"Having conceived the identity of the jar and the pedestal, the knower of the ritual procedure..."
With a decoction of milky trees, or with that produced from the bark of the *palāśa* tree. || 3-629 ||

Or with waters from sacred fords, well-scented with camphor, fragrance, and flowers, one should perform the ritual according to the rules by identifying oneself [with the deity], reciting the *mātṛkā* in reverse order.
In the same manner, one should fill [the vessel] with the root-mantra while perceiving it as the deity;
in the conch, one should place the eight fragrances which grant all desires, filled with boiled water. (3.631)
Having stirred [the contents], one should worship within that jar after invoking the kalās;
first the ten kalās of Fire, and then the twelve of the Twelvefold Self (Dvādaśātman).
Furthermore, the knower of mantras should recite the root mantra in reverse order one hundred and sixty times after [the recitation of] Soma.
With a concentrated mind, meditating upon the deity of the mantra,
the expert in the tantras should perform the ritual of the installation of life-force (prāṇapratiṣṭhā).
One should pour the decoction, which consists of the *kalās* and is situated within the conch, into the pitcher;
or [one may fill it] with auspicious waters scented with fragrant paste, flowers, and so forth. (Merutantra, 3.635)
Having filled the conch with water such as decoctions and the like, one should stir the eight fragrances within it; now, the [fragrances] for each respective deity are proclaimed.
Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, gorocana, saffron, madana, red sandalwood, barley, and so forth are declared to belong to Gāṇapatya. (3.637)
Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, coraka,
saffron, gorocana, jaṭāmāṃsī, and musk— these are known as the eight fragrances of Śakti.
With water, saffron, kuṣṭha, red sandalwood,
sandalwood, mālava, aguru, and camphor, this is the eight-fold fragrance (aṣṭagandhaka) belonging to Śambhu.
Hrīvera, candana, kuṣṭha, aguru, kuṅkuma, mura, sevyaka, and jaṭāmāṃsī—this is declared to be the Vaiṣṇava [incense]. (3.640)
They know the eightfold solar fragrance (*saura-gandhāṣṭaka*) to consist of water, saffron, kuṣṭha, red sandalwood, sandalwood, tamāla, aguru, and camphor. (3.641)
With *gorocanā*, *arka*, musk, camphor, *aguru*, saffron, sandalwood,
elephant ichor, vermilion, and lotuses— (3.642).
Through the combination of the eight fragrances and by the power of the preceptor, the wise know that water endowed with potency will thus come to be in the jar. (3.643)
First, one should worship the ten digits associated with Fire:
Dhūmrārcis, Ūṣmā, Jvalinī, Jvālinī, and Visphuliṅginī.
One should worship Suśrī, Surūpā, Kapilā, and both Havyavāhā and Kavyavāhā;
thereafter, one should worship the twelve solar kalās.
Tapinī, Tāpinī, Dhūmrā, Marīci, Jvālinī, Ruci, Suṣumṇā, Bhogadā, Viśvā, Bodhinī, Dhāriṇī, and Kṣamā. (3-646)
Thereafter, the best of gurus should worship the sixteen digits of the moon:
Amṛtā, Mānadā, Pūṣā, Puṣṭi, Tuṣṭi, Rati, and Dhṛti.
Śaśinī, Candrikā, Kānti, Jyotsnā, Śrī, Prīti, Aṅgadā, Pūrṇā, and Pūrṇāmṛtā are the digits born of Soma who bestow splendor. (3.648)

Having brought together and firmly established the fifty *kalās* produced from the divisions of the Vedas and others, along with the Moon (*indu*), one should worship them within the water-pot (*kalaśa*).
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, Śānti, Indhī, Dīpikā, Recikā, Mocikā, Pārā, Sūkṣmā, and likewise Sūkṣmāmṛtā. (3-650)
She is the one who nourishes with the nectar of knowledge, the all-pervading one whose form is space;
she is the infinite one, the prosperity of creation, as well as memory, intelligence, and splendor.
Lakṣmī, Dyuti, Sthirā, Sthiti, Siddhi, Jarā, Pālinī, Kṣānti, Īśvarī, Rati, Kāmā, Varadā, and likewise Hlādinī. (3.652)
Prīti, Dīrghā, Tīkṣṇā, Raudrī, Bhayā, Nidrā, and Tandrikā; Kṣut, Krodhinī, Kriyā, Utkārī, Mṛtyu, Prītā, and Dāruṇā. (3-653)
One should worship Asitā and likewise Anantā in the middle of each [section] with the mantras "h saḥ śuciṣat," "ṣaṭ," and "pratadviṣṇustave. (3.654)
The wise one should worship the *Tariyambaka*, the *Gāyatrī*, and likewise the *Viṣṇuyoni*—the digits arising from the fivefold divisions of the *Tāra*. (3.655)
Having invoked the ten Kalās beginning with Sṛṣṭi and having caused them to be present,
one should worship after muttering the two verses beginning with "haṃsaḥ śuciṣat."
Having performed the stabilization of the vital breath (prāṇa), one who knows the ritual procedure should worship those digits (kalās),
such as Jarā and the others, Tīkṣṇā and the others, and Pītā and the others.
The wise one should also worship Nivṛtti and the others according to the stated method.
The letter *a* and the letter *u* are proclaimed [as the first two], while the letter *m* consists of the Bindu and the Nāda.
Śakti and Śānta—these seven are proclaimed as the divisions of Dhruva; these last two divisions are indeed described separately. (3-659)
(Siddhāntasāra):
Having meditated upon the deity, one should pour the water contained in the conch—which consists of its [the deity's] kalās—into the jar; this is the implied meaning.
(From the Śāradā-tantra:
Afterwards, with the tender sprouts of the *aśvattha*, *panasa*, and *cūta* trees... || 3.660 ||
The Guru, with the thought that they were celestial trees bound together by *indravallī* creepers,
covered the mouth of the jar with my cup, which was filled with fruit and unbroken grains.
One should duly plant the branches of the kalpa-trees with the thought of obtaining their fruit;
thereafter, one should wrap the water-pot with a pair of stainless linen cloths.
In the *Merutantra*, this is proclaimed as the installation of the principal pitcher (*pradhānakumbha*).
Now, in the directions beginning with the east, in the vicinity of the arches (*toraṇa*), [the following occurs]. (3-663)
One may construct mandalas according to one’s desire, including those with eight petals;
above that, one should arrange heaps of *śāli* rice at each door. (3.664)
Above that, one should place a full water-pot and worship these [deities] therein:
Dhruva in the east, Dharā on the right (south), Vākpati in the west, and [Guru] in the north.
Then one should properly place Vighneśa and the other *mūrtis* starting from the southeast (āgneya) and so forth;
one should worship Amṛta, Durjaya, Siddhārthaka, and Maṅgala.

Furthermore, one should worship Indra and the other world-protectors (lokapālas) in the directions starting from the east, in sequence, within the mandalas upon the water-jars (kumbha), with their respective mantras.
Airāvata, Puṇḍarīka, Vāmana, Kumuda,
Añjana, Puṣpadanta, Sārvabhauma, and Supratīka were at his front.
Then the Guru, having gone to his own altar, should sit upon his seat;
the most excellent Guru should contemplate the Form [of the deity] within that [seat] by means of the root mantra.

Having invoked the chosen deity into that image, one should worship it; having worshipped the image with the root mantra, one should [worship] the wish-fulfilling tree upon this branch. (From the Śāradā-tantra, 3.670)
Having invoked [the deity], the practitioner of mantra should worship the deity of the mantra within that [liṅga]. According to the *Merutantra*,
one should perform the invocation and other rites ninefold upon the image and so forth.
First, the invocation (āvāhana) should be performed while reciting the root mantra three times;
the deity, having arrived from the heavenly realm in a subtle form, enters into the images.
Having meditated thus while remaining steady, the wise one brings the deity from its own place, having caused it to emerge through the opening of the nostril via the path of the *suṣumṇā*.
One should place a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) in the hands and offer it upon the head of the deity.
(From the *Siddhāntasāra*):
Having taken up the handful of flowers with the *trikhaṇḍa* mudrā... (3.674).
Having meditated upon the deity as described, while reciting the root mantra, one should also say: "O God, come, come! ending with the name of the deity followed by the vocative particle *saṃbuddhi*.
Furthermore, having recited the root mantra once more, one should bring Śiva from his own place;
here, the term "Śiva" refers to each respective deity (*Mahākālasaṃhitā*).
Then, having gathered the flower with the *trikhaṇḍā* mudrā, the wise one [should proceed].
Having assumed the *karakacchapikā* posture, one should perform the meditation (*dhyāna*) of the Goddess;
for whichever mantra there is a specific meditation, it should be performed exactly as it has been proclaimed.
By that very yoga of meditation, the meditator should meditate upon the Mother of the World,
carrying her from the center of the heart-lotus through the opening of the nostril-passage.
Having brought the Goddess onto the flower, one should place that flower upon the yantra;
[one should invoke] the splendor of the God into that image by means of the mudrā called āvāhanī. (Merutantra 3.679)
Reciting the root mantra, one should establish [the deity]; this is considered the invocation (*āvāhana*).
Then, one should perform the stabilization (*saṃsthāpana*), saying: "Stay here! Stay here! (3.680).
At the end of the root [mantra], one should recite the name of the deity, and at its end,
one should display the āsthāpanīya mudrā and perform the visualization.
"Once born, become firm"—thus one should pray afterwards:
"O Lord of Gods, easily accessible through devotion, accompanied by all your retinues. (3.682)
"Remain steadfast for as long as I shall worship you.
Having thus prayed to the Lord of Gods, one should perform the rite of invocation (*saṃnidhāpana*).

Having recited the root mantra and addressed the deity with the word "O Perfectly Awakened One" (saṃbuddha), one should say twice, "Be present here," so that [the deity] is brought into one's own presence. (3.684)
One should satisfy the deity established there with the *saṃnidhāpana* mudrā;
then, having uttered the root mantra, one should perform the *saṃnirodha* [of the deity].
Having uttered the words ending in "saṃbuddhya," one should say "saṃniruddho bhava" twice; thus, filled with compassion, one should practice the cessation of the state of devotion. (3.686)
One should contemplate the deity as having become firmly established within the image;
then, reciting the root mantra, one should perform the rite of making the deity face-to-face.
Afterwards, one should say, "May they awaken," and also, "Be present before me.
One should meditate upon the deity in front of oneself, with a face as a lotus, most serene.
"One should display the mudrā for bringing [the deity] face-to-face; that is how it is remembered.
Then, having recited the root mantra, one should perform the veiling (avaguṇṭhana) of the deity. (3.689)
One should show [the gesture] with the words, "May they awaken; be veiled. And having displayed the *avaguṇṭhana* (veiling) mudrā, one should contemplate as follows: || 3-690 ||
The God, deluded by devotion, has his eyes wide open with wonder;
this is the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa performed upon the heart and other limbs of the God.

Having performed the placement of the six-limbed mantras and having uttered the root mantra, one should then say: "May the deity be fully awakened; thus, you have become one who has performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa. (3.692)
One should meditate upon the deity as possessing limbs, for the deities of the limbs are established therein;
because that which is non-different is the purpose of those things that possess different natures. (3.693)
Through the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa (the integration of the limbs), the limbs become one with the possessor of the limbs.
I shall now describe the rite of amṛtīkaraṇa (the transformation into nectar): having established the deity upon the seat...

Having properly formed the *dhenumudrā* over the head of the deity, one should meditate that a rain of nectar falls; then, with water for the *argha* offering, [one should perform the sprinkling]. (3.695)
One should sprinkle [the water] three times with the root mantra, three times with the Dīpinī mantra, and again three times with the Mātṛkās from the letter *a* to the letter *kṣa*. (3.696)
The Vāgbhava [syllable], the pair of words, "O Thou Who Speakest Words," and the Vāgbhava again;
then *krīḥ*, "O Wet One," "O Moistening One," "Moisten," and also "Great Agitation. (3-697)
Form the pair *kāmabīja*, which is *sau*; form the pair *mokṣa*. This is the *prāsāda* and the *parāprāsāda*, consisting of thirty-seven syllables.
The mantra called Dīpinī is said to increase the splendor of the deity;
it consists of the root-mantra followed by the vocative case-ending and the name of the deity rendered as nectar (amṛtīkṛta). (3.699)
One should say "bhava" and so forth; this is known as the immortalization (amṛtīkaraṇa).
I shall now describe the supreme transformation (paramīkaraṇa); one should bind the great mudrā (mahāmudrā).
Having recited the root-deity as before, O you of supreme form,
and having uttered the words "Become one with me" (kṛto bhava), one should meditate upon the head of the deity.
"And the rain of supreme nectar..."—thus [it is said].
The characteristics of the mudrās for invocation and so forth have been stated in the *Lakṣaṇasaṃgraha*:
"Having formed the añjali with both hands, [place them] upon the root joint of the ring fingers. (3.702)
One should place the two thumbs [within the palms]; this mudrā is considered the āvāhanī (invocation). When turned face downwards, it is indeed called the sthāpanī (establishment).
From the joining of two fists with the thumbs raised is the *saṃnidhāpanī*;
that same mudrā, when the thumbs are inserted inside, is considered the *saṃrodhinī*. (3.704)
The two fists held open and facing each other constitute the gesture of bringing [something] before one;
the fist formed with the right hand has its index finger extended and pointing downward. (3.705)

When this *avaguṇṭhana-mudrā* is rotated all around the limbs of the deity, it constitutes the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), which is the act of making [the deity] complete (*sakalīkṛti*).
The rite of immortalization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*) is performed with the *dhenumudrā*, which is defined as follows:
the little fingers and ring fingers are again joined together, facing one another. (3.707)
Likewise, the Dhenu-mudrā, which bestows the nectar [of immortality], arises from between those two index fingers;
it consists of the thumbs interlaced with one another and the remaining fingers extended. (3.708)
O beloved, one should employ these mudrās in the rite of invoking the deity for the sake of making this Great Seal (mahāmudrā) joyful and supreme. (3.709)
Regarding the first five mudrās here, they recite in sequence: "Come here! Stay here! Be present here! and "Be present here! Be manifest before me here! (In the *Uḍḍīśa*, it is said:
"Therefore, for the worship of the deity who is already fully present..."
Here, "invocation" (āvāhana) is said to be the act of bringing [the deity] into presence with reverence.
Therefore, by the mere display of the *āvāhana-mudrā*,
the wise have declared that the placement (*niveśana*)— the installation (*sthāpana*)— of the Lord within the yantra occurs;
[the deity] then accepts the worship being offered, as well as grace (*anugraha*) and so forth.
Its capacity to act is what is called its "proximity" (sāṃnidhya);
indeed, one should contemplate this proximity as persisting until the completion of the ritual action. (3-712)
That cessation has been taught with devotion by those most skilled in mantra;
it is the reality that is the abode of bliss, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss.
Therefore, in this case, the entire [universe] should be meditated upon as pervading during the veiling (avaguṇṭhana);
having performed the ritual of totalization (sakalīkaraṇa) with these mantras, one should then achieve oneness.
One should effect the immortalization of the limbs together with the possessor of the limbs;
forgiveness of their transgressions should be understood as the supreme act of honoring them. (3.715)
"Of offenses" means: of those offenses consisting in the conceptualization of the undivided Brahman as having limitations through the performance of mudrās such as invocation (*āvāhana*).
(In the *Meru* [Tantra], beginning with "touching the heart of the Deity," it says:
"One should perform the installation of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*), and likewise one should say 'in my place'. (p. 222)
Indeed, the entire name of the deity here is exactly as previously stated.

"‘This is my place’: after the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), this [rite] must be performed upon one’s own body. The meaning is that the specific distinction lies in that which is the installation of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhāpana*). And therein, we have written down the concise method as stated in the *Jñānārṇava*.
In detail, however, [it is said in the *Merutantra*]:
‘The sages of the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.’"
The *chandas* are the *Ṛg*, *Yajus*, and *Sāman*; the deity, however, is the power of breath (*prāṇaśakti*).
The Ṛṣi is on the head, the meters on the face, and the deities on the heart.
"Āṃ Vijayāyai namaḥ" is for the secret place; "Hrīḥ Śaktaye namaḥ" is for the feet. (3-718)
At the navel: *namaḥ klīṃ kīlāya niyogo 'susthitau*.
Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ maḥ; the *ka*-group with the anusvāra, facing the sky. (3-719)

Having recited the five principles (pañcatattva), one should place the syllable ĀḤ within oneself; likewise, one should place the seed-syllable OṂ ĀḤ HRĪḤ KROḤ, the CA-group of consonants, and the pentad beginning with sound (śabda) into the heart.

Having pronounced "ātmane ī" for the head, [one places] the consort of the Fire-dweller (the letter *ra*) and those seed-syllables (*u*). Likewise, one should place the *ṭa*-group and the letters beginning with the ear (*śrotra*, i.e., *śa*). 3-721.
Having uttered "tadātmane" and "ū," one should say "vaṣaṭ" for the *śikhā*;
these are the seed-syllables (*bīja*), and this [mantra] is for the speech and other [senses]. (3-722)
Having uttered "aimuktvā kavacāya," one should say "hu" immediately thereafter;
then the four seed-syllables previously mentioned, and likewise the labial class (pavarga). || 3-723 ||

Speech and the rest should likewise be in the beginning; for the eye, it ends with that [letter]. There is also the fourfold seed-syllable *a*, and the *ya*-group starting with the mind (*manas*). (3.724)
One should utter "tadātmane" followed by the final vowel (Svarānta), and then "astrāya phaṭ";
in this very manner, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) starting from the thumbs and ending at the palms of the hands.
Having sequentially assigned [the syllables] Ā, HRĪḤ, and KRO at the navel, below the throat, and below the head—ending there—and also upon the eight petals of the heart-lotus. (3.726)
From the east, one should sequentially place the letters ending with the heart (ha) within the pericarp, according to their groups:
ra, la, ha, ṣa, va, ca, ma, ca, sa, śa, and kṣa. || 3.727 ||
Then one should assign [the syllables] to the directions and meditate upon the power of breath (prāṇaśakti) situated in the heart.
Seated upon a red lotus on a ship in the ocean of jewels,
she holds in her lotus-like hands a noose, a goad, a sugarcane bow, five arrows, a trident, and a skull-cup.
I bow to the goddess who is red and has three eyes. || 3-728 ||
Placing the hand upon the heart, one should say: "The primordial seed-syllable and the eight beginning with *yā*, the *haṃsaḥ so'haṃ*—my vital breaths are situated here. (3-729)
Having spoken thus, and likewise again, "My life-force remains here";
having said that once more, he should then say to me, "And all my sense-faculties [remain]. (3-730)
Having spoken that again, let my speech, mind, and sight go forth;
having come here through the ears, nose, and breath, may they then remain in happiness for a long time.

Having uttered the mantra ending with the wife of fire (svāhā) preceded by the *tāra* (oṃ), one should meditate on the body as consisting of light; thus there is the stabilization of the vital breath (*prāṇasaṃsthiti*).
The words "mametyādi" (beginning with "mine," etc. are intended for the purpose of establishing one's own vital breaths.
Likewise, one should then display the mudrās as prescribed in the ritual manuals (kalpa) for each respective deity.
Then one should worship the God with whatever offerings can be obtained according to one's capacity.
In another tantra:

Having performed the root-installation (*mūlanyāsa*) in its entirety upon the form of the deity, one should present the ritual services (*upacāra*), beginning with the seat and ending with the flowers. (3.734)
As for the ritual services (*upacāra*), [it is said in the *Navaratneśvara* on p.
224]: "Fragrance, flowers, incense, lamp, and food offering—these five services bestow the fruit of absolute liberation. (3.735)
Thus are the five services (pañcopacāra).

Water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), as well as the bath, the honey-mixture (madhuparka), and the sipping water (ācamana), followed by the offerings beginning with fragrance and ending with the food offering—these are the ten services in their proper order. (3-736)
(In the Mahākālasaṃhitā:
Water for the feet, water for sipping, water for bathing—these four in succession;
as well as fragrance, flowers, incense, a lamp, and the food offering. (3.737)
And again, the water for sipping; these ten are proclaimed.
Thus are the ten services (*daśopacāra*).
(From the *Kularatnāvalī*)
Water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), water for sipping, the bath, and again water for sipping.
Fragrance, unbroken rice grains, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and betel leaf—these are declared to be the twelve services in worship. (3.739)
Thus are the twelve services (*dvādaśopacāra*).
According to the *Navaratneśvara*:
"The seat, welcome, water for the feet (*pādya*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), and water for sipping (*ācamanīyaka*)."
And the honey-mixture, water for sipping, the bath, garments, and ornaments. || 3.740 ||
One should employ perfume, jasmine flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and sandalwood in the worship; these are the sixteen services.
Thus are the sixteen services. (In the Śāradā-tantra, however:
water for the feet, the arghya offering, water for sipping, bathing, garments, and ornaments;
Incense and flowers, incense-sticks and lamps, as well as food offerings and water for sipping.
Betel, worship, hymn, libation, and prostration—
one should employ these sixteen services in the ritual of worship.
Thus it is said in the *Navaratneśvara*:
"The seat, welcome, water for the feet, the offering of honor, and water for sipping."
Bathing, clothing, the sacred thread, and all kinds of ornaments.
Incense, flowers, as well as incense smoke, lamps, food, and libations; likewise garlands, ointments, prostration, and the ritual dismissal. || 3-745 ||
The mantra-practitioner should perform the worship with the eighteen services.
Thus are the eighteen services (*aṣṭādaśopacāra*).
(From the *Sundarīrahasyavṛtti*)
The same applies to sitting, anointing, massaging, and looking at [the disciple]. (3.746)
Then indeed, the honoring with clarified butter and other substances, followed by the bathing and invocation,
as well as the water for the feet, the guest-offering, the water for sipping, the bath-water, and the honey-mixture.
Furthermore, water for sipping, a garment, a sacred thread, ornaments, perfumes, flowers, as well as incense and lamps; 3-748.
Betel leaves, food offerings, and likewise garlands of flowers; ointments, beds, as well as chowries and fans. || 3-749 ||
Beholding the mirror, as well as prostration immediately thereafter;
singing, instrumental music, canopies, hymns of praise, fire-offerings, and circumambulation. (3.750)
The offering of a tooth-stick and then the dismissal of the deity—these are to be known as the thirty-six services in the worship of the gods. (3.751)
Thus are the thirty-six services (*upacāra*).
In this manner, the sixty-four services and others are to be found in other tantras,
such as the *Kuloḍḍīśa*.
Whatever may be difficult to obtain among all the ritual services,
one should mentally visualize all of that and provide it by means of scattering flowers.
In each instance, one should offer water at intervals between the ritual services.
(Sārasaṃgraha) The procedure for the offering of the ritual services has been described.
One should offer the seat to the left of the Deity while reciting the *mūla-mantra*. (3.753)
The seat is said to be of six kinds—made of flowers, wood, cloth, leather, silk, or metal—and it causes delight to the deity. (3.754)

The *pauṣpa* [seat] is fashioned from fragrant flowers. The *dārumaya* [seat] is made of wood, either carved from thorny wood or joined together with sandalwood and other materials. The *vāstra* [seat] is made of cotton (*kārpāsa*). The *kauśeya* [seat] consists of blankets and the like. The *kauśaya* is a seat-mat (*viṣṭara*) made of twenty-seven blades of *kuśa* grass.
As it is said in the *Ḍāmara*:
"A braid of twenty-seven *darbha* grasses, adorned at its tip with a knot..."
"The *viṣṭara* is proclaimed as the defining characteristic in all sacrifices"—thus [ends the verse]. (3-755)
*Taijasa* refers to that made of gold and the like, excluding iron, lead, and so forth. *Cārma* refers to the skin of deer, tigers, and the like. (In the *Jñānamālā*):
"I shall describe the procedure for ritual service after having provided a comfortable seat."
Then, one should utter a greeting of welcome and inquiries regarding his well-being in his presence.

Having meditated thus upon the deity, together with his limbs and retinue, who has come here for the purpose of worship, one should offer a welcome at the end of the root mantra: "svāgatam" (welcome). (Merutantra 3.757)
In the *Jñānamālā*:
"One should offer water for the feet (*pādya*) to the lotus-feet of the deity with the *hṛdayāṇu*;
that is to say, with the mantra 'namaḥ', which is the *hṛdayāṇu*."
Then, according to the *Yāmala*, one should offer the arghya with well-perfumed waters into the two lotus-hands.
"In the *Jñānamālā*, however, it is stated:
'Then the preceptor should offer the *arghya* upon the head with the *śiromantra*.
By 'with the *śiromantra*' is meant [the mantra] *svāhā*."
It is also stated by Mahākāla: "The practitioners should offer the *arghya* upon the head with the *svāhā* mantra. (3-759)
(p. 227) (In the *Kramadīpikā*):
After the offering of the *argha*, the offering of the *pādya* is mentioned:
"Having offered a seat and uttered 'Welcome'..."
Likewise, [he prepares] the water for honor, the water for washing the feet, and the water for sipping.
(Siddhāntasāra) 3.760:
One should offer the water for the feet with the heart-mantra, the arghya-water with the wife of fire (svāhā),
the water for sipping with *svadhā*, and the honey-mixture with that same mantra.
(From the Śāradā-tantra: One should offer water for sipping (ācamanīya) into the mouth with the *svadhā* mantra;
that [offering] is said by those who know the mantras to consist of jasmine, cloves, and *kaṅkola*. (3.761)
Likewise: "Then, with the *svadhā* syllable, one should offer the *madhuparka* into the lotus of the mouth;
clarified butter mixed with curd and honey—this is what has been declared by the wise. (3.762)
In the *Kuloḍḍīśa*, however, it is stated that even milk and sugar constitute part of the *madhuparka*:
"Having prepared the *madhuparka* consisting of honey, sugar, clarified butter, curd, and likewise milk, one should offer it according to the prescribed rite. (3.763)
Honey is greater than all [other ingredients], while curd, clarified butter, and sugar are equal;
milk, however, is slightly less than all of them—this is declared to be the *madhuparka*. (3.764)
(In the *Śāradā-tilaka*:
"With that very mantra, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamanīyaka*) with water.
By "with that very mantra," it is meant: with the mantra ending in *svāhā*.
In this regard, Sudhārṇava says:
"And with the seed-syllable of Varuṇa, one should offer the water for sipping (ācamanīya). (3.765)

"The preceptor should offer the *madhuparka* into the mouth with the *jalamantreṇa* [water-mantra]," according to the agreement of this statement from the *Yāmalasvatantra*. Following this, some adopt the reading "with the *svadhā* mantra" or elsewhere "with the *sudhā* mantra"; since the word *sudhā* denotes nectar (*amṛta*), they say that one should offer the *madhuparka* and the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) with its seed-syllable, the letter *va* joined with the nasal drop (*bindu*).

The author of the *Tantrasāra*, however, maintains that since the offering of the *arghya* is prescribed with the word *svāhā*, which signifies renunciation (*tyāga*), the word *svadhā*—which is used in conjunction with it—is understood to signify renunciation when the offering of *ācamanīya* is performed, and not the seed-syllable of Varuṇa, because that [seed-syllable] lacks the inherent meaning of renunciation.
And thus, in the *Kulasāra*:
"Having first uttered the mantra, one should then worship in this manner. (3-766)
Then follows the dative case, and after that, a word expressing the sense of renunciation;
in this sequence, O Goddess of the Gods, one should arrange the ritual offerings.
As for that:
"Then the preceptor should offer the *madhuparka* with the water-mantra;
thereafter, he should offer the *madhuparka* into the lotus of the mouth with the *svadhā*-syllable. (3.768)
"With that same mantra, one should perform the sipping of water (ācamana);
and with the Vāruṇa seed-syllable, one should offer the water for sipping"—thus [it is said]. (3.769)

These two statements must be established according to the distinction of castes (*varṇa*), because Śūdras lack the entitlement to utter the word *svadhā*. Thus, since terms such as *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *svadhā*, and *vauṣaṭ* signify the act of relinquishment (*tyāga*), they maintain that the offering of services (*upacāradāna*) should be performed with those very mantras; however, the presentation of services using mantras other than these is devoid of any authoritative basis (*pramāṇa*).

Some say that because the offering of the *madhuparka* and the *ācamanīya* with the *svadhā* mantra is accepted by all Tantras, in the phrase "with the water-mantra" (*jalamantreṇa*) and so forth, the meaning of the instrumental case is "conjunction"; thus, one should give [the offerings] with the *svadhā* mantra conjoined with the water-seed syllable (*vaṃ*). Others, however, reconcile it by stating that the water-mantra is for the preparation of the *ācamanīya*, whereas the *svadhā* mantra is for its actual offering.
In the *Nibandha*: "One should offer the bath, clothing, ornament, scent, and flower with the *hṛdaya* [mantra]."
With the heart-mantra and the word "namaḥ.
However, in the Kālīkalpa it is stated:
"One should offer the bath and the fragrance with the heart-mantra, and the flowers with 'vauṣaṭ' as well. (3-770)
Then, saying "I offer," one should give everything, O Maheśvarī.
"Everything" means garments, ornaments, incense, lamps, and so forth. However, a specific rule regarding the offering of food (*naivedya*) has been stated in the *Siddhāntasāra*.
I offer [this] with the Tattvamudrā, using the wives of the fire of the heart.
"O Maheśānī, one should offer the most excellent *naivedya* to the deity"—thus [it is said]. (In the *Merutantra*:
"Having anointed [the image] with fragrant oils, [one should bathe it] with fragrant *āmalaka* and other such substances. || 3-772 ||
Having performed the ritual rubbing with unguents, one should then bathe [the deity] with warm water;
one should consecrate [the deity] with scented water and with the root-mantra according to one's capacity.
With milk, curd, clarified butter, honey, and sugar, each separately,
one should perform the ritual bathing with fragrant water and cause [the deity] to be clothed in two garments. (From the Śāradā-tantra, 3.774)
The garments have been described (in the *Merutantra*):
for Viṣṇu and Vagalāmukhī, yellow silk cloth; for Śiva and Sarasvatī, white [cloth]; and for Pārśvanātha, white [cloth]. (3-775)
The garment of Śakti, Arka, and Vighna is red; that of Bhauma and Saugata is also [red];
that of Bhairava, Kālī, and others is black; and that of Rādhā and others is blue.
That which is flawless, free from stains, and never worn before—whether made of cotton, silk, or wool—is distinguished as excellent. (3.777)
From a vessel defiled by oil and the like, disease arises; from one with holes, suffering occurs;
from one belonging to another, poverty results; and from one that is worn out, the loss of life ensues. (3.778)
From a burnt object, misfortune occurs; from one offered with a face turned away or hung upon the body, there is harm;
from one pierced by a needle, boils and the like arise; and from a dirty one, a loss of luster. (3.779)
If the water is taken up while wet, there is the loss of one's son; if it is unwashed, there will be wretchedness;
and if it is defiled by phlegm, urine, or the like, there occurs a false accusation. (3.780)
In that very same [text]:
"Then, having offered the sacred thread (yajñopavīta), one should present the ornaments.
One should employ the name of the deity, ending in the nominative case and followed by 'namaḥ', at the beginning of the worship and other rites. (3.781)

These [ornaments] may be of various kinds, distinguished by differences such as crowns and the like, and should also be understood by the wise according to the distinctions between male and female. (3.782)

p. 230) Fragrance is said to be of five kinds (in the *Siddhāntasaṃgraha*): that produced by friction, that which is a refined perfume (*parimala*), that produced by crushing, that originating from living beings, and that known as *kṛṣṇasāra*; thus fragrance is considered to be of five types. (3-783)

That produced by friction (*saṃgharṣaja*) arises from rubbing sandalwood and the like. *Parimala* is that produced by the crushing of fragrant substances. That produced by grinding (*kṣodaja*) arises from the powder of gorocanā and similar materials. That originating from living beings (*prāṇisaṃbhava*) includes musk and the like. *Kṛṣṇasāra*, however, is the essence drawn forth from fragrant substances such as sandalwood; it is well known in the vernacular as *atara*. Regarding that very point:
"The three supreme types are the yakṣa, the divine (*daiva*), and the gandharva, along with the *kardama*."
The means for achieving dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa is entrusted to the deity.

Three types of *kardama* (unguents) are mentioned in that very same [text]: "With musk, *kakkola*, black agallochum, and white *abhraka*, that which brings joy to the deities is to be known as *yakṣakardama*. (3.785)
That very same substance, when combined with *rocanā*, is called *devakardama*;
when joined with *paṭīra*, it is to be known as *devapaṅka* or *gandharvakardama*.
*Kuraṅgamada* is musk; *sitābhra* is camphor; *paṭīra* is sandalwood. (From the *Puraścaraṇacandrikā*): Sandalwood produced in Malaya is unadulterated and very cooling.
Auspiciously ground with camphor, agallochum, musk, and cold water.
(Merutantra) One part of musk and two parts of mustaka; half of that [of each] are elā, jaṭāmāṃsī, tvak, kuṣṭha, and śilārasa. (3.788)
Caturbhāga, bālaka, and likewise nakhī fried in ghee;
sugandhi, kokilā, lohavāṇa, and likewise rājavacā.
Eight parts of keśara, sixteen of murā, kālāguru, akasīra, kālīya, and then vārddhaya; || 3.790 ||
One should grind the parts of *sevantikā* and *arka* with sandalwood; this ointment named *kāmoda* satisfies the King of Deities. (3.791)
The different types of flowers are described in that very same [text]:
"Flowers are said to be of five kinds: supreme, inferior, excellent, middling, and low; I shall describe their characteristics. (3.792)
The supreme golden flower is indeed always suitable;
it should be offered after anointing [the image], and it shall again become worthy of worship. (3.793)
Furthermore, silver and copper flowers are also proclaimed;
these too are always suitable for use, whether they are three years old or one year old.
Tulasī, Ketakī, Padma, Karavīra, and Mālatī—
these five they call the most excellent, while ten others are likewise considered middling.
The Mallikā, Kunda, Mandāra, Tagara, Arjuna, and Kiṃśuka; the Pārijāta, Aśoka, Bilva, and Campaka as well. (3.796)
Gold that differs from this and lacks fragrance is said to be inferior;
one should offer those [substances] prescribed in the ritual procedures for their respective mantras. (3.797)
Now, regarding those things prohibited in that very same context:
one should not offer a bud that has fallen to the ground, one eaten by insects, one clinging to the fingers, one that has been smelled, one that is withered, or likewise one that is stale. (3.798)

[Food] that has a pungent odor or is foul-smelling, or is defiled by worms, hair, and the like; [or food] [offered] with impure vessels, animal parts, or clothing, by those of contemptible character. (3.799)
That which is brought from elsewhere is prohibited, as is bathing at midday;
likewise, that which is offered face-downward is not desired in the rite of the handful of flowers.
There is no fault of being stale in the case of *tulasī*, *bilva*, *campaka*, lotus, *vakula*, and *agastya* flowers, nor in those from the houses of garland-makers. (3.801)
One should not worship Īśa with *ketakī* or *kuṭaja* flowers, nor Hari with *varvarī* or unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*);
one should not worship Durgā with *dūrvā* grass, nor Divākara with *bilva* leaves. (3.802)
One should worship Lambodara with Tulasī leaves that are free from stalks.
The specific flowers for each deity have been stated [in the Padma Purāṇa]:
"With auspicious Dūrvā grass, plantain leaves, Bilva leaves, and [leaves] excluding Tulasī... (3.803).
One should worship the Lord of the Gaṇas with water-born and land-born flowers that are white and red;
one should worship Śāradā with *mālatī*, *kunda*, *mandāra*, and *kumuda* flowers.
Karavīra, the javā flower, the lotus, and likewise the kokanada;
the blue lotus, the aśoka, the bandhūka, and likewise the pomegranate.
Ketaka, mallikā, and arka are dear to the Sun at the three junctions of the day;
so too are kanaka, kumuda, kunda, tagara, and kaṇṭakārikā.
Girikarṇī and bilva leaves are forbidden in the worship of the Sun;
likewise, the hayāri flower, the lotus, the kairava lily, and nāgakeśara.
Jātī, sevantikā, droṇapuṣpa, as well as nīlotpala, arkapuṣpa, apāmārga, unmatta, and likewise kuṭaja. || 3-808 ||
The *śamī* flower and the *bilva* leaf are exceedingly dear to Hara;
likewise, the *ketaka*, the *japā* flower, the *śirīṣa*, and the *damana*.
One should avoid the vibhītaka, atimukta, sarja, bandhūka, yūthikā, and even the white viṣṇukrāntā when performing the worship of Śiva.
Mālatī, mallikā, yūthī, campaka, nāgakeśara, pāṭalā, kunda, mandāra, kahlāra, and atimuktaka. || 3-811 ||
The *karṇikāra*, *kuruvaka*, *kadamba*, *karavīraka*, *tamāla*, *vakula*, the blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), and the *kamala* and *kairava* lotuses. (3-812)
The *sevantikā*, the *ketaka*, the *damana*, the *munipuṣpa*, the *dhātrī* flower, the leaf of the *śamī*, and the leaf of the *apāmārga*. (3.813)
The sprouts of soft and even tough grasses, the *śatapatrikā*, the blossom-cluster of the mango tree, and the *tulasī* are dear to Hari. (3.814)
One should avoid for the worship of Viṣṇu flowers that are wild, or like the *arka* flower, or scentless, or excessively red, as well as those that have a pungent odor. (3.815)
One should offer red flowers and bilva leaves to Nṛsiṃha;
one should avoid the ketakī flower, while all other matters are as previously described.
(In the Kālītantra:
With various offerings and oblations, with various beautiful flowers,
with auspicious leaves of Apāmārga and Bhṛṅga— excluding Tulasī— (3.817).
They should always be worshipped with devotion by men for the swift attainment of results. (In the Muṇḍamālā:
One should likewise offer flowers that are red, black, and white. (3.818)
O beloved, white flowers, the javā flower, and likewise the karavīra; as well as tagara, mālatī, jātī, sevantī, and yūthikā. || 3-819 ||
Dhattūra, aśoka, bakula, white and black aparājitā, vakapuṣpa, as well as bilva, campaka, and nāgakeśara. (3.820)
Mallikā, jhiṇṭikā, kāñcī, and that which is proclaimed as raktam; arkapuṣpa, varvara, bandhūka, and priyamvadā. (3-821)
On the eighth day, Pārvatī is especially pleased;
all the deities are satisfied by a red lotus flower.
Whether with black or white flowers, Kālikā becomes a granter of boons; one should worship her with fragrant white and red lotuses and with *kula* flowers. (Matsyasūkta 3.823)
With auspicious bilva, maruvaka, and other flowers—excluding tulasī—and especially with honey-colored flowers mixed with vajra flowers. (3.824)
One should offer every flower with a mind endowed with devotion;
she should always be worshipped with devotion, for she bestows fruits swiftly upon men. (3.825)
With *vajra*, *puṣpa*, and other [flowers] (as stated in the *Kālikāpurāṇa*):
"The flower is the *kokanada*, the *padma*, the *japā*, and the *bandhūka*."
Among all species of flowers, the red flower is preeminent. || 3-826 ||
(Yāmalatantra): One should offer the vajra-flower to Kālikā for the sake of attaining accomplishment;
the yoni-flower is for Maheśa, and it is called the vajra-flower. (3.827)
The threefold nature of the *vajrapuṣpa* is stated in the *Muṇḍamālā*:
"That [girl] who is unmarried up to the age of sixteen is the best, granting all accomplishments;
she who has been taken by force is middling, increasing worldly enjoyments. (3.828)
O Goddess, by the power of the *rajoyoga*, another [substance] arises on earth that bestows inferior pleasure; the *svayambhūkusuma* is thus born in three types. (3-829)
"Unmarried" means not yet enjoyed; "married" means already enjoyed. In another tantra:
"Just as Kālikā is pleased when the vajra-flower is offered..."
Neither by gold, nor by jewels, nor likewise by touchstones.
In the absence of the *vajrapuṣpa*, one should worship with the *javā* flower;
or Kālikā, the source of all auspiciousness, is to be worshipped with the *arka* flower. (3.831)
*Kālikā* is the presiding deity of the Southern Tradition (*dakṣiṇāmnāya*). However, in the Northern Tradition (*uttarāmnāya*), the prohibition of *arka* flowers is stated in the *Mahākālasaṃhitā*:
"With *tulasī*, *apāmārga*, *dhattūra*, and *sindhuvāraka*..."
"One should never worship the Goddess with *arkapuṣpa* flowers or *vāsaka*. — 3.832.
The [prescribed flowers] are mentioned in that very same place:
"With *śirīṣa*, *karṇikāra*, *campaka*, and *kovidāraka* trees;
with *vakula*, *mandāra*, *kundapuṣpa*, and *kuraṇṭaka* flowers. (3-833)
With creepers of the Brahma-tree, even with soft sprouts of dūrvā grass, with *kāñcanāra*, *aśoka*, *punnāga*, and *ketakī* petals; || 3.834 ||
With *sephālikā*, *yūthī*, *jātī*, and *damana* flowers, as well as with *śatapatra*, *mallikā*, unfading blossoms, and *bandhujīvaka*.
With *jhiṇṭī* flowers, *japā* blossoms, *karavīra*, and *kiṃśuka*;
with *parijāta*, *pāṭala*, and even *padma* and blue lotuses (*nīlotpala*).
With *mādhavī* vines, *maruvaka* flowers, and also *aparājitā*, with *aśana* trees, *kadamba* trees, and *droṇa* flowers along with *kesara*.
The best of practitioners should worship the Goddess with these flowers;
O fair-faced one, just as the bilva leaf is most pleasing to the Goddess.
There is nothing else among flowers that produces such joy;
therefore, one should diligently offer the bilva leaf endowed with its three folds.
Likewise: "A flower garland fashioned from various flowers should be offered.
The different types of garlands are described in that very same [text].
With flowers of a single species, or even of different species. || 3-840 ||
O Dear One, a garland may consist of a single color or even of various colors;
furthermore, it should be known as threefold according to its circumference.
That garland which reaches down to the heart and is fragrant should be known as the *vaikakṣikā*, worn across the shoulder in a manner that covers everything. (3.842)
The flower garland that hangs down from the navel is called Sādhārī;
it should be known as Madhyamā when it is greater than the previous one on the left side. (3.843)
That which hangs down to the ankles and rests upon the lotus-feet is known as the *vanamālā* (forest garland); it is the most excellent of all garlands. (3.844)
Now, regarding the second vidyā: (In the Nīlatantra) one should worship according to the prescribed rite on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days;
one attains the perfection of the command (*ājñāsiddhi*), as well as the *javā* flower and the *varvarī*. (3.845)
One should offer sandalwood, arka flowers, and white aparājitā;
he shall be pleased by a garland of bandhūka flowers just as by the gift of a goat. (3.846)
(From the *Triśaktiratna*): One should worship with *vajrapuṣpa* flowers mixed together for the sake of attaining accomplishment (*siddhi*).
In the absence of *vajrapuṣpa*, one shall obtain accomplishment through mere recollection. (3.847)
One with a clear mind should offer flowers, excluding *tulasī* and *mālatī*.
(From the *Matsyasūkta*):
The best flowers are the red *koka*, the *bandhūka*, and the *śatapatraka*. (3-848)
A pair of varvarī flowers, as well as a pair of karṇikāra flowers,
along with vaka, mandāra, āmra, and karavīra flowers, are recommended.
(In the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*):
One should avoid the *mālatī* flower; one should avoid the *tulasī* leaf. (In another tantra):
One should worship Caṇḍasundarī everywhere with *vajrapuṣpa* flowers.
The meaning is that even when offering another ritual accessory, one should say: "Vajrapuṣpaṃ pratīccha svāhā" (Accept the adamantine flower, svāhā).
(In the Śrīvidyā-paddhati:
"Whatever lotuses there are here, whether white, black, or red..."
The red flowers, such as the *japā* and *bandhūka*, even those growing on land, [are used]. || 3-851 ||
One should offer white flowers that are fragrant and exclude the *mallikā*, as well as yellow flowers and likewise *bilva* leaves. (3.852)
One should avoid scentless flowers, black flowers, and tulasī;
for by the mere scent of tulasī, the beautiful goddess becomes enraged. (3.853)
(p. 237) One should not worship Mother Tripurā even with *palāśa* flowers;
however, for rites performed for specific desires (*kāmya*), the *mallikā* is not prohibited.
As it is said in the *Jñānārṇava*:
And with *mallikā*, *mālatī*, *jātī*, *kundas*, and *śatapatraka* flowers.
"And one should worship for the duration of one month with cool white lotuses"—thus [it is said] in the *Kaulālavīya*:
"Of Sundarī, Bhairavī, Kālī, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Vivasvat... (3.855).

"A worship devoid of *tulasī*—that worship shall be fruitful. In some versions, the reading is "becomes fruitless" (*viphalati*), but even there, by eliding the vowel *a* (*akāra-praśleṣa*), the meaning results in "it becomes fruitful. The reading "of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Vivasvat," as written by the author of the *Puṣpacintāmaṇi*, is erroneous; for a prohibition of *tulasī* in the worship of Viṣṇu has never been heard of, even in a dream. (In the case of a persistent [objection]:)
Bhuvaneśvarī is especially pleased by red flowers.
In the same way, Chinnamastā [is pleased] by yellow flowers; Vagalāmukhī by *guñjā* seeds; and Mātaṅgī especially becomes a granter of boons [when worshipped] with *guñjā*. (3.857)
(In the *Muṇḍamālā*):
"Dhūmāvatī, the supreme goddess, is pleased by the *dhattūra* plant of the cremation ground alone.
The word "alone" (*eva*) is intended to express excellence; it does not exclude connection with anything else.
One should worship all the vidyās with flowers offered according to the Śrīvidyā ritual.
Thus, from the statement in another tantra (*Merutantra*):
"The *kunda*, *mandāra*, *kumuda*, *mālatī*, *padma*, and *ketaka* [flowers]."
The one called Nandyāvarta, as well as Jātī, Kahlāra, and Campaka.
Flowers such as the red lotus are indeed extremely dear to Lakṣmī.
As for Durgā, [the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa* states]:
"The jasmine, the blue lotus, the lotus, the *śamī*, the *punnāga*, and the *campaka*... (3.860).
The aśoka, the karṇikāra, and especially the droṇapuṣpa;
the karavīra, the japā flower, saffron, and the nāgakeśara.
O best of men, O Bhārata, he who, endowed with faith and devotion, offers these flowers to Caṇḍikā for the sake of merit— (3.862)
Having obtained all desires without exception, he shall become an attendant of the illustrious Durgā.
Likewise: the Punnāga, Campaka, Kunda, Yūthikā, and Navamallikā [are also offered]. (3.863)
Tagara, arjuna, mallī, bṛhatī, śatapatrikā, as well as kumuda, kahlāra, vilva, pāṭala, and mālatī. (3.864)
Javā, vicakila, aśoka, red and blue lotuses, damana, marupatra, and śatapuṣpa are for the sake of increase. (3.865)
Likewise: "Whoever worships Caṇḍikā with fragrant perfumes and flowers, or even with a garland of *mukti* beads, shall obtain the fruit of a horse sacrifice. (3.866)
Likewise: "O best of men, listen to the fruit of merit for him who offers a garland made of a thousand blue lotuses to Caṇḍikā. (3.867)
Having become an attendant of Śrī Durgā for thousands of millions and hundreds of millions of years, he rejoices in the world of Rudra.
Regarding the planets as well, it is said in that same [text]:
"One should worship the Sun with *hayāri* flowers and the Moon with *kadamba* flowers; one should worship Mars with *japā* flowers and Mercury with *campaka*. (3.869)
The Guru is to be worshipped with *śatapatra* flowers, Bhārgava with *jātī* flowers, Paṅgu with *mallikā* blossoms, and Vidhuntuda with *kunda* flowers. (3.870)
And Ketu [is worshipped] always with various flowers during the times of pacification. (In the *Yāmala*):
"The gods are pleased by flowers; the gods are established in flowers. (3-871)
Furthermore, what is the use of saying too much? The word *puṣpa* (flower) is a metaphorical designation (*matallikā*).
The supreme light residing within the flower is propitiated by means of the flower itself. (3.872)
The flower is the means for achieving the three aims of life (trivarga) and bestows nourishment, prosperity, heaven, and liberation.
Brahmā dwells at the root of the flower, while Keśava dwells within its center.
Mahādeva resides at the tip of the flower, and all the gods are situated upon the petals;
therefore, a person endowed with devotion should always worship the God with flowers. (3.874)
(Kriyāsāra) "One should always worship with all flowers, whether prescribed or prohibited;
the yoga of devotion is the cause here for [the worship] of all deities. (3-875)

The worship of the Goddess is always praised, whether performed with aquatic or terrestrial flowers, and whether they are prescribed or forbidden, provided it is done with a mind imbued with devotion. (3.876)
(Merutantra) In the absence of flowers, one may use young shoots; in their absence, buds;
in their absence, fruits or leaves; and in their absence, grass sprouts. (3.877)
In that interval:
"Whether it be a flower or a leaf, it should be offered exactly as it has grown—be it from the *vilva*, the *khadira*, or the *dhātrī* fruit. (3.878)
Neither the *tamāla* nor the lotus is defiled even when cut or broken.
(In the *Mālinītantra*,) O Supreme Goddess, one should worship with leaves in the absence of flowers. (3.879)
If even leaves are not available, one should worship with those produced from trees, shrubs, and the like;
if even those growing in that place are unavailable, one should worship with their fruit.
One should perform worship with unbroken grains or water, or in their absence, with white mustard seeds; if even those are unavailable, one should perform mental worship.
(p. 240) (In the *Merutantra*): "Then, at the conclusion of the offering of flowers, one should perform the worship of the enclosures (*āvaraṇārcana*).
This [procedure] belongs to the Gauḍa and other traditions; elsewhere, however, it should be understood that the worship ends with the incense, lamp, and food offering (*naivedya*)."
In the *Siddhāntasāra*:
Having first uttered the mantra, one should then utter the word "pādukā" preceded by "śrī. (3.882)
Having uttered the [name] in the accusative case, one should worship with the words "I worship.
(In the *Somabhujaṅgāvalī*:
Then the wise one should worship three times with the root mantra. 3-883.
Having received the command of the Great Goddess, one should worship the retinue;
the first ritual method is with the six limbs, while the second is by means of the Gurus.
The third [mandala] consists of the retinue; the fourth is formed by the world-protectors (lokapālas); and the fifth is said to consist of their weapons. This is the general sequence. || 3-885 ||
(From the *Yāmala*):
Thereafter, one should likewise worship the deities of the limbs with water for the feet and other offerings. (From the *Merutantra*)
With the letters of the Mātṛkā, accompanied by the bindu and encapsulated by the mantra.
One should worship the limbs of the deity in sequence with perfumes, flowers, and so forth;
likewise,
one should worship the heart-mantra and the others in the filaments, beginning from the southeast corner.
The eye of Agni and the weapon in the directions— these limb-deities are to be meditated upon as having rays that are white like frost, crystal, dark, blue, black, and ruddy.
The principal female deities, bearing the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, are situated respectively in the southeast, northeast, southwest, northwest, and the center. (3.889)
In the Tūrṇāyāga:
O you who are compassionate toward those who have come for refuge, grant me the fulfillment of my desired goal.
With devotion, I offer to you this worship of the first enclosure (prathamāvaraṇa). (3-890)
Thus one should offer a handful of flowers and prostrate with extreme devotion;
in this manner, one should offer each successive enclosure (āvāraṇa) by its respective name. (3.891)
In the *Merutantra*:
"In the worship of the enclosure (*āvaraṇa*), the east is to be known as being in front of the deity;
the worship of the attendants beginning with that [east] is performed by proceeding clockwise. (3-892)
(Mānasollāsa):
"Between the one to be worshipped and the worshipper, the direction toward the east is proclaimed by the wise;
that which is to the south of it shall be the south, and that to the north shall be the north. (3.893)
(Jñānārṇava) O Goddess, when one extracts the wheel while facing north, then, O Goddess, the northern direction is indeed the eastern direction; of this there is no doubt. (3-894)
When the mantra-practitioner, facing westward, draws forth the wheel, then the western direction should be known as the eastern direction; of this there is no doubt. (3-895)
When the practitioner facing the southern direction draws forth the wheel, then the southeast becomes the southwest, and the northeast becomes the southwest. (3.896)
At that time, the eastern quarter alone is the Rakṣas, while the southeast corner possesses fire.

Facing the western direction and so forth pertains specifically to optional (*kāmya*) worship. However, in the case of daily (*nitya*) and other regular worship, there is a restriction to only two directions, as stated in [the *Śyāmārahasya*] and other tantras: "The eastern part is prescribed for the priest, while the left side is the southern part according to those who know the Āgamas."
One should know the northern portion to be skillful and supreme; by the wise, the western seat is declared [to be the best]. || 3.897 ||

"East" means in front. "Foremost" means facing oneself; therefore, the meaning is that behind the deity is indeed the west. As for the fact that some worship Indra and the others according to the natural order of east and so forth, that is devoid of authoritative proof. (In the Śāradā-tantra:
"The deities mentioned in the ritual manual should be worshipped in sequence from the west."
First, one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) together with their primary retinues.

(From the *Merutantra*, p. 242) The meditations on the world-protectors, Indra and the others, endowed with their weapons, lineages, and presiding deities, are as follows in order from the eastern direction:
"Indra, the lord of the gods, yellow in color, the all-pervading one mounted upon Airāvata... (3-899).
I worship the thousand-eyed one, two-armed, holding a yellow vajra;
I worship the Lord Agni, the sovereign of splendor, red in color, with a white śakti in his hand.
I bow to Yama, the lord of the departed, who is well-adorned, whose mount is a ram, whose limbs and eyes are red, who is dark-complexioned, and who stands upon a buffalo. (3.901)
[He beheld] the cruel Niṛti, the lord of the Rākṣasas, who holds the staff of death, is surrounded by terrifying messengers, and is seated upon a corpse.
Smoky-colored, with a sword in hand and a tawny beard and mustache,
he stands upon a crocodile, holding a lotus in his hand that resembles lightning.
I salute Varuṇa, the lord of aquatic creatures, who has a radiant body and a protruding belly;
and the supreme Vāyu, the lord of the vital breaths, who is smoke-colored and holds a red goad in his hand. (3.904)
I worship Kubera, the lord of the Yakṣas, who is white in complexion, holds a white mace, and runs with great speed mounted upon Vātapramī.
One should visualize Meduḷa, mounted upon a lion-throne,
accompanied by Citriṇī, the Lord of Knowledge, holding a blue trident, and having a bull as his vehicle.
Three-eyed, with the crescent moon upon his brow, wearing a mass of matted hair,
white in color, the lord of the worlds, the creator, auspicious, with a red lotus in his hand.
I worship Him who is mounted upon a swan, chanting the Vedas, fair-complexioned, and adorned with a circle of hoods by the lord of serpents upon His head. (3.908)
I worship the one who bears the discus, who is infinite, who pervades the universe, and whose belly is full and elevated.
(In the *Śāradā*:
the thunderbolt, the spear, the staff, the sword, the noose, the goad, and the mace. 3-909.
One should know that their weapons are, in order, the trident, the wheel, and the lotus;
they are yellow, white, bright as the sky, red like lightning, white, and black. (3.910)
Diamonds and other gems are proclaimed to have a reddish-pink luster like that of kuruvinda;
when the root of the hand is joined, all the fingers are extended. (From the *Yāmala*) 3-911.
One should display this mudrā of the Lords of the World (Lokeśvaras) during their worship.
In another tantra: [one should likewise worship] Gaṇeśa, Vaṭuka, Kṣetrapāla, and Yoginī. (3-912)
One should worship with scents and flowers according to the sequence starting from the east (as stated in the *Merutantra*).
Then, having again uttered the root mantra, [one should worship] "to her who possesses the limbs" (*sāṅgāyai*) and "to her who is accompanied by the retinue" (*saparīti*).
The practitioner should utter the name of the goddess Vārāhī ending in the dative case, and three times he should worship her with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings while saying "namaḥ. (3.914)
In another tantra:
"Having performed the worship of the enclosure, one should offer incense and lamps.
The various types of incense are described in the *Merutantra*:
One should burn incense for Gaṇeśa; guggulu is said to be his favorite.

The resin of the Sarja tree belongs to the Goddess; that produced from Devadāru belongs to Maheśa; and black agallochum (kṛṣṇāguru) is for Viṣṇu; [incense] that is cool is considered dear to Bhāskara.
I shall describe the ten ingredients of Śakti: śaileya (1), malayodbhava (2), nakha (3), kuṣṭha (4), and sarjarasa (5); one should prepare these in single parts each. (3.917)
