Two parts each of *śilārasa* (6), *aguru* (7), and *jaṭāmāṃsī* (8) are prescribed; six parts of *mākṣika* (9) and eight parts of white sugar (10)—this incense is known as "Deluder of Power" (*śaktimohana*). (3.918)
One part each of *harītakī*, *sarjarasa*, *mura*, and *māṃsī*;
three parts of *lākṣā*; and four parts each of *śailaja* and *musta*. (3-919)
Nakha is said to consist of five parts, Kuṣṭha is declared to consist of six parts, and Guḍa consists of twelve parts; this is the ten-fold formula of Arka, Īśa, Vighna, and Viṣṇu.

Honey (1), musta (2), ghee (3), fragrance (4), guggulu (5), agallochum (6), bitumen (7), sarala resin (8), silha resin (9), and white mustard (10) constitute the ten-fold incense for the remaining deities. (3.921)
(In another tantra:
The preceptor should incense the deity with low-intensity smoke made from guggulu, aguru, uśīra, sugar, honey, and sandalwood, mixed with clarified butter. (3.922)
White sugar, clarified butter, honey, guggulu, agallochum, and sandalwood—
this six-component incense is always dear to all the gods.

O beautiful one, here [in this rite], the *roga*, *rogahara*, *rogada*, and *keśa* [incenses], as well as the specific leaves of the *surataru* and *jatu*, along with *vaktra*-free *vārida*, *mustā*, and incense-sticks (*dhūpavarti*), are recommended. (3-924)
Guggulu, sarala, dāru, patra, that which originates from Malaya, hrīvera, aguru, kuṣṭha, guḍa, sarjarasa, and ghanasāra. || 3-925 ||
Harītakī, nakhī, lākṣā, jaṭāmāṃsī, and śailaja—
these sixteen ingredients are known as the sixteen-fold incense for rites pertaining to the gods and the ancestors.
Honey, musta, ghee, fragrance, guggulu, agaru, śailaja, candana, sihlaka, and siddhārtha—this ten-ingredient incense (daśāṅga-dhūpa) is recommended. (3.927)
In the *Yāmala*: the ten-ingredient incense is for Śyāmā; that of sixteen ingredients is for Sundarī;
that of eighteen ingredients is for Tārā; and that of eight ingredients is for Bhairavī. (3.928)
For Chinnamastā, five ingredients are preferred; for others, six.
In the absence of these, guggulu, aguru, and sandalwood are used for all vidyās.
245) (In the *Merutantra*): Having worshipped the bell with the heart-mantra (*hṛdāṇu*), the lord-mantra (*nātha*), and the weapon-mantra (*astra*), one should ring it.
In that very same [text]:
The syllable *tāra* (oṃ), the word *jayadhvani* (victory-sound), the mantra *mātaḥ* (O Mother), and *agnigehinī* (the wife of Agni).
The eleven-syllable mantra of the bell bestows all accomplishments;
it is used for the invocation, the water offering (arghya), the incense, the flower, the food offering (naivedya), and the lamp. || 3-931 ||
One should ring the bell, especially during the offering of incense and lamps;
at other times, one should sound it except during the actual moment of worship.
One who desires accomplishment should not perform worship without this [mantra], O Rāghavabhaṭṭas.
Having sprinkled the incense vessel with the Astra-mantra and worshipped it with the Hṛdaya-mantra... (3.933)
While ringing the bell consecrated with the Astra-mantra, one should burn guggulu incense.
Regarding the substance for incense, it is said in the *Kulārṇava*:
"It dispels the foul odor of all great defects that have been shaken away. (3.934)
It is called "incense" (*dhūpa*) because it generates supreme delight.
The varieties of lamps are described in the *Kuloḍḍīśa*:
"The first is a lamp of ghee; the second arises from sesame oil. (3-935)
Lamps made from mustard oil, resin from fruit, or produced from water-born [lotus] seeds; those produced from curd and those produced from food—these seven types of lamps are proclaimed. || 3-936 ||

The wick may be made from lotus fibers (1), or from darbha grass fibers (2), or it may be made from water-born plants (3), or from banyan bark (4), or even from the interior of cotton (5). || 3-937 ||
In the *Yāmala*, it is traditionally taught that there are always five kinds of wicks for the purposes of lighting lamps:
the wick may be white or red, but never yellow nor black. (3.938)
Cotton that is free of seeds, as well as its threads, or a new white cloth, is recommended for the wick. (3.939)
One should never give a garment that is worn out or soiled. (On Mount Meru,) [the vessels] are made of metal, silver, iron, clay, or coconut shell. (3-940)
Alternatively, a lamp-vessel made from the king of grasses (palmyra palm) is praised;
one should prepare the lamp in this manner as a means for pleasing the eyes. (3.941)
(Yāmale) One should present the perfume, flowers, and ornaments in the front part;
likewise, the incense should be on the left or in front, but never on the right. (3-942)
(Merutantra) One should not offer incense on the ground, nor on a seat, nor likewise in a water-pot; rather, having placed it in a vessel in whatever manner appropriate, one should present it. 3-943.
Fat mixed with marrow is not desired; for Viṣṇu, it should be produced from wood.
(In the Yāmala:
One should offer the lamp to the right or in front, but never to the left. 3-944.
Likewise: on the right [side] there is [a lamp] combined with ghee, and on the left, combined with oil; on the right there is a white wick, and on the left, a red wick. (3.945)
Having worshipped the bell with its own mantra, preceded by its sound, one should offer a lamp according to one's means, accompanied by various musical instruments. (Merutantra 3.946)
In that very place: "One should display a lamp aloft using cow's ghee or oil, with a wick containing camphor; but never with fat or similar substances. (3.947)
One should not offer a lamp by mixing various oils such as ghee and the like;
having mixed the oil, one shall go to the Tāmisra hell. (3.948)
One should whirl and display the form resembling the whirling of a pigeon;
then one should recite this verse regarding all the limbs of the deity. (3-949)
Brilliantly luminous, greatly radiant, dispelling darkness everywhere—may this lamp, whose light is both internal and external, be accepted. (3-950)
On the right, a mustard-seed lamp; on the left, a lamp of sesame oil.
On the right, a white wick; on the left, a red wick. (3.951)
A lamp should be offered upon trees, but never on the ground;
for a person who places a lamp on the earth causes distress to the earth itself.
One who possesses a burning lamp incurs sin and surely reaches hell for a hundred years;
one must never extinguish that lamp, for it causes the destruction of prosperity.
(In the Kālikā Purāṇa:
"That whose heat extends even four finger-breadths from the lamp is not known as a 'lamp'; indeed, it is heard of as the 'flood-fire' (oghavahni). (3.954)
One should never give for the purpose of a wick a garment made of hemp or silk that is worn out, soiled, or already used. (3.955)
One must never extinguish a lamp prepared for the sake of the gods;
the thief of the lamp shall become blind, and the one who extinguishes it shall become one-eyed.
The earth, which endures everything, cannot endure these two things:
a kick from the foot upon what should not be done, and likewise the heat of a lamp. (3.957)
In that interval,
O Goddess of Gods, one should offer the lamp while holding it with the tip of the thumb,
whirling it in the shape of a circling pigeon until it reaches the eyes.
The substance of the lamp has been described [in the Kulārṇava]:
"By the complete abandonment of the great darkness of long-standing ignorance and of egoism..."
And because it reveals the supreme reality, it is called a lamp. (3.959)
(In the *Yāmala*): The food offering (*naivedya*) should be placed on the right side or in front, but never behind;
cooked food is for the left of the deity, and raw grain is for the right of the deity. (3.960)
There is also a distinction regarding food offerings based on whether they are cooked or uncooked;
however, there is no rule anywhere regarding the placement of lamps and food offerings in front [of the deity].
The words of the Rudrayāmala:
"In vessels made of fire-born [metals]—that is, in those of gold, silver, or likewise copper—or even on a stone slab or upon a lotus leaf. (3.962)
A wise person should prepare the food offering (naivedya) either on a plate made of sacrificial wood;
but in the absence of all these, it may be made of clay, provided it is fashioned by one's own hand.
But according to the statement in the *Sārasaṃgraha*:
"Having placed [the vessel] upon a square mandala within a circle, one should place it in a golden vessel together with its base, and consecrate it according to the path of the scriptures. (3-964)
Having sprinkled it with the weapon-mantra (astramantra) and protected it with the wheel-gestures (cakramudrā),
one should purify it with the wind-seed-syllable (vāyubīja) and burn it with the fire-seed-syllable (vahnibīja).
Touching it with the tip of his right hand, he should consecrate it with the *sudhā* seed-syllable;
then, having displayed the *dhenu-mudrā*, he should worship it with perfumes and flowers.
Having worshipped the deity, one whose mind is undistracted should offer handfuls of flowers;
[he should present] divine, well-prepared *paramānna* (milk-rice) placed in a golden vessel. (Merutantra 3.967)
"Accept this [food] endowed with the six flavors in five ways for my success.
Having recited the root mantra ending in *svāhā*, one should offer the water.
Touching the vessel with both hands at the conclusion of the food offering (naivedya), one should say "namas.
Having offered water into the right hand of the deity, one should recite this: || 3-969 ||
"Thou art the under-layer of nectar, svāhā"—this is the nine-syllable [mantra].
One should display with the left hand [the gesture] resembling a full-blown blue lotus. (3.970)
Having displayed the *prāsa-mudrā*, one should perform the five *prāṇāhuti* offerings.
The *mudrās* for *prāṇa* and the others are described right there:
"The joining of the little finger, the ring finger, and the thumb is the *mudrikā* of *prāṇa*. (3.971)
Having grasped the *prāsa* [noose] with that [hand], one should recite "To Prāṇa, Svāhā!
By joining the index finger, middle finger, and thumb, one should utter the *apānaka*.
Then one should say "to Vyāna" ending with *svāhā*;
then, by joining the middle finger, the ring finger, and the thumb, one should offer [the oblation] with *svāhā*. || 3-973 ||
Having set aside the youngest [wife], he should offer with all [the others] to Udāna the wife of Agni;
then, having uttered "Svāhā" to Samāna with all [the wives], he should cast in a mouthful of food.
In another tantra: "One should touch the little finger and the ring finger with the tips of one's own thumbs; this is the first mudrā here."
Likewise, another [mudrā] consists of the index and middle fingers, and the ring and middle fingers joined at their middles. (3.975)
The ring finger, the index finger, and the middle finger;
likewise, the fourth [finger] together with the little finger;
and the fifth is taught to be from the middle [of the fingers].
The mudrās of Prāṇa and the others are joined with their respective mantras. || 3-976 ||
(From the Merutantra:
Then, having rendered pure water nectar-like with the *dhenumudrā* in a vessel made of gold or other materials, it should be offered to the deity while reciting this mantra: || 3.977 ||
Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods! This supreme offering brings complete satisfaction;
it is not previously offered to others, pure, in its natural state, and perfectly cool. (3.978)
"Accept this supreme water, filled with supreme bliss.
Having spoken thus, one should place the water vessel to the left of the deity.
Food cooked for the sake of the gods should be offered with three types of grains:
prepared by frying in ghee, cooked in milk, or processed solely over fire. (3-980)
It is proper that it be smeared with sugarcane mud; this is praised for a Śūdra.
Then one should offer a handful of flowers and perform the binding with the Astra-mantra.
Having made the directions a curtain, one should place [the offerings] all around the Lord;
then one should utter "Namaḥ" again over the nectar-like food offering.
Then, having displayed the *dhenumudrā*, one should visualize the deity as partaking of the food;
having recited the root mantra one hundred and eight times, one should offer water.
Having offered water for sipping (ācamana) at the conclusion of the food offering (naivedya), one should perform the ritual of the fire oblation (homa).
In that very same place:
"Having thus performed the worship with incense, lamps, and food offerings... (3.984).

Likewise: Having prepared an excellent sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) on the southern side of the altar, and having established and consecrated the fire, one should commence the Vaiśvadeva rite. || 3.985 ||
Then, according to the prescribed rule, one should worship the deity there with perfumes and other offerings;
having first performed oblations there with the *vyāhṛtis* preceded by the *praṇava*.
One should perform the oblation with milk-rice and clarified butter using the root mantra;
thereafter, having offered twenty-five times, one should offer again with the *vyāhṛti* mantras.
Having worshipped her with sandalwood paste and other offerings, one should join her to the form on the pedestal;
then, having dismissed the fire, one should offer an oblation of milk-rice prepared for the rite of emanation.
To the attendants [he offers oblations] accompanied by sandalwood paste, flowers, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*).
(p. 251) Here, the *vaiśvadeva* offering is indeed the daily fire-sacrifice (*nityahoma*).
(In the *Siddhāntasāra*)
Having completed the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, one should indeed offer the bali-oblation to the spirits (bhūtas).
In the Śākta [tradition], however, the wise practitioner should offer the *bhūtabali* at the conclusion of the *balidāna*.

The meaning is that wherever—in the Vaiṣṇava rites or other rituals—the procedure for offering the *bali* as it will be described later does not exist, the *bhūtabali* should be offered at this very time. (From the *Merutantra*)
Having meditated that the deity is satisfied, [one should offer] the food offering (naivedya) from which the essence has departed.
Then, having reflected, he should place that bowl in the direction of the Rākṣasas;
next, the purification of the site for the food offering should be performed with cow-dung water using the *astra* mantra.

Having taken the remnants of the deity's food, one should say, "Homage to the consumer of the floral offerings (nirmālya)," and then, having cast them out toward the northeast, one should wash one's hands.
One should again offer water for sipping (ācamana) as well as a hand-paste (karodvartana).
Having given pure water for sipping, one should scent the hands with fragrant substances.
Having reflected for a moment, the wise one should then take a mouthful of water with this mantra: "Thou art the covering of nectar, svāhā. (Gautamīya, 3.994)
(In the *Yāmala*):
One should offer all the ritual implements and so forth at the end of the root mantra;
if one is unable [to do so physically], one should offer them mentally, for this ritual action must not be omitted. (3-995)
Regarding the second vidyā, however, a specific rule is stated in the *Nīlatantra*:
"Having made everything consist of mantra, one should offer it to the deity; one should recite:
'O glorious Ekajaṭā, accept this vajra-flower. (3.996)
The practitioner [should worship] with the root-mantra ending in *agnipriyā* (namas), accompanied by the *satāra* (the five stars).

"Tāra" refers to the *praṇava* (oṃ); its application at the very beginning is established by tradition (*saṃpradāya*). Furthermore, according to the author of the *Sudhārṇava*, this mantra is entirely uncontradicted for the worship of all deities, including those headed by Tārā.
Regarding the subject of Śrīvidyā, however, [it is stated in the *Mānasollāsa*]:
The mantra-practitioner should always recite the mantras while performing the ritual services with full awareness.
Likewise, it is stated: "And all the mantras for ritual services are proclaimed to begin with the three *tārās*.
And the three *tārās* are *śrīṃ*, *hrīṃ*, and *klīṃ*. (In the *Yāmala*)
In the *Jñānārṇava*, it is said: "Vāṅ, Māyā, and Kamalā.
Furthermore: "One should offer a mouthful of water (*culluka*) after having given excellent betel. (3.998)
It was blended with cardamom, cloves, camphor, nutmeg, and other ingredients,
and made fragrant by portions of *tāla* leaves, camphor, and *pūga* nuts.
(Merutantra) Then one should offer to Viṣṇu the twelve-fold betel preparation:
1. Khadira, 2. Elā, 3. Lavaṅga, 4. Indu, 5. Cūrṇa, 6. Parṇa, and Tamālaka.
Combined with the petals of the jasmine bud (jātīkośadala), its bark, musk (kastūrī), and saffron (kesara),
along with the betel nut (pūgīphala), this is declared to be the ten-ingredient incense (daśāṅga) for the Sun.
The five-fold powder (pañcāṅga) of Vighneśvara, however, is devoid of musk and jasmine garlands; it consists of khadira wood, leaves, betel nut, and camphor.
There, one should likewise show the mountain of the Goddess together with the *jātī* flower-casket of the Great Lord; and one should arrange the mirror along with the parasol and the fly-whisks.
Now, the ritual gestures (*upacāramudrā*):

For the seat, there should be the lotus gesture (*padmamudrā*), with both hands facing downward. This is the gesture used when inquiring after one's welfare; for that same inquiry, it is repeated with the hands facing upward. (3.1004)
The *svāgata* (welcome) gesture should be the *arghya* mudrā, while the *añjali* is said to be [the gesture for] salutation;
when the ring finger and the thumb are joined, that same gesture is called the *pādya* mudrā.
The wise one, having made the right hand palm-upward with its surface slightly hollowed, should keep the four fingers—excluding the little finger—joined together and raised. (3-1006)
O fair-faced one, this mudrā with the fingers facing downward and not bent is prescribed for the ritual rinsing (ācamana);
for the offering of honey-mixture (madhuparka), the mudrā should have the thumb touched.
O Supreme Goddess, the fist formed with the right hand facing downwards, released by the little finger— this is declared to be the mudrā of bathing.
Having placed the right hand palm upwards, one should then touch its middle finger with the thumb; this is proclaimed as the mudrā of the garment.
This very same [mudrā], through the touching of the ring finger, is known as the Ornament (bhūṣaṇa);
indeed, through the touching of the little finger, it is the mudrā of the sacred thread (upavīta). 3-1010.
One should touch the tip of the little finger with the tip of the thumb; this is the *mudrā* of fragrance.
In another tantra it is said: "O Pārvatī, [one should join] the middle, ring, and thumb fingers at their tips. (3-1011)
The practitioner should offer pure fragrance with the root mantra,
and he should present flowers upon the yantra using the thumb and forefinger.
Having turned the hand face down, one should join the tip of the thumb with the tip of the index finger;
O Supreme Goddess, this mudrā is called Puṣpā.
Just as with the incense, O Goddess, so should the wise preceptor offer incense; he should do so with the middle and ring fingers at the middle joint. (3.1014)
O Goddess of gods, having grasped the lamp with the tip of the thumb, one should offer it.
Likewise: O Maheśvarī, one should touch the tip of the forefinger with the tip of the thumb. (3.1015)
This is declared to be the mudrā of incense, which brings delight to all the gods.
O Goddess, the preceptor should touch the tip of the ring finger with the tip of the middle finger. (3.1016)

The *naivedya-mudrā* is said to bring satisfaction to the deity. Elsewhere it is stated: "Having performed the raising [of the offering] three times with the *gāyatrī* and the root-mantra... (3.1017).
O Goddess, one should present the food offering with the mudrā called Tattva;
one should give the water for rinsing the mouth with the root mantra, and the betel leaf with the Tattva-mudrā.
Having performed worship with the root mantra according to the specific mantras prescribed in each respective ritual manual,
one should offer the bali-oblation to the deity and then present the bali-oblation to the obstructing spirits and others. (Siddhāntasāra 3.1019)
(In the Jñānārṇava:
"O Dear One, having fashioned mandalas in the northeast, southeast, southwest, and northwest corners as before, one should then worship them as before. (3.1020)
And one should offer the oblation of food as before for the sake of all prosperity, O Great Goddess, to the Vaṭukas, to the Yoginīs, and to their beloved ones. (3.1021)
One should offer the bali-oblation to Gaṇeśa and Kṣetrapāla as before.
(In the *Samayācāra*:
One should give [the offering] to Vaṭuka in the south and to the host of Yoginīs in the north. (3-1022)
One should offer the *bhūtabali* in the east and the *kṣetrapālabali* in the west;
likewise, the offering for Vaṭuka is prescribed with the thumb and the ring finger. (3-1023)
One should offer the bali to the Yoginīs by joining the little finger and the thumb;
one should offer the bali to the Kṣetrapāla with the thumb and the index finger.
O beloved, the *bhūtabali* is said to be performed with all the fingers;
however, for the *tathyamuṣṭi*, make the middle finger stand upright like a staff.
The great mudrā of the elephant’s tusk is for the bali offering of Gaṇeśa;
and with all the fingers [joined together], O Dear One, it is said to be the bali offering for the bhūtas. (1026)
The acceptable substances have been described in the *Mahākālasaṃhitā*,
first regarding the Right-hand Practice (*dakṣiṇācāra*):
"Black gram rice, as well as parched grain, fried grain, or even flour."
Either flattened rice, or grains of rice, or even boiled rice.

Either curd-mixture (āmikṣā) or gruel (yavāgū), or likewise rice-and-pulse porridge (kṛsara), milk-rice (pāyasa), or curd sprinkled with clarified butter (ājya), or cooked foods, or fruits. || 1028 ||
In the Vāmācāra [tradition], O fair-faced one, liquor that is burnt, fried, or even made into a sauce should be offered as the *vali* oblation. 1029.
This bali offering is not proclaimed as being common to all;
rather, this bali can only be given by a specific qualified person.
The mantras for the *vaṭukas* are as follows (*Jñānārṇava*): "Come, come, O Son of the Goddess," ending with "O Lord" (*nātha*) at the end of "O *Vaṭuka*";
then "O you with tawny hair" (*kapila*), ending with "O you resplendent with a mass of matted locks" (*jaṭābhārabhāsura*), followed by "O Three-eyed One" (*trinetr*). (1031)
And at the very end: "O Jvālāmukha, destroy, destroy the obstacles!
Accept this offering (bali) together with all ritual services," [ending] with the two-word step.
The mantra of Vaṭuka is said to be joined with the wife of Vahni (the fire-goddess, Svāhā).
O Goddess, one should offer the oblation to Vaṭuka with this mantra.
At the conclusion of the practice, one should recite this mantra of the power of the Yoginīs:
"To the Yoginīs, svāhā," together with the syllable *kvaṃ* and in the *sragdharā* meter. (p. 256)

Whether above the cosmic egg, or in heaven, in the expanse of the sky, on the surface of the earth, in the partless realm, in the netherworld, in fire, in water, or in wind— wherever they may be situated;
or those who have established their feet in sacred fields, pīṭhas, upapīṭhas, and so forth, with offerings of flowers, incense, and the like;
May the goddesses Prītās, who are always worshipped by heroes and honored by the virtuous, protect us through the rite of auspicious offerings.
In the *Jñānārṇava*, however, after reciting the aforementioned verse, it says:
"O Great Goddess, at the end of this is the seed-syllable of the Yoginī. (1034)
To [the mantras] ending with *sarvavarṇa*, one should write the word *yoginī*;
having written the armor (*kavaca*) and the weapon (*astra*), one should again write the wife of fire (*vahnijāyā*). || 1035 ||
"O Goddess, by means of this mantra, one should offer the bali-offering to the Yoginīs," so it was said.
She [replied]: "One should again write the letter *kṣa*, conjoined with the six long vowels. (1036)
Furthermore, one should draw the field-square (kṣetrapada) along with the guardian, incense, lamps, and so forth;
having drawn it together with the offering (bali), one should then say: "Take, take! (gṛhṇa gṛhṇa). || 1037 ||
O beautiful one, this is the mantra of Kṣetrapāla, joined with the wife of Vahni (the fire-goddess, svāhā).
O Goddess, with this mantra, one should offer the bali-oblation to Kṣetrapāla.
Having written the triad gā, gī, and gū, one should utter Gaṇapati ending in -ṅ.
After *vara*, after *varada*, and after *sarva*, one should write *jana*. (1039)
Having said, "Bring [him] under my control," one should offer the oblation (bali) with the mantra consisting of two parts and ending with the wife of Vahni (svāhā);
thus one should present the oblation to Gaṇeśa.
However, in the *Siddhāntasāroddhṛtasāmānyapaddhati*, the offering of the *bali* to Gaṇeśa and the others is stated to proceed clockwise starting from the east:
"The preceptor should present the *bali* to Gaṇeśa, Vaṭuka, and Kṣetrapāla, and to the Yoginīs, proceeding clockwise starting from the east. (1041)
Mahākāla has also stated the sequence beginning with Gaṇeśa:
"One should subsequently offer [the oblation] to Gaṇādhipati and then to Vaṭuka," and so forth.
In reality, however, the sequence beginning with Gaṇeśa pertains to the Dakṣiṇa-mārga (Right Path), while the sequence beginning with Vaṭuka pertains to the Vāma-mārga (Left Path).
One must certainly perform the worship of Vaṭuka at the beginning, starting from the left.
"Vaṭuka is the principal deity on this path; therefore, the first offering is made to the gods.
This is according to the statement in the *Merutantra* concerning the section on the Vāmamārga.
Now, the *bhūtabali* (offering to the spirits) [according to the *Merutantra*]:
Having sat upon his seat, the practitioner of mantra should then offer the bali-oblation to the bhūtas.
Having prepared a mandala in the northeast,
one should place there a vessel filled with food, rich in side dishes and water, and adorned with flowers and other offerings.
Having worshipped the spirits there, one should then offer them a bali-oblation: "Those who are fierce, whose deeds are fierce, and who dwell in fierce places... (1045)
The yoginīs of fierce form, those who are lords of the hosts (gaṇas), those who move on the earth, those who move in the sky, and those who dwell in the intermediate space; || 1046 ||
"May all of you, with joyful minds, accept this offering (bali).
With the left hand, one should present the vessel containing water. || 1047 ||
Having taken up a handful of flowers, one should pray to the spirits. || 1047ef ||
May all the beings who dwell here upon the earth, having received this offering presented according to the ritual, attain satisfaction and depart.
May they forgive these [faults] here; let there be homage to them. || 3-1048 ||
Having offered a handful of flowers and bowed, let them dwell at their ease; then, one should dismiss the spirits with the *nārāca* mudrā, reciting "bhūtāni. (3-1049)
(From the *Śāradātilaka*):
Having recited the root mantra one thousand times with undistracted mind, he should offer that recitation to the deity for the sake of attaining all prosperity. (3.1050)
In the Merutantra:
"One should recite the root mantra without weariness one thousand and eight times, or half of that, or three hundred, or even one hundred and eight. (3-1051)
When the recitation is completed, one should place the rosary upon the head;
then, taking water from the *argha* vessel into the hand, one should recite this: || 3-1052 ||
You are the protector of the most secret among secrets; accept this recitation performed by us.
O Lord, Master of the World, may spiritual accomplishment be mine through your grace.
Having offered water into the right hand of the deity, one should present it;
likewise, thereafter, with songs of praise and preceded by the ringing of a bell. (3.1054)

The Brāhmaṇa [should worship] with the Vedic mantras and so forth; the Kṣatriya with the Saṃhitās and so forth; the Vaiśya with the Purāṇas and so forth; but the Śūdra with the Prākṛta texts and so forth. (3-1055)
(From the *Yāmala*):
Thereafter, the wise one, having circumambulated the deity with devotion, should bow down;
"having circumambulated" means having performed a clockwise circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇīkṛtya*).
The fruit of circumambulation is stated in another tantra: "Whatever fruit a man obtains by giving the earth to those who know the Vedas," [that same fruit he obtains by circumambulating]. (3-1056)
One obtains that fruit through devotion by performing a circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇā*) of Kṛṣṇa. The mention of "Kṛṣṇa" is an elliptical designation (*upalakṣaṇa*).
The various types of circumambulations have been described in the *Yāmala*.
O Goddess, one should perform a circumambulation of the triangle-shaped Śakti.
The half-moon is said to be behind Maheśa;
and the practitioner of mantra [should perform] the circumambulation of Śiva according to the sequence of the half-moon. (3-1058)
One should not cross the *somasūtra* by alternating between the right and left sides;
rather, extending the right hand while keeping one's own head bowed, one should proceed again. (3-1059)
One should show the right side [of the body] and be mentally inclined toward the right;
one should properly perform the circumambulation of the deity three times, keeping it to the right.
Whether it be a single cubit in measure or even a single circumambulation,
seeing Viṣṇu at an improper time destroys previously accumulated merit.
In another tantra: One should perform one circumambulation for Caṇḍī, seven for the Sun, three for Vināyaka, four for Keśava, and half for Śiva. (3.1062)
The various types of prostrations are described in the *Viṣṇukalpalatā*:
"With those two hands, with the two knees, with the chest, with the head,
with the eyes, with speech, and with the mind— thus is the eight-limbed prostration (aṣṭāṅga-praṇāma) proclaimed."
With both arms, with knees joined, with the head, with speech, and with the eyes. (3-1078)
This five-limbed prostration (*pañcāṅga-praṇāma*) is the most excellent among all forms of worship.
Likewise: "The wise person who, upon seeing Kṛṣṇa, should prostrate by falling to the ground... (3.1063).
Having abandoned the sins accumulated over a thousand births, he shall attain Vaikuṇṭha.
(Viṣṇudharma) A wise person [should prostrate] with both knees, both hands, and the head. (3-1064)
Having offered salutations to the God, one shall obtain all desires;
indeed, as many atoms as there are upon a person's forehead [so many worlds shall be attained]. (3.1065)
O best of Brahmins, for as many years as there are atoms in the earth that belong to one who bows here to Madhusūdana,
for that many years he is glorified in the heavenly world.
(From the *Śāradā-tantra*):
Then, in the direction of Śambhu, the Guru should scatter [the grains] from what was previously collected;
he should [place] a water-pot filled with water and joined with gold, cloth, and other [ornaments]. (3.1067)

Having established [the image] upon it, one should worship the weapon-deity (astradevatā), who is seated upon a lion, holding a sword and a shield, possessing a terrible form, and facing westward. || 3-1068 ||

Having worshipped with the *calāsana* and taken it up again, the Guru [should protect it] with water poured from the mouth of a vessel, saying, "Protect [it] for the sake of the world-protectors (*lokapālas*). (3-1069)
Having announced the command of the deity and circumambulated [the site] from left to right, one should recite the weapon-mantra and establish [the deities] as before. || 3-1070 ||
Having worshipped its mouth once more with perfumes and other offerings while remaining on a steady seat,
[one should prepare] the *karkarī*, the *vardhanī*, and the *ghaṭī* with its stalk.
(From the *Kriyāsaṃgraha*)
Then, having placed the water-jar (karkarī), which has the form of a weapon, in its proper place; || 3-1071 ||
The preceptor should perform the consecration of the fire in his own sacrificial pit.

In this third chapter— which possesses a confluence of excellent compositions, abounding in streams of nectar variegated by the wonderful diversity of words that purify beings with marvelous power; and which provides the aesthetic wonder of a heap of pearls made manifest by sound reasoning— [the following is presented].
This very point has been reached here in this *Puraścaryārṇava* composed by the illustrious Naradeva. (3-1072)

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Worship of the Deity Preceded by the Selection of the Guru," within the *Dīkṣā-vidhi* (Ritual of Initiation) of the *Puraścaryārṇava*, composed by the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja Śrī Pratāpasiṃha.
Now, the procedure for the consecration of the fire is demonstrated.

Regarding that, first the consecration of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) is stated in the *Merutantra*: "The practitioner of the Vedic path should perform the installation of the fire according to the ritual manual."
The Tantrika should perform eighteen purifications of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
One should visualize [the site] with the root mantra, sprinkle it with water while reciting the weapon mantra (*astramantra*),
and strike the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) three times with *kuśa* grass while reciting the weapon mantra.
Then, sprinkling the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with the armor-mantra (kavaca-mantra) is prescribed;
the digging of the pit according to the measurement of finger-breadths (aṅgula) is performed with the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra).
One should extract that clay with the thumb and ring finger while reciting the Astra mantra;
then, one should fill it again with pure clay while reciting the Hṛdaya mantra.
Then one should level it, sprinkle it with the Astra-mantra, and protect it with the Kavaca-mantra;
one should crush it with wood or other materials using the Astra-mantra so that it becomes firm.
One should sweep the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with kuśa grass while reciting the Kavaca mantra,
and then one should apply a coating of cow-dung and water using the same Kavaca mantra.
With the Kavaca mantra, one should contemplate the digits of fire, sun, and moon within the sacrificial pit;
then, one should encircle it with each girdle using a cord made of three strands.
Then one should perform the worship of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) three times with the armor mantra (varma-mantra). [The formula is:
"Oṃ, to such-and-such a pit, āsanaṃ namaḥ. (4–8)
One should perform the entire worship with modifications such as "This is the arghya," and one should likewise perform the worship of the navel and the girdles.
Then one should contemplate that pit as being made firm like a vajra by means of the Astra-mantra. (In the Śāradā-tantra:
"The making of the vajra is performed with the Astra-mantra, and [the purification] with auspicious kusha grass and the Hṛdaya-mantra. (4.10)
One should protect the crossroads and the hall for the dice-game with the armor-mantra.
In the sacrifice, one should consecrate the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) with these aforementioned consecrations.
Alternatively, one should consecrate those [seeds] with the four [rites] beginning with inspection;
then, [the scattering of seeds] is performed with *darbha* grass whose tips are uncut and which has been empowered with the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*). (4.12)
One should adorn the entire wall of the pit with armor;
thus is described the consecration of the pit known as the "axle-board" (akṣapāṭa). || 4-13 ||
Thus it is stated in the Nāradapañcarātra. (In the Merutantra:
"In the case of a left-hand homa, however, there are indeed only the first four purificatory rites."
In the *Nāradapañcarātra*:
"If, however, at the time of commencing the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) have not been performed... (4.14).
"And once you have attained perfection, all these [deities] shall indeed be subject to your command in due order.

The meaning is that if these purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) were not performed at the time of constructing the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), they must necessarily be performed once that [pit] has been completed.
(In the *Śāradā-tantra*)
One should draw three lines each, directed toward the east and the north, with the heart-mantra.
Regarding the sequence of drawing here (*Sautrāmaṇītantra*):
one should draw [the lines] starting from the south, with the head facing east and north;
one should draw [the lines] starting from the west, with the head facing north and positioned in front. (4-16)
Having written three lines each in this manner, one should sprinkle them with the *vāgbhava* [mantra]. (In the *Śāradā-tantra*:
"The deities for those lines pointing eastward are traditionally held to be Mukunda, Īśa, and Purandara. (4.17)

At the northern ends of the lines, one should draw [the figures of] Brahmā, Vaivasvata, and Indu with the root mantra, using either *darbha* grass or a sacrificial ladle (*sruva*). (From the *Yāmala*) 4-18.
(Merutantra) Above the triangle is a hexagon; therein is the worship of the six [deities] beginning with Viṣṇu, Īśa, and Vāsava, within the pair of triangles. (p. 263) 4-19.
(In the Śāradātilaka and the Amalaka, however:
"Alternatively, one should draw a circle, a hexagon, and a triangle there;
O Goddess, one should draw a triangle surrounded by a hexagon"—thus [it is said]. (4-20)
The drawing of the triangle, hexagon, and so forth, is stated according to another alternative view. (In the Śāradā-tantra:
"Having sprinkled all [the materials] with the Tāra mantra, one should then worship the Yoga-pīṭha."
In the *Merutantra*:
"And [one should place them] upon the filaments of that lotus, proceeding clockwise starting from the eastern petal. (4-21)
One should worship these at the center and the ends: Jayā and Vijayā, as well as the one named Ajitā, Aparājitā, Nityā, and Vilāsinī.
Then, in that place, reciting "Hrīḥ! Obeisance to the one seated upon the lotus of all powers," [one should worship] Dogdhrī, Aghorā, and Maṅgalā.
Having offered a handful of flowers into the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should worship Bhuvaneśvarī.
In another Tantra: "Salutation to the nature of the yoga-pīṭha of Vāgīśvarī and her Lord. (4-24)
This is the *pīṭha-mantra* beginning with *hrīm*; having invoked [the deity] into this, one should worship her.
In the *Merutantra*, under the heading "One should worship Bhuvaneśvarī," it says:
"There, one should worship Śiva as intoxicated with passion, and likewise the Goddess in her menses. (4-25)
"One should meditate upon and worship [the goddess] within the Gaṇeśa, Śaiva, and Śākta [traditions]"—thus it is said in the *Śāradā*:
"One should worship Vāgīśvarī, who has bathed after her menses and resembles a blue lotus. (4.26)
One should worship [the deity] joined with Vāgīśvara using the ritual offerings.
Regarding the alternative forms of Bhuvaneśvarī and Vāgīśvara, it is stated in the *Gaṇeśavimarṣiṇī*:
"One should worship Vāgīśī with the seed-syllable of Śakti, and Vāgīśa with the mantra of the one to be accomplished. (4-27)
The word "should worship" (*pūjayet*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
In the *Rudrayāmala*, however,
the two mantras for Śiva and Śakti are said to end with the word "namaḥ."
Having worshipped these two three times each, one should prostrate with this mantra.
"I bow to Vāgīśvarī, who has bathed after her menses, adorned with all ornaments, and united with Vāgīśvara, for the sake of attaining all perfections"—thus it is said. (4.29)
In the Vaiṣṇava [tradition], however, Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa are to be worshipped in the place of Vāgīśvarī and Vāgīśvara. As it is said in the *Tattvasārasaṃhitā*:
"There, one should contemplate Lakṣmī as being in her menses, and Agni as being united with the Lord Nārāyaṇa through the act of sexual union. (4.30)
The same applies to the Saura [tradition] as well. As it is said in the *Merutantra*:
"In the Vaiṣṇava and likewise in the Saura [traditions], one should contemplate Lakṣmī as being in her menses;
one should meditate on the fire born from the union with Nārāyaṇa. (4.31)
And here:
Sovereignty, elevation, splendor, emanation, fame, humility, contentment, excellence, and growth—these are declared to be the nine powers. (4.32)

Thus end the powers of the *pīṭha*. According to the statement, "Having offered the seat beginning with the seed-syllable (*bīja*)," the *pīṭha-mantra* is: "Obeisance to the essence of the Yoga-pīṭha of Śrī Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa.
In the case of Śrīvidyā, however, [it is said in the Jñānārṇava]: "Kāmeśvarī, full of desire and joined with her season, is in the center of the *kuṇḍa*."
Having invoked and fully worshipped [the deity], one should bring the fire into its interior.
(From the Śāradā-tantra):

Having brought fire produced from a sun-crystal or the like, or that which has come from the house of a Vedic scholar, one should place it in a vessel and discard the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters. 4-34.
(p. 265) (According to the Gautama tradition:
[One should kindle] a fire produced from stone, or one produced from a fire-drill, or one born in the house of those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), or it may be a forest fire. 4-35.
One who has obtained [an animal] by chance but is unfit for the sacrificial rite, or one received from a Brāhmaṇa who maintains no sacred fires (niragni), shall yield only half the merit. (4.36)
The sacrificial fire shall grant a fourth part of the fruit to one who has received [the initiation] from a Kṣatriya;
however, that act of oblation performed by a Vaiśya or a Śūdra becomes fruitless.
(From the Uḍḍīśa):

Whether produced in the house of one learned in the Vedas, or born from a sun-crystal, or even produced from a fire-drill, it should be placed in a vessel made of gold or other precious materials. (4.38)
The practitioner should bring it covered with a copper vessel or similar object;
or else, he should place what has been brought in a brass bowl on all sides.
In the *Merutantra*:

A young girl, a married woman, or a woman whose husband is living, having purified herself and wearing clean garments, should collect fire from a forest, from a jewel, or from the house of a brahmin. (4.40)
When a beautiful copper vessel or similar container has been covered with another vessel, one should perform the bringing forward of the fire; or else, one may do so in a new earthen bowl.
One should place the fire into the vessel with the Astra-mantra and cover it with the Kavaca-mantra;
[this should not be done] in a worn-out earthenware pot, a skull-cup, a broken vessel, or likewise on a firebrand.
One should not perform the bringing forward of the fire (*agnipraṇayana*), for it brings about the danger of the loss of [one's] health.
Regarding the specific procedure for discarding the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters (*kravyāda*), another Tantra states:
"Having established the fire with the *astra* mantra and having covered it with the *kavaca* mantra... (4.43).
O Dear One, one should cast away the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters toward the southwest with the Astra-mantra.
(Also in the Mantramuktāvalī:
Having brought [the remains] with the Astra-mantra, one should abandon the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters in the southwest.
The wise practitioner should establish the portion belonging to the gods in front with the root mantra.
And in the *Uḍḍīśa*, it is stated: "One should discard the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters in the southwest using the *kūrca* and *astra* mantras. (4-45)
(Regarding Gaṇeśvara as well:
One should discard the portion for the flesh-eaters with the root mantra ending in *huṃ* and *phaṭ*.
(Also in the Kriyāsāra:)
He who eats raw flesh in places such as cremation grounds is called Vahni.
One should abandon even a small portion of his name, such as "flesh-eater" (*kravyāda*), from the fire.
Then the preceptor should perform the consecration (*saṃskāra*) for him according to the rule, by means of the rites of inspection (*vīkṣaṇa*) and so forth. (From the *Śāradā-tantra*, 4.47)
Then, while recollecting the unification of the earth with the digestive fire and the lunar fire,
one who mutters [the mantra] with the seed-syllable of fire brings consciousness into the fire.
(Merutantra) Having diligently invoked the radiant energy in the form of a lamp-flame, one should effect the unification of the earthly element with the digestive fire and the lunar fire. 4-49.
Then, having recollected [it] by means of the seed-syllable of fire, one should join his consciousness [to it].
The "Vaindava" fire is situated between the eyebrows.
(In the Uḍḍīśa):
Shining in every direction, according to the analogy of one lamp [igniting] another lamp.
Then, one who knows the mantra should worship by means of the armor-mantra through the path of the breath;
the practitioner of mantra, having consecrated [the offering] with the Tāra-mantra, renders it nectar-like by means of the dhenumudrā. (From the Śāradā-tantra, verses 4–51).
Having first protected it with the Astra-mantra and subsequently enveloped it with the Tanutra-mantra,
the preceptor should circumambulate it three times while worshipping it above the sacrificial pit.
Then, while reciting the *tāra-mantra*, he should circumambulate the fire from left to right, keeping it to his right,
with his knees touching the ground and facing the fire.
(On page 267: With the thought that it is the seed of Śiva, he should cast this [seed] into the womb of the Goddess. (Also in the *Merutantra*:
There, in the womb of the Goddess, the preceptor should have his knees touching the ground. (4–54)
Having meditated upon it as the seed-syllable of Śiva, one should quickly cast the fire [into the pit];
and having placed both knees on the ground, one should [place] the *kūrca* seed-syllable and the fire [therein]. (Uḍḍīśa, 4.55)
Ending with "caitanya" and concluding with "namaḥ," one should awaken the pure [fire] with this;
then, perceiving it as the seed-syllable of Śiva, one should cast the fire into its womb.

In the *Tripurāsārasamuccaya*, it is stated: "The practitioner of mantra should place this [deity] within the womb [of the triangle], facing himself; thereafter, he should place the fire with the root mantra."

"By means of the meditation on the seed-syllable of Śiva" refers to the Śaiva and Śākta traditions; however, in the Vaiṣṇava and other systems, it should be understood as "by means of the meditation on the seed-syllable of Viṣṇu" and so forth.
(In the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā, however:
"Having uttered the seed-syllable of Fire, one should install the fire upon the seat."
And likewise, [one should do so] through the path of the *yoni* or directly facing oneself. || 4.57 ||
Through the path of the *yoni*, by means of the opening of the *yoni* placed above the girdle (*mekhalā*).
(In the *Merutantra*): One should perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) for the God and Goddess with the intention that it is the end of sexual union.
(From the Śāradā-tantra:
Afterwards, one should offer water for sipping (ācamanīyaka) to both the God and the Goddess. || 4.58 ||
Then the preceptor should kindle that fire with this mantra, having uttered the pairs [of syllables]: *cit piṅgala hana daha paca*. (4-59)
"O Omniscient One, command me, svāhā"—this is the mantra previously proclaimed (in the Rudrayāmala).
O Goddess, [the mantra consists of] *hrīḥ*, *hroḥ*, a pair of *jvala*s, and then a pair of *prajvalat*s. (4-60)
"The wise one should kindle the fire with the mantra *huḥ phaṭ svāhā*—thus it has been said. (4.60ef)
The kindling [of the fire] is performed with the mouth, or with a handful of *kuśa* grass, *palāśa* leaves, and so forth.
As it is said in the *Merutantra*: "One should blow upon the fire with the mouth alone, for this [fire] was indeed born from the mouth."
Not with kuśa grass, nor with leaves such as those of the palāśa tree, nor with any other non-purificatory [material].
Also in another tantra:
"They should perform the oblation and offer into the fire using the hands, winnowing baskets, ladles, and so forth;
one should not blow upon the fire, nor should one do so with fans and the like. (4.62)

"One should blow upon the fire with the mouth alone, for it was born from the mouth; as for the common saying that 'one should not blow on the fire with the mouth,' that refers to [ordinary] fire. — 4.63.
In that regard, the Jvālinī mudrā should also be displayed, and it is as follows:
having made the two wrists level and the hands with fingers extended, having joined the two middle fingers, one should insert the two thumbs into their midst. (4.64)

"This is that supreme mudrā, Jvālinī, for the rite of homa"—thus it is stated in the *Yāmala*. Then, having risen from that [posture] and having properly formed the hollow of the hands according to the rule, the wise one [should proceed]. (4-65)
I worship Agni, the blazing one, the knower of all beings, the consumer of oblations—pure, golden-hued, kindled, and facing in every direction. (4.66)
He should sit before the fire according to the rule with this mantra.
(Uḍḍīśa) Having silently cast into the fire a fuel-stick the size of a span, saturated with ghee at both its base and tip, one should place the deity upon the tongue [of the fire]. (4.67)
In the *Śāradā*, it is said:
"The practitioner of mantra should place [the syllables] throughout his own body—in the tongue, the fire-god (the anus), the genitals, the anus, the head, the mouth, the nose, and the eyes. (4.68)

The letters from *sa* to *ya*, joined with *vahni* (the letter *ra*), *ārghīśa* (the letter *ha*), and provided with the bindu (*m*), are declared by the teachers to be the seven mantras of the tongues of fire. (4.69)
p. 269) The tongues are said to be of three kinds according to the distinction of qualities in their functions: Hiraṇyā, Kanakā, Raktā, and another, Kṛṣṇā, which is considered Suprabhā. (4-70)
Bahurūpā and Atiraktā are the *sāttvika* [deities] in sacrificial rites.

*Vahni* is the syllable *repha* (ṛ); *ira* is the syllable *ya*; *arghīśa* is the long *ū* vowel (*ū*). Here, in the *sāttvika* tongue, the sequence of Bahurūpā and Atiraktā follows the order of the seed-syllables (*bīja*) and not the order of the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), because Bahurūpā is to be placed upon all the limbs.
As it is said in another Tantra:
And [one should apply it] in sequence to the penis, anus, head, mouth, nose, and eyes. (4.71)
"One should place that multiform goddess, who is intensely red, upon all her limbs"—so say Rāghavabhaṭṭas.
But in reality: "Hiraṇyā, Gaganā, Raktā, Kṛṣṇā, and Suprabhā. (4.72)
"O Maheśānī, [the goddesses] Bahurūpā and likewise Atiriktā—immediately after this, O Goddess, one should place each one upon the linga, the anus, and the head. (4.73)
"Then one should place [the syllables] on the mouth, the nose, the eyes, and all the limbs," according to the statement in the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*.
Thereafter, the practitioner of mantra should install the tongue of the Fire-god within his own body. (4.74)
In the heart, the navel, the anus, the head, the mouth, the nose, and the eyes, as well as in all the limbs and on the tongue, they will be described as being of three types. (4.75)
Hiraṇyā, Gaganā, Raktā, Kṛṣṇā, Suprabhā, Bahurūpā, and Atiraktā— these seven tongues are of the nature of sattva.

Thus, according to the statement in the *Tantramantraprakāśa*, the placement (*nyāsa*) for one who is intensely passionate (*atiraktā*) should be performed on all limbs. Furthermore, the author of the *Sudhārṇava* maintains that if the statement written by Rāghavabhaṭṭa is authoritative, then there is indeed an option (*vikalpa*). In the *Merutantra* as well, the very same sequence mentioned in the *Tantramantraprakāśikā* is stated. In the *Śāradā*, it says:
"Padmarāgā is golden, and another is Bhadralohitā, the third."
Immediately after Lohitā are Śvetā, Dhūminī, and Karālikā. || 4.77 ||
The tongues of fire prescribed for rites performed for specific desires (kāmya-karma) are:
Viśvamūrti, Sphuliṅginī, Dhūmravarṇā, and Manojavā. (4.78) p. 270)
Lohitā, Karālā, and Kālā are said to belong to Tamas;
these seven are employed by practitioners of mantra in cruel rites.
The tongues of those whose seed is auspicious—the immortals, ancestors, gandharvas, yakṣas, nāgas, and piśācas—shall be equal in luster to their respective names. (4.80)
The seven Rākṣasas are declared to be the presiding deities (adhidevatā) of the tongues.

The mention of presiding deities is for the purpose of ritual placement (nyāsa) and worship in the respective locations of those tongues, so that the various tasks of the gods and others may be accomplished through the tongues. (4.81)
"By offering oblations, those deities are considered to grant the desired accomplishment.

From this statement in the *Prapañcasāra*, the author of the *Sudhārṇava* maintains that [the mantra] is for the purpose of the fire-oblation when the oblation is performed with the respective substance upon each respective tongue.
(*Kriyāsāra*)
Bhṛgu is the seer (ṛṣi) of this [verse], the Gāyatrī is the meter (chandas), and Agni is the deity (devatā). || 4-82 ||
The seed-syllable is *ra* and the power is *svāhā*; one should assign the seers (*ṛṣi*) and so forth as before. (In the Śāradā-tantra:
"One should assign the mantras of the limbs of Fire to the body according to the method already stated. (4.83)
Sahasrārcis, Svastipūrṇa, Utthita Puruṣa, Dhūmavyāpin, Saptajihva, and Dhanurdhara—these are the names in sequence. (4.84)
The six-limbed mantras have been declared together with their respective seed-syllables;
thereafter, the preceptor should install the eight forms of Jātavedas.

One should perform the placement (nyāsa) upon the crown, the shoulders, the sides, the buttocks, the anus, the hips, and the sides of the limbs, following the direction of circumambulation; these are now described in their proper order.
Jātavedas, Saptajihva, he who is named Havyavāhana, another named Aśvodaraja, and furthermore the one called Vaiśvānara. (4.87)
Kaumāratejas would be Viśvamukha, who is remembered as Devamukha. (p.
271) Tārā, Agni, and so forth, ending with *namas*, are the forms of Fire. (4.88)

Having prepared the seat, one should contemplate the form of that [deity]. "The seat" refers to the pedestal (*pīṭha*) upon the body—this is the implied meaning. Therein, having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) starting from the foundational power (*ādhāraśakti*) up to the fire-mandala (*vahni-maṇḍala*), one should place the powers of the pedestal (*pīṭhaśakti*) upon the filaments and in the center. In that very place, one should also place the pedestal with the mantra: *raṃ vahniyogapīṭhāya namaḥ*. It is said in that same [text]:
"One should worship [the deity] within its own mandala upon the pedestal, which possesses the nine powers of the lords of the pedestal. (4.89)
Yellow, white, reddish, black, smoky, intense, emitting sparks,
beautiful, and flaming— these are declared to be the nine powers of fire.
Having offered a seat with its own seed-syllable, one should fashion the form with the root-mantra—thus [it is said]. (4.90ef)
Now, regarding meditation on that very same [deity]:
one should meditate upon him who possesses a desired power, holding a svastika and the gesture of fearlessness aloft with his long arms, and who has the luster of a hibiscus flower.
One should meditate upon the Fire-god, adorned with golden ornaments, seated upon a lotus, possessing three eyes, wearing a crown of matted locks, and bound with his hair.
The *Dhyānāntara* is described [in the *Rudrayāmala*] as resembling the *bandhūka* flower, with the luster of well-refined gold;
seated upon a lotus for the sake of the sacrificer, it is adorned with two faces. (4.92)
The god, composed of the seven meters, stationed above his celestial chariot,
with three necks and three lotus-feet, is the destroyer of the offerings to gods and ancestors.
It is adorned with the four horns of the Brahman, Adhvaryu, Udgātṛ, and Hotṛ;
it consists of five vessels, and includes the Pāśupata, Kāpila, and Mahā-mata systems.
The Buddhist and the Vedic—these are his six tawny eyes;
the meaning of the Vedas is his four ears, and the sound consisting of the Śrauta scriptures is his voice. (4.95)
Resplendent with the tips of his matted locks tied down to the netherworld (pātāla),
adorned with golden ornaments, and graced with golden earrings.
Seated in the center of a red lotus, established in the svastika posture, with his third lotus-foot resting against the region of his back. (4.97)
Always resounding and shining with his own splendor,
he holds a spear, a thunderbolt, and the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles in his four arms directed toward the cardinal directions.
Holding a trident, a palm-leaf fan, and a golden vessel of ghee in his three left arms, and wearing red garments; 4.99.
Hiraṇyā, Kanakā, Raktā, and Kṛṣṇā are situated on the face of Dakṣa;
Suprabhā, Vātiraktā, Bahurūpā, and Jihvikā [are likewise located there].
These knowers of tastes are eternally situated upon your two faces;
with these seven tongues, your split-open mouth is endowed.
(From the Śāradā-tantra: Then one should sprinkle with pure waters upon the girdle;
one should spread darbha grass, devoid of a pith, around the middle of the girdle. (4.102)
(Kuloḍḍīśa):
Having performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa) in this manner, one whose body is thus sanctified should perform the strewing of the sacrificial grass.
Having sprinkled [the area] with the water of the arghya offering, [he should do so] over the girdle situated in the center.
With the tips pointing north in the eastern direction, then with the tips pointing east in the south;
with the tips pointing north in the west, and likewise with the tips pointing east in the north. (4.104)
Having covered the base, one should spread [the grass] three times around;
likewise, one should arrange a garland of lamps upon all the girdles.
(In the *Gaṇeśvaravimarṣiṇī*):
One should surround the fire with *darbha* grasses whose tips point eastward and northward;
that is to say, with tips pointing eastward on the south and north sides, and with tips pointing northward on the east and west sides.
(From the *Merutantra*:
In a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with a single girdle (*mekhalā*), one should spread [the grass] beneath the girdle. (4-106)
On a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) with two or three ridges,
or on a mound made of sand, one should spread [the grass] upon the outer ground during the second [rite].
In the *Śāradā-tantra*,
the most excellent of teachers should place the boundary-sticks (*paridhi*) in the directions, excluding the east; thus says Kātyāyana.
They place the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) around [the fire], which are fresh, from a single tree, arm-length in size, and made of *palāśa*, *vaikaṇṭaka*, *kāśmarya*, and *bilva* wood.
(From the *Merutantra*: "Those produced from *palāśa*, *kāśmarī*, *bilva*, and *vikaṇṭaka*...")

One should place the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), which originate from a single tree, are not moist, and are one cubit in length, upon a vessel outside the sand of the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍilaka*).
(Also in the *Tripurāsārasamuccaya*:
"One should place the enclosing sticks upon a vessel outside the sand of the sacrificial mound. (4-109)
In the *Śāradā*, it is said:
"Having worshipped them in a clockwise direction, the forms of Brahmā and the others [should be installed] therein.
In the *Sautrāmaṇītantra*:
The knower of the ritual procedure [should act] in the center of the sacrificial pit.

The powers of the seat of fire (vahner-āsana-śaktayaḥ) are to be worshipped one above the other, in sequence, with the mantras beginning with the common power (sādhāra-śakti) and ending with the lotus-seat (padmāsana).

The seat-śaktis— the previously mentioned pedestal-śaktis— are to be worshipped in sequence at the bases of the petals starting from the east and in the center. A specific detail regarding this is stated in the *Merutantra*:
In the center of the pit, however, there should be a golden pericarp containing a hexagon.
One should visualize an eight-petalled lotus joined with various filaments, surrounded by four gates, and encircled by three squares.
Having worshipped the sacrificial seat (pūjāpīṭha) of that Fire, as well as Maṇḍūkaka and the others there, and the Yoga-seat (yogapīṭha) which is the essence of knowledge—thus [it is said]. (4.114)
Likewise, the worship of the previously mentioned *pīṭhaśaktis* on the eight petals has been described.
"The twelve-syllable heart-mantra for the Lotus-Throne of All Powers (*sarvaśaktikamalāsana*) is declared to be the mantra of Fire (*vahni*) in the worship of all *pīṭhas*" (4.115).
(From the Śāradātilaka):
One should worship the visualized fire in the center with perfumes and other offerings using this mantra:
"O Vaiśvānara, O Jātavedas, come here after [the invocation]. (4.116)
Accomplish all rites at the end of the word *lohitākṣa*;
this mantra, beloved of Agni, is said to conclude with the wife of fire (*svāhā*). || 4.117 ||
One should worship those possessing the luster of tongues of flame in the center and in all six corners.
Here, the grammatical connection is that one should worship in the six corners and in the center. It has been stated that in the corners, the sequence begins with Īśāna.
(Somaśambhu).
In the spheres of Rudra, Indra, Vahni, Māṃsāda, Varuṇa, and Anila.
The six tongues of fire, beginning with Hiraṇyā, are situated in sequence; however, Bahurūpā is in the center—thus [it is said]. (4.119)
(In the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā:
Hiraṇyā has a tongue directed toward the northeast; Kanakā is situated in the east;
Raktā is in the southeast; Kṛṣṇā is in the southwest; and the other is considered to be Suprabhā. (4.120)
Atirikta, Marujjihvā, Svanāma, Svaguṇaprabhā, Triśikhā, Madhyamā, Jihvā, Bahurūpā, and Samāhvayā. (4-121)
"One stands on the right, blazing; the other is on the left.
Immediately after their respective seed-syllables, they should be addressed as follows... (4.122)
(Also in the *Gaṇeśvaravimarṣiṇī*):
Then one should worship the tongues in the six corners and in the center.
Hiraṇyā, possessing the luster of molten gold, is situated in the direction of the Trident-bearer (Śiva). (4.123)
The goddess Gaganā, the color of lapis lazuli, is situated in the eastern direction;
the tongue, resembling the rising sun and red in color, is situated in the direction of Agni (the southeast). (4.124)
Kṛṣṇā, resembling a blue lotus, is situated in the south-western direction;
Suprabhā, with the luster of a ruby, is situated in the western direction.
And there is an additional [light] of saffron color situated in the northwest;
it is multiform, appearing according to its true nature, and situated in the south and north. || 4-126 ||
These [deities], radiant with flames, also grant the boons of the vara and abhaya gestures. || 4-126ef ||
(Also in the *Tripurāsārasamuccaya*):
Possessing the beautiful color of well-refined gold, she stands in the eastern direction of the Trident-bearer.
She who is the color of beryl and named Kanaka sits in the direction of Vāsava.
That which is red, with the color of the rising sun and so forth,
is the tongue of Agni, well-situated and green;
that which is black has the luster of a full-blown blue lotus.
She clung to the quarters of the sky surrounded by demons.
Suprabhā, blazing with a luster like that of a ruby, is situated in the direction of Varuṇa;
she who resembles a flower of great silver is Atilohitā in the direction of Gandhavaha. (4.129)

That tongue, which possesses many forms and is known by its true name, is situated above and to the right; a specific rule regarding the fire-oblation (*homa*) has been stated [in the *Gaṇeśavimarṣiṇī*].
Fuel sticks for Hiraṇyā; a sacrificial pap (caru) with clarified butter for Gaganā;
white mustard seeds for Bahurūpā; and likewise barley grains for Raktā.
One should offer parched grain (lāja) during the Kṛṣṇā [night], but roasted barley flour (saktu) during the Suprabhā;
sesame seeds (tila) during the Atiraktā, and always [offer them] during the Kanakā. (4.131)
The practitioner should offer all substances in all rites.
In another tantra, the fruit resulting from these [offerings] is proclaimed in sequence according to the distinction of the desired aim:
4-132. The fruit, however, is declared for these [substances] in succession according to the difference in the object of desire.
The first [Gaganā] is considered for subjugation and attraction; Gaganā is also held for paralyzing. Raktā is for causing enmity and delusion, while Kṛṣṇā is for rites of killing. (4.133)
Suprabhā is considered suitable for rites of pacification (śāntika) and nourishment (puṣṭi), while Suraktā is intended for rites of eradication (uccāṭana);
each, appearing in many forms, bestows the fruits of all desires. (4.134)
As stated in the *Merutantra*:
"If the tongue is seen directed toward its own respective direction, just as the ritual action is performed, then there is success in the form of flames; conversely, the opposite occurs. (4-135)
Regarding the Vaiṣṇava [fire], however, other tongues are mentioned in that very same place:
"Prabhā, Dīpti, Prakāśā, Marīci, Tāpanī, Karālā, and Lelihā—these are the tongues for rites pertaining to Viṣṇu. (4.136)
Situated in the northeast, east, southeast, southwest, west, northwest, and the center, all the tongues stand with their hands shining with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness. (4.137)
In the *Śāradā*, it is said: "One should worship the deities of the limbs according to the stated method upon the filaments;
on the petals, one should worship the Form (Mūrti), who holds a spear and a svastika. (4.138)
Then one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) in the directions according to the stated characteristics.
Here, the worship of the world-protectors should be performed upon the *darbha* grass placed on the girdle (*mekhalā*).
This is stated in another tantra:
In the corners, in the six [petals], in the center, and also upon the filaments with the tongues. || 4-139 ||

Then, outside with the limb-mantras (aṅgamantras), one should worship the lords of the directions starting from the east upon the darbha grass resting on the girdle, in sequence with the eight forms (mūrtis).
(p. 277) (In the *Tattvasārasaṃhitā*):
Having arranged the vessels according to the rule many times, the knower of mantras, having inspected them with a purifier and having placed them face upwards—4-141.
One should wash the vessel again, fill it with pure water,
offer unbroken grains (akṣata) and a purifier (pavitra), fill it once more, and set it down.
In the northern direction, that vessel is called *praṇītā* by the wise;
then, having taken a little of the *praṇītā* water from it, with those waters—
One should sprinkle the collection of materials for the sacrificial implements with the root mantra;
then, having invoked Brahmā, one should worship him with the root mantra.
Elsewhere as well:

having spread darbha grass with its tips pointing toward the northeast on the left, and having placed vessels in pairs above that— first with their openings facing downward and then likewise with their openings facing upward—

Then, having filled [the vessel] with water purified by the *hṛdaya-mantra*, and having sprinkled all the sacrificial materials (*havyajāta*) located on the left with these and other *kūrca*-blades while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*: 4-145.
Thus it is stated in another tantra:
"The *praṇītā* vessel, filled with water, should be placed to the north of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
All the groups of vessels are to be placed in sequence starting from the *praṇītā* vessel. (4.146)
The vessel for clarified butter, the vessel for the sacrificial porridge accompanied by cow's milk, the large and small ladles, cow's ghee, rice grains, and the roots of *kuśa* grass. (4.147)
Three fuel-sticks of *pālāśa* wood, and thereafter a full vessel;
according to the procedure prescribed in one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra*, [this should be done] to the east of the direction of Vāyu. (Merutantra 4.148)

The *sruva* and *sruk* ladles, the *praṇītā* vessel, the pair of *prokṣaṇī* vessels, the clarified butter pot (*ājyasthālī*), the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), the fuel (*idhma*), and handfuls of *kuśa* grass. (4.149)

Then, one should arrange all the vessels with their openings facing downward, as well as the materials for the fire oblation (homa), the sacrificial offering (bali), and the perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), and so forth. (4.150)
Having sprinkled them with the purifier (pavitra) and placed them face upwards,
one should fill the pair of *prokṣaṇī* vessels with auspicious water.
In another tantra:
Having spread darbha grass with the tips pointing east upon one’s own left side, [one should place] vessels made of gold and other materials according to one’s means for the ritual. (4-152)
One should arrange the vessels in pairs with their openings facing downward; then, having turned the vessels face upward, one should fill them with water and other substances. (4.153)
(Yāmala):
To the north of the fire, on his own left, the best of preceptors, having spread darbha grass with its tips pointing eastward, should then set out the vessels. (4.154)
The word "one's own" should be understood as meaning "facing east.
(Also in the *Tripurāsārasamuccaya*:
"Then, having spread darbha grass on the left side..."

The wise one should then place all the vessels, whose openings face downward, above those [deities] who have reached the tips of the directions desired by the beloved of Pulomā’s daughter, in the form of pairs.

Then, when these vessels have been turned face up, having filled one vessel with water and having clearly visualized the sacred bathing places (tīrthas) therein, he should sprinkle [the other vessels] with that water using *kūrca* grass.
The collection of substances situated on the left side with the heart. || 4-156 ||
Regarding the vessels as well, there is a specific rule for that very same [rite]:
"The vessels may be made of gold, or silver, or likewise of copper, or even of clay; however, in rites such as *śāntika* and others, [the materials] are supreme here in these ritual acts."
(279) These vessels made from śelu, akṣa, drum, and śigru trees are highly recommended for acts such as inciting enmity, expulsion, destruction, and killing. (4.157)
Śaulva is copper. Śelu is the bahuvāraka plant. Akṣadruma is the vibhītaka tree. Śigru is the śobhāñjana plant. (In the Merutantra:
One should choose a peaceful Brāhmaṇa who has been initiated into the deity and the mantra.
One should cause him to sit upon a seat of kuśa grass on the southern side of the sacrificial pit.
"I, of such-and-such a lineage, choose you, of such-and-such a lineage, as the Brahmā priest in this homa which constitutes a limb of the initiation. (4-159)
Having clothed him with garments, ornaments, and so forth, one should worship him;
or one may employ a *kuśa* boy if no Brāhmaṇa can be found. (4.160)

(From the Śāradātilaka: Thereafter, having taken up the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles with both hands and turned them face downwards, the preceptor should heat them three times in the fire after taking up *darbha* grass. (4.161)
One should purify their tips, bases, and middles with those [mantras] in due order;
having grasped them with the left hand, one should sprinkle them with the right.
Having heated those two again, the minister should cast the darbha grasses into the fire and place them upon a bed of kuśa grass on his own right side.

In another tantra: Having taken up the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, facing upwards and downwards respectively, one should heat them three times in the fire and touch them with the roots, middles, and tips of *darbha* grass. (4.164)
Having heated them again thirty times, one should cast the two [ends] face-downward into the fire and place the Śaktis—
beginning with Icchā— in order upon the root, middle, and tip.
One should install Śakti in the *sruc* and Śambhu in the *sruva* by means of the heart-mantra (*hṛdayāṇu*). "Icchādikā" means desire, knowledge, and action (*icchā-jñāna-kriyā*).
(In the Śaiva Āgama, however...)
Having taken up the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles respectively with their faces turned upward and downward, || 4-166 ||
Having heated them in fire, one should touch them three times with the roots, middles, and tips of *darbha* grass.
Their necks should be wrapped with three threads, and they should be worshipped with flowers and other offerings.
Having placed those two upon the *kuśa* grass, it is said [in the *Merutantra*]: "It should be on the right.
(Merutantra 4.168): "One should purify their tips with the tips of the *kuśa*, and their middle parts with the middle parts."
Having thus cleansed the roots with the roots in three ways, one should heat them;
holding those two with the left hand, one should sprinkle them with the water from the *prokṣaṇī* vessel.
Again, he should heat those two with the tip of his right hand;
then, having cast kuśa grass into the fire, he should place them upon a bed of kuśa grass on his own right side.
Having placed the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles behind [the fire], one should thereafter perform the consecration of the clarified butter (*ājya*). (In the *Śāradā-tantra*, verse 4.171:
"Then, having taken the vessel for the clarified butter, one should sprinkle it with water empowered by the weapon-mantra (*astra*)."
Having poured clarified butter into it and consecrated it with the rites of inspection and so forth—as stated in another tantra:
"Having taken cow's clarified butter, it should be consecrated with the root mantra alone. (4.172)
Having meditated upon one's own form as consisting of Brahman, one should heat it over the fire;
(as stated in the Śaiva Āgama:
having taken cow's clarified butter, it should be consecrated with the root mantra alone. (4.173)
"And having meditated upon one's own form as consisting of Brahman"—
this was stated with reference to the "bovine" [product] as the best option.
As it has been said in the *Piṅgalāmata*:
Cow's ghee is declared to be the best, while that produced from a buffalo is middling.
"The birth of a goat is the lowest; therefore, that which comes from a cow is praised"—thus [it is said] in the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā (4.175):
"Having placed the mantra upon the ghee, one should display the mudrā known as 'the Cow'."
(From the Śāradā-tantra:
Having removed the embers for the sake of Vāyu with the Heart-mantra, one should offer [the oblation] upon them;
this is designated as *tāpana* by the teachers who know the Tantras. (4-176)
Having kindled a pair of *darbha* blades and cast them into the clarified butter (*ājya*), he should throw them into the fire;
this is the "purification" (*pavitrīkaraṇa*) performed by the preceptor with the Heart Mantra.

Having consecrated the clarified butter with a pair of blazing *darbha* blades while reciting the armor-mantra (*varma*), one should cast the *darbha* into the fire; this is declared to be the "illumination" (*abhidyotana*).

Having displayed blades of *darbha* grass blazing in clarified butter while reciting the *astra-mantra*, the Guru should cast them into the fire; this is considered the rite of illumination (*udyotana*).
Having taken clarified butter and applied it to the embers,
one should touch water with the thumb and the ring finger while holding two *darbha* blades, each measuring a span (*prādeśa*).

Having held [the ladle], one should purify the ghee with the Astra-mantra; this is the purification of the ghee. Likewise, with the Hṛdaya-mantra and two Kuśa blades, [one should purify it] facing oneself.
One should perform the immersion in ghee; thus, six purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) are proclaimed.
[The phrase] "with the thumb and the ring finger" implies that this refers to both hands. [The verb] "one should purify" implies [the action is performed] facing the fire.
This has been stated in the *Śaivāgama*:
With two blades of darbha grass, each a span in length, held between the tips of the thumb and the ring finger.
Having held [two blades of grass] facing the fire, one should perform the *utplava* with the weapon-mantra (*astra*).
(In the *Śāradā-tantra*:
"A pair of *darbha* blades, one span in length and tied together at the knot, should be placed within the clarified butter. (4.183)
Having cast [the breath] and divided it into two parts, one should visualize the two wings as white and its opposite;
again, one should place the iḍā channel in the left part and the piṅgalā in the right.
Having meditated on the *suṣumnā* in the center, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) according to the prescribed rule.
Regarding that, the manner of holding the *sruva* ladle is stated in the *Nāradīya*:
"The sacrificer indeed perishes from seeing the base of the *sruva*. (4-185)
Therefore, one should protect the base of the *sruva* ladle at the time of the fire offering (*homa*).
It is declared that [damage] at the tip causes disease, while that in the middle is remembered as causing grief. (4.186)
It is declared that [a vessel] at its base causes harm; how then does one hold the *sruva*?
Having omitted four finger-breadths at the base, and likewise sixteen at the tip. (4.187)
One should hold [the thread] at four finger-breadths (vedāṅgula) from its center using the conch-gesture (śaṅkhamudrā).
As stated in another tantra:
"Having left five finger-breadths (pañcāṅgula) on the outside, one should hold it using the conch-gesture. (4-188)
(In the Homasāra: Having set aside six finger-breadths from the base, or indeed four finger-breadths, || 4-189 ||
Having covered the root [of the thumb] at the forearm, one should wear it with the *śaṅkha-mudrā*.
In another tantra:
"Taking clarified butter with the *śruva* ladle, one should offer it as oblation with the hand turned downward. (4-190)
(In the Bhairavatantra:
"An oblation poured into the mouth of Vaiśvānara with a hand that has not been purified by the *haviḥ-uktāna* rite leads to the destruction of the priest's sight; the sacrificer perishes. (4.191)
(In the supplement,
however,) it is stated: "With the hand turned palm-upward, with the fingers joined and the tip of the thumb pressed [against them], one should offer the oblation while remaining silent" (4.192).
Bhairava says: Three mudrās are prescribed for the fire-oblation (homa): the Mṛgī, the Haṃsī, and the Śūkarī.
The Mṛgī is formed by the little finger and the index finger; the Haṃsī is that in which the little fingers are released. (4.193)
The *śūkarī* is proclaimed as the mudrā that causes the contraction of the hands;
the *mṛgī* is for one desiring a son, and the *haṃsī* bestows all fruits. (4.194)
(Śāradāyām, p. 283) In all rites of sorcery (*abhicāra*), the *śūkarī* [mudrā] is taught by the wise.
With the *sruva* ladle, the Guru takes clarified butter from the southern portion while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*. (4-195)
One should offer oblation to Agni with "Svāhā" into the right eye of the Fire;
likewise, taking [the oblation] from the left, one offers it into the left eye of the Fire.
Then one should offer oblations with the mantra "To Soma, svāhā" using the Heart-mantra;
having taken clarified butter from the left portion with the Heart-mantra, [one offers it] into the left eye of the fire. (From the Merutantra, 4.197)
"The renunciation [of the offering] is always considered by us to be 'To Soma, svāhā! (as stated in the Śāradā-tantra):
