having taken ghee from the center [of the fire], [one offers it] into the eye on the forehead of the Fire. (4-198)
One should offer oblations with the heart-syllable, saying "Svāhā to Agni and Soma";
having taken ghee from the southern portion with the sacrificial ladle (sruva) while reciting the heart-mantra.
One should offer oblations to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt with the mantra "Svāhā" into his mouth;
then one should pour the remainder of the clarified butter (saṃpāta) into the [other] portions according to the sequence of the offerings.
Thus the Guru should perform the illumination of the eyes, the lead, and the faces;

he should cause [the remnants] to fall upon the respective parts. This means that from whichever part the clarified butter was taken for the oblation, one should pour the remains of the oblation back into that same part.
As it is said in the Śaivāgama:
One should sequentially cast the remaining portion of the oblation, the clarified butter, into the fire with the utterance "svāhā"—thus [it is said]. (4.201)
(From the Śāradā-tantra: "One should again offer oblations with clarified butter using the *vyāhṛtis* together with the stars (*tārās*).

Herein: *oṃ svāhā*, *bhūḥ svāhā*, *bhuvaḥ svāhā*, *svaḥ svāhā*, and *oṃ bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ svāhā*. One should sacrifice five oblations with these five mantras, both individually and collectively," according to the statement in the Nārāyaṇīya-tantra.
(From the *Uḍḍīśa*): One should perform the *vyāhṛti-homa* for the Goddess and offer four oblations with the mantra beginning with *Tārā*. (4.202)
"Bhūḥ" is for Agni and the great Earth, beloved of Fire;
"Bhuvaḥ" is from the word for Vāyu and for the intermediate space (antarikṣa) by virtue of its sound. || 4-203 ||

The forms *agnyādityacandramasaḥ* (Agni, Āditya, and Candramas), as well as *nakṣatre* (in the locative singular) ending in *-ṅi*, and those ending in *-bhyas* from the words for the directions (*digbhyaḥ*), and [the form] *mahate* (in the dative singular)—these are the beloveds of Vahni (Fire). 4-204.
(From the Śāradā-tantra: The most excellent of preceptors should offer oblations three times with the fire-mantra;
he should then perform the rites for the fire, beginning with the impregnation (garbhādhāna), in their proper sequence. (4.205)
With eight oblations of clarified butter, each accompanied by the syllable Om individually,
[one performs] the impregnation (garbhādhāna), the rite for a male child (puṃsavana), and then the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana).
Immediately thereafter, the birth-rite (jātakarma) should take place, as well as the naming ceremony (nāmakaraṇa);
after that, the rite of going out of the house (upaniṣkramaṇa), and finally, the first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana) is prescribed.
The tonsure ceremony (cūḍā), the initiation (upanayana), then the Mahānāmnī, the Mahāvrata, followed by the Upaniṣad, and finally the Godāna, the marriage, and death. (4.208)
One should perform the *garbhādhāna*, *puṃsavana*, and *sīmāntonnayana* rites for my [embryo].
Once born from the womb of Vāgīśvarī, one should meditate upon the Fire-god as before. (4.209)
Then, having performed the *jātakarman* rite, one should carry out the cutting of the umbilical cord;
after purifying the birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), one should then perform the naming ceremony according to the prescribed rule.
For the satisfaction of that deity for whom there is fire, preceded by his name,
[are performed] the tonsure, the initiation, and likewise the Mahānāmni-vrata of Agni.
The Mahāvrata, the Upaniṣad-vrata, the Godāna, the Samāvartana, and the Udvāha [are the rites] belonging to the Śākta [tradition], preceded by the Vāgbhava [syllable]. (4.212)
Likewise:
"Having first uttered the *praṇava*, one should utter the name of the rite; 'I accomplish [this], svāhā!'—this is the rule for all rites. (4-213)
(From the Śāradā-tantra):
Those rites ending with marriage are prescribed for auspicious acts; those ending with death are designated for cruel deeds by those who know the Agamas of Fire. 4-214.
(Uḍḍīśa):
Having completed the birth rites and for the sake of dispelling fatigue, [one should offer] a fuel-stick the size of a span, soaked at both its root and tip with clarified butter. (4.215)
Reciting "Oṃ, svāhā to Kāmeśvara and Kāmeśī," the mantra-practitioner should cast [the oblation] three times;
then, he should unite the parents of the fire within his own body.
One should perform the naming of the fire using the name of one's chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*).
In the case of *Śrīvidyā*, this is done with "Kāmeśvara and Kāmeśvarī"; elsewhere, it should be understood as "Vāgeśvara and Vāgīśvarī.
(In the *Pūrṇayāga*)
Having offered eight oblations of clarified butter, one should perform the naming ceremony.
One should perform the rite with the root mantra, saying, "You are such-and-such a guide.
Having thus meditated upon the newborn as having this form, one should perform the birth-rite (*jātakarman*). (From the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā*, 4.218)
Having removed the stalk and then purified the *sūtaka*,
one should assign it the name "Śivāgni" (the Fire of Śiva) and perform oblations preceded by the *huti* offering.
Having performed the dismissal of his parents, and having carried out for him the sacraments beginning with the tonsure and the initiation, and ending with the marriage ceremony; (4.220)
As for the method of removing the stalk, [it is stated] in the Śaiva Āgama:
"Then, for the removal of the stalk here, one should offer five fuel-sticks soaked in clarified butter at the tip and at the base with the Astra-mantra of the fire. (4-221)
(Vāyavīyasaṃhitā) (p. 286):

Those [stems] should be from the Palāśa tree or other sacrificial trees, twelve finger-breadths in length, straight, not withered of their own accord, possessing their bark, free from blemishes, and uniform. 4-222.

"Alternatively, they are prescribed as being ten finger-breadths long, or equal in measure to the little finger; or, in the absence [of these], even all [other materials] may be offered when they are one span (prādeśa) in length. — 4.223.

In the *Śāradā-tilaka*, after describing the dismissal of the parents [of the deceased] at the conclusion of all the purificatory rites for the fire, the oblation of five fuel-sticks (*samidh*) is prescribed during the removal of the umbilical cord.
Then it says: "Having fully worshipped his two parents, one should unite them with one's own self;
one should offer five fuel-sticks, drenched with clarified butter at their roots and tips. (4.224)
(In the *Kriyāsāra*):

Having performed the dismissal of the two parents, one should perform all the sacraments beginning with the tonsure (*cūḍā*) and the initiation (*upanayana*); at the conclusion, one should dismiss the two deities. (4.225)
And for the purpose of dispelling fatigue, having offered three excellent fuel-sticks,
one should offer one oblation each with the name of the seed-syllable and the tongue [of fire] (merutantre). (4-226)
Then one should offer oblations to the limbs [of the deity], as well as the eight forms (mūrtis) of Agni,
the world-protectors beginning with Indra, and after that, their weapons.
The wise one, with the mantra preceded by Oṃ and ending with Svāhā, should offer oblations at the conclusion of the word Svāhā while meditating upon the deity of the mantra. (4.228)
In a mantra that already ends with *svāhā*, another *svāhā* should not be added. As it is said in the *Mantraprakāśa*:
"One should not add *namaḥ* at the end of what already ends in *namaḥ*, nor *dviṭha* at the end of what already ends in *dviṭha*.
O Śivā, this rule applies everywhere, whether in worship or in the offering of oblations. (4.229)

*dviṭhaḥ svāhā*. Here, by the letter *ṭha*, the *bindu* is indicated due to its similarity in form (*lipisāmyāt*). Two *bindus* constitute the *visarga*, and that is of the nature of Śakti; therefore, Rāghavabhaṭṭa maintains that by the word *dviṭha*, the fire-śakti (*agniśakti*) is called *svāhā*. However, according to the traditionalists (*sāṃpradāyikāḥ*), *dviṭha* is actually a technical term (*paribhāṣikī saṃjñā*). (In the *Merutantra*:
having taken clarified butter four times with the *sruva* ladle, one should pour it into the *sruc* offering-spoon.)
Having covered it with that very [substance], the Guru himself, standing, should offer it into the fire. (4.230)
Then, with the mantra of Agni ending in *vauṣaṭ*,
the practitioner should address the deity situated in the middle tongue, whose body is a mass of flames.
With the mantra of Gāṇapati, preceded by the ten divisions beginning with Tārā and joined with each preceding one, he should first offer ten oblations.
And one should offer oblations four times with that entire [mantra] itself; furthermore, according to the *Śāradā-tantra*,
one should offer ten oblations with the mantra of Vighneśvara.
This fire-sacrifice is remembered as common to all tantras.
In that very [text] it is said: "Then, once the fire has been consecrated, one should cook the sacrificial porridge (caru) with cow's milk. (4-234)
In a new vessel made of copper or another material, cleansed with the Astra-mantra,
one should place rice grains produced from the Śāli variety, consecrated by the root mantra.
Having thrown fifteen handfuls [of water] while reciting the Astra-mantra,
and having washed the mouth of the vessel, he should cover it with the Kavaca-mantra.
Facing the east, the lord of adepts should cook the sacrificial porridge (caru) with the root mantra;
once it is prepared, he should offer the "heated sprinkling" (taptābhighāraṇa) with clarified butter using the sruva ladle.

Thereafter, the Guru should lower that vessel with the *kavaca* mantra upon the maṇḍala strewn with kuśa grass over which the *astra* mantra has been recited, according to the prescribed rite. (4.238)
Having divided that into three parts, the preceptor should set aside one portion for the deity, offer another into the fire, and consume the remaining portion himself.
"One should eat together with the disciple"— the manner of the fire-oblation (*homa*) and the meal will be explained further on. (From the *Merutantra*)
Then, having properly worshipped the seat of the deity in the fire, the Guru [proceeds].
There, one should worship the chosen deity assuming the form of fire, twenty-five times with clarified butter while reciting the mantra of the one to be accomplished (sādhya). (4.241)
The fire-mouthed mantra-practitioner performs this unification of the faces;
contemplating the oneness of the self, the fire, and the deity, the knower of the self [proceeds]. (4.242)
Then, one should offer eleven oblations of clarified butter with the root mantra;
this is indeed called "the joining of the channels" by the best of teachers.

One should offer one oblation for each of the ritual procedures beginning with the limbs (*aṅga*). At the end, ten oblations should be offered with the root mantra (*mūla*). As it is stated in the *Tripurāsārasamuccaya*:
"One should offer one oblation for each member of the retinue and ten oblations for the Goddess. (4-244)
In all the fire-pits located in the directions starting from the east, the Guru should duly carry forth the fire into the consecrated pits according to the prescribed path. (Merutantra 4.245)

Then, having honored all the officiating priests with sandalwood paste and other offerings, they should perform oblations with the root mantra for the aforementioned deity, together with all the surrounding retinues.

With twenty-five oblations of milk-rice mixed with clarified butter—here, in all the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*), the placement of the fire is performed by the Preceptor (*ācārya*); however, it should be understood that the consecration of the other pits is performed by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). Regarding the phrase "they should offer": the Preceptor and the officiating priests are to be understood as the agents. "With milk-rice" means with the *caru* consisting of the second portion of the previously mentioned *caru*. Twenty-five oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) are to be offered prior to the *caru* oblation. And so it is stated in the *Śāradā*:
Then, other sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) should also be consecrated according to the prescribed rule.
The preceptor, composed in mind, should leave the fire in the eastern and other directions;
the officiating priests [should worship] the goddess, who is accompanied by her limbs and enclosures, with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.

There, they should offer oblations twenty-five times with clarified butter and likewise with sacrificial porridge mixed with clarified butter, using the root mantra of their chosen deity as previously described.
(Somaśambhu) [states]: "One-third of the sacrificial pap (*caru*), measured as three mouthfuls, or eight mouthfuls in measure, [should be offered] while avoiding looking at it or touching it. (4-250)
When eating from a leaf-cup of *palāśa*, or when eating from a leaf of the *pippala* tree,
the practitioner of mantras should cause [the deity] to eat with the *hṛdaya-mantra* and cause [him] to rinse with pure water for sipping.
(From the Śāradā-tantra:

Having brought the disciple who has sipped water and performed the ritual purification of the limbs (sakalīkṛta), the preceptor [should provide] a staff of the measure of a palm tree, produced from a milk-tree or similar source, over which the heart-mantra has been recited. (4.251)
Then, one should give a tooth-stick to the disciple who is disciplined in nature;
having diligently cleansed the teeth and washed it, one should discard it. (4.253)
(Also in the Merutantra:

One should give to the disciple a tooth-stick of the prescribed length, measuring one *vitasti*, over which the heart-mantra has been recited; having cleansed his teeth with it, he should discard the washed stick. (4.254)

The examination of the tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*) must be performed even before entering the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*); however, the traditional teaching (*saṃpradāya*) holds that in this context it refers merely to the cleansing of the teeth. Some say that the examination should be performed at this very point; others, however, maintain that its examination must indeed be performed on both occasions. As stated in the *Śāradā*:
"Having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) according to rule, and being protected by the binding of the topknot (*śikhābandha*),"
Having performed [the rites] together with him upon the altar on a bed of darbha grass, the Guru—
He should sleep on that [mat] for that night; this is declared to be the consecration (*adhivāsa*).
(In the *Nārāyaṇīya*):
Furthermore, that disciple, having sipped water (*ācānta*) and being protected by the tying of the topknot (*śikhābandha*), [should be seated]. (4.256)

Having prepared the altar, the Guru should sleep upon it together with him on a bed of *darbha* grass; according to the *Piṅgalāmata*, he should have him sleep facing east, resting his head against the *svapnamānava* [the dream-man]. (4-257)
(Vāyavīyasaṃhitā) p. 290):
On the right side of the deity, he should cause that disciple to undergo the preparatory rite (*adhivāsana*), being pure upon a bed spread with fresh grass and covered with a new cloth. (4.258)
(From the *Merutantra*):

Having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) according to the rules, the practitioner of mantra should then secure him with the binding of the topknot (*śikhābandha*) so that he is well-protected.
On the sacrificial altar, he should sleep upon a bed of kusha grass during the night together with his disciple; thus has the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) been described by the Anu.
In the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*:
Having performed the worship of the Guru’s feet, fasting and with senses subdued, one should go to a bed of *darbha* grass at night; having seen a dream, one should report it. (4.260)

In the *Yoginītantra* and the *Merutantra*, it is said: "For one who is awake, that which rises far away— the divine— having encompassed these mantras, he, being restrained, [recites] them three times."
Eating little, eating alone, and sleeping on his right side, he should examine his dream according to the instructions.
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, wielder of the trident, whose vehicle is the bull,
O Eternal One, declare to me what is desirable and undesirable while I am asleep.
Thus, having slept upon a bed strewn with kusha grass with a disciplined mind, he beholds at the end of the night a dream, whether auspicious or inauspicious. (4.263)

In the *Piṅgalāmata* and the *Merutantra*: "The *tāra* (oṃ), followed by *hili* twice, then *śūlapāṇaye*, and ending with *dviṭha* (svāhā)—this is proclaimed by Śambhu as the mantra of Svapnamānava. (4.264)
Homage to the victorious three-eyed one, to the tawny-hued great soul;
homage to the left-handed one, to the one of universal form, to the lord of dreams. 4-265.
"O Maheśvara, by your grace, I shall accomplish the success of all undertakings without exception; this account of mine in the dream is entirely true. (4-266)
(From the *Mantratantraprakāśa*):
Oṃ, salutation to Viṣṇu, the all-pervading Lord, who is the heart of all the worlds, the universe itself, whose form is the universe, and the sovereign of dreams. 4-267.
This mantra for the Dream-Man (svapnamānava) was taught by Nārada and others (in the Nāradīya):
"You are the very nature of the Supreme Brahman; you move within [all beings], the sustainer of the universe. (4.268)
"O Lord, reveal to me in a dream my auspicious or inauspicious destiny";
having uttered this, one should pay homage while kneeling upon the ground. (4.269)
Being serene and restrained in speech, one should lie down upon it and contemplate what is desired.
Now, regarding auspicious dreams: (In the Yoginītantra), his vision is of three kinds: that which is according to reality and that which is not according to reality. (4.270)

The vision of those who are self-restrained and established in their own state is born of non-defilement; however, that which is contrary to reality arises from the disorder of those who are not established in their own state. (4.271)
That which is not produced by external causes and is mental is said to have a result that corresponds to reality. || 4-271ef ||
According to the established doctrine of the Āgamas:
in the first [case], digestion occurs after one year; in the second, after half a year;
and in the third, after a quarter of a year.
That which ripens in a watch [of the night], in the fourth quarter of the night, or that which is seen to ripen immediately upon emission; || 4-272 ||
Likewise: "In a dream, one indeed beholds the deity desired by oneself, facing in all directions; the Guru, with a countenance gracious with favor, like the stainless orb of the moon. (4.273)
One should recognize the appearance of the Gaṅgā, the Bhāgīrathī, the Sun, a *liṅgin*, or the Īśvara-liṅga there as a sign of success in the manifestation of a dream. (4.274)
(In the Nāradapañcarātra:
Gaining land, wounding [an enemy], crossing the ocean, worshiping the fire, performing oblations when the fire is blazing, and likewise victory in battle. (4.275)
[One should avoid] the mounting of swans, cranes, and peacocks;
and [the sight of] a maiden, an umbrella, a chariot, a lamp, a palace, a lotus, and a river. (From the *Mahākapila-pañcarātra*, 4.276)
An elephant, a bull, a garland, sea foam, a tree, a mountain, a horse, meat from the middle part [of an animal], and liquor and spirits. (4.277)
Having seen all such [omens], one shall attain success;
when, in dreams during rites performed for specific desires, one sees a woman. (4.278)
One should recognize prosperity in that dream-vision, as well as crossing rivers and oceans, and likewise traveling through the sky. (4.279)
The rising of the sun, the blazing of the sacrificial fire,
and the sight of the moon's orb along with the planets, lunar mansions, and stars.
Climbing upon the roof of a palace or even the top of a temple;
climbing upon elephants, horses, bulls, or lions; and climbing upon trees or mountain peaks. (4.281)
Traveling by celestial chariot, the sight of one who has mastered the mantra, and other such signs—having beheld these, a man shall attain perfection. (4.282)
In a dream, however, one may see the drinking of liquor, the eating of raw meat, being smeared with worms and excrement, and being sprinkled with blood. (4.283)
Food consisting of curd-rice, white garments and ointments, a lion-throne, a chariot, a vehicle, a banner, and royal consecration. (4.284)
One feels joy upon seeing jewels, ornaments, and so forth in a dream;
likewise, the teacher, the deity, a brahmin, a maiden, cows, elephants, horses, and the lion [are auspicious signs]. (Nāradapañcarātra 4.285)
Beholding a mirror, a conch, a kettledrum, stringed instruments, and yellow pigment; chewing betel, as well as saluting a woman who is pregnant; 4-286.
Prepared food, raw meat, liquor, women, the remnants of wine, an umbrella, a vehicle, white clothing, as well as other such things, and white sandalwood. (4.287)
A necklace is a string of pearls; the full moon is risen;
the sun has fierce rays; and a river is a great ocean. (4.288)
A blossoming tree, rice, yellow pigment, saffron, honey, parched grain, white mustard seeds, seed-grain, a new vessel, and milk-rice. (4.289)
Furthermore, even the preceptor is seated nearby and the Gāyatrī has come under his control;
all such dreams are declared auspicious, bestowing the fruits of spiritual perfection and liberation. (4.290)
(In the Nāradīya):
"The seizing of others' wives, as well as approaching those who should not be approached, being bitten by a white serpent, and being bound with chains and the like. (4.291)
Weeping, beating, running about, and striking one's limbs [are punishments for stealing] earth, iron, tin, bronze, or even lead from a contemptible person. (4.292)
The attainment of a mineral element, as well as flowers, both fruit and jewels, a fan, and fanning the fire by oneself or by another. (4.293)
The wise have declared other auspicious signs such as these in the *Merutantra*:
a full water-pot, a mirror, a pair of fish, clarified butter, and yellow pigment (*rocanā*). (4.294)
A corpse devoid of weeping, weapons, banners, Bhāradvāja, a king, the sound of the Vedas, and a singer. (4.295)
If a practitioner sees in a dream a whip, auspicious songs, a goad, or whatever is dear to his heart, he shall attain accomplishment. (4.296)
For one afflicted by disease, there shall be no suffering, and he shall attain ordinary happiness;
this occurs when, amidst rites for desired objects, he sees a woman in his dreams. (4.297)
She desires the crossing of rivers and oceans, wandering in the sky,
the rising of the sun, and even the eclipses of the moon and the sun.
Climbing onto a palace, a tower, an elephant, a horse, a bull, a mountain, or fire;
eating boiled rice with curd, and eating raw meat. (4.299)
Smearing oneself with worms and excrement, being sprinkled with blood, chewing betel, drinking liquor, and saluting those who are to be executed. (4.300)

The appearance of the sun with its rays intensely bright and the person being healthy is a sign of the accomplishment of one's purpose; likewise, a woman wearing white garments, white garlands, and white unguents [is a favorable omen].
For whomsoever one embraces in a dream, for that person prosperity is manifest in every direction—
in their seat, bed, drink, body, vehicle, and home.
While it is blazing, one should wake up; his prosperity will be manifest in every direction.
Furthermore, the bite of a white serpent occurs on his right hand. (4.303)
Within ten days there will be gain; one who is ill shall be freed from disease;
or he may be bound by fetters or arm-cords, or a son shall be born.
His stability increases by drinking milk, while his wealth diminishes;
a Brahmin drinking wine mixed with blood shall obtain knowledge and supreme wealth.

Seeing curd brings joy, and with *godhūma* grain there is the arrival of wealth. (p. 295) One should know that seeing prepared food signifies the arrival of a beloved person, and likewise, with white mustard seeds, there is gain. 4-306.
From obtaining curd, there will be wealth; from obtaining ghee, there will be victory.
From eating ghee, there is distress regarding wealth; but from consuming curd, there is victory.
Having seen the worship of the *liṅga* and other [emblems], one shall achieve victory in worldly affairs;
moreover, he who eats ghee and milk-rice in the midst of a pond or similar body of water [shall likewise succeed]. (4.308)
One should know him to be a lord of the earth by his steady lotus-like eyes;
for cows, deities, ancestors, Brahmins, and kings possess divine marks. (4.309)
Whatever they say of a man in a dream will come to pass exactly so;
even if one should wrap a village or a city with entrails.
In a village there shall be a kingdom of a mandala, and in a city one shall become a sovereign;
there shall also be the swallowing of the moon, stars, and sun, as well as their search.
The swallowing up of lands, waters, and oceans; the act of slaying enemies;
victory in disputes and gambling; and likewise victory over one's foes. (4.312)
The milking of a mare, a buffalo, a lioness, a cow, an elephant, and so forth; and the favor of a guru, a brahmin, a beloved deity, a siddha, or others—these are auspicious. (4.313)
Bathing, royal consecration, the cutting off of one's own head, death, crossing over the waters of sacred fords, and likewise leaping over poison; (4.314)
The birth of a cow, a horse, or a mare, as well as the acquisition of fire;
likewise, embracing another's wife, obtaining her, and even weeping. (4.315)
Smearing with excrement, seeing the Kunda, Jātī, Vakula, and the Lord of the Earth;
victory in battles, gambling, and conflicts, and imprisonment in fetters. (4.316)
The acquisition of livestock, humans, and wild animals, as well as mastery [of them]; the appearance of a crest, and the wearing of white garments, flowers, and sandalwood paste. (4.317)
When one sees food in a vessel made of jewels, pearls, gold, and so forth, then it should be known that success has arrived for the practitioner. (4.318)
For those distressed by their tasks, there shall be the accomplishment of their business; for others, the arrival of wealth.
Now, regarding inauspicious dreams: a woman wearing black garments, with black perfumes and ointments [is seen]. (4.319)
The night in which she embraces him in a dream is his last;
likewise, with a red woman he suffers disease, and with one as pale as dawn, grief.
A quarrel with a blue [cow], slaughter with a yellow one, and misfortune with a parrot-colored one;
likewise, [the sight of] the skin of a barren woman, chaff, bones, salt, charcoal, and fuel. (4-321)

A libertine, a eunuch, one intoxicated, oil, a woman with matted hair, an enemy, forest herbs, a sick person, grass, a renunciant, a naked person, one anointed with oil, and one afflicted by hunger. (4.322)
A man with disheveled hair falling down, blood from a mutilated limb, a lizard wounded by an arrow, a fight between two cats, cotton, and a pregnant woman in her menses. (4.323)
Molasses, buttermilk, a dyer, mud, a widow, strife in the home, the slipping of garments and such, and likewise a fight with a buffalo; || 4.324 ||
A blind man, a hunchback, one of foul speech, a deaf man, a lame man and a hunchback, a dwarf, an empty jar, and a washerwoman with soiled garments. (4.325)
If these are seen, no purpose will be served; the sick man shall meet his death.
[Likewise, one should avoid seeing] the Aśoka, the Karavīra, or the Palāśa tree in flower. (4.326)
Even in a dream, having seen water, a man may encounter grief;
likewise, there is the entering into another form and traveling toward the southern direction. (4.327)

Bathing by immersing oneself in mud brings about the destruction of one's sons and wife; one should avoid bathing in rivers such as the Ganges or the Indus, and black water is to be avoided, for it is not auspicious. (4-328)
Having discarded cotton, ashes, bones, and the like, one should eat that which brings auspiciousness;
wearing red perfumes, garments, and garlands, or being dressed in black, one should face the south. (4.329)
Mounted upon a donkey, a camel, or a buffalo, he does not live for three months;
or there is a fall into a pit in his house, or his door is shut. (4.330)
And he who does not rise from that state lives for only one year;
there is vomiting, urination, defecation, the production of offspring, and death. (4.331)
He who sees semen in a dream has a lifespan of ten months;
he is struck by deformed black men with raised weapons. (4.332)
Or if he is struck with stones, his death will occur without a doubt;
likewise for one mounted upon a buffalo, a camel, or a donkey, or one who is smeared with oil and has a shaven head.
For one who has set out toward the southern direction, death is certain;
he shall see the collapse of a palace or the falling of the moon and the sun from the sky.
There shall be a loss of authority over mountains and trees, as well as the decline of one's own lineage and subjugation by disease. (4.335)
The sweeping of the house was omitted, as was the smearing with cow dung or even with clay;
having crossed the river, he arrived and put on another garment on the bank. (4.336)
A sick person shall be freed from disease, and loss occurs for one who is healthy. Male-named deer and birds, as well as the female osprey, the sow, and the *ralā* bird [are auspicious]. (4.337)
The Piṅgalā, Chucchukā, Pallī, Vāmāṅga, Kokilā, and Śivā; animals and birds bearing female names; Śrīkaṇṭha, the monkey, and the Ruru deer [are auspicious on the left]. (4.338)
If the chikkara, pippala, bhāsa, crow, hyena,
and cock are seen on the right side of the patient, there will be the destruction of the disease for the sake of the practitioner's success.
From the inquiry of one who is healthy, there is gain; however, due to the reversal of directions, it is not auspicious. (p.

298) Now, regarding the reporting of dreams (according to the *Nibandha*): the most excellent Guru, having purified himself and performed the ritual rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*), with flowers in his hand, [should address] the disciple. (4-340)
Having bowed his head with joy, he should report the dream to him—whether it occurred in a dream, before his very eyes, or even if it were a marvel that brings delight. (4.341)
If one should see [an omen] unexpectedly, it must not be told to anyone except the Guru.
Now, regarding the pacification of bad dreams (*duḥsvapnaśānti*): having seen a bad dream, one shall attain success through the fire-oblation (*homa*). (From the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*, 4.342)
(In the Piṅgalāmata:
When it is auspicious, his [rite] shall be auspicious; when inauspicious, he should offer a hundred oblations. 4-343.
"By means of the Astra [mantra]," thus the wise one [should proceed] in sequence—[as stated in the Merutantra]:
"One should offer a hundred fuel-sticks (*samidh*) that are moist with milk and smeared with clarified butter. (4.344)
A Śūdra, having bathed with *palāśa* leaves while reciting the *Gāyatrī*, and eating sacrificial food (*haviṣya*),
should offer a lamp at the house of a Brahmin, in the temple of Viṣṇu, or in a shrine of Śiva.
Having seen such an inauspicious dream, one should take up the mantra in another way;
for if it is taken [in the first way], there will surely be loss, or one should otherwise reflect thus.
(O Sage, in the *Nāradapañcarātra*): Having seen [the toothbrush twig], one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) prescribed for the toothbrush twig;
or, for the sake of pacification, with clarified butter alone using the *siṃha-mantra*. (4.347)

There is an optionality regarding the *astramantra*, the *gāyatrī*, and the lion-mantra (*siṃhamantra*). "Oṃ vajranakha daṃṣṭrāyudhāya mahāsiṃhāya hūṃ phaṭ namaḥ"—this is the mantra of the lion (as declared in the *Merutantra*).
Now, the ritual duties for the day of initiation (according to the *Merutantra*): having risen at dawn, one should again perform the twilight prayers, bathing, and so forth.
The preceptor, the disciple, and the officiating priests should proceed toward the sacrificial hall.
All of them should offer oblations in their respective fire-pits with sesame seeds mixed with ghee,
repeating the mantra to be accomplished one thousand and eight times.
Or one should offer one hundred and eight oblations with substances prescribed by the ritual injunctions (*śrībhaviṣye*).
The oblation of clarified butter and other materials should be made with a *sruva* ladle held face-downward. (4.350)
One should offer oblations of sesame seeds and other materials with the right hand turned upward according to the divine rite (*daiva*);
[as stated] in the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā*:
"The clarified butter, the fuel sticks, and so forth, are offered with the *sruva* ladle; the remainder is offered with the *sruc* ladle or with the hand. (4.351)
In that regard, one should offer oblations using either the divine (*divya*) or the sage’s (*ārṣa*) sacred path;
likewise, one should offer into a fire that is not blazing, nor even into one that is merely kindled by moderate means. (Mahākapilapañcarātra 4.352)
When the blazing, licking fire is kindled, one should offer oblations for the accomplishment of the rite.
(Also in the *Bahvṛcapariśiṣṭa*:
"He who offers oblations into the sacrificial fire while it is smoky [and] facing downwards... (4.353).
"The sacrificer shall become blind along with his sons," so says the Śruti.
(Also in the Chandogya Pariśiṣṭa:
"The man who offers oblations into a fire that is without flames or into one whose embers are extinguished... (4.354).
He becomes one with weak digestion, afflicted by disease, and impoverished. || 4-354ef ||
(From the *Tripurāsāra*):
From performing the fire-oblation (*homa*) on the ear of the fire-altar, there is affliction by disease; on the eye, blindness; and on the nose, freedom from disease.
The cutting of the substance should be performed on the head; by means of that, the wise man should constantly perform the oblation ending with the mouth. (4.355)
In another tantra: "Where there is wood, there is the ear; where there is smoke, there is the nose;
where there is a small flame, there is the eye; and where there is charcoal, there is the head. (4.356)
Where the blazing flame is, that is the tongue of Jātavedas.
Also elsewhere:
"Fire with smoke should be known as the head, and fire without smoke as the eye. (4-357)
The ear becomes burning and thin, while the nose, as if touched by wood, feels as though fire is blazing there, resembling pure crystal. (4.358)

That face should be understood there as measuring four finger-breadths in size (from the *Navadurgākalpa*); where there is wood, there are the ears, and where there is smoke, there are the nostrils. (4-359)
Where there is a slight glow, that is the eye; where there is ash, that is the head;
and where the fire blazes intensely, that is proclaimed to be the tongue.
In the *Śāradā-tantra*, it is said:
"The preceptor should meditate on Vaiśvānara as standing during oblations of fuel-sticks (*samidh*);
as reclining during oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*); and as seated during all other matters. (4.361)
Likewise: "The beautiful color of Suvarṇaretas is proclaimed to be like gold, vermilion, the young sun, saffron, and honey. (4.362)

The sound of fire that resembles the roar of a kettledrum, a rain-cloud, or a lordly elephant brings auspiciousness; it is like the fragrance of the nāga, campaka, punnāga, pāṭala, and yūthikā flowers. (4.363)

That which resembles the scent of a lotus, a blue lotus, a white water-lily, clarified butter, or guggulu resin is declared by those who know the tantras to be the auspicious fragrance of fire. (4.364)
Cocks whose crests turn clockwise, are free from trembling, and resemble umbrellas bring auspiciousness to the sacrificer, especially for his kingdom. (4.365)
Smoke as white as a jasmine flower or the moon is declared to bring auspiciousness from fire;
however, black smoke when the fire is black in color will destroy the sacrificer.

A white [flame] quickly destroys the kingdom; one resembling the sound of a crow brings misfortune; and a sound like the braying of a donkey, or like the roar of fire, causes total destruction. (4.367)
If the fire has a putrid odor, it will bring grief and suffering to the giver;
if its crest is broken, it causes death and the loss of wealth. (4.368)
Smoke resembling the wing of a parrot, or possessing a luster like that of a pigeon, always causes the loss of horses and cattle. (4.369)
When such defects have occurred, the preceptor should offer twenty-five oblations of clarified butter with the root mantra as an act of atonement.
"In the *Tripurāsārasamuccaya*, it is stated:

'In these cases of defects, the lord of practitioners should perform a propitiatory rite (*śāntika*) by offering one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter with the Weapon-mantra (*astra*), and then perform the worship of the wheel (*cakrapūjā*). (4-371)

(From the Śāradā-tantra: Then, having had the disciple—who has thoroughly cleansed his teeth and so forth, who has bathed, and who is composed—drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), he should lead him to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa). || 4.372 ||
(Also in the *Prayogasāra*):

Having drunk the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) as prescribed and having sipped water according to the rule, one should then cause [the initiate] to enter the sacrificial site by the southern door. (4.373)
(From the Śāradātilaka): Having beheld that consciousness within the heart-lotus with divine vision,
the Guru, having united it with his own self, should perform the purification of the paths (adhva-viśodhana).
In another tantra:
"Having taken that consciousness situated in the heart, which has the form of a shimmering star, one should then cause it to enter into one's own heart by means of the goad mudrā. (4.375)
(From the *Ṣaḍanvayamahāratna*):

Purification (*śodhana*) is the contemplation of the unity of the cause of the principles (*tattva*s); it is the contemplation of the oneness of consciousness within that [unity] of the phonemes (*varṇa*), and so forth, as well as the digits (*kalā*). (4.376)
In the *Śāradā* it is said: "The path of the digits (*kalādhvan*), the path of the principles (*tattvādhvan*), and the path of the worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*)—these are the triad;
and the path of the phonemes (*varṇādhvan*), the path of the words (*padādhvan*), and the path of the mantras (*mantrādhvan*)—these are the supreme triad. (4.377)
In that regard, the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā* states: "Therein, three paths are declared to be verbal (*śābda*) and three to be objective (*ārtha*).
[This is] in another Tantra.
The path of mantra, the path of words, and the path of phonemes—thus they are designated by name. (4.378)

The path of the worlds (*bhuvanādhvā*), the path of the principles (*tattvādhvā*), and likewise the path of the energies (*kalādhvā*)—in this context, the exposition follows the order of dissolution (*saṃhārakrama*); however, it should be understood as the order of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*) according to the *Śāradā-tantra*. According to the *Merutantra*:
These digits, however, should be contemplated by the Guru upon the feet of the disciple.
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, Śānti, and likewise Śāntyatītā—these are the five; now the sequence of purification is described. (4.380)

And the Guru, touching the disciple with a *kūrca* [bundle of grass], should offer oblations into his own fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) using sesame seeds soaked in ghee, reciting "Tārā" and so forth, and "O path of such-and-such! (*amukādhvāna*). (4.381)
One should offer eight oblations with the mantra ending in *dviṭha* (*phaṭ*) to purify [the path];
one should then contemplate the path of the *kalās* as dissolved into the path of the *tattvas*.
Then, in the region of the *liṅga*, one should contemplate these principles (*tattvas*):
those pertaining to Gaṇeśa and those pertaining to Śiva; therein, they are six and three. (4.383)
Namely: Śiva and Śakti, Sadāśiva and Maheśvara, and Vidyā—these are the five pure [principles], and there are seven that are both pure and impure. (4-384)
Māyā, Vidyā, Kalā, Rāga, Kāla, and Niyati; then Puruṣa and the pure principles: Prakṛti, Buddhi, and Ahaṃkṛti. (4.385)

"The mind, the ten sense organs, the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), and the five gross elements—these are pure. This means they are devoid of the three impurities known as *āṇava*, *kārmaṇa*, and *māyīya*. Among these, *āṇava* is the failure to recognize one's own true state as Sadāśiva; *kārmaṇa* is the cognition "I am a possessor of merit and demerit"; and *māyīya* is the notion of selfhood (*ātmatva*) with respect to the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) and so forth. "They are pure and impure. This means they are pure because they are free from the three impurities by virtue of being causes, but they are impure because they possess those [impurities] by virtue of being effects.
Now, the Vaiṣṇava principles (*tattva*) are indeed measured at thirty-two. (4.386)

The individual soul (jīva), vital breath (prāṇa), mind (manas), intellect (buddhi), the subtle elements (tanmātra), the five gross elements (bhūtapañcaka), the ten sense organs (indriya), the heart-lotus (hṛtpadma), as well as the sun, moon, and fire; || 4-387 ||
Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha; as well as the solar [deities], the elements, the subtle essences, the mind, the ego, and the senses.

"Nature (prakṛti) and intellect (buddhi)—thus [the group] numbering twenty-four [is taught] in the Śāradā[tantra]. Then there are the five kalās beginning with Nivṛtti, and then again the Bindu and the Kalā. (4.389)
They know that *nāda* is *śakti*, while *sadāpūrva* is *śiva* prior to *prakṛti*;
subsequently, *ātmavidyā* is *śiva*, and *vidyā* is *śiva* himself once again. (4.390)
All reality and the principles (tattvas) have been declared as belonging to the threefold nature;
indeed, this path of principles (tattvādhvan) has been described by those who know the various Āgamas. (4.391)
In the Merutantra, there are exactly ten principles of power (śaktitattva): Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva;
likewise Śiva, Vidyā, and Ātman; and again Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva. (4.392)
Furthermore, one should perform the oblation for all the principles (tattvas) again according to the previous method;
one should then contemplate the path of the principles as dissolved into the path of the worlds (bhuvana).
The fourteen worlds are to be contemplated by the disciple at his navel;
these are, in order: Pātāla, Rasātala, and Mahātala. (4.394)
Talātala, Sutala, Vitala, Atala, and Bhūr;
then Bhuvar, Svar, Mahar, Janas, and Tapas, in that order. (4.395)
The path of the worlds is real; however, the modification for the oblation and so forth is as before.
One should contemplate the dissolved path of the worlds within the path of the phonemes.
One should contemplate the letters from *a* to *kṣa* within the heart;
one should then contemplate the path of letters as dissolved into the path of words. (4.397)
Then, one should contemplate the *homa-hau* as before here on the forehead;
thereafter, the path of the word (*padādhvan*) consists of the nature of the words and phonemes of the root mantra.
One should perform the offerings, oblations, and so forth on the path of words (padādhvan) as previously described;
one should then contemplate the path of words as dissolved into the path of mantras (mantrādhvan). || 4.399 ||
Having completed the mantra, one should contemplate the path of mantras upon the head of the disciple:
"The fire-oblation is 'OḤ'; as before, I am dissolved here into the supreme Śiva. (4.400)
When [the breath] is situated in the *brahmarandhra*, one should meditate; from this, the purification of the paths (*adhvaśodhana*) occurs.
The supreme Guru should emanate [the path] through the process of emanation, ending in dissolution, up to the limit of Śiva. (4.401)
And the lord of teachers, having beheld that disciple with his divine vision, should unite that consciousness residing within him with that very [reality]. (4.402)
(Also in the Śāradā-tantra):
"One should gradually lead those [elements] to dissolution; having caused them to merge into Śiva, ending with Śiva, one should generate [them] again by way of emanation. (4.403)
Beholding that child with his divine vision, the supreme teacher should once again project that consciousness, which resides within himself, into the disciple. (4.404)
(Kriyāsaṃgraha) For those of Śūdra and mixed castes, purification of the path is not prescribed;
one should effect their liberation from sin by means such as offering water for the feet. 4-405.
Having offered ten oblations with the root mantra,
and then having offered one oblation each to the presiding deities, one should then perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
(From the Śāradā-tantra: Having offered the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the sacrificial ladle (*sruva*) using the root mantra, the preceptor [should proceed].
(From the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā: p. 305)
Then, having filled the sacrificial ladle with the ghee remaining from the oblation, || 4.407 ||
Having placed a flower before it, he should cover her with a downward-facing *sruva* ladle together with *darbha* grass, while standing with palms joined (*añjali*) at the root [of the mantra].
One should offer oblations with the mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, pouring a continuous stream with speed;
having filled the *sruc* ladle with clarified butter, one should place a flower upon it with its face turned downwards. (From the *Merutantra*) 4-409.
Having placed the *sruva* ladle upon the *sruc* vessel, one should drop a flower there with the left and right hands joined together like a conch shell.
Having gathered [the materials] and stood up, and having placed them crosswise at the navel,
he, being well-restrained, [should offer] with the mantra "pūrṇā darvi" and the root mantra.
One should offer three *pūrṇāhuti* oblations that fulfill all desires;
this has been prescribed for a *śrotriya*, but another may also perform the *pūrṇāhuti*.
With the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ* and ending in *svāhā*, one [offers] to the left;
with the *mūrdhānaṃ divam* mantra and the *saṃśravaṇa* mantra, one maintains the flow [of the offering]. (Agnipurāṇa 4.413)
Having stood up, one should offer the full oblation, but never while remaining seated.
(From the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*):
Having offered with the sacrificial oblation, one should offer three purifying oblations (*puṇāhuti*) using the *sruva* ladle. (4.414)
With the mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*— [as stated] in the *Nāradapañcarātra*:
"In the absence of ghee, however, one should complete it with whatever substance serves as the oblation. (4.415)
One should place ghee upon that, and above that, saffron and other substances;
having recited the root mantra ending with "namaḥ," while stepping forward with the left foot first, [as in the *Tūrṇāyāga*]. (4-416)

Then the mantra-practitioner should offer the *pūrṇāhuti* with the thought that it is supreme nectar; according to the *Merutantra*, the right-handed practitioner should perform the *pūrṇāhuti* while placing the right foot forward. (4-417)
In the *Śaktihoma*, the practitioner of the left-hand path (*vāmamārgī*) should place the left foot forward in every respect.
Then, having taken up the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and filled them with clarified butter once again— (from the *Gautamīyatantra*, 4.418).
Having cast the materials for the oblation and established those two again at the navel,
one should then offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the mantra "brahmārpaṇam".

From this time forward, regarding the vital breath and the intellect within the body, and by virtue of my authority over all actions, whatever has been remembered, spoken, or performed by me through mind, speech, action, the two hands, the feet, the stomach, or the genitals—during the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep—may all that become an offering unto Brahman; Svāhā!
This is the mantra for the offering unto Brahman, prescribed for the rite of *brahmārpaṇa*. (4.420)
Having thus performed the rite of the fire-oblation (homa), [one should worship] the deities of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and the altar (sthaṇḍila),
as well as the guardian deities of the directions (dikpāla) and the deities of the ritual sowing of seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa).
The Guru should also pour [the water] into the jar and contemplate his identity with Kṛṣṇa;
"Kṛṣṇa" is used here according to the intended meaning of the context. (From the *Merutantra*)
Furthermore, the knower of mantras, having again worshipped with perfumes and other offerings using the root mantra, [should proceed].
Having raised [the deity] from the fire-pit, the preceptor should install the deity in the jar;
(in the *Śāradā*:
"The Guru, having raised the deity together with the limbs and the enclosures, [should place them] in the jar. (4.423)
Having again offered oblations with the *vyāhṛtis* to the various parts of the fire, such as the tongue and so forth,
and having given one oblation for each, he should sprinkle himself with water.
Having prepared the fire and arranged his own enclosing sticks (paridhi) and the surrounding grass (paristara),
the practitioner of mantras should burn these in an occasional rite (naimittika), but he should not burn them in a regular daily rite (nitya).

p. 307) "One should complete the oblation again with the *vyāhṛtis* and the *mahāvyāhṛtis*, preceded by the *mahāvyāhṛtis*," according to this statement. As for the procedure for that, [it is found] in the *Gautamīya*:
Then, one who knows the ritual procedure should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with water in this manner.
Oṃ bhūr! To Agni and to the great Earth, with Svāhā;
likewise, bhuvaḥ! To Vāyu and to the great Intermediate Space, with Svāhā. (4.427)
Svāhā to one’s own self, to the moon, to the directions, and to the lunar mansions!
Om bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, svāhā to the moon, to the lunar mansions, to the directions, and to the Great One! Having thus joined the fire—its procedure is described in the *Gaṇeśvaravimarṣiṇī*.
O Agni, O you of great power, who accomplishes all rites!
"Even when another ritual action has arrived, perform the presence [of the fire] with reverence.
Having thus made this prayer with the mantra, one should also dismiss the fire. || 4.429 ||
(Merutantra) Then, having dismissed Brahmā, one should cause it to be given to a Brāhmaṇa:
a copper vessel fashioned with a measure of thirty-two palas. (4-430)
Having filled it with rice grains, along with gold and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), one should give it to a Brahmin for his satisfaction; this is declared to be the "Full Vessel" (pūrṇapātra).
Then, one should cast the enclosing sticks (paridhi) into the fire after spreading the sacrificial grass around it; thus it is said in another Tantra:
"Eight handfuls make a *kuñci*, and eight *kuñci* make a *puṣkala*. (4-432)
And four abundant [offerings] constitute what is called the *pūrṇapātra*. (In the *Śāradātilaka*:
One should bind the eyes of the disciple with a cloth using the *netra-mantra*. (4.433)
In the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*, it is stated: "Having bound the eyes with a new white cloth... (p.
308). In the *Piṅgalāmata*:
One should bind his eyes with a cloth for the eyes while reciting the Netra-mantra.
(From the Śāradā-tantra: Having taken that disciple by the hand, he should lead him from the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) to the mandala;
then, having filled his joined palms with flowers according to the ritual rule. (4.435)
One should cast [the substance] into the pitcher while reciting the root mantra for the pleasure of the deity.
(In the *Nārāyaṇīya*:
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the body of the disciple, one should lead him around [the pitcher] clockwise. (4.436)
Having led [the disciple] to the western door, one should cause him to cast a handful of flowers.
(From the *Merutantra*) Having thus removed the blindfold, one should cause him to enter upon a bed of *kuśa* grass. (4-437)
Then the supreme guru should cause the disciple to recite this mantra:
"For one blinded by the darkness of ignorance, with the collyrium-stick of knowledge... (4.438)
Salutation to that venerable Guru by whom the eye has been opened.
(In the Piṅgalāmata:
Having filled his joined palms with flowers, he should offer them upon the yoga-pīṭha. 4-439.
The falling of flowers in the northwest, north, or east is auspicious for a favorable [result];
then the teacher, having repeatedly withdrawn and generated [the self] in due order, performs the self-sacrifice (ātmayāga).
Then one should perform the ritual placements (*nyāsa*) on the body of the disciple using the respective mantras;
this constitutes the self-sacrifice (*ātmayāga*) and the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*).
(From the *Prayogasāra*)
By means of the aspect of the qualities (guṇāṃśa), one should bring the elements, such as earth and the rest, to dissolution.
Just as they were established as a single mass through the application of the process of withdrawal,
one should then contemplate that same mass by means of the very process of emanation.
(In the *Mantratantraprakāśa*):
Having sat upon a pure seat, one should dissolve its form. (p.
309) One should dissolve the earth, which is conjoined with the sense of smell and [the qualities] such as fragrance, into water—and so forth. (4-443)
(From the Śāradā-tantra:
Having worshipped the chosen deity residing in the water-pot with the fivefold offerings, one should perform the ritual of sakalīkṛti within it according to the method taught in the Tantra. (4.444)
The teachers have stated that this interval is for requesting a boon from the presence of the God:
"O Goddess, abode of compassion, refuge of all presences! (4.445)
O compassionate Mother, worthy of refuge, show mercy toward this child;
O Sovereign of the Gods, protect him from the fetters beginning with the *āṇava*.
O Goddess, O support of compassion, show mercy to this wretched one;
let him be connected even with shares of both this world and the next.
"Let all one's devotion be offered to him who is the refuge of the partless"—thus [it is said in] the *Kriyāsaṃgraha* and *Meru* Tantras.
Then, having taken the vessel for the *arghya* offering and reciting the root mantra, the knower of mantras [should proceed]. (4.448)
Whatever action has been performed by me, whether good or evil,
accept all of that, O Lord of the gods of gods, as my supreme act of worship.
Having thus offered the water for the arghya, the wise one should place a small portion in the deity's right hand; thereafter, the worship is considered completed.
Having bowed with devotion to the Lord of Gods, one should ask for forgiveness with these verses:
"Whatever leaf, flower, fruit, or water has been offered by me through mere devotion... (4.451)
Please accept with compassion this offered food that has been presented;
I do not know how to perform the invocation, nor do I know how to perform the dismissal.
I do not even know how to perform worship; you are my refuge, O Supreme Lord.
In deed, thought, or speech, there is no other refuge for me but you.
O Supreme Lord, you are the witness of all beings through your internal movement.
(From the *Merutantra*) Then one should dismiss the deity along with the hosts of his attendants. (4.454)

Likewise: Having meditated upon Śiva in the form of light, [one should contemplate] that entire multitude of rays dissolved completely into the body of the deity, and [say] "Forgive me" again and again. (4.455)

Having worshipped oneself in the form of the deity according to the prescribed rite, one should ask for forgiveness and then cause the deity to ascend into the lotus of one's own heart (as stated in the *Kriyāsaṃgraha*). 4-456.
Then, having offered the *arghya* and other oblations, one should worship the deity wearing the remains of the previous offering (*nirmālya-vāsina*).
One should construct a mandala in the northeast, devoid of gates and lotuses.

For one who consumes the remains of the offering (nirmālya) for the sake of worship during the five-fold worship of the Āyatana, exactly five [deities] must be worshipped; one should worship starting from Īśa up to the center.
Lambodara is the splendor of Gaṇeśa, Caṇḍa that of Vivasvat;
Viṣvaksena is said to be that of Hari, and Caṇḍeśvara that of Maheśitṛ.

I am the mantra of Caṇḍeśvarī, the consort of Bhava; one should act accordingly regarding what is to be licked, sucked, eaten, and drunk, as well as the remains of offerings (nirmālya), garlands, and ointments.
"I give this to you, who partakes of the remains of the offering (nirmālya), by the command of Śrī Śiva.
Having thus given the remainder of the food offering (naivedya) and bowed down, one should dismiss [the deity]. || 4-461 ||
Likewise:
"The practitioner of mantras should wear the remains of the offering upon his head while reciting the root mantra" (from the *Prayogasāra*).
Then, in the northeastern direction, [he should worship] him whose form has been arranged according to the mantra.
On the square altar of the pedestal, with darbha grass tips in his hand,
he should consecrate his own disciple who follows the principle of the Self (ātmatattva).
(Somaśambhu, p. 311):
In the northeast direction from the sacrificial hall, one should perform the rite of bathing in the bathing pavilion;
there, one should construct an altar two cubits in length and eight finger-breadths in height. (4-464)

Having placed a seat made of *śrīparṇa* wood and other materials there, and having seated the disciple— who is bowed low— upon that seat facing east, he should perform the ritual of personification (*sakalīkaraṇa*) and worship him.
In that very same [text]:
"The bath is with the face turned toward that [deity]; for eating, the face is turned eastward; and for liberation, it is as before.
Also elsewhere:
Having established the mandala with its orientation toward the northeast, one should place those seeking liberation facing north.
For the sake of the meal, the teacher should have the disciples enter there facing the east;
while the five musical instruments resound, the teacher, together with the benedictions of the Brahmins, [should proceed]. (From the Śāradā-tantra, 4.467)
Having duly excavated the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and having placed the celestial trees located at its opening upon the head of the child while mentally reciting the Mātṛkā, [he should proceed].
The knower of the Self should sprinkle him with water consecrated by the root mantra,
using the Mātṛkā and the reverse Mātṛkā,
filled with the letters from *kṣa* to *a*, and accompanied by the mantras beginning with the three-fold utterance of the principles (*tattvas*).
Thus, according to the statement in the *Kramadīpikā*:

"Having joined [the mantra] to the head of the disciple while reciting the reverse alphabet (*vilomamātṛkā*), and likewise having recited the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*), one should perform the consecration of the deity. (4.470)
And because of the statement in the *Gautamīyatantra*:
"Likewise, having again taken up the Vardhinī, who has the form of a weapon, once she has been worshipped..."
One should quickly sprinkle it with well-prepared waters for the sake of protection.
With the remaining water, the Guru should cause the disciple to sip;
then, having performed the ritual integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*), the knower of the Self [should regard] him as being of the nature of the deity.
Having risen and put on two clean garments, the disciple, having sipped water and become restrained in speech, should sit in the presence of the guru. (4.473)
The supreme teacher should worship the deity who has been transferred into the disciple with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, while contemplating the identity of the two.
Then one should impart the knowledge to that disciplined person, preceded by the offering of water.
(From the Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā:
Then, having placed one's own hand upon his head, one should recite [the mantra] a hundred times. 4-475.

Or he may offer one hundred and eight [libations] preceded by water; having diligently performed the entire network of ritual placements (*nyāsa*) upon his body, the Guru [should do so]. (From the *Gautamīya*) 4-476.
With a full heart, one should recite the mantra three times into the right ear;
O wise ones, the learned man should speak it into the right ear of the Brahmin, preceded by the offering of water.

But to others, the wise one should speak the mantra in this very same way; however, in the *Kulāmṛta*, it is said that he should recite the *vidyā* three times into the ear, or even when [the recipient] lacks understanding. (4.478)
Then, in the *Dīpikā*,
the Guru [should] properly bestow the supreme mantra, endowed with the [names of the] sages and so forth, three times into the left ear of the disciple who is of priceless worth.
Elsewhere as well:
"One should recite the Vidyā three times into the right ear with a single utterance;
this is the rule for the twice-born, while for women and Śūdras it is from the left. (4.479)
In another tantra:
"May these two yield equal results"—thus should the preeminent sage, with a serene countenance, address that disciple. (4.480)
(Merutantra) p.
313): The Guru should contemplate the Vidyā, consisting of light, as departing from himself;
the disciple should contemplate it as having arrived, bowing especially with the words, "I am prostrate. (4-481)
The disciple should recite one hundred and eight times as instructed by the guru, or indeed twenty-eight times, or else eight times. (4.482)
The disciple should contemplate the identity of the Guru, the deity, and his own mantra;
the seeker, filled with devotion, should repeatedly offer prostrations to the Guru. (4.483)
(In the *Kriyāsaṃgraha*):
The Guru should raise up the disciple who has fallen at his feet:
"Arise, child! You are liberated; be one who perfectly observes the conduct. (4-484)
"May fame, fortune, beauty, intelligence, longevity, strength, and health always be yours.
(From the *Gautamīya-tantra*) Having recited the mantras beginning with Gaṇeśa, the Guru should speak according to the tradition. (4.485)
The bestowal of the mantras of Gaṇeśa and others occurs in the case of initiation into the Pañcāyatana system.
(In the Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā:
"And having properly worshipped the King of Wheels (Cakrarāja) nearby, the Preceptor..."
One should fashion a beautiful name joined with the first syllable.
Having then united oneself with the heavy human [bodies], all the gurus should be remembered with perfect prostrations. (4.487)
Having written the vidyā upon the ground, one should worship it properly with flowers and other offerings;
O Dear One, one should show the vidyā, recited a hundred times, to the disciple.
If there should be great devotion in the disciple who is prostrate,
then one should mutter the supreme mantra into his right ear with a single utterance.
(In the *Tantrārāja*):
A disciple endowed with the aforementioned characteristics and adorned by proper conduct, purified over many days by means of the five and six-peaked vidyās. (4-490)
Having consecrated him with water-pots and seated him within the Śrīcakra,
one should contemplate the wheel in the center, at the base, the heart, and the head.
Having invoked [the deity] from one's own heart, established [her], and worshipped her together with the ritual placement (nyāsa),
one whose mind is filled with the Self of the Goddess should recite the Vidyā three times into the ear.
One should joyfully contemplate the oneness of the deity, the guru, the mantra, and one's own self-nature;
standing before them, one should recite [the mantra] a hundred times and dwell in their presence for three days.
If that mobile power does not reach the Guru, there is no doubt;
therefore, one should dwell near him, performing worship, prostrations, and so forth. (4.494)

One should dwell with devotion for three days in the presence of the Guru for the sake of accomplishment; otherwise, there is no doubt that the spiritual power residing therein will return to the Guru. (From the Gautamīya-tantra) 4.495.
(From the *Mantratantraprakāśa*):

A mantra that has not been received from a preceptor, or one that has been received but for which the ritual fee (*dakṣiṇā*) has not been given—even if it is recited constantly—does not bestow accomplishment (*siddhi*). (4-496)

Having given to the guru a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) consisting of one's entire wealth or half of it, free from stinginess regarding one's possessions, the reception of the mantra is then considered appropriate.
(In another tantra:
"If one does not have abundant cattle, land, gold, or many houses, fields, and so forth, then [one should give] half of that, or half of that, or even a tenth part of it. (4-498)
One should give food, clothing, and so forth without distress, according to one's wealth.
(In the *Brahmasaṃhitā*):
"O Nārada, it is certain that an action performed without a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is in vain. (4-499)
"Give me my lute, along with my rosary and water-pot;
then, O great sage, receive the mantra from me according to the prescribed rite."
An action performed devoid of the prescribed rules does not bestow success at all.
(In the *Gautamīya*):
One intent on liberation should give the preceptor a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consisting of half of one's wealth. (4.501)
Or one may give half of that, according to one's capacity and with devotion;
one should not practice stinginess regarding wealth, for such a deed would bring about misfortune.
Then, one should offer cows, land, gold, garments, and so forth to the guru, as well as to the guru’s son, his wife, and his disciple, according to one's own capacity. (4.503)
One should give garments and ornaments, and a desired kingdom according to one's wish;
one should give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the officiating priests, accompanied by garments and ornaments.
(Merutantra) One should respectfully give ornaments and garments to the officiating priests;
then, with the thought of offering them to the Lord, one is gladdened by the blessings of the twice-born. (4.505)
The disciple should give half of his own wealth to the guru, or half of that, or even a tenth part, provided he is free from stinginess regarding his possessions. (4.506)
Likewise, one should give cows, land, gold, forests, houses, fields, and so forth, as well as food, clothing, and other necessities without hardship, according to one's wealth. (4.507)
Adopting another method, one should diligently please the Guru, with a mind perpetually dependent on him and devoted solely to his contemplation. (4.508)
The best of practitioners should be adorned with the dust from the lotus-feet of that [deity];
thereafter, [he should worship] with various kinds of foods to be eaten, licked, sucked, and others as well.
One should feed the Brahmins properly and bestow abundant sacrificial fees;
according to the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā, one should give the pavilion to the preceptor along with the implements of sacrifice. (4.510)
(In the Nārāyaṇīya and Mahākapila Pañcarātras:
Having imparted the mantra, the preceptor should indeed recite it a thousand times for his own success.
Also elsewhere:
One should recite [the mantra] one thousand and eight times for the attainment of those who are deficient in their own power.
(In the *Kulāmṛta*):
One should instruct the disciple, who has prostrated like a staff, in all the rules of conduct:
the daily rites of bathing and twilight prayers, as well as the occasional and optional rites. (4–512)
The Guru should explain the methods for accomplishing the mantras to the disciple.
On the day of initiation, fasting is prohibited; as it is said in the *Yoginītantra*: "If the Guru, having bestowed the mantra, should observe a fast... (4.513).
In the hell of great darkness, one becomes a worm; it cannot be otherwise.
When a mantra-practitioner, having bestowed initiation, observes a fast, [the result is as stated]. (4.514)
The Lord, always enraged at him, would depart for his city after pronouncing a curse;
then, having consumed the remnant of the oblation in a quantity equal to a hen’s egg— (from the *Bṛhatsiddhāntasāra*)— 4-515.
Having offered the fourfold food-oblation (naivedya) presented to the deity to the devotees, they two should then eat it as they please. (4.516)
The words "the teacher and the disciple" are to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. (In the *Merutantra*:
"A Śaiva, however, is entitled to the *nirmālya* and *prasāda* of Śiva."
Another enters hell; there is no fault in the union of the five.
Whether they be non-Śaivas or Śaivas, those who with devotion [visit] the Svayambhū-tīrtha-liṅga or even its sacred shrine (prasāda) are liberated from a multitude of sins.
(Siddhāntasāra) Having stayed for three days in the teacher's household, on the fourth day, having worshipped the deity and carrying the teacher’s command upon his head, he should go home. (4-519)

Now, the specific procedure for the *vīradīkṣā* (hero’s initiation): there, having performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), the placement of the *mātṛkā* (*mātṛkānyāsa*), the sixfold placement (*ṣoḍhānyāsa*), and so forth, upon both his own body and the body of the Śakti, and having performed the installation of the water-pot (*kalaśa*) and the setting out of the *śrīpātra* and other vessels, the Guru—by means of the sequence of the *dūtīyāga*, having produced and consecrated the substance arising from the *kuṇḍa* and *gola*, and having likewise performed the consecration even of fish, meat, and so forth—worships the Deity according to the sequence of the *vīrapūjā*.
Then, at the time of imparting the mantra to the disciple, [he says]: "O Maheśānī, O Kuleśvarī, having placed the vessel in the hand of the disciple—"
This vessel of heroes, as described by Vīracūḍāmaṇi: "Drink this pure nectar, the medicine for the disease of worldly existence. (4.520)
"This is the cause for the total severance of the bonds of the bound beings (*paśu*), as proclaimed by Bhairava.
Thus, according to the sequence of the *Kulārṇava*, he should place [the vessel] into the hand of the disciple.
The disciple, likewise, with this very mantra, having recited "I drink" (*pibāmi*) instead of "let it be drunk" (*pīyatām*), [should drink].
With the mind as the sacrificial ladle, one should offer the oblation of dharma and adharma into the fire of one's own self, which is kindled by them.
"By means of the path of the *suṣumṇā*, I eternally offer the functions of the senses"—with this and other such mantras, one should drink. Then the guru should impart the mantra.
Regarding that, [it is said] in the *Yāmala*:
Having written this together with the seers and the rest, one should place it within the earth.
Having worshipped [the deity] with flowers and other offerings, the guru should then show it to the disciple;
if there is great affection for the disciple, then the guru should speak it into the ear.

If the disciple is an even greater recipient of the teacher's affection than that, then the most excellent teacher should indeed bestow this [initiation] preceded by the ritual rinsing of the mouth (gaṇḍūṣa). || 4.524 ||
Even if he is free from conceptual thought, the disciple should receive it with a joyful mind;
for in its absence, there will be no accomplishment, and he may incur the curse of the deity. (4-525)
(In the Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā:
One should sprinkle the auspicious [disciple] three times with sprouts placed in the water-pot;
when he has been thus consecrated, he becomes a preeminent leader among teachers. (4-526)
One who is endowed with the reality of the mouthful (gaṇḍūṣa-tattva) is then worthy for the worship of Śiva;
otherwise, O Pārvatī, there can be no accomplishment for one possessed of conceptual construction (savikalpa).
If a doubt arises in the disciple regarding the offering of the mouthful of water (gaṇḍūṣa), he shall find no accomplishment anywhere; even Śrīvidyā turns her face away from him.
The remainder is the same as the initiation of the animal sacrifice (*paśudīkṣā*).
Regarding the second initiation of knowledge (*vidyādīkṣā*), the specific detail stated in the *Nīlatantra* is that one should perform one thousand and eight oblations (*homa*) with *vilva* leaves.
Alternatively, one should make one hundred and eight, or indeed twenty-eight.

One should offer milk-rice, rice mixed with sesame, sweetmeats, and candied sugar; having presented the oblation, one should indeed offer the flesh of a goat and the most excellent meat of a monitor lizard.
One should diligently offer the *rambhā* flower and the *sāramatsya* fish;
then, having offered barley with milk, one should offer *śāli* rice together with honey.
"One should satisfy one's own guru with gifts such as cows, land, gold, and clothing"—thus it is said in the *Merutantra*.
In this way, the ritual initiation (*kriyāvatī-dīkṣā*), which bestows prosperity, has been described. (4-532)
This sequence of initiation is declared for kings, wealthy vaiśyas, brahmins, and industrious men who desire success accompanied by enjoyment. (4.533)
Thus, the initiation involving ritual action (kriyāvatī-dīkṣā) is complete.

It is worthy of veneration as a confluence of rivers of excellent compositions, characterized by a stream of nectar variegated by the wonderful diversity of words that purify beings through marvelous supernatural powers.
The fourth [chapter], a lofty wave in the *Puraścaryārṇava* composed by the illustrious Naradeva, has come forth, radiant with the luster of hands [of pearls] made clear by manifest reasoning. 4-534.

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Ritual of Initiation into Kriyāvatī," in the *Puraścaryārṇava*, composed by the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja Śrī Pratāpasiṃha Sāh. © 2011 Muktabodha Indological Research Institute.
